Subject: Year-end team note draft
From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen

- Team —
- As we wrap 2024, we keep coming back to how much hard, unglamorous work it took to turn enterprise learning into product that is clearer, more repeatable, and easier for customers to trust on day one.
- We made real progress on the parts of Scaffold that decide whether a customer gets set up quickly, gets their first source connected, sees a live sync, invites teammates, and feels like the product can support a serious deployment.
- Project Mercury pulled a lot of that into focus, but this was not just one project or one team. Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone carrying customer context helped reduce one-off setup work and turn it into something we can ship repeatedly.
- Atlas also got stronger in the ways that matter most once customers are live: better auth and verification paths, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer docs, faster first technical reads, and less thrash on issues that used to bounce around.
- The numbers behind that progress are meaningful: median time from workspace creation to first connected source moved from 2.4 days in Q1 to 0.9 days in Q4; the share of new workspaces reaching a first live sync within 14 days rose from 41% to 63%; teammate invitations on activated workspaces increased from 28% to 47%.
- In the core Mercury setup flow, workspace creation success improved from 93.8% to 97.9%; first-source connection completion moved from 54% to 72%; and first successful sync on connected workspaces increased from 68% to 84%.
- Enterprise-readiness and repeatability improved together: admin-role setup on new enterprise workspaces rose from 61% to 88%; median time to close high-priority Atlas issues dropped from 2.6 business days to 0.9; and the auth / webhook / connector docs refresh deflected 37% of repeat enterprise implementation questions in the second half.
- More important than any single metric, people kept showing up for each other while we were changing the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through that rarely gets enough credit.
- Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, for caring about the details customers actually feel, and for helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder.
- We’re proud of what this team shipped this year, and we’re excited for what we can build from here.

Subject: Thank you for what we built together in 2024

Team —

As we wrap up 2024, we keep coming back to how much hard, often unglamorous work it took to turn enterprise learning into a product that is clearer, more repeatable, and easier for customers to trust from day one.

We made real progress across the moments that matter: getting customers set up quickly, connecting their first source, seeing a live sync, inviting teammates, and feeling confident that Scaffold can support a serious deployment.

Project Mercury brought much of that work into focus, but this was never just one project or one team. Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone who carried customer context helped reduce one-off setup work and turn it into something we can ship repeatedly.

Atlas also grew stronger where it matters most after customers go live — with better authentication and verification paths, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer documentation, faster technical support, and less thrash around issues that used to bounce between teams.

A few year-end markers of that progress:

• Customers are reaching their first connected source in a median of 0.9 days, down from 2.4 days in Q1.

• The share of new workspaces reaching a first live sync within 14 days rose from 41% to 63%.

• Activated workspaces with teammate invitations increased from 28% to 47%.

• In the core Mercury setup flow, workspace creation success improved from 93.8% to 97.9%, first-source connection completion rose from 54% to 72%, and first successful sync on connected workspaces increased from 68% to 84%.

• On the enterprise side, admin-role setup on new workspaces rose from 61% to 88%, while median time to close high-priority Atlas issues fell from 2.6 business days to 0.9.

• The refreshed authentication, webhook, and connector documentation helped deflect 37% of repeat enterprise implementation questions in the second half of the year.

More important than any single metric, people kept showing up for one another while we changed the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through — much of it work that rarely gets enough credit.

Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, caring about the details customers actually feel, and helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder.

We’re proud of what this team shipped this year, and excited for what we can build from here.

Happy holidays,

Devon

Working purpose
Board / leadership recap of the Northstar-led Series B path and what it means operationally.

- Scaffold is raising an $18M Series B led by Northstar Ventures.

What this round says
Northstar underwrote the round on the bounded story we can actually support: Mercury activation and admin-path improvement are real, the current Evergreen read is useful enterprise signal, hybrid MAU pricing is credible, and we did not need to invent a vanity-growth version of the business to get there.

Why the narrow process was the right call
We kept the path through Sofia and the current Mercury evidence set instead of reopening a broader fundraising process. That let us hold the story to something defensible rather than smoothing over uneven expansion or spending another month creating theatrical price tension. At this point, that trade looks right.

Remaining steps
The remaining steps are largely closing mechanics: board consent, signature packet circulation, and final document cleanup. The only substantive governance items left are the Sofia board-seat / board-size mechanics, the written-consent structure, and the matching director-designation language.

Operating implication
This round gives us enough room to operate against the current Mercury / enterprise-expansion path without continuing to manage every decision like a survival bridge. It does not change the underlying product truth: activation/admin progress is real, expansion is still uneven, and enterprise-readiness follow-up is still work we need to do rather than a claim we can make.

Northstar completed final diligence on the existing Mercury package and is closing an $18M Series B with Scaffold on February 22. The package held because it stayed on current evidence rather than a broadened process story.

The main lesson from this process is that a narrower, defendable path beat extra weeks of fundraising theater. We should treat that as a useful operating constraint even once the money is in.

Narrow process, defensible package, no fundraising theater.

[2023-10-03T08:18:00-07:00] Devon’s first cut for Elena is here:

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Subject: first cut / Elena Mercury calibration
Date: Tue, Oct 3, 2023 7:42 AM PT

First cut below. This is meant as a calibration note, not a process-launch deck.

Main places I'd like your pass:
- whether the pricing section is too detailed for a first pre-read
- how directly to say expansion is uneven without making the whole thing feel like a shrug
- whether we say Evergreen by name in the pre-read or keep that for the conversation

---
Mercury / October calibration draft for Elena Volkov

Why this note
We are considering a selective October reopen, starting with a short list and using this as a calibration conversation rather than a broad process update. The goal is to test whether the Mercury story is now honest and credible enough to reopen narrowly.

What has changed since February
- Product signal is less theoretical. The design-partner wave produced real evidence on setup, activation, and admin friction.
- The activation/admin story is better than it was earlier in the year because the team corrected the biggest early setup and handoff failures.
- Pricing is now structured instead of bespoke.
- Evergreen put us through a real regulated-buyer procurement/security process, which surfaced enterprise-readiness gaps with much more specificity than we had before.

September Mercury package — usable summary

Board-facing context
- The quarterly cohort view is directionally better in the recent design-partner wave than in the earliest Mercury cohorts.
- That improvement is useful context, but it is not proof that retention or expansion is solved.

Operating read
- Activation improved after the onboarding/admin fixes in the design-partner wave.
- Admin friction came down in the latest wave.
- Expansion remains uneven: some accounts deepen after setup, others stall after initial usage.
- The package is best used as evidence that the team improved the early path and clarified the failure points, not as proof of a finished growth engine.

How to talk about Evergreen
What Evergreen gives us
- a real buyer process in a regulated environment
- concrete evidence on where Mercury still needs deeper enterprise-readiness work
- a better read on packaging gaps around security/admin expectations and procurement handling

What Evergreen does not give us
- proof that enterprise readiness is solved
- proof that the motion is repeatable across multiple accounts
- proof that procurement converts cleanly into expansion

Pricing frame

Pilot
- $2,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 50 monthly active developers

Growth
- $7,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 200 monthly active developers

Overage
- $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Enterprise add-ons
- SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls are separate add-ons only after those features ship
- we should be explicit that those are not being pre-sold as current capability

Caveats to keep explicit
- Expansion is still uneven.
- Evergreen is a strong signal, but still a single signal.
- Enterprise-readiness gaps are clearer than before; they are not closed.
- This would be a narrow October reopen, not a broad fundraising process.
- I do not think we should put random investor coffees on the calendar off this package.

Questions to test with Elena
1. Is this package materially more credible than the February version?
2. What would make the Evergreen signal feel repeatable rather than anecdotal?
3. Is the current pricing frame disciplined enough, or does it still read as early?
4. How much more explanation do we need on uneven expansion before widening beyond a short list?

Rough email shell
Elena —
We took another pass at the Mercury package and wanted to use a short conversation for calibration, not to launch a broad process. The current story is stronger on three dimensions: the design-partner wave improved activa…

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury release-risk readout — 2023-07-14
arguments.body:
Mercury release-risk readout — 2023-07-14

Attendees: Morgan Chen, Leo Park, Jake, Priya, Marcus

Scope
- Release risk and evidence only; this is not a platform roadmap or an owner-split launch ledger.
- Focus: where Mercury can still surprise us at the seams, especially activation behavior tied to auth/org state and thin dogfood evidence.

1. Org-invite roles vs activation-state seam

Risk
- The invited-member branch is the highest platform-seam risk. Rendering depends on server role and source state, which may not settle simultaneously after invite acceptance.
- A user may accept an invite and receive the org-role update while still between source states, potentially showing the wrong branch or CTA.

Evidence
- Only 2 real dogfood invited-member accounts have been tested end to end.
- One bug-bash pass required refresh/re-entry before the expected branch settled.
- Confidence is still driven more by happy-path staging than repeated real dogfood coverage.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Run more real invited-member dogfood accounts across admin-first and invitee-first orderings.
- Verify no path creates an activated-looking state without a real source or first live sync.
- Confirm sample data remains visually separate and preview-only and cannot shift the branch into an activated-looking state.
- Watch CTA selection on first load after invite acceptance.
- Distinguish wrong-CTA rendering from stale-state timing.

Room notes
- Design intent remains four branches; there is no pseudo-activated middle state.
- This is a release risk because it crosses auth/org state, not merely copy or UI.

2. Release-readiness evidence gaps

Risk
- Implemented is not the same as proven. Thin evidence remains a material launch risk even where code may be close.

Evidence
- Invited-member branch has only 2 real dogfood accounts.
- Queued-sync retry logs are sparse, even after removing fake progress/countdown behavior.
- Failed-sync screenshots are cleaner, but sample depth remains shallow.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, high confidence that the evidence gap exists; lower confidence about how many user-facing bugs remain underneath it.

Next verification
- Run a targeted dogfood pass exercising each branch with saved screenshots and logs.
- Capture at least one real queue -> retry -> recovery trace for queued sync.
- Separate “path unproven” from “path actually broken.”

3. Failed-sync cleanup and normalization

Risk
- The failed state is not fully verified across every normalized bucket.

Evidence
- One screenshot still leaks a raw vendor string.
- Existing fixes appear to cover the obvious path, but auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown/retry have not all been confirmed equally clean.
- Retry action looks better, but bucket text and UI still need proof on every branch.

Severity / confidence
- Medium severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Retest each failed bucket with captured UI.
- Confirm no raw vendor strings leak.
- Confirm retry remains idempotent.
- Keep the warning-circle direction; the open issue is verification, not icon reconsideration.

4. Later polish vs potential blockers

Not currently main blockers
- Setup-guide copy tightening, unless it causes a wrong action or real confusion in the invited-member branch.
- Small-width spacing, unless it clips or overlaps on a supported width.
- Failed-state icon polish, unless it obscures state meaning.

Guidance
- Keep branch distinctions crisp.
- Do not let a polish list become a second scope track before the next Mercury cycle.

Explicit exclusions
- No abstract platform recommendations.
- No provider debate or broader auth rewrite scope.
- No SSO/admin-depth wishlist.
- Do not convert this readout into an owner-split launch ledger yet.

Questions to verify next
- Can we prove invited-member rendering across real role/source-state permutations, not just the happy path?
- Do we have enough queued-sync retry evidence to say recovery is understandable without fake progress?
- Is failed-sync normalization complete across all buckets, or only mostly clean on the common path?
- Which gaps are real launch blockers versus thin proof on otherwise-correct behavior?
- What is the smallest next dogfood pass that materially raises confidence before wider exposure?

Bottom line
- The main release risks are the invited-member auth/org/source-state seam, insufficient real-world evidence for readiness, and incomplete end-to-end verification of failed-sync normalization. The next step is a focused dogfood pass that produces branch coverage, screenshots, logs, and a real queued-sync recovery trace before widening exposure.

arguments.message: Mercury release-risk readout (7/14): the main risks are (1) invited-member auth/org/source-state timing that may produce the wrong branch or CTA, (2) thin real dogfood evidence—especially invited-member coverage and queued-sync retry/recovery traces—and (3) incomplete end-to-end verification of failed-sync normalization across all buckets. Next step is a focused dogfood pass with branch screenshots/logs and a real queue → retry → recovery trace. Setup-copy, spacing, and icon polish remain later unless they cause confusion or obscure state. This was a release-risk/evidence readout, not an owner-split launch ledger.

[2023-07-25T13:07:00-07:00] Sarah's design-partner questions are the right input for Thursday, but I don't want them dressed up as fundraising collateral.

From: Sarah Kim <sarah@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Cc: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>, Jake <jake@atlas-test.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Jul 2023 08:41:00 -0700
Subject: Mercury design-partner readiness questions

Sending the recurring launch-readiness questions I'm hearing in prospective design-partner conversations. I'm deliberately not naming anyone here because the conversations are still exploratory, but the themes are pretty consistent and seem useful before the Thursday checkpoint.

1) Source setup failure cases
- If the first source connection fails, what does the user actually see?
- Can they tell the difference between auth/permissions trouble, source unavailable/timeout, and an unknown failure without us translating it for them?
- Does recovery look self-serve, or does it feel like they would need vendor/API knowledge to continue?

2) Admin handoff
- If an admin starts setup and then invites an operator or teammate, does the invited person land in a sane next step?
- What happens if the invited member arrives before the first source is fully connected?
- Is the line between "waiting on admin/first source" and "something is broken" obvious?

3) Time to first sync
- How long from first connection to first live sync in the normal case?
- If the sync is queued or retried, what reassures the user that the system is working without inventing fake progress?

4) Which failure states are actually understandable
- Which states are legible on first read to an external user?
- Which ones still make sense only if someone from our side narrates what happened?

5) What evidence creates enough confidence to try Mercury
- a clean first-run path end to end
- one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails
- proof that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle
- clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state
- a credible sense of time-to-first-sync, even if it's a range rather than a promise

My read is that this is product-readiness input, not deck material. It's basically the bar people are using to decide whether they would be comfortable trying Mercury with a real but bounded workflow.

Create a one-page internal checklist for the Mercury headcount checkpoint: what external launch-readiness feedback we need before deciding any second Mercury engineering req. Keep it as product-readiness input only, not board, investor, or B-round material.

arguments.title: Mercury headcount checkpoint — external launch-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
MERCURY HEADCOUNT CHECKPOINT
External launch-readiness evidence required before deciding on a second Mercury engineering requisition
Internal product-readiness input only — not board, investor, or B-round material

Decision standard
Do not treat design-partner interest or recurring questions as evidence by itself. Before deciding on a second Mercury engineering req, review concrete evidence from bounded, real-user or realistic external design-partner workflows and identify the product gaps that still block a credible first run.

Checklist: evidence we need

[ ] 1. First source connection failure is understandable
    • Capture what an external user sees when the first source connection fails.
    • Distinguish auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown failure without internal narration.
    • Show a self-serve recovery path, or name the precise product gap if recovery still requires vendor/API knowledge.
    Evidence to bring: screenshots or recording of each state, observed user interpretation, recovery outcome.

[ ] 2. Admin-to-operator handoff is sane
    • Test an admin starting setup, then inviting an operator or teammate.
    • Verify the invitee lands on a clear next step, including arrival before the first source is fully connected.
    • Make “waiting on admin/first source” clearly different from “something is broken.”
    Evidence to bring: end-to-end invite path, timing, failure/edge-case notes, and unresolved handoff defects.

[ ] 3. Time to first sync is credible
    • Measure first connection → first live sync in the normal case across more than one bounded workflow where possible.
    • Exercise queued and retried syncs.
    • Confirm the UI reassures users that work is progressing without inventing fake progress or implying a guarantee.
    Evidence to bring: observed range, sample size/workflows, queue/retry behavior, and user comprehension.

[ ] 4. Failure states are legible on first read
    • Ask external participants to interpret setup, waiting, timeout, retry, and unknown-failure states without coaching.
    • Separate states they understand unaided from those that still require someone on our side to narrate.
    Evidence to bring: verbatim interpretations, misread states, severity, and proposed product changes.

[ ] 5. Confidence to try Mercury with a real but bounded workflow
    • Validate a clean first-run path end to end.
    • Show one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails.
    • Demonstrate that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle.
    • Clearly separate sample/preview data from real activated state.
    • Provide a credible time-to-first-sync range, not a promise.
    Evidence to bring: design-partner notes, observed workflow boundaries, activation/preview screenshots, and explicit blockers.

Headcount decision prompts

• Which gaps are launch blockers versus polish, and what user evidence supports that distinction?
• What additional engineering capacity would remove a specific blocker, rather than merely accelerate general roadmap work?
• If a second req is approved, what measurable product-readiness outcome must it own, by when, and how will we verify it with external users?
• If the evidence is insufficient, what smallest next design-partner test closes the uncertainty before we make the req decision?

Required checkpoint packet

[ ] One compact evidence table: workflow, participant/context, observed behavior, user interpretation, severity, owner, next gate.
[ ] Links to recordings/screenshots and the current build/version used.
[ ] Explicit list of states requiring internal narration.
[ ] Observed time-to-first-sync range with caveats and no roadmap or launch promise.
[ ] Clear recommendation: approve, defer pending evidence, or do not add the second req.

Out of scope

Fundraising narrative, board/investor collateral, B-round positioning, market-sizing, pricing, roadmap promises, and generalized hiring justification. Keep this checkpoint anchored to external product-readiness evidence only.

arguments.title: Mercury activation empty states — working decision note (v7 review)
arguments.body:
Mercury activation empty states — working decision note

Working-team material; not for external circulation.
Source: Figma export for Mercury / Activation empty states, page “Activation empty + transitional states,” section “v7 review.” Exported 2023-06-19 17:18 PT.

Purpose
Separate product decisions from release-readiness and implementation constraints so the next review can close the remaining gaps without using Figma comments as the sole source of truth.

PRODUCT DECISIONS

1. No source connected — admin
- The state has one job: get an admin to connect a real source.
- Primary CTA: “Connect a data source.”
- Secondary option may link to the setup guide.
- Sample import must not appear on this card in a way that reads as activation.
- If sample import remains in v0.2, label it “preview only.” It must not produce a success state, “you’re ready” language, or a green-check treatment for sample data.

2. Invited member before first source
- Do not show a generic blank page.
- Explain that the workspace exists but an admin still needs to connect the first source.
- A non-admin must not be teased with a CTA they cannot complete.
- The user should land in a coherent explanatory state rather than dead air.

3. First sync queued
- Treat this as a transitional state, not an empty state.
- Reassure the user that the source was found and the first live sync is running.
- Do not use a fake percentage, countdown, stepper, or language implying precise/resumable progress.
- Neutral copy such as “This usually takes a couple of minutes” is acceptable if it remains accurate.
- Add a docs link only when the state has run long enough to justify it; do not add it by default if it creates noise.

4. Sync failed
- Make the state actionable, not merely apologetic.
- Provide retry plus help docs.
- Keep copy at the product level; do not expose connector internals or raw vendor errors.
- Day-one failure presentation does not need five distinct user-facing variants.
- Support contact is not part of the state unless support routing is wired.

5. Sample data
- Sample data must not create an activated-looking success card.
- If retained in v0.2, it belongs to a sandbox/preview branch with its own copy and no shared “activated” treatment.
- Sample import may help exploration but cannot masquerade as a live source connection.

6. Measurement language and success framing
- Do not expose internal activation-measurement language in the UI.
- User-facing copy should talk about connecting a real source and seeing the first live data arrive.
- Invite acceptance is not equivalent to activation.
- Sample data is not equivalent to activation.
- No celebratory success card until real data is present; invite acceptance and sample data must not feel equivalent to that outcome.

7. CTA labels locked for now (C-221 resolved)
- No source: “Connect a data source”
- Invited member: “View setup guide”
- Queued: no primary CTA
- Failed: “Try again”

8. Mobile copy
- Shorten invited-member and failure-state copy so the CTA remains usable on small widths, including iPhone SE.
- Prefer cutting words over shrinking type.

RELEASE-READINESS / IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS

1. State derivation
- Distinguish “member lacks permission” from “organization has no source yet.”
- Use server-provided role/source state, including org_has_connected_source where applicable.
- Do not infer the client-side role from the session token; token-based guessing can flicker on refresh and create false CTAs.
- Wait for server role/source state before rendering the invited-member branch. A short loading state is preferable to showing the wrong action.

2. Queued-state behavior
- Define and implement a threshold for when queued becomes “taking longer than usual.” QA cannot test that branch until the timeout is agreed.
- Do not promise an ETA or percentage that the system cannot substantiate.

3. Failure handling
- Normalize connector failures before release into these implementation buckets:
  - auth / permissions
  - source unavailable / timeout
  - unknown / retry
- Map those buckets to simplified product copy.
- Retry must be idempotent; double-clicking must not create duplicate jobs.

4. Event and activation mapping
- Engineering, QA, and Anna need one agreed event mapping behind the scenes.
- invite_sent is supporting activity only, not activation.
- sample_import_completed stays out of the activation definition.
- Product copy should remain free of the internal formula/measurement language.

5. QA freeze
- Final invited-member and failure strings are needed before QA screenshots are frozen.
- Small-width rendering must be checked for both states, including CTA position on iPhone SE.

6. Success trigger implementation
- Engineering needs a concrete trigger definition for the success treatment. Candidate checkpoints discussed were real_source_connected, first_live_sync_completed, or both in practice.
- Do not fill the product-definition gap with a fake happy path; carry it to the next review if it cannot be resolved now.

UNRESOLVED ITEMS FOR NEXT REVIEW

1. Success trigger: Should the success treatment fire on real_source_connected, first_live_sync_completed, or only after both are true?
2. Queued timeout: What exact threshold changes the state to “taking longer than usual,” and what copy/docs behavior follows that transition?
3. Long-running queued state: When exactly should the docs link appear?
4. Support routing: Is support contact wired for v0.2? If not, confirm docs-only behavior for the failed state.
5. Activation/event contract: Finalize the canonical event mapping and ownership for engineering, QA, and Anna, including how real-source connection and first live sync relate to activation.
6. Failure copy mapping: Approve the simplified user-facing copy for each normalized failure bucket while keeping vendor details out of the UI.
7. Final strings: Lock the shortened invited-member and failure-state strings before QA screenshot freeze.
8. Sample-data scope: Confirm whether sample import remains in v0.2; if yes, approve the sandbox/preview branch, labels, separate event names, and explicit exclusion from activation treatment.
9. Loading branch: Confirm the exact loading behavior and copy while server role/source state is pending.
10. Ownership/checklist: Assign one canonical home and owner for the release-readiness checklist and the event/QA contract so these constraints do not remain split across Figma comments and review threads.

Proposed next-review output
- Approved success trigger and event mapping.
- Agreed queued timeout and long-running-state behavior.
- Confirmed support/docs decision.
- Final mobile-safe strings.
- Explicit v0.2 decision on sample data.
- Named owner and canonical location for the release-readiness checklist.

bookend_end.content:
Created the internal working decision note, separated into:

- Product decisions
- Release-readiness and implementation constraints
- Unresolved items for the next review
- Proposed next-review outputs

Morgan, small dogfood diagnostic from this morning. This is internal-only; I haven’t moved any of it into board/external views.

```text
workspace            terminal state                  observed events                                     sample preview rows
mdf-01               activated                       real_source_connected -> first_live_sync_completed   0
```

What’s muddying the dashboard is the `sample_import_completed` noise across the same five workspaces. Right now the dogfood panel makes the cohort look more activation-ish than it really is because those preview rows sit next to the real-source / live-sync events.

Decision logic

- Keep the diagnostic internal and directional.
- Treat only `real_source_connected` and `first_live_sync_completed` as activation-relevant events.
- Count `first_live_sync_completed` as completed activation.
- Keep workspaces with `real_source_connected` followed by a sync failure in a connected-but-failed/exception bucket—not as completed activation.
- Treat `invite_sent` without a source connection as not activated.
- Exclude `sample_import_completed` and preview rows entirely from the activation-facing cut. If useful, show them in a clearly labeled internal “sample/preview exception” bucket.
- Do not patch board or external views from this diagnostic.

Short answer for Anna:

“Let’s keep this cut internal and directional. For the activation-facing view, use only `real_source_connected` and `first_live_sync_completed`; preview/sample activity should not count toward activation. arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury release-risk readout — 2023-07-14
arguments.body:
Mercury release-risk readout — 2023-07-14

Attendees: Morgan Chen, Leo Park, Jake, Priya, Marcus

Scope
- Release risk and evidence only; this is not a platform roadmap or an owner-split launch ledger.
- Focus: where Mercury can still surprise us at the seams, especially activation behavior tied to auth/org state and thin dogfood evidence.

1. Org-invite roles vs activation-state seam

Risk
- The invited-member branch is the highest platform-seam risk. Rendering depends on server role and source state, which may not settle simultaneously after invite acceptance.
- A user may accept an invite and receive the org-role update while still between source states, potentially showing the wrong branch or CTA.

Evidence
- Only 2 real dogfood invited-member accounts have been tested end to end.
- One bug-bash pass required refresh/re-entry before the expected branch settled.
- Confidence is still driven more by happy-path staging than repeated real dogfood coverage.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Run more real invited-member dogfood accounts across admin-first and invitee-first orderings.
- Verify no path creates an activated-looking state without a real source or first live sync.
- Confirm sample data remains visually separate and preview-only and cannot shift the branch into an activated-looking state.
- Watch CTA selection on first load after invite acceptance.
- Distinguish wrong-CTA rendering from stale-state timing.

Room notes
- Design intent remains four branches; there is no pseudo-activated middle state.
- This is a release risk because it crosses auth/org state, not merely copy or UI.

2. Release-readiness evidence gaps

Risk
- Implemented is not the same as proven. Thin evidence remains a material launch risk even where code may be close.

Evidence
- Invited-member branch has only 2 real dogfood accounts.
- Queued-sync retry logs are sparse, even after removing fake progress/countdown behavior.
- Failed-sync screenshots are cleaner, but sample depth remains shallow.

Severity / confidence
- High severity, high confidence that the evidence gap exists; lower confidence about how many user-facing bugs remain underneath it.

Next verification
- Run a targeted dogfood pass exercising each branch with saved screenshots and logs.
- Capture at least one real queue -> retry -> recovery trace for queued sync.
- Separate “path unproven” from “path actually broken.”

3. Failed-sync cleanup and normalization

Risk
- The failed state is not fully verified across every normalized bucket.

Evidence
- One screenshot still leaks a raw vendor string.
- Existing fixes appear to cover the obvious path, but auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown/retry have not all been confirmed equally clean.
- Retry action looks better, but bucket text and UI still need proof on every branch.

Severity / confidence
- Medium severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Retest each failed bucket with captured UI.
- Confirm no raw vendor strings leak.
- Confirm retry remains idempotent.
- Keep the warning-circle direction; the open issue is verification, not icon reconsideration.

4. Later polish vs potential blockers

Not currently main blockers
- Setup-guide copy tightening, unless it causes a wrong action or real confusion in the invited-member branch.
- Small-width spacing, unless it clips or overlaps on a supported width.
- Failed-state icon polish, unless it obscures state meaning.

Guidance
- Keep branch distinctions crisp.
- Do not let a polish list become a second scope track before the next Mercury cycle.

Explicit exclusions
- No abstract platform recommendations.
- No provider debate or broader auth rewrite scope.
- No SSO/admin-depth wishlist.
- Do not convert this readout into an owner-split launch ledger yet.

Questions to verify next
- Can we prove invited-member rendering across real role/source-state permutations, not just the happy path?
- Do we have enough queued-sync retry evidence to say recovery is understandable without fake progress?
- Is failed-sync normalization complete across all buckets, or only mostly clean on the common path?
- Which gaps are real launch blockers versus thin proof on otherwise-correct behavior?
- What is the smallest next dogfood pass that materially raises confidence before wider exposure?

Bottom line
- The main release risks are the invited-member auth/org/source-state seam, insufficient real-world evidence for readiness, and incomplete end-to-end verification of failed-sync normalization. The next step is a focused dogfood pass that produces branch coverage, screenshots, logs, and a real queued-sync recovery trace before widening exposure.

arguments.message: Mercury release-risk readout (7/14): the main risks are (1) invited-member auth/org/source-state timing that may produce the wrong branch or CTA, (2) thin real dogfood evidence—especially invited-member coverage and queued-sync retry/recovery traces—and (3) incomplete end-to-end verification of failed-sync normalization across all buckets. Next step is a focused dogfood pass with branch screenshots/logs and a real queue → retry → recovery trace. Setup-copy, spacing, and icon polish remain later unless they cause confusion or obscure state. This was a release-risk/evidence readout, not an owner-split launch ledger.

[2024-02-05T09:36:00-08:00] Jake needs a release call on a live-sync support edge.

Discord DM — Jake → Morgan Chen
Mon, 5 Feb 2024 09:17 PT

Dropped the evidence links on MER-1279 this morning, but short version here because I need a release call.

We have a live-sync support edge that feels like real customer-facing release material, not just cleanup.

What support is seeing
- In two current Mercury workspaces over the last four days, the retry actually ran after a source timeout, but the UI stayed stale long enough that the user could not tell whether recovery succeeded.
- Shape is the same in both cases: pending state sticks too long, old timeout messaging can hang around in the same session, and the operator assumes the retry is still broken until they refresh.
- Support had to manually tell both accounts to refresh / re-open the page to see the recovered state.

Affected accounts
- Evergreen Bank test workspace
- one other current Mercury workspace from the same bounded live-sync path

Impact
- No duplicate sync jobs and no data-loss signal in the logs
- But it burns trust right at first live sync, creates repeat-click / did-this-actually-run support traffic, and makes the current recovery path look less reliable than it is
- Three support touches so far off two accounts; same question each time: did the retry happen or is it still stuck?

What I think belongs in this week's release
Customer-impacting:
- MER-1749 narrowed reconcile patch so retry status refreshes correctly after timeout recovery without a page reload
- MER-1823 stale timeout-banner cleanup so a successful retry actually clears the old timeout message in-session

Nice-to-have cleanup that I would leave out unless the branch is boring:
- retry helper-text cleanup
- timeout-banner copy polish
- minor pending-state wording cleanup that does not change behavior

Timing
- Leo says one more bounded timeout replay plus post-deploy smoke would make him comfortable shipping MER-1749 + MER-1823 in a small release Wednesday or Thursday this week
- If that last replay is noisy, I'd rather hold the copy cleanup and only ship the pieces that reduce support ambiguity

Question
Do you want the real support edge in this week's release, or do we keep punting and treat everything here as follow-on cleanup?

Draft an internal decision note for Jake and Leo: treat MER-1749 and MER-1823 as customer-impacting release work if the remaining timeout replay and smoke stay clean, and keep the helper text / banner copy polish / pending-state wording out unless the branch is genuinely boring. The note should separate trust/support impact from nice-to-have cleanup and avoid implying any sync-engine or retry-policy change.

Internal decision note — live-sync support edge

Decision

Treat MER-1749 and MER-1823 as customer-impacting release work for this week, targeting a small Wednesday or Thursday release, provided the remaining bounded timeout replay and post-deploy smoke stay clean.

Why this belongs in the release

This is a trust and support issue in the live-sync recovery experience:

- In two current Mercury workspaces, the retry completed after a source timeout, but the UI remained stale or continued showing the old timeout state.
- Users could not tell whether recovery had succeeded without refreshing or reopening the page.
- Support has handled three touches across the two accounts, all driven by the same question: did the retry actually run, or is it still stuck?
- There is no duplicate-job or data-loss signal. The customer impact is ambiguity at a high-trust moment: first live sync and recovery from failure.

Release scope

- MER-1749: ship the narrowed reconcile patch so retry status refreshes correctly after timeout recovery without requiring a page reload.
- MER-1823: clear the stale timeout banner in-session after a successful retry.

These changes should be framed as UI/state-reconciliation fixes that make the existing recovery result visible. They do not change the sync engine, retry policy, retry behavior, or job execution semantics.

Release gate

Ship if:

- The final bounded timeout replay is clean.
- Post-deploy smoke confirms that a recovered retry updates the visible status without a page reload.
- A successful retry clears the prior timeout message in the same session.
- There is no unexpected change to job counts, retry behavior, or error handling.

If the replay is noisy, hold the release rather than broadening scope. Reassess the two customer-impacting fixes with the failure evidence before shipping.

Keep out of this release

Unless the branch is genuinely boring after the required validation, leave these out:

- Retry helper-text cleanup.
- Timeout-banner copy polish.
- Minor pending-state wording changes that do not alter behavior.

Those are follow-on cleanup, not part of the trust/support fix. Avoid bundling them into the release unless they are demonstrably low-risk and add no validation or rollback complexity.

arguments.title: Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read
arguments.body:
Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read

Purpose
This pre-read frames Thursday’s discussion around the practical gaps and risks in the two hosted auth paths tested in the sandbox. It is intentionally not a final provider recommendation and does not reopen custom auth.

What we know so far

- Sessions: Clerk reached a working middleware/server-check flow faster. Auth0 works but required more setup and exposes more policy/tenant configuration.
- Magic links: Clerk was the simpler end-to-end sandbox path. Auth0 passwordless worked but had more redirect/state-handling friction.
- Organization invites: Clerk’s organization model maps well to the basic team-invite flow. Auth0 would leave more invite and membership stitching to us.
- SSO/admin: Auth0 appears stronger for deeper admin controls, domain/IdP management, and earlier enterprise-style SSO needs.
- Pricing: The ramp/MAU economics of Clerk plus org features remain unresolved; Auth0’s implementation cost is higher, while its future enterprise/contract shape may be more predictable.
- Staging validation: Any validation must use the standard deployment pipeline. No one-off staging shortcut should be used for auth testing.

Questions for Thursday

1. Session lifecycle
   - What is the expected behavior when a user accepts an invite or changes organization membership while a session is active?
   - How will refresh, revocation, and re-authentication behave across those transitions?
   - What evidence do we need from each path before calling this flow proven?

2. Magic-link reliability
   - What are the exact link-reuse and expiry semantics for new and returning users?
   - What should support see and do when a link is expired, reused, or associated with the wrong browser/session?
   - What redirect/state guarantees are required so users do not lose the return path?

3. Organization and invite edge cases
   - How do we handle an invitee who already has a personal workspace and then joins a team workspace?
   - What happens when an invite is revoked, resent, accepted twice, or accepted after membership changes?
   - Which membership and workspace invariants must be enforced by the provider versus Mercury?

4. Enterprise/admin scope
   - Is normal session auth plus invites sufficient for the launch scope?
   - Which domain, IdP, admin, audit, or SSO capabilities are launch requirements versus later requirements?
   - What is the earliest credible date by which enterprise requirements could change the implementation choice?

5. Cost and operational shape
   - What usage assumptions should we use for MAU, organizations, and invite volume?
   - What pricing breakpoints or org-feature charges need validation before a provider decision?
   - What support, observability, and incident-response responsibilities remain with Mercury for each path?

6. Validation and rollout
   - What is the smallest staging matrix that exercises sessions, magic links, invite acceptance, org switching, revocation, and failure recovery?
   - Who owns the test evidence and sign-off for each unresolved flow?
   - What must be green in the standard pipeline before auth changes can be promoted?

Non-decisions for this meeting

- No final provider recommendation.
- No reopening of custom/in-house auth.
- No commitment to enterprise SSO, domain management, or advanced admin controls before scope is confirmed.
- No assumption that sandbox success proves refresh, invite/org handoff, link reuse/expiry, or production-scale behavior.
- No pricing or MAU commitment until usage assumptions and provider pricing details are validated.
- No staging validation through one-off deploys, direct kubectl, or other paths that differ from the path we would ship.
- No launch approval based solely on the happy path; failure, recovery, and support workflows remain part of the acceptance bar.

Scope risks to resolve or explicitly accept

- Session refresh and state continuity after invite acceptance or organization changes are unproven.
- Personal-workspace to team-workspace handoff may create duplicate, orphaned, or incorrectly scoped membership state.
- Magic-link reuse, expiry, and redirect/state behavior could create avoidable support load or account-access confusion.
- Auth0’s additional flexibility may expand implementation and ownership scope if requirements are not bounded.
- Clerk’s MAU/org-feature economics may become less predictable at higher usage.
- Enterprise SSO/admin requirements could arrive after implementation work has committed us to a less suitable shape.
- Provider-specific failure modes, logs, rate limits, recovery paths, and support tooling have not yet been compared systematically.
- A staging shortcut would give us misleading confidence and increase the risk of shipping an auth path that was not validated through the real deployment controls.

Deploy-discipline checks

- Use the standard/current deployment pipeline for every staging auth validation.
- Confirm the tested commit, environment, configuration, and provider tenant are recorded with the test evidence.
- Do not use direct kubectl or a one-off shortcut for staging auth testing.
- Verify secrets, redirect URLs, callback URLs, and environment separation through the normal configuration path; do not paste or manually mutate production values.
- Record pipeline result, deploy identifier, and rollback path before treating a test as comparable to a ship-ready flow.
- Keep any pre-green notes and findings in the engineering release channel/process until the deployment is green; do not broaden distribution prematurely.
- Define rollback and session invalidation behavior before testing a provider change against shared staging data.

Suggested Thursday outcome

Leave with a bounded validation matrix, named owners for each open question, explicit launch-versus-later scope, and a list of evidence required before the provider decision. The meeting should produce criteria and follow-up work—not a provider selection.

What support is seeing
- In two current Mercury workspaces over the last four days, the retry actually ran after a source timeout, but the UI stayed stale long enough that the user could not tell whether recovery succeeded.

Impact
- No duplicate sync jobs and no data-loss signal in the logs
- But it burns trust right at first live sync, creates repeat-click / did-this-actually-run support traffic, and makes the current recovery path look less reliable than it is
- Three support touches so far off two accounts; same question each time: did the retry happen or is it still stuck?

What I think belongs in this week's release
Customer-impacting:
- MER-1749 narrowed reconcile patch so retry status refreshes correctly after timeout recovery without a page reload
- MER-1823 stale timeout-banner cleanup so a successful retry actually clears the old timeout message in-session

Nice-to-have cleanup that I would leave out unless the branch is boring:
- retry helper-text cleanup
- timeout-banner copy polish
- minor pending-state wording cleanup that does not change behavior

Timing
- Leo says one more bounded timeout replay plus post-deploy smoke would make him comfortable shipping MER-1749 + MER-1823 in a small release Wednesday or Thursday this week
- If that last replay is noisy, I'd rather hold the copy cleanup and only ship the pieces that reduce support ambiguity

Question

Internal decision note — live-sync support edge

Decision

Treat MER-1749 and MER-1823 as customer-impacting release work for this week, targeting a small Wednesday or Thursday release, provided the remaining bounded timeout replay and post-deploy smoke stay clean.

Why this belongs in the release

This is a trust and support issue in the live-sync recovery experience:

- In two current Mercury workspaces, the retry completed after a source timeout, but the UI remained stale or continued showing the old timeout state.
- Users could not tell whether recovery had succeeded without refreshing or reopening the page.
- Support has handled three touches across the two accounts, all driven by the same question: did the retry actually run, or is it still stuck?
- There is no duplicate-job or data-loss signal. The customer impact is ambiguity at a high-trust moment: first live sync and recovery from failure.

Release scope

- MER-1749: ship the narrowed reconcile patch so retry status refreshes correctly after timeout recovery without requiring a page reload.
- MER-1823: clear the stale timeout banner in-session after a successful retry.

These changes should be framed as UI/state-reconciliation fixes that make the existing recovery result visible. They do not change the sync engine, retry policy, retry behavior, or job execution semantics.

Release gate

Ship if:

- The final bounded timeout replay is clean.
- Post-deploy smoke confirms that a recovered retry updates the visible status without a page reload.
- A successful retry clears the prior timeout message in the same session.
- There is no unexpected change to job counts, retry behavior, or error handling.

If the replay is noisy, hold the release rather than broadening scope. Reassess the two customer-impacting fixes with the failure evidence before shipping.

Keep out of this release

Unless the branch is genuinely boring after the required validation, leave these out:

- Retry helper-text cleanup.
- Timeout-banner copy polish.
- Minor pending-state wording changes that do not alter behavior.

Those are follow-on cleanup, not part of the trust/support fix. Avoid bundling them into the release unless they are demonstrably low-risk and add no validation or rollback complexity.

arguments.title: Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read
arguments.body:
Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read

Purpose
This pre-read frames Thursday’s discussion around the practical gaps and risks in the two hosted auth paths tested in the sandbox. It is intentionally not a final provider recommendation and does not reopen custom auth.

What we know so far

- Sessions: Clerk reached a working middleware/server-check flow faster. Auth0 works but required more setup and exposes more policy/tenant configuration.
- Magic links: Clerk was the simpler end-to-end sandbox path. Auth0 passwordless worked but had more redirect/state-handling friction.
- Organization invites: Clerk’s organization model maps well to the basic team-invite flow. Auth0 would leave more invite and membership stitching to us.
- SSO/admin: Auth0 appears stronger for deeper admin controls, domain/IdP management, and earlier enterprise-style SSO needs.
- Pricing: The ramp/MAU economics of Clerk plus org features remain unresolved; Auth0’s implementation cost is higher, while its future enterprise/contract shape may be more predictable.
- Staging validation: Any validation must use the standard deployment pipeline. No one-off staging shortcut should be used for auth testing.

Questions for Thursday

1. Session lifecycle
   - What is the expected behavior when a user accepts an invite or changes organization membership while a session is active?
   - How will refresh, revocation, and re-authentication behave across those transitions?
   - What evidence do we need from each path before calling this flow proven?

2. Magic-link reliability
   - What are the exact link-reuse and expiry semantics for new and returning users?
   - What should support see and do when a link is expired, reused, or associated with the wrong browser/session?
   - What redirect/state guarantees are required so users do not lose the return path?

3. Organization and invite edge cases
   - How do we handle an invitee who already has a personal workspace and then joins a team workspace?
   - What happens when an invite is revoked, resent, accepted twice, or accepted after membership changes?
   - Which membership and workspace invariants must be enforced by the provider versus Mercury?

4. Enterprise/admin scope
   - Is normal session auth plus invites sufficient for the launch scope?
   - Which domain, IdP, admin, audit, or SSO capabilities are launch requirements versus later requirements?
   - What is the earliest credible date by which enterprise requirements could change the implementation choice?

5. Cost and operational shape
   - What usage assumptions should we use for MAU, organizations, and invite volume?
   - What pricing breakpoints or org-feature charges need validation before a provider decision?
   - What support, observability, and incident-response responsibilities remain with Mercury for each path?

6. Validation and rollout
   - What is the smallest staging matrix that exercises sessions, magic links, invite acceptance, org switching, revocation, and failure recovery?
   - Who owns the test evidence and sign-off for each unresolved flow?
   - What must be green in the standard pipeline before auth changes can be promoted?

Non-decisions for this meeting

- No final provider recommendation.
- No reopening of custom/in-house auth.
- No commitment to enterprise SSO, domain management, or advanced admin controls before scope is confirmed.
- No assumption that sandbox success proves refresh, invite/org handoff, link reuse/expiry, or production-scale behavior.
- No pricing or MAU commitment until usage assumptions and provider pricing details are validated.
- No staging validation through one-off deploys, direct kubectl, or other paths that differ from the path we would ship.
- No launch approval based solely on the happy path; failure, recovery, and support workflows remain part of the acceptance bar.

Scope risks to resolve or explicitly accept

- Session refresh and state continuity after invite acceptance or organization changes are unproven.
- Personal-workspace to team-workspace handoff may create duplicate, orphaned, or incorrectly scoped membership state.
- Magic-link reuse, expiry, and redirect/state behavior could create avoidable support load or account-access confusion.
- Auth0’s additional flexibility may expand implementation and ownership scope if requirements are not bounded.
- Clerk’s MAU/org-feature economics may become less predictable at higher usage.
- Enterprise SSO/admin requirements could arrive after implementation work has committed us to a less suitable shape.
- Provider-specific failure modes, logs, rate limits, recovery paths, and support tooling have not yet been compared systematically.
- A staging shortcut would give us misleading confidence and increase the risk of shipping an auth path that was not validated through the real deployment controls.

Deploy-discipline checks

- Use the standard/current deployment pipeline for every staging auth validation.
- Confirm the tested commit, environment, configuration, and provider tenant are recorded with the test evidence.
- Do not use direct kubectl or a one-off shortcut for staging auth testing.
- Verify secrets, redirect URLs, callback URLs, and environment separation through the normal configuration path; do not paste or manually mutate production values.
- Record pipeline result, deploy identifier, and rollback path before treating a test as comparable to a ship-ready flow.
- Keep any pre-green notes and findings in the engineering release channel/process until the deployment is green; do not broaden distribution prematurely.
- Define rollback and session invalidation behavior before testing a provider change against shared staging data.

Suggested Thursday outcome

Leave with a bounded validation matrix, named owners for each open question, explicit launch-versus-later scope, and a list of evidence required before the provider decision. The meeting should produce criteria and follow-up work—not a provider selection.

arguments.title: Mercury auth — open questions for Friday decision window
arguments.body:
Mercury auth — internal open-questions note
Friday, June 9 decision window

Context
The June 8 readout established that the Clerk sandbox session path and magic-link path work at demo level. It did not establish a provider decision, production readiness, or a deployment path. This note keeps those questions open and identifies the evidence required before any prod conversation.

What is working so far
- Clerk sandbox session path: end-to-end happy path demonstrated.
- Magic-link path: working at demo level.

Open questions for Friday

1. Provider baseline
- Is the current Clerk sandbox result sufficient to use as the baseline for the next implementation pass, or do we need a comparative check against another provider before committing?
- What exact product and engineering requirements must the provider satisfy for Mercury v1: session handling, magic links, organization invites, SSO, admin operations, auditability, supportability, and failure/error states?
- What admin surface would we still need to build around the provider, especially for organization management, invite recovery, access changes, and operational intervention?
- Which unresolved provider limitations are acceptable for v1, and which are launch blockers?
- What is the fallback/exit plan if the provider cannot cleanly support the required invite or admin behavior?

2. Organization-invite behavior
- What is the intended accept flow for an existing user versus a new user?
- After acceptance, what landing page and organization context should be guaranteed?
- How should expired, revoked, duplicate, or already-accepted invites behave?
- What happens when the invitee is signed into the wrong account, has no account, or belongs to multiple organizations?
- Which recovery and support paths are self-serve, and where would operations need to intervene?
- What telemetry and error states are required to make these cases diagnosable?

3. SSO and admin depth
- Which SSO capabilities are required for the target customers and launch scope?
- Which admin controls are provider-native versus owned by us?
- Do we need domain verification, role/group mapping, provisioning/deprovisioning, audit logs, or other enterprise controls in v1?
- What is the minimum viable admin surface, and what is explicitly deferred?

4. Staging discipline and release checks
- Confirm that all auth validation runs through the standard staging pipeline; no shortcut path and no direct/manual production deployment.
- Run a clean staging pass for:
  - Session creation, persistence, expiry, logout, and failure states.
  - Magic-link issuance, delivery, expiry, replay prevention, and failure states.
  - Organization invites for existing users and new users.
  - Invite acceptance landing behavior and organization context.
  - Wrong-account, duplicate, expired, revoked, and multi-organization cases.
  - Required admin and operational recovery flows.
- Record the build/commit, environment configuration, test accounts, results, and any deviations.
- Verify staging logs, telemetry, and alerting are sufficient to investigate failures without handling sensitive credentials or links unsafely.
- Confirm rollback/recovery steps before considering any production discussion.
- Identify who signs off on the staging evidence and who owns each unresolved issue.

arguments.body:
Subject: December all-hands packet — presenter notes and Q&A calls

Hi HR,

Thanks for the revised packet. The run of show works for me, and I’m aligned with removing the open-mic block and keeping Q&A structured around the pre-collected questions with routed follow-up.

A couple of calls on the question handling:

- Question 3 can stay live, provided Devon keeps the answer to the monitoring-versus-operating tradeoff. It should stay grounded in the current Q4 hardening priorities, without turning into a broader roadmap discussion.
- Question 11 should name Jake on the follow-up slide, rather than referring only to “the product owner.”

For my section, I’ll keep the company update short and high-level, then bridge into current work. My Mercury update will stay within the current bounded-testing flow: magic links, org invites, preview-only sample data, the real-source connection, and the first live sync, followed by what this testing is clarifying about how we work this month.

For live Q&A, let’s stay with the approved current topics:

- What bounded Mercury testing has changed about how we work this month.
- Current Q4 hardening priorities and what remains outside sprint scope.
- Why onboarding remains a monitoring/guarded-rollout effort rather than a broader polish pass.
- One useful Honeycomb debugging/observability workflow example.

The following should remain async or out of scope for the live session: whether January Northstar means fundraising is active again; whether SSO, audit history, or admin controls are on the roadmap because of Mercury customer questions; Mercury pricing or enterprise-package questions; and 2024 hiring priorities.

Please route follow-up as follows:

- API v2 support-path issues: Rishi.
- Holiday support/on-call path: HR plus the support lead.
- Recurring Mercury support questions: Jake.
- Additional all-hands questions: HR.

Presenter notes

0:00–0:04 — Welcome and housekeeping
- Acknowledge that questions were collected in advance.
- Set expectation that the Q&A will be structured and that routed follow-up will be handled after the session.

0:04–0:12 — Morgan company update
- Keep this high-level and brief.
- Bridge directly from the company update into current work; do not open new strategy or fundraising threads.

Suggested transition: “I’ll keep the company update brief and focus on the work in front of us now. That leads into what we’re learning from bounded Mercury testing and how it is shaping our operating focus this month.”

0:12–0:22 — Morgan: Mercury bounded-testing update
- Describe the current flow only:
  1. Magic links.
  2. Organization invites.
  3. Preview-only sample data.
  4. Connection to a real source.
  5. First live sync.
- Explain what the current testing clarifies: where the seams are, what needs monitoring and guarded operation, and which issues belong in hardening rather than a broad polish pass.
- Avoid implying a general availability launch, a wider rollout, or commitments beyond the current test scope.

0:22–0:32 — Devon: Q4 hardening priorities
- Cover the current hardening priorities and explicitly state what stays out of sprint scope.
- For question 3, keep the answer focused on the monitoring/operating tradeoff: what we are choosing to observe and operate carefully now instead of expanding the surface area for polish.

0:32–0:40 — Jordan: debugging/observability example
- Give one concrete Honeycomb workflow example: start from the affected request or user flow, use traces and relevant attributes to isolate the failing seam, compare the surrounding events, and use that evidence to decide whether the issue is a code defect, an integration boundary, or an operational condition.
- Keep it useful and current without turning it into a tooling tutorial.

0:40–0:56 — Structured Q&A
- Take only the approved live topics listed above.

UI fixes
- After a source-timeout recovery, the live-sync retry status now refreshes in the current session without requiring a page reload or reopening the page.

- The deploy did not change the sync engine, retry policy, retry execution semantics, or job behavior. It made the existing recovery result reconcile correctly in the UI and removed stale messaging.
- Verification after deployment showed a clean timeout replay, no duplicate sync jobs, and flat alerting during the initial monitoring window.

In short, this was a scoped live-sync UI/state-reconciliation fix intended to remove the “did the retry actually run?” ambiguity; it was not a broader change to the underlying sync or retry system.

Best,
Morgan

arguments.title: Northstar close package — internal note and investor recap
arguments.body:
NORTHSTAR CLOSE PACKAGE
22 February 2024

INTERNAL TEAM NOTE

Team —

Northstar has confirmed the close of Scaffold’s $18M Series B. Northstar Ventures led the round, and Sofia Alvarez’s board seat is effective at close. The final board and stockholder signatures are in, the amended and restated certificate has been filed, and the release call is complete.

The operating message stays deliberately plain: we raised on a bounded case we can defend, not a widened growth story. Mercury activation and the first-admin path are better; hybrid pricing is credible; Evergreen is the clearest current enterprise-pattern signal; and expansion still has to be earned.

Our post-close work is straightforward:
- Protect the activation gains and improve the first-admin-to-second-admin handoff.
- Make the enterprise-readiness backlog legible and shippable: SSO timing, admin-change audit history, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet.
- Turn the Evergreen signal into repeatable evidence without customer-specific exceptions.
- Build retention evidence and enterprise expansion milestones rather than telling a fast Series C story.

Thank you to everyone who got this across the line. We should treat the financing as room to execute, not a reason to change the facts.

— Morgan


FINAL INVESTOR RECAP

Subject: Scaffold financing update

Investors —

Scaffold has closed an $18M Series B led by Northstar Ventures, with Sofia Alvarez joining the board at close.

I want to keep this note plain: the financing gives us workable room to execute on a bounded case we can defend, not a reason for a victory lap. The case underwritten through diligence is the same one we have been using: better Mercury activation and admin flow, credible hybrid pricing, Evergreen as a real enterprise-pattern signal, and expansion that remains unsolved.

In the bounded Mercury flow:
- September: 24 accounts; 15/24 activated within 7 days (63%), and 12/24 reached first live sync within 7 days (50%).
- October: 27 accounts; 19/27 activated within 7 days (70%), and 16/27 reached first live sync within 7 days (59%).

Here, activation lift means more real-source connection and week-one live sync, not preview or sample behavior.

Our hybrid pricing remains:
- Pilot: $2,500/month for up to 50 monthly active developers.
- Growth: $7,500/month for up to 200 monthly active developers.
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers.

Evergreen remains the clearest current enterprise-pattern example because the bounded flow worked for a second-admin group without customer-specific exceptions. It also keeps the next backlog explicit: SSO timing, admin-change audit history, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet.

MAU remains the honest ramp measure; we are not reframing the model around seats or directories, and there is no Evergreen carveout. Expansion after initial admin and setup remains uneven and still has to be earned. We are not reading this financing as proof that enterprise readiness is complete or that Mercury expansion is suddenly clean.

Post-close, our focus is retention evidence and enterprise expansion milestones—not a fast Series C narrative.

Narrow process, defensible package, no fundraising theater.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold

messages.content:
[2024-12-27T10:12:00-08:00] Can you tighten Devon’s year-end note into something HR can format as-is? I want it to still feel like a team thank-you, not a board memo, and the metric bullets should come through as lighter year-end language instead of three dense blocks.

Subject: Year-end team note draft
From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen

- Team —
- As we wrap 2024, we keep coming back to how much hard, unglamorous work it took to turn enterprise learning into product that is clearer, more repeatable, and easier for customers to trust on day one.
- We made real progress on the parts of Scaffold that decide whether a customer gets set up quickly, gets their first source connected, sees a live sync, invites teammates, and feels like the product can support a serious deployment.
- Project Mercury pulled a lot of that into focus, but this was not just one project or one team. Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone carrying customer context helped reduce one-off setup work and turn it into something we can ship repeatedly.
- Atlas also got stronger in the ways that matter most once customers are live: better auth and verification paths, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer docs, faster first technical reads, and less thrash on issues that used to bounce around.
- The numbers behind that progress are meaningful: median time from workspace creation to first connected source moved from 2.4 days in Q1 to 0.9 days in Q4; the share of new workspaces reaching a first live sync within 14 days rose from 41% to 63%; teammate invitations on activated workspaces increased from 28% to 47%.
- In the core Mercury setup flow, workspace creation success improved from 93.8% to 97.9%; first-source connection completion moved from 54% to 72%; and first successful sync on connected workspaces increased from 68% to 84%.
- Enterprise-readiness and repeatability improved together: admin-role setup on new enterprise workspaces rose from 61% to 88%; median time to close high-priority Atlas issues dropped from 2.6 business days to 0.9; and the auth / webhook / connector docs refresh deflected 37% of repeat enterprise implementation questions in the second half.
- More important than any single metric, people kept showing up for each other while we were changing the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through that rarely gets enough credit.
- Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, for caring about the details customers actually feel, and for helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder.
- We’re proud of what this team shipped this year, and we’re excited for what we can build from here.

Subject: Thank you for what we built together in 2024

Team —

As we wrap up 2024, we keep coming back to how much hard, often unglamorous work it took to turn enterprise learning into a product that is clearer, more repeatable, and easier for customers to trust from day one.

We made real progress across the moments that matter: getting customers set up quickly, connecting their first source, seeing a live sync, inviting teammates, and feeling confident that Scaffold can support a serious deployment.

Project Mercury brought much of that work into focus, but this was never just one project or one team. Engineering, product, design, support, and everyone who carried customer context helped reduce one-off setup work and turn it into something we can ship repeatedly.

Atlas also grew stronger where it matters most after customers go live — with better authentication and verification paths, more usable webhook and connector behavior, clearer documentation, faster technical support, and less thrash around issues that used to bounce between teams.

A few year-end markers of that progress:

• Customers are reaching their first connected source in a median of 0.9 days, down from 2.4 days in Q1.

• The share of new workspaces reaching a first live sync within 14 days rose from 41% to 63%.

• Activated workspaces with teammate invitations increased from 28% to 47%.

• In the core Mercury setup flow, workspace creation success improved from 93.8% to 97.9%, first-source connection completion rose from 54% to 72%, and first successful sync on connected workspaces increased from 68% to 84%.

• On the enterprise side, admin-role setup on new workspaces rose from 61% to 88%, while median time to close high-priority Atlas issues fell from 2.6 business days to 0.9.

• The refreshed authentication, webhook, and connector documentation helped deflect 37% of repeat enterprise implementation questions in the second half of the year.

More important than any single metric, people kept showing up for one another while we changed the product under real customer pressure. That takes judgment, patience, and a lot of follow-through — much of it work that rarely gets enough credit.

Thank you for sticking with the hard parts, caring about the details customers actually feel, and helping build a company that learns and gets better instead of just getting louder.

We’re proud of what this team shipped this year, and excited for what we can build from here.

Happy holidays,

Devon

messages.content:
Sep 18 Operating-Posture Read
45 minutes

Purpose

Assess Q3 operating evidence, fall financing posture, and whether the evidence warrants revisiting staffing. This is an operating read, not a data-room, investor-packet, customer-decision, or default hiring-reopen meeting.

Agenda

0:00–0:03 — Frame the read and decision boundaries
Owner: Sofia

- Confirm the three questions:
  1. What does the final August close show about Q3 operating posture?
  2. What does the fall financing posture require us to watch or decide?
  3. Does the evidence justify revisiting staffing now?
- Confirm that the only inputs are the final August close, the narrow owner-lane read, and the unfinished Compass evidence gate.
- Establish a parking lot for data-room refresh, investor materials, customer-facing Compass decisions, and unrelated roadmap or hiring topics.

0:03–0:13 — Final August close: Q3 operating evidence
Owner: Devon
Supporting input: Jake, limited to current-state support-quality evidence

Focus:

- Actual Q3 operating evidence from the finalized August close.
- Material variance, trend, or execution signal that changes the operating posture.
- Known caveats or evidence gaps.
- What is confirmed versus still interpretive.

Prep asks:

- Devon: Bring the final August close and a concise view of the few facts that materially affect the operating read.
- Jake: Bring current-state support-quality notes only; no advanced-admin research, CSV export scoping, or new product investigation.
- No data-room refresh or investor-packet translation.

0:13–0:22 — Narrow owner-lane read
Owner: Anna

Focus:

- What each relevant owner lane is carrying now.
- Concrete capacity, dependency, or execution constraints evidenced by the read.
- Whether any constraint is durable enough to affect fall planning.
- Explicitly distinguish an observed owner-lane issue from a broader org-design or hiring conclusion.

Prep ask:

- Anna: Bring the narrow owner-lane read with named evidence, current constraints, and unresolved dependencies.
- Keep the discussion to the lanes already in scope; do not broaden it into an org redesign or general hiring review.

0:22–0:31 — Compass evidence gate
Owner: Leo

Focus:

- Current status of the unfinished internal Compass evidence gate.
- What evidence is complete, what remains missing, and who owns the next evidence step.
- Whether the remaining gap affects the operating posture or simply requires continued follow-through.
- Any ambiguous contract or log detail needed to interpret the evidence.

Prep ask:

- Leo: Bring the gate status, specific missing evidence, accountable owner, and next checkpoint.
- Keep contract/log questions to facts needed to resolve ambiguity.
- Do not turn this into a customer-facing Compass decision, relaunch signal, or roadmap obligation.

0:31–0:40 — Fall financing posture
Owner: Sarah

Focus:

- What the August close and owner-lane evidence imply for the fall financing posture.
- The relevant timing, thresholds, risks, and decision points already supported by the evidence.
- What needs monitoring versus what requires action now.
- Whether the posture changes the staffing question.

Prep ask:

- Sarah: Bring the bounded fall financing view tied to the operating evidence, including assumptions and decision triggers.
- No investor packet, fundraising narrative, data-room work, or new external outreach decisions.

0:40–0:45 — Staffing test, decisions, and owners
Owner: Sofia, with Morgan

Use this test:

- What evidence would justify revisiting staffing?
- Do we have that evidence now?
- If not, what specific signal or checkpoint would cause the question to reopen?

Close with:

- Decisions made.
- Evidence still missing.
- One owner and date for each follow-up.
- Topics explicitly parked.
