arguments.title: Mercury offsite closeout — owners, cuts, launch blockers
arguments.body:
Mercury offsite closeout
Owners, cuts, launch blockers
Photo transcription / closeout notes — 2023-05-12

Purpose
This is working material, not a deck. Ship work, owners, cuts, and blockers. The weekly spine is Jake. If discussion turns into narrative polish, cut it.

Launch bar
- Activation works without founder handholding.
- The expansion path is visible in the product, not in slides.
- The top admin pain is reduced enough that calls stop repeating the same three complaints.
- Every blocker has one owner.

ACTIVATION

Owners
- Priya: path, copy, and screens.
- Jake: implementation, feature flag, and rollout sequence.
- Anna: event definitions and success cut.

Needed by next review
- Single primary CTA: connect first source.
- Invite teammates becomes optional after first value, not before.
- Use sample data only if there is no real event in the first session.
- Define the activation event chain in plain English and as actual events.

Blockers
- Billing gate timing is unresolved:
  - Before the first real run is probably too much friction.
  - After first value is better, but requires an abuse cap / usage limit.
- Event names are still fuzzy. Anna needs an exact handoff; Jake will not wire to vibes.
- Role-setup copy is too abstract. Admins do not know what changes later versus now.
- Feature-flag rollout criteria are not written anywhere.

Scope cuts
- No template gallery for v1.
- No SSO in the first-run path.
- No advanced permissions setup during activation.
- No logo upload or custom branding in first-run.

Decisions / guardrails
- “First value” means connected source plus first successful action, not an invited teammate.
- Stop debating the empty-state illustration.
- Do not reopen the entire settings IA here.

EXPANSION

Owners
- Jake: overall.
- Priya: upgrade moments and UI.
- Anna: usage-threshold sanity check and measurement.

What stays in
- Expose the upgrade trigger where usage actually hits the limit.
- Provide one clean in-app path from cap hit to plan / owner action.
- Show the admin why the workspace is constrained.
- Keep copy light; no packaging essay.

Blockers
- Mercury feature-flag rollout remains ambiguous:
  - Who flips it?
  - What are the merge criteria?
  - Where is the rollback note?
  - What is the target date?
- The usage-threshold cut is noisy; choose one number the team will actually use.
- Upgrade copy is split between product / admin language and billing language.

Scope cuts
- No annual-plan flow work for launch.
- No seat-management overhaul.
- No contract-specific enterprise branching in product.
- No pricing-story work in this room.

Decisions / guardrails
- The expansion path must exist even if monetization details evolve later.
- If it requires sales explanation every time, it is not launch-ready.

ADMIN PAIN

Owners
- Jake: backend, account actions, and audit surfaces.
- Priya: admin home and settings grouping.
- Anna: tag incoming issues by severity and frequency.

Repeated pain to fix
1. Permissions / roles are unclear.
2. Bulk user actions are too manual.
3. There is no clean audit trail for “who changed what.”
4. The wrong person gets admin / billing noise.
5. Settings are scattered across too many places.

Blockers
- Audit-log scope is unclear: which events are mandatory for launch?
- CSV / import failures do a poor job explaining what broke.
- The permission-model explanation is too hand-wavey for security-conscious customers.
- Notification-routing rules are not explicit enough.

Scope cuts
- No full settings redesign.
- No granular notification matrix.
- No admin analytics dashboard.
- No custom role builder.

Decision / guardrail
- Fix repeated pain, not every admin complaint anyone has ever had.
- If a problem matters only after launch scale, write it down and move on.

CROSS-CUTTING
- Jake runs the weekly from this; Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon can pressure-test logic, but should not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner comes to weekly with: what moved, what slipped, and what we cut.
- Customer examples beat opinions.
- Keep the launch-blocker list short and named.

OPEN BLOCKERS TO CARRY FORWARD
1. Billing gate timing.
2. Activation instrumentation definitions.
3. Mercury feature-flag rollout owner plus merge / rollback criteria.
4. Admin audit-log minimum scope.

DECISIONS DUE
- Decide billing-gate placement and abuse-cap / usage-limit approach.
- Lock the activation event chain and exact event-name handoff.
- Name the Mercury feature-flag rollout owner; document merge criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- Set the single usage threshold for the expansion path.
- Define the minimum launch audit-log event scope.

MONDAY GUARDRAIL
Do not let Monday become “can we make this story cleaner.”

Next Mercury weekly — compact internal recap

Purpose: keep the weekly on owners, cuts, blockers, and decisions due; do not turn it into launch-story polish.

Owners
- Jake runs the weekly and owns implementation / rollout coordination.
- Priya owns activation and upgrade UI, copy, screens, and admin-home grouping.
- Anna owns instrumentation, measurement, threshold sanity checks, and issue tagging.
- Morgan joins for scope calls and unblockers.
- Devon pressure-tests logic only; no investor-copy work.

What moved / what to carry
- Activation: primary CTA is connect first source; teammate invite follows first value; sample data is fallback only.
- Expansion: keep the in-product cap-hit to plan / owner path; show why the workspace is constrained.
- Admin: focus on permissions, bulk actions, audit trail, routing, and settings grouping.

Cuts to hold
- No v1 template gallery, first-run SSO, advanced activation permissions, custom branding, annual-plan flow, seat overhaul, enterprise branching, pricing-story work, full settings redesign, notification matrix, admin analytics dashboard, or custom role builder.

Open blockers / decisions due
1. Billing-gate placement and abuse cap / usage limit.
2. Exact activation event chain and event-name handoff.
3. Mercury feature-flag rollout owner, merge criteria, rollback note, and target date.
4. One usable expansion threshold.
5. Minimum launch audit-log scope.

Weekly check-in format
Every owner reports: what moved, what slipped, and what we cut. Bring customer examples, not opinions. Keep the blocker list short and named.

Guardrail
Do not let Monday become “can we make this story cleaner.”

arguments.title: Compass June closeout packet — June 4 evidence read
arguments.body:
COMPASS JUNE CLOSEOUT PACKET
June 4 evidence read

Status: Evidence packet only. Final cut/keep decision: PENDING.

Purpose and boundary
This packet consolidates the June closeout evidence for a narrow owner-group read. It is not a customer-facing launch, product commitment, dashboard, GTM proof point, staffing trigger, or Series C/investor narrative.

Executive read
- Limited internal behavior changed: Compass prompts generated a small number of owner follow-ups and improved account-team preparation and questions.
- No verified customer behavior change: no customer asked to use Compass, changed workflow because of a prompt, or took a visible action attributable to a prompt.
- No repeatable customer-growth motion is established.
- Evidence is sufficient for a bounded internal operating read, with dates, sources, account boundaries, and caveats attached. It is not sufficient for broader exposure, customer proof, GTM claims, hiring, or portfolio-level repeatability.
- Enterprise-readiness intake remains owner-routed and evidence-gated.
- Final cut/keep decision is intentionally left pending for the June 4 read; the evidence below supports discussion, not a pre-decided disposition.

1. Behavior-change evidence

Changed internally
- Owner follow-up hygiene and preparation/question quality improved in limited examples.
- 2025-04-25, “Compass review wrapped”: the renewal-risk/admin-friction prompt helped owners notice specific follow-up work and ask better questions; the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt was legible to internal account owners.
- 2025-05-06, “First-May Compass observation notes”: Sarah requested one missing audit-lookup timestamp in the Evergreen appendix; an Acme account owner sanity-checked a renewal-risk note before a customer conversation; Nadia added one expansion-timing script question after first live sync. Implementation remained owner-group-only.

Not demonstrated
- No customer used Compass, changed workflow because of a prompt, or took a visible action because of it.
- No attributable customer adoption, expansion intent, or repeatable customer-growth motion.
- Do not convert internal follow-up into customer proof.

Interpretation
- Observed: limited internal follow-up and preparation improvement.
- Not observed: verified customer behavior change, customer workflow change, adoption, or repeatable growth motion.
- Still unknown: whether a larger, dated sample can show attributable and repeated account or customer behavior change.

2. Prompt evidence and caveats

Signal A — renewal-risk / admin-friction follow-up
- Evidence: owners noticed specific follow-up work and asked better questions. Examples include the missing Evergreen audit-lookup timestamp and the Acme owner’s pre-conversation sanity check.
- Sources: 2025-04-25 “Compass review wrapped”; 2025-05-06 “First-May Compass observation notes.”
- Boundary: Evergreen is annual-account current-state context; Acme is limited to Acme’s own live-only signals.
- Caveat: an internal follow-up does not establish churn, product weakness, customer demand, or causality. Admin handoff, role confusion, procurement/security packaging, activation drag, and product gaps remain distinct possibilities.
- Routing: Anna for definitions/caveats; Sarah for account-thread evidence; Nadia for pattern capture; Jake/Leo for implementation and seams as needed.

Signal B — post-first-live-sync expansion follow-up
- Evidence: the prompt was legible to internal account owners; Nadia added one script question about expansion timing after first live sync on 2025-05-06.
- Source: 2025-04-25 “Compass review wrapped”; 2025-05-06 “First-May Compass observation notes.”
- Caveat: script usability and one added question do not establish expansion intent, committed demand, customer behavior change, or repeatable growth. Keep readiness basis and observed usage attached to any future example.
- Routing: Nadia for pattern capture and customer-success/customer-growth use cases; Jake for product sequencing; Leo for data/platform seams as needed.

Signal C — account-note/source-quality prompt
- Evidence: 2025-05-06 exposed a missing audit-lookup timestamp in the Evergreen appendix. The 2025-05-11 prep notes say source quality is strongest in Sarah’s Evergreen thread and uneven elsewhere. The 2025-04-25 review says Leo’s source-recency handling is acceptable for continued owner-group use but not for broader exposure claims.
- Caveat: source hygiene supports bounded internal use; it is not evidence of Compass impact or portfolio-wide repeatability.
- Routing: Sarah for account-thread and note hygiene; Leo for source-recency/data seams; Anna for definitions and caveats.

3. Account-source quality

Current assessment
- Sarah’s Evergreen thread is the strongest source-quality example, bounded to Evergreen’s annual-account current state. It is not proof of repeatability beyond Evergreen, customer-growth proof, or staffing justification.
- Acme remains live-only and limited to Acme’s own signals. Do not use Evergreen-derived material for Acme, and do not generalize Acme beyond its own review.
- Portfolio-wide quality remains uneven. The missing audit-lookup timestamp is a concrete completeness gap; the 2025-05-11 review explicitly calls out uneven quality outside Sarah’s Evergreen thread.
- Source-recency handling is acceptable for continued owner-group use, but does not support broader exposure claims.

Use with confidence within boundary
- Dated source records with named account, source type, provenance, and direct observation separated from inference.
- Sarah’s Evergreen current-state evidence within its annual-account boundary.
- Acme’s own live-only signals, without cross-account generalization.

Qualify or exclude
- Undated, stale, duplicated, incomplete, or unattributed notes.
- Account-level claims without a source, sample/account boundary, or direct excerpt.
- Evergreen extrapolated into a portfolio or growth claim.
- Acme evidence used outside Acme’s live-only scope.
- The separate Acme API v2 export-timeout issue as evidence that a Compass prompt worked; that is operational evidence, not Compass behavior-change evidence.

4. Owner-routed enterprise-readiness intake

Routing model
Route only specific, evidenced needs with a named accountable owner and next step. Weak or unowned items remain open questions, not commitments.

- Sarah Kim — customer-thread continuity and account evidence hygiene: preserve customer statements, observed usage, support-derived facts, procurement context, provenance, and recency.
- Devon — commercial and procurement framing and decision context.
- Nadia Singh — pattern capture, scripts, and customer-success/customer-growth use cases; distinguish evidence from inference.
- Jake — product implementation and sequencing; keep any test lightweight and owner-group-only unless separately approved.
- Leo Park — data/platform seams and source-recency handling; reuse existing signals and event paths rather than building a separate scoring service or platform layer.

Required intake fields
- Account/source and collection date.
- Specific enterprise-readiness need or question.
- Direct evidence, exact quote, or artifact.
- Business impact.
- Dimension: product, security, legal, procurement, or implementation.
- Requested decision/follow-up.
- Accountable owner and supporting owner(s).
- Priority/timing and disposition.

Closeout status
- Routing model: established and named.
- Broad enterprise-readiness motion: not established.
- Unowned or weakly evidenced requests: not roadmap, GTM, or staffing commitments.

5. June 4 readout questions

- Did the limited internal follow-up improvement persist across more than the current small sample?
- Is any observed action attributable to a Compass prompt rather than ordinary account work?
- Which sources meet the minimum provenance, recency, account-boundary, and direct-observation standard?
- Is there a concrete enterprise-readiness artifact and accountable owner, or only an open question?
- What is the smallest next test that distinguishes cleaner internal follow-up from attributable account/customer behavior change?

6. Disposition frame — decision intentionally pending

The June 4 read should decide whether any narrowly scoped Compass work remains worth keeping as internal prompt-evidence work and what, if anything, should be cut. This packet does not make that final decision in advance.

Candidate keep criteria for discussion
- Owner-group-only prompt experiments with a clear trigger and bounded purpose.
- Evidence tied to date, source, account/sample, observed action, and caveat.
- Limited internal learning about preparation, follow-up questions, or routing.
- Source-quality work that preserves provenance, recency, source type, and fact-versus-inference separation.
- Enterprise-readiness items with a concrete artifact, accountable owner, and next step.
- A small next test designed to distinguish internal follow-up improvement from attributable account/customer behavior change.

Candidate cut criteria for discussion
- Customer-facing Compass launch or customer-facing proof.
- Dashboard rebuild, broader customer analytics surface, reporting layer, data platform, or separate scoring service.
- GTM proof, repeatable customer-growth claims, or expansion demand inferred from prompt legibility or script use.
- Hiring-trigger language, new requisitions, or staffing conclusions from Compass prompt usage or Evergreen alone.
- Series C or investor narrative.
- Claims without dated source, sample/account boundary, provenance, or account-level support.
- Duplicate, stale, incomplete, or unattributed account evidence.
- Broad signal inventories that do not change the June 4 decision.
- Unowned enterprise-readiness requests and speculative roadmap commitments.

Decision record
- Final cut/keep decision: PENDING at packet creation.
- Decision owner/group: June 4 narrow evidence read.
- Required standard: preserve open questions where evidence is incomplete; do not expand the read into launch, dashboard, GTM, hiring, or Series C work.

- Account/sample: Evergreen annual-account current-state context; Acme live-only review of Acme’s own signals. Sample is small.
- Caveats: these are internal owner actions, not customer behavior. Evergreen cannot be generalized. Acme evidence cannot be used outside Acme’s own live-only review. The prompt does not establish that “renewal risk” is churn, product weakness, or customer demand; admin handoff, role confusion, procurement/security packaging, activation drag, and product gaps remain distinct possibilities.
- Owner: Anna for definitions/caveats; Sarah for account-thread evidence; Nadia for pattern capture; Jake/Leo as needed for implementation and seams.

Signal B — post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- Prompt/trigger: expansion-timing follow-up after the first live sync.
- Observed evidence: the prompt was legible to internal account owners; on 2025-05-06, Nadia added one script question about expansion timing after first live sync.
- Source/date: 2025-04-25 “Compass review wrapped”; 2025-05-06 “First-May Compass observation notes.”
- Account/sample: internal owner-group use; no customer action recorded.
- Caveats: script usability and one added question do not establish expansion intent, committed demand, customer behavior change, or a repeatable growth motion. Keep readiness basis and observed usage attached to any future example.
- Owner: Nadia for customer-success/customer-growth use cases and pattern capture; Jake for product sequencing; Leo for data/platform seams as needed.

Signal C — account-note/source-quality prompt
- Prompt/trigger: require evidence source, date, provenance, recency, and fact-versus-inference separation before follow-up.
- Observed evidence: 2025-05-06 notes exposed a missing audit-lookup timestamp in the Evergreen appendix; 2025-05-11 says source quality is strongest in Sarah’s Evergreen thread and uneven elsewhere; 2025-04-25 says Leo’s source-recency handling is acceptable for continued owner-group use but not for broader exposure claims.
- Source/date: 2025-04-25 “Compass review wrapped”; 2025-05-06 “First-May Compass observation notes”; 2025-05-11 “Prepare Monday board-cycle evidence review.”
- Caveats: source hygiene supports bounded internal use; it is not evidence of Compass impact or portfolio-wide repeatability. Keep “not enough evidence” available where provenance, recency, or attribution is incomplete.
- Owner: Sarah for account-thread and note hygiene; Leo for source-recency/data seams; Anna for definitions and caveats.

3. ACCOUNT-SOURCE QUALITY

Current read
- Sarah’s Evergreen thread is the strongest source-quality example, but it is bounded to Evergreen’s annual-account current state. It is not proof of repeatability beyond Evergreen, customer-growth proof, or staffing justification.
- Acme remains live-only and limited to Acme’s own signals. No Evergreen-derived materials should be used for Acme, and Acme should not be generalized to other accounts.
- Portfolio-wide quality remains uneven. The 2025-05-06 missing audit-lookup timestamp is a concrete completeness gap; the 2025-05-11 review explicitly calls out uneven quality outside Sarah’s Evergreen thread.
- Source-recency handling is acceptable for continued owner-group use, per the 2025-04-25 review, but does not support broader exposure claims.

Quality assessment
- Evergreen current-state thread: high within its stated boundary; qualify for annual-account context only.
- Acme live-only own-signal review: bounded/usable for Acme’s review when the live evidence is explicit; not portable.
- Other account sources: medium-to-low / uneven until provenance, recency, source type, and attribution are checked consistently.
- Overall: sufficient for narrow internal review with caveats; insufficient for broad customer, GTM, repeatability, or staffing claims.

Evidence to rely on
- Dated source records with named account, source type, provenance, and direct observation separated from inference.
- Sarah’s Evergreen current-state evidence within its annual-account boundary.
- Acme’s own live-only signals, without cross-account generalization.

Evidence to qualify or exclude
- Undated, stale, duplicated, or unattributed notes.
- Any account-level claim that lacks a source, sample/account boundary, or direct excerpt.
- Evergreen extrapolated into a portfolio or growth claim.
- Acme evidence used outside Acme’s live-only scope.
- The separate Acme API v2 export-timeout issue as evidence that a Compass prompt worked; it is operational evidence, not Compass behavior-change evidence.

4. OWNER-ROUTED INTAKE

Routing conclusion
Enterprise-readiness intake remains owner-routed rather than an undifferentiated customer-growth sink. Route only specific, evidenced needs with a named accountable owner and next step. Weak or unowned items remain open questions, not commitments.

- Sarah Kim — customer-thread continuity and account evidence hygiene. Preserve customer statements, observed usage, support-derived facts, procurement context, provenance, and recency.
- Devon — commercial/procurement framing and decision context.
- Nadia Singh — pattern capture, scripts, and customer-success/customer-growth use cases; distinguish evidence from inference.
- Jake — product implementation and sequencing; keep the test lightweight and owner-group-only unless separately approved.
- Leo Park — data/platform seams and source-recency handling; reuse existing signals and event paths rather than building a separate scoring service or platform layer.

Required intake fields
- Account/source and collection date.
- Specific enterprise-readiness need or question.
- Direct evidence, exact quote, or artifact.
- Business impact.
- Dimension: product, security, legal, procurement, or implementation.
- Requested decision/follow-up.
- Accountable owner and supporting owner(s).
- Priority/timing and disposition.

Status by closeout
- Routing model: established and named.
- Evidence of a broad enterprise-readiness motion: not established.
- Unowned or weakly evidenced requests: do not convert into roadmap, GTM, or staffing commitments.

5. CUT / KEEP RECOMMENDATION

KEEP
- The two narrow owner-group prompt experiments: renewal-risk/admin-friction follow-up and post-first-live-sync expansion follow-up.
- Prompt-level evidence that is tied to a date, source, account/sample, observed action, and caveat.
- Limited internal evidence that prompts improve owner preparation, follow-up questions, or routing.
- Source-quality work that preserves provenance, recency, source type, and fact-versus-inference separation.
- Enterprise-readiness items with a concrete artifact, accountable owner, and next step.
- A small next test designed to distinguish cleaner internal follow-up from attributable account/customer behavior change.

CUT
- Evidence outside the May board-cycle boundary unless explicitly labeled context.
- Customer-facing Compass launch or customer-facing proof.
- Dashboard rebuild, broader customer analytics surface, reporting layer, data platform, or separate scoring service.
- GTM proof, repeatable customer-growth claims, or expansion demand inferred from prompt legibility or script use.
- Hiring-trigger language, new requisitions, or staffing conclusions from Compass prompt usage or Evergreen alone.
- Series C or investor narrative.
- Claims without dated source, sample/account boundary, provenance, or account-level support.
- Duplicate, stale, incomplete, or unattributed account evidence.
- Broad signal inventories that do not change the June 4 decision.
- Unowned enterprise-readiness requests and speculative roadmap commitments.

June 4 decision output
1. State plainly that limited internal follow-up changed, while verified customer behavior and repeatable growth motion did not.
2. Show only the strongest dated prompt examples, with source-quality caveats.
3. List owner-routed intake items only when the evidence and owner are explicit.
4. Record keep/cut decisions above.
5. Preserve open questions where evidence is incomplete; do not expand the read into launch, dashboard, GTM, hiring, or Series C work.

The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities. That matters because those were real gaps for a set of larger customers, and now they are real capabilities we can point to without stretching the story.

Second, on platform and customer trust: Atlas support and release handling are on a steadier path. Customer-facing Atlas issues now route through the support rotation, Leo takes the first technical read, and Jake continues to own product priority and sequencing. That split is not glamorous, but it is important. It means customer issues are getting a cleaner technical read, product tradeoffs are staying with the right owner, and we are not pretending a process gap is solved by everyone swarming it.

Third, on the market side: our enterprise push is producing better conversations, but I want to be careful about what that does and does not mean. It means larger accounts are taking Scaffold more seriously when they look at setup, admin expectations, and reliability questions. It does not mean we suddenly have a broad enterprise machine, and it does not mean every larger-customer request should bend roadmap gravity.

That distinction matters a lot right now. The board discussion last month was constructive precisely because the facts are more real now, not because we told a bigger story. The line remains the same: more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.

Cutoff: June 18, 2024

Hiring pace after the Series B

- The February 22 Series B did not lead to broad hiring acceleration. The operating posture remains evidence-led, with hiring tied to retention, enterprise expansion, and Mercury launch-readiness evidence rather than to the financing itself.
- One planned leadership hire was completed: Nadia Singh joined as Head of Customer Growth on April 15.
- Nadia’s initial mandate is to build a repeatable customer-growth motion around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and cross-functional handoffs. Her role is not a generic sales or bespoke enterprise-roadmap function.

Monday Mercury readout

Headline

The Sunday cut continues to show an activation and admin-setup pattern, but the taxonomy should remain a working classification rather than a confirmed causal model.

Readout

1. Activation friction

The strongest current signal is around activation and setup completion.

- activation_start: 83% in both Looker and Mixpanel after the corrected definition.
- sync_enabled_week1: 38% in both systems and holding.
- retained_activity_week2: 32% in Looker versus 26% in Mixpanel. The gap is still present, but the weakness is concentrated in workspaces with unresolved admin setup:
  - unresolved admin setup: 18% / 12%
  - setup resolved by day 7: 44% / 39%

Working interpretation: unresolved admin setup is associated with weaker week-two retained activity. This supports keeping the row in the activation-friction bucket, but does not by itself establish that setup friction is the sole cause.

2. Admin handoff / role confusion

The first-action and invite rows continue to point toward an admin-side transition or coordination issue.

- admin_first_action: 62% / 61%, matched within rounding.
- invite_sent_week1: 49% / 49%, stable.

Working interpretation: the two rows are consistent with an admin handoff or role-confusion pattern. The metrics do not distinguish between those explanations, so the bucket should be presented as a useful pattern label, not a confirmed diagnosis.

3. Expansion stalls after first live sync

There is no active stall signal in the current repeat-admin-action row.

- repeat_admin_action_week3: 18% in both systems.

Working interpretation: this row is clean this week and does not support calling expansion-after-sync a current problem. It remains a bucket for monitoring, not a conclusion from this cut.

- It is a weekly directional internal cut, not the quarterly cohort or board layer.
- It does not provide enough account-level evidence for procurement or security-packaging conclusions.
- It does not establish a true product gap.
- Bucket labels do not change account, commercial, or product ownership.

“After the definition correction, the activation and admin rows are directionally stable across Looker and Mixpanel. The clearest current pattern is lower week-two retained activity among workspaces with unresolved admin setup, while workspaces that resolve setup by day seven do not show the same drop. We are therefore using ‘activation friction’ as the current working bucket, not as a confirmed causal diagnosis. Admin handoff / role confusion remains a plausible pattern based on first action and invite activity, and the repeat-admin-action row does not show an active post-sync expansion stall this week. Procurement, security packaging, and true product-gap conclusions require account-level evidence.”

tests.request: Post a blocking review on scaffold/mercury#3198. The failed-sync screen exposes raw connector errors and each retry click enqueues another job. Explain the required corrections.

input.body:
Blocking review

The failed-sync flow has two correctness and security issues that must be fixed before merge:

1. Raw connector errors are exposed in the UI. Do not render connector/provider exception text directly. Return a safe, stable user-facing error (with actionable next steps), and keep the raw error only in protected server-side logs/telemetry. Ensure logs are redacted for credentials, tokens, request headers, customer data, and other connector payload details; include a correlation/sync ID so support can trace the failure.

2. Each retry click enqueues another job. Make retry idempotent and enforce one active retry per sync: disable or gate the control while a request is in flight, but also enforce deduplication server-side (idempotency key/unique constraint plus an atomic status transition) so repeated or concurrent requests cannot create duplicate jobs. Return the existing job/result for a duplicate retry, and make the UI reflect the actual queued/running/completed state rather than allowing another enqueue.

Please add regression coverage for raw-error redaction and for rapid double-click/concurrent retry requests, verifying that only one job is created and that the user sees the safe error.

checks.observed:
Blocking review

The failed-sync flow has two correctness and security issues that must be fixed before merge:

1. Raw connector errors are exposed in the UI. Do not render connector/provider exception text directly. Return a safe, stable user-facing error (with actionable next steps), and keep the raw error only in protected server-side logs/telemetry. Ensure logs are redacted for credentials, tokens, request headers, customer data, and other connector payload details; include a correlation/sync ID so support can trace the failure.

2. Each retry click enqueues another job. Make retry idempotent and enforce one active retry per sync: disable or gate the control while a request is in flight, but also enforce deduplication server-side (idempotency key/unique constraint plus an atomic status transition) so repeated or concurrent requests cannot create duplicate jobs. Return the existing job/result for a duplicate retry, and make the UI reflect the actual queued/running/completed state rather than allowing another enqueue.

Please add regression coverage for raw-error redaction and for rapid double-click/concurrent retry requests, verifying that only one job is created and that the user sees the safe error.

parameters.title: Decision record — selective October investor reopen (Devon conversation)
parameters.body:
Date: September 28, 2023
Source: Devon conversation voice memo, September 28, 2023, 17:36 PT

Decision
We are reopening a selective investor path in October. This is not a September restart and not the beginning of a broad process.

Sequence and scope
- Elena Volkov is first, as warm context and because she previously provided useful retention feedback.
- The Elena conversation is for calibration on the real Mercury story, not to signal that we are broadly raising.
- Keep the investor list short and continue narrowing it. Devon owns continued trimming of the short list.
- No broader outreach until the package is ready.
- Random investor coffees and opportunistic September calendar fill stay out. Anyone not clearly on the short list waits until the package is ready or does not happen.

Package framing
The package should use:
- September Mercury metrics, framed as helpful progress from the design-partner wave: improved activation and reduced admin friction, cleaner pricing, and real enterprise pull.
- Evergreen as evidence of real enterprise demand and procurement seriousness.
- Hybrid pricing to make the commercial story legible.

Required caveats
- Expansion remains uneven. The September Mercury package is usable only with the bounded internal framing: helpful progress, not proof that retention or expansion is solved.
- Evergreen is not proof that enterprise readiness is complete. Preserve the gaps around SSO, audit history for admin changes, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and the packet's need to stand better on its own.
- Do not imply enterprise add-ons or make bespoke roadmap promises from the hybrid-pricing presentation.

Gate before outreach beyond Elena
Run one more clean pass on the package so the story is clear without hand-waving on expansion or enterprise gaps.

Language and board notes
- Approved language: “selective October reopen” and “October prep.”
- Avoid: “process is on.”
- “We have proof points” is too loose unless the same sentence preserves the caveats.
- Board-note language must describe preparation, not a launched process.

Durable outcome
Selective October reopen, not a rushed September restart or broad process; Elena is first as warm context; the short list keeps narrowing; the package uses September Mercury metrics, Evergreen’s enterprise-readiness signal, and hybrid pricing while preserving the uneven-expansion caveat; random investor coffees stay out until the package is ready.

messages.content:
[2023-09-27T19:31:00-07:00] Devon’s rough pass for tomorrow is here.

From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Wed, 27 Sep 2023 19:12:00 -0700
Subject: Thursday prep — rough October investor path

Morgan —

Rough pass before tomorrow so we can decide whether to put real walls around this instead of letting random September inbound set the agenda.

What I think is supportable now

- We finally have a real Mercury story grounded in external use, not just planned-launch narrative.
- The September package is usable if we keep the framing disciplined: activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave; Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context; the corrected weekly cuts are helpful operating read, not proof.
- Evergreen is useful evidence in two ways: (1) there is real enterprise pull serious enough to get procurement/commercial attention, and (2) the enterprise-readiness gaps are now concrete rather than abstract.
- Hybrid pricing gives us a cleaner commercial frame. Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands is much easier to explain than the earlier seat-ish ambiguity.

What I do not think we can blur

- We cannot tell a “retention is solved” story. It still is not.
- We cannot present expansion as clean. Some rows are moving; some are still uneven.
- We cannot use Evergreen’s procurement motion as proof that enterprise readiness is already there. Their feedback is basically the current gap list: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, clearer admin vs billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without one of us live-explaining it.
- We cannot let the pricing decision imply enterprise add-ons are in-market beyond what is actually shipped.

How I would frame the investor path

I think there is a version of reopening that is disciplined and a version that turns into cosplay. The disciplined version is: selective, October, and explicitly based on whether the investor can underwrite the real Mercury story. Not “market is hot again, let’s spray meetings.”

Elena feels like the right first conversation in that frame. She already engaged seriously once and her pass was thoughtful, not generic. If we go back to her, the point is calibration and context: does the more honest Mercury picture change the read at all? That is very different from treating Elena as the start of a broad process.

Short-list criteria

Only keep firms that can handle all of the following without pushing us into story inflation:
1. uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention
2. enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped
3. a usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young
4. a deliberately narrow process instead of a manufactured auction

Rough list

1) Elena Volkov — warm-context bucket
- Best use: first calibration conversation
- Why: prior feedback was substantive; she'd pressure-test the actual story
- Caveat: only useful if we stay honest about what still is not proven

2) Firm A — possible fit if we keep the narrative operational
- Tends to understand infra/devtools motion
- Biggest risk is they will immediately push on expansion consistency

3) Firm B — possible fit if the commercial story is crisp
- Could appreciate the cleaner pricing frame
- Risk is enterprise checklist bias if the packet still requires too much live explanation

4) Firm C — maybe
- Thoughtful and patient
- Might be more useful as signal than as an actual lead if we are keeping the list tight

September inbound / coffee noise

I have three stray September asks that I think should probably stay out:
- two mutual-intro coffee requests that feel more social than decision-relevant
- one “in town next week” inbound that looks like calendar tax
Given where we are, I think saying yes to these just makes the whole thing feel broader than it is.

Questions for tomorrow
- Are we comfortable calling this a selective October reopen internally, or do we want even tighter language?
- Is Elena definitely first, or do we want one more p…

Decision-prep read

Bottom line

There is enough for a disciplined, selective October calibration process—but not enough for a broad fundraising reopen or a “traction is now proven” narrative.

The honest frame is:

“Mercury has moved from planned-launch narrative to externally observed usage and a clearer commercial model. Activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave, and enterprise demand is real. Retention and expansion are not yet fully proven, and enterprise readiness still has specific gaps we are actively closing.”

I would use “selective October calibration” internally rather than “reopen” unless the team wants to signal a more active process. The operating behavior should remain the same: one conversation first, a very small list only if that conversation and the package support it.

What can support the story

1. External use, not just roadmap
   - Mercury now has a credible external-use basis.
   - The design-partner wave provides evidence that activation and admin friction improved.
   - This is a meaningful change from a planned-launch story, but it should not be inflated into proof of durable product-market fit.

2. September data as operating evidence
   - Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context.
   - The corrected weekly cuts are useful for understanding operating movement.
   - Neither should be presented as definitive proof of retention or expansion.

3. Evergreen as both demand and diagnostic evidence
   - Evergreen demonstrates that enterprise interest is serious enough to reach procurement and commercial review.
   - More importantly, its feedback turns enterprise-readiness concerns into a concrete, bounded gap list.
   - That supports a story of real pull plus known execution work—not a claim that enterprise readiness is complete.

4. Cleaner commercial framing
   - Hybrid pricing, with Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands, is easier to explain than the earlier seat-like ambiguity.
   - The model is clearer, but still young.
   - The pricing decision must not imply that enterprise add-ons are already shipped or broadly in-market.

Gaps we cannot blur

- Retention is not solved. Do not use “retention is improving” as shorthand for “retention is durable” or “retention is solved.”
- Expansion is uneven. Some rows are moving, but the overall picture is not clean enough to present as a consistent expansion engine.
- Evergreen procurement interest is not enterprise readiness. The current gap list remains:
  - SSO timing
  - audit history for admin changes
  - clearer separation between admin and billing-owner roles
  - a procurement packet that does not require live explanation from the team
- The commercial model is clearer, not mature. Do not present usage-based pricing as a validated enterprise monetization system.
- Enterprise add-ons should be described only according to what is actually shipped.
- The selective process itself matters. A broad set of meetings would create pressure to turn partial evidence into a larger story.

Short-list criteria

Keep a firm only if it can engage constructively with all four of these:

1. Uneven expansion and not-yet-solved retention
   - They should be able to underwrite progress without demanding that the data be cleaner than it is.

2. Scoped enterprise-readiness gaps
   - They should distinguish “important work remains” from “there is no enterprise opportunity.”
   - They should not require premature promises on SSO, audit controls, admin permissions, or procurement timing.

3. A usage-based commercial model that is clearer but still early
   - They should understand MAU-based platform bands without forcing the company into a more mature pricing narrative than the evidence supports.

4. A narrow, deliberate process
   - They should be comfortable with calibration before process-building.
   - Avoid firms or partners whose default response is to manufacture urgency, auction dynamics, or story inflation.

messages.content:
[2023-10-03T08:18:00-07:00] Devon’s first cut for Elena is here:

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Subject: first cut / Elena Mercury calibration
Date: Tue, Oct 3, 2023 7:42 AM PT

First cut below. This is meant as a calibration note, not a process-launch deck.

Main places I'd like your pass:
- whether the pricing section is too detailed for a first pre-read
- how directly to say expansion is uneven without making the whole thing feel like a shrug
- whether we say Evergreen by name in the pre-read or keep that for the conversation

---
Mercury / October calibration draft for Elena Volkov

Why this note
We are considering a selective October reopen, starting with a short list and using this as a calibration conversation rather than a broad process update. The goal is to test whether the Mercury story is now honest and credible enough to reopen narrowly.

What has changed since February
- Product signal is less theoretical. The design-partner wave produced real evidence on setup, activation, and admin friction.
- The activation/admin story is better than it was earlier in the year because the team corrected the biggest early setup and handoff failures.
- Pricing is now structured instead of bespoke.
- Evergreen put us through a real regulated-buyer procurement/security process, which surfaced enterprise-readiness gaps with much more specificity than we had before.

September Mercury package — usable summary

Board-facing context
- The quarterly cohort view is directionally better in the recent design-partner wave than in the earliest Mercury cohorts.
- That improvement is useful context, but it is not proof that retention or expansion is solved.

Operating read
- Activation improved after the onboarding/admin fixes in the design-partner wave.
- Admin friction came down in the latest wave.
- Expansion remains uneven: some accounts deepen after setup, others stall after initial usage.
- The package is best used as evidence that the team improved the early path and clarified the failure points, not as proof of a finished growth engine.

How to talk about Evergreen
What Evergreen gives us
- a real buyer process in a regulated environment
- concrete evidence on where Mercury still needs deeper enterprise-readiness work
- a better read on packaging gaps around security/admin expectations and procurement handling

What Evergreen does not give us
- proof that enterprise readiness is solved
- proof that the motion is repeatable across multiple accounts
- proof that procurement converts cleanly into expansion

Pricing frame

Pilot
- $2,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 50 monthly active developers

Growth
- $7,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 200 monthly active developers

Overage
- $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Enterprise add-ons
- SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls are separate add-ons only after those features ship
- we should be explicit that those are not being pre-sold as current capability

Caveats to keep explicit
- Expansion is still uneven.
- Evergreen is a strong signal, but still a single signal.
- Enterprise-readiness gaps are clearer than before; they are not closed.
- This would be a narrow October reopen, not a broad fundraising process.
- I do not think we should put random investor coffees on the calendar off this package.

Questions to test with Elena
1. Is this package materially more credible than the February version?
2. What would make the Evergreen signal feel repeatable rather than anecdotal?
3. Is the current pricing frame disciplined enough, or does it still read as early?
4. How much more explanation do we need on uneven expansion before widening beyond a short list?

Rough email shell
Elena —
We took another pass at the Mercury package and wanted to use a short conversation for calibration, not to launch a broad process. The current story is stronger on three dimensions: the design-partner wave improved activa…

[2023-08-01T09:06:00-07:00] Jake’s first-wave shape is finally concrete enough to review with Devon.

Discord group DM — Jake, Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
2023-08-01 08:47 PT

Jake:
Pulled together a first-pass view on the external Mercury design-partner wave.

My proposal is to use Evergreen Bank as the enterprise-shaped candidate in the first wave.

Why Evergreen:
- They are likely to stress the exact admin/security edges we still care about: admin handoff, role/state clarity, auditability questions, and how trustworthy the early sync/failure path feels.
- That gives us a real test of the standard Mercury path without immediately turning the rollout into bespoke build work.
- Put differently: hard enough to expose whether the product is enterprise-ready on the current path, but still within the boundaries of the product we are actually trying to ship.

I’m keeping the rest of the wave deliberately lighter; the enterprise question is whether Evergreen should be the anchor stress case.

On Acme, I would keep them in the not-now column.
- The NDA scope thread is still muddy enough that sending fresh Mercury material feels like asking for a document fight instead of product signal.
- I do still think their prior feedback is useful internally, especially on admin pain, failure-state legibility, and procurement/security questions.
- I would use that feedback to sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279, but not send Acme new packet/screens/notes unless the NDA thread gets narrowed first.

MER-1279 rows this would pressure-test most directly:
- invited-member/admin handoff confidence
- queued-sync trust / retry confidence
- failed-state legibility and recovery
- admin/security questions that show up before anyone asks for one-off treatment

Not calling any of those closed. This is just the cleanest first-wave shape I can see right now.

If you both agree with the direction, I can turn it into a tighter wave outline before the review.

Give me decision questions for that Devon review, not an announcement. I want them to pressure-test three things: why Evergreen Bank is a good enterprise stress case for admin/security without dragging us into bespoke work, what exactly keeps Acme out while the NDA scope thread is unresolved, and which parts of Acme’s prior feedback can still sharpen internal blocker rows in MER-1279 without sending Acme anything fresh.

Devon review — decision questions

1. Evergreen as the enterprise stress case
- What specific admin/security behaviors do we need the first wave to expose?
- Does Evergreen exercise those behaviors through the standard Mercury path, or are we already assuming custom workflow, permissions, integrations, or support?
- What would count as useful enterprise signal from Evergreen without turning their participation into a bespoke implementation?
- Which risks are we intentionally testing now, and which enterprise requirements are explicitly out of scope for this wave?
- What evidence would make us conclude that Evergreen is the wrong anchor—or that the standard path is not ready for this stress case?

2. Why Acme stays out for now
- What exactly remains unresolved in the NDA scope thread?
- Which categories of Mercury material are still unsafe or ambiguous to send under the current scope?
- Is the blocker the legal permission to share, the risk of starting a document-negotiation loop, or both?
- What narrow resolution would be sufficient to reconsider Acme, and who owns getting us there?
- Until that resolution exists, are we aligned that Acme receives no fresh packets, screens, notes, or other Mercury materials?

3. Using Acme’s prior feedback internally
- Which parts of Acme’s existing feedback are clearly usable without sharing anything new: admin pain, failure-state legibility, procurement/security questions, or specific examples?
- How should those points sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279 without being treated as fresh customer validation?
- Which rows should be updated first: invited-member/admin handoff, queued-sync and retry trust, failed-state recovery, or admin/security clarity?
- What evidence would distinguish a real launch-readiness blocker from a useful design concern or future enterprise requirement?
- Who will convert the usable feedback into explicit blocker criteria, and what would we need to see before calling any row materially improved?

4. Decision at the end of the review
- Do we agree to make Evergreen the first-wave enterprise-shaped stress case on the standard Mercury path?
- Do we agree to keep Acme out until the NDA scope is narrowed?
- Do we agree on the specific Acme feedback that can inform MER-1279 internally, with no new external sharing?

Working thesis

Find an enterprise-growth operator who can turn Mercury/Evergreen-like customer pull into a repeatable motion: identify the right use cases, build internal champions, navigate procurement, and expand adoption without turning Scaffold into a bespoke-services shop.

This is not a classic VP Sales search. It is also not a mandate to sell whatever a large account requests.

1. Profile to look for

Possible profile labels:

- Enterprise Growth Lead
- Strategic Expansion Lead
- Product-Led Enterprise Growth
- Enterprise Partnerships and Expansion
- Customer Development Lead

The title is secondary. The core profile is someone who has repeatedly translated strong product demand into durable enterprise adoption, with enough product judgment to protect the standard product boundary.

2. Primary mandate

- Make enterprise pull repeatable rather than founder-dependent.
- Convert successful initial deployments into broader, durable usage.
- Develop a disciplined land-and-expand motion around clear product value.
- Help the company understand which enterprise signals are genuinely repeatable.
- Improve the path from activation to procurement to expansion.
- Feed recurring customer patterns back into product, packaging, onboarding, and pricing.
- Establish qualification criteria for when an enterprise opportunity is strategically attractive.

3. What “Mercury / Evergreen-like” should mean

Search for evidence that the person can:

- Recognize a strong use case before it is fully obvious in the pipeline.
- Find and develop an internal champion.
- Map the economic buyer, technical stakeholders, users, security, and procurement.
- Navigate enterprise process without losing the original product-led value.
- Turn one successful team or workflow into broader organizational adoption.
- Separate a repeatable requirement from a one-off accommodation.
- Document the motion so another team member can reproduce it.
- Measure expansion through real usage and adoption, not just signed logos or contract value.

4. Explicit non-goals

The role should not be framed as:

- A traditional VP Sales role with a broad bookings mandate.
- A quota-first organization-building exercise.
- A license to pursue every large logo.
- A custom implementation or solutions-engineering business.
- A source of bespoke product commitments.
- A replacement for product-market-fit work.
- An executive hired mainly to add process, forecasting, or layers of management.

5. Experience signals

Strong candidates may have:

- Built an enterprise motion from an existing product with demonstrated pull.
- Led strategic expansion after an initial successful deployment.
- Worked across product, engineering, customer success, and procurement.
- Sold technically complex products without overselling roadmap commitments.
- Created repeatable qualification, champion, and expansion playbooks.
- Managed a small number of high-value accounts deeply rather than relying on volume.
- Operated effectively in an early-stage or ambiguous environment.
- Personally closed or expanded important accounts, rather than only managing a sales team.

6. Capabilities to test

Commercial judgment

- Can distinguish “important customer” from “good customer.”
- Knows when to walk away from an attractive but structurally bad deal.
- Understands price, scope, implementation burden, and expansion economics.

Product judgment

- Can translate customer requests into underlying needs.
- Can identify which requests belong in the core product.
- Will protect standardization when a bespoke build would create long-term drag.

Enterprise navigation

- Can build a multi-threaded account strategy.
- Understands procurement, security, legal, budgeting, and executive sponsorship.
- Can maintain momentum through a long buying process without manufacturing urgency.

- Turns individual wins into documented patterns.
- Defines leading indicators for activation, ad…

arguments.body:
INTERNAL LEADERSHIP RECAP
February 26 leadership reset

Operating line
More room, same discipline. We will build a defensible story, not a bigger story.

Mercury operating ownership
• Jake owns Mercury execution and the weekly launch-evidence path. MER-1279 remains the internal operating ledger for launch-relevant evidence, with links back to source evidence rather than summary theater.
• Leo Park owns platform seams, release discipline, and cases where sync trust or system behavior crosses from cleanup into architecture or system-risk work.
• Priya owns activation and onboarding UX, admin/setup clarity, and failure-state legibility. Settled design decisions remain settled unless new evidence changes the conclusion.
• Anna Martinez owns retention evidence, cohort-definition discipline, and the board-consistent outside-reader package.
• Morgan Chen owns board follow-through, sequencing, dates and promises, not-yet lines, and the hiring sequence.

Enterprise-readiness lane
The next-phase scope remains bounded to:
• SSO timing
• Admin-change audit history
• Clearer separation between the admin and billing owner
• A standalone procurement packet

Devon Hayes and Sarah Kim own current-state commercial and procurement packaging, using shipped or current product facts only. Jake and Leo provide current product facts and seam-risk input; they must not backdoor roadmap promises into customer material.

No Evergreen-specific commitments, feature dates, or enterprise add-on quoting before the relevant work ships. Evergreen Bank remains a useful stress case for the current path, not a reason to turn wave-one learning into bespoke-build behavior.

The enterprise-readiness review remains a separate lane from current Mercury release work. Sarah keeps the customer-coordination lane; owners now take back their operating lanes.

Board and investor follow-through
The first post-close board framing will focus on defensible retention evidence and repeatable enterprise expansion learned through Mercury and Evergreen—not a rush to spin a Series C story. MER-1279 and Leo Park’s risk readout are internal operating evidence, not board or investor proof claims.

Anna Martinez and Morgan Chen will keep the board pack tight: retention truth, expansion truth, and bounded enterprise-readiness next steps.

Hiring decision
The second Mercury engineering requisition is not reopened.

The first new search to scope is a customer-growth / GTM leader—not an immediate Mercury engineering search. The role is intended to build a repeatable customer-growth motion from Mercury- and Evergreen-like pull without turning accounts into bespoke commitments or product-roadmap negotiating sessions.

Devon Hayes and HR will draft the initial role description. Morgan reviews it before it goes beyond the small reset group.

If Mercury engineering hiring is reconsidered later, the existing evidence rule applies:
• Senior hire for repeated platform or architecture seam failures requiring independent ownership
• Implementation-heavy mid-level hire for hardening or throughput constraints
• No requisition if the current split can close the remaining work

Near-term cadence
• Keep the short weekly Mercury truth check focused on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and material product change.
• Keep enterprise-readiness review as a separate lane from Mercury release work.
• Close-thread handoff is complete: Sarah retains customer coordination, while operating owners resume their respective lanes.

Core decisions to carry forward
Mercury ownership is explicit. Enterprise-readiness scope is bounded. No one should use the close as permission to describe Mercury as enterprise-ready now or to reopen every deferred initiative.

input.body:
Hi team,

A reminder of the principle agreed in the February 2024 leadership reset: “more room, same discipline” — or, in the longer form, “defensible story, not a bigger story.” The raise gave us more operating room; it did not make Mercury a solved enterprise story, create permission for side-quest expansion, or authorize reopening every deferred initiative.

Can you confirm whether there was a subsequent decision that the raise authorized reopening every deferred Mercury enterprise item? My understanding remains that the enterprise-readiness scope was intentionally bounded to the agreed sequence—SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet—with no automatic dates, Evergreen-specific commitments, or enterprise add-on quoting before the relevant work shipped.

Thanks,
Morgan

Based on the excerpts you summarized, the clean position is: accept a documentation and account-follow-up cadence, but reject any language that converts future admin work or usage economics into renewal entitlements.

Counter-redline guidance

Suggested replacement:

“During the Term, the parties may schedule a quarterly review of the administrative capabilities currently available in the Services and ordinary account follow-up items. The review is limited to current-state functionality and does not create or imply any commitment regarding future functionality, roadmap items, scope, packaging, pricing, service levels, or delivery dates.”

“Accepted in principle, subject to clarifying that the review covers shipped, current-state capabilities and ordinary account follow-up only. It is not a roadmap, delivery, packaging, or pricing commitment.”

2. Granular role editor or equivalent admin capability: reject

Suggested comment:

“Not accepted. A granular role editor or equivalent advanced-admin capability is not part of the renewal baseline and cannot be committed through this agreement. Please remove this reference.”

Do not soften this to “planned,” “targeted,” “expected,” or “under consideration.” Those formulations could still be read as a commitment.

3. Delivery dates, milestones, or packages: reject

Delete any reference to:

- A delivery date or target date
- A development milestone
- A named package or included tier
- “During the Term” language tied to future functionality
- “At no additional charge” language for future admin capability

“Not accepted. The annual agreement should not establish a delivery date, feature package, milestone, or inclusion obligation for future functionality. Any future capability remains subject to product prioritization and would require separate written agreement if it were ever to be offered on different terms.”

4. Overage cap or waiver: reject

“Usage will continue to be measured and billed under the standard monthly-active-developer accounting and existing overage treatment applicable to the subscription.”

Suggested comment:

“Not accepted. The renewal does not change the standard monthly-active-developer measurement or existing overage treatment. Please remove the proposed cap, waiver, or other limitation on overage charges.”

Do not describe standard overage treatment as a new product, department package, pricing change, or commercial exception. The point is continuity with the existing Growth terms.

Suggested language:

“Research, exploration, prototypes, beta functionality, and other future administrative capabilities are not included in the Services or the annual subscription baseline unless separately agreed in writing.”

Suggested comment:

“Please clarify that advanced-admin research and future functionality are outside the annual baseline and are not subject to the quarterly current-state review commitment.”

Assessment

“Non-binding roadmap appendix” is not safe enough. “Non-binding” may not prevent the appendix from later being used as:

- “Granular sync-operator controls”
- “Future sync-operator functionality”
- “Planned admin enhancements”
- “Under consideration”
- “Future phase”

“Administrative capabilities currently available to Evergreen as of [Effective Date] are listed below for reference only. “This appendix is not a product roadmap and does not describe planned, promised, targeted, or committed future functionality. No future feature, enhancement, permission model, role, operator control, or sync capability is included in or implied by this appendix.”

“For clarity, the availability or future delivery of any additional administrative or sync-operator functionality is not a condition of this renewal.”

“Evergreen has separately raised requests regarding additional administrative controls. Those requests are not part of this renewal schedule, are not included in the current service description, and do not create a commitment to deliver future functionality.”

I would prefer deleting even this acknowledgment from the customer-facing schedule and keeping it in internal procurement notes.

arguments.title: Compass April 25 Review — Prep
arguments.body:
Compass April 25 Review — Prep

Review date: April 25, 2025
Scope: Owner-group use only
Prepared for: Compass review

1. Review objective

Determine whether Compass is producing a useful, evidence-bounded improvement in account-team follow-up, without treating cleaner internal follow-up as customer behavior change or broader product proof.

The review should answer:
- Are account teams taking different actions because of Compass, or are they only documenting/following up more cleanly?
- What evidence supports continued owner-group use?
- Which claims remain unsupported and must stay out of customer-facing, board, and hiring narratives?

2. Current position and evidence gate

Current position: There is still no observed customer behavior change. Keep the evidence gate narrow.

The April 25 gate is limited to:
- Continued use in the owner-group surface.
- Prompt-level implementation for both prompts.
- Evidence that account-team behavior changed, if any, distinguished from cleaner internal follow-up.
- Source quality, recency, definitions, dates, and caveats for each reviewed signal.

The gate does not evaluate or authorize:
- Customer-facing proof or customer-facing guidance.
- Broader exposure claims.
- A dashboard rebuild or a reporting layer.
- Board-dashboard framing.
- Hiring implications before the May board-cycle gate.

3. Review sections

A. What shipped / what is in scope

Owner: Jake
Evidence owner: Jake, with Leo for source-recency context

Confirm that both prompts remain prompt-level implementation in the owner-group surface. No dashboard rebuild is in scope. Record the exact owner-group surface and prompt versions used for the review.

Decision question:
- Is the current prompt-level implementation sufficient for continued owner-group use?

B. Signal definitions and evidence bundle

Owner: Anna
Evidence owner: Anna

For every signal discussed, bring:
- Definition.
- Evidence source.
- Evidence date or date range.
- What is directly observed versus inferred.
- Caveats and known gaps.
- Provenance and recency status.
- The explicit state “not enough evidence” where the record does not support a conclusion.

Decision question:
- Can each conclusion be traced to a dated source with its limitations visible?

C. Source recency and exposure boundary

Owner: Leo
Evidence owner: Leo

Confirm that source-recency handling is acceptable for continued owner-group use. Treat source recency as a quality condition for internal use, not as evidence for broader exposure claims.

Decision question:
- Does recency support the narrow internal-use decision, without being overstated as proof of wider applicability?

D. Account and evidence boundaries

Owner: Sarah
Evidence owner: Sarah

Evergreen:
- Keep evidence limited to the annual-account current state.
- Do not generalize Evergreen evidence beyond that current-state context.

Acme:
- Keep the review live-only.
- Review only Acme’s own signals.
- Do not use Acme signals as evidence for other accounts or customer-facing claims.

Decision question:
- Does each account remain within its defined evidence boundary?

E. Behavior-change test

Owner: Nadia
Evidence owner: Nadia, with account-team participants supplying examples

Use the scripts as preparation material, not as proof by themselves. The review must distinguish:
- A changed account-team action or decision attributable to the signal/prompt; from
- More consistent, cleaner, or faster internal follow-up with no demonstrated behavior change.

For each claimed behavior change, capture:
- Account/team and date.
- Prior behavior or baseline, if known.
- New action observed.
- Signal or prompt involved.
- Evidence source and direct excerpt/reference.
- Alternative explanation.
- Confidence and caveat.

Decision question:
- Is there evidence of changed account-team behavior, or only improved internal follow-up hygiene?

4. Evidence-owner checklist

Jake:
- Confirm both prompts and the owner-group surface.
- Confirm no dashboard rebuild is required or implied.

Leo:
- Document source-recency handling and its limits.
- State explicitly that recency does not support broader exposure claims.

Anna:
- Supply definitions, evidence sources, dates, and caveats.
- Separate fact from inference and mark unsupported conclusions as “not enough evidence.”

Sarah:
- Enforce Evergreen’s annual-account current-state boundary.
- Enforce Acme’s live-only, own-signals boundary.

Nadia:
- Bring scripts and behavior-change examples.
- Test changed account-team behavior versus cleaner internal follow-up.

Morgan:
- Hold the evidence gate narrow.
- Keep customer-facing proof, board-dashboard framing, and hiring implications out of the review’s approved claims.

5. Decision boundaries

May continue after the review if supported:
- Owner-group use of both prompts at prompt level.
- Internal preparation and follow-up using the documented evidence and caveats.
- Source-recency handling for the owner-group context.

Must remain out of scope / unapproved:
- Customer-facing proof, guidance, or claims.
- Any claim that Compass caused customer behavior change.
- Broader exposure or generalization beyond the defined account evidence.
- Board-dashboard framing.
- Hiring implications before the May board-cycle gate.
- Dashboard rebuild, reporting layer, data platform, or separate scoring service for account-note quality.

6. Proposed review decisions to record

1. Continue, narrow, or pause owner-group use of the two prompt-level implementations.
2. For each signal, record: owner, recipient, action, evidence bundle, caveat, and source-quality requirement.
3. Record whether account-team behavior changed; if not demonstrated, record “not enough evidence” and describe any internal follow-up improvement separately.
4. Confirm Evergreen and Acme evidence boundaries were respected.
5. List claims explicitly rejected for this review: customer-facing proof, broader exposure, board-dashboard framing, and hiring implications before the May board-cycle gate.
6. Identify the smallest next test needed to distinguish behavior change from cleaner internal follow-up.

7. Review output

The review should end with a short decision log containing:
- Decision and owner.
- Evidence relied on, with dates and sources.
- Caveat or unresolved gap.
- Allowed audience: owner-group/internal only unless separately approved.
- Smallest next test.

Default conclusion if no new evidence is presented: continue only the narrow owner-group use that is supported, make no customer-facing or broader claims, and carry the behavior-change question forward as unresolved.

bookend_end.content:
Created the Compass April 25 review prep document with:

- Review objective and narrow evidence gate
- Sections for implementation, definitions, source recency, account boundaries, and behavior change
- Named evidence owners: Jake, Leo, Anna, Sarah, Nadia, and Morgan
- Evergreen and Acme evidence boundaries
- Explicit decision boundaries around customer-facing proof, broader exposure, dashboards, board framing, and hiring
- Proposed decisions and review-output format

messages.content:
Product-copy edits to make

1. Audit surface
- Keep: “View audit events”
- Remove: “Export audit log”
- Add supporting copy such as: “Review audit events recorded for this workspace.”
- Do not mention CSV, downloads, reports, or compliance artifacts unless that functionality actually exists.
- If users are likely to ask about CSV, state plainly in support documentation: “Audit events are currently view-only; CSV/download is not available.”

2. SSO surface
- Replace “SSO required” with wording that describes configuration, for example:
  - “Configure SSO for this workspace”
  - “Workspace SSO settings”
  - “SSO is managed by workspace admins”
- Make clear that this is workspace-level configuration, not bank-wide policy enforcement.

3. Admin role surface
- Keep the “Admin” role label.
- Make the relevant powers visible beside it, for example:
  - “Can resend invitations”
  - “Can remove members”
- Use explicit action labels such as “Resend invitation” and “Remove member” rather than relying on the role name to communicate authority.

Support-safe explanations

- “View audit events” opens the current audit view. It should not be described as exporting a log or producing a downloadable report.
- CSV or downloadable audit reports are not available unless the product explicitly provides that function.
- The SSO wording refers to settings for the individual workspace. It does not mean SSO is already required or enforced across the bank.
- “Admin” identifies the role, while the visible permissions explain what that role can do in the current surface.
- The resend and remove actions are the relevant visible powers here; avoid implying broader administrative or compliance authority than the interface actually provides.
- Avoid describing the surface as “compliance-ready.” Describe only the available view, settings, and actions.

Procurement phrases not to endorse

- “Export audit log”
- “Downloadable audit report”
- “CSV export” or “CSV available,” unless implemented and verified
- “Compliance-ready”
- “SSO required”
- “SSO enforced”
- “Bank-wide SSO policy”
- “Admin has full control”
- Any statement that treats the “Admin” label alone as proof of authority or implies permissions beyond the visible resend/remove actions

messages.content:
Subject: Re: Mercury admin wording follow-up

Hi Sarah,

Thanks for pulling these through. Here is customer-safe wording that keeps the current product copy, the supporting explanation, and the procurement interpretation distinct:

Current product copy

- Activity surface: “View activity history”
- SSO surface: “Configured by workspace admin”

Support explanation

“View activity history” refers to the present-state activity view available in the product. It is not intended to suggest that a CSV export, downloadable audit log, or separate report artifact is available behind the label.

“Configured by workspace admin” describes the workspace-level configuration state for SSO. It indicates that the setting is managed by a workspace administrator; it does not state that SSO is already enforced as a bank-wide policy.

Procurement-sensitive distinction

We are intentionally avoiding language that could be read as either:

- a contractual or reporting commitment, such as “Export audit log”; or
- a statement that bank-wide SSO enforcement is already in effect, such as “SSO required.”

This keeps the labels aligned with the current product surfaces without implying capabilities or policy enforcement beyond what the product currently represents.

Best,
Morgan Chen · Scaffold

HR follow-up:

Thanks for the questions from today’s all-hands. Here’s the written follow-up on the product questions:

Q4 hardening does not mean all planned feature work slips again. It means we are raising the ship bar and prioritizing the issues that could affect reliability, correctness, data handling, permissions, or safe onboarding. Those release-blocking issues are in the first pass; lower-severity edge cases, polish, and non-blocking feature work will follow in the longer tail.

For Mercury, the current promise is bounded design-partner testing—not full enterprise readiness. SSO, admin-change audit history, and role separation are follow-up enterprise controls, not requirements of the current bounded-testing promise. Design partners can participate because the testing is scoped, opt-in, monitored, and limited to preview/sample data; real-source connections are not included at this stage.

We’ll continue using the collected-question format for future all-hands questions. We will post written answers where appropriate rather than reopening live Q&A. Fundraising-related questions will remain parked and are not part of this follow-up.

[2023-06-13T14:04:00-07:00] Review is done. Notes below.

June 13 Mercury activation / onboarding review — Morgan notes

Attendees: Morgan Chen, Priya, Marcus, Jake

- Priya walked the activation and onboarding frames in Figma and kept anchoring on the file as the source of truth for flow decisions.
- Marcus said the problem is that ready in Figma has been reading as safe to ship even when release-risk items are still open.
- Concrete examples raised in room:
  - stuck credential / retry handling on first source connection
  - org-invite dead-end risk on the current auth branch
  - admin fallback / visibility concerns before the deeper admin path exists
- Priya’s point: those issues can require follow-up work or even a design change, but they should not be litigated as open-ended design vetoes in comment threads after the core flow decision has already been made.
- Marcus’s point: if implementation risk has nowhere explicit to live, it spills into Figma comments or Discord because that is where people are already looking.
- Both acknowledged they have been half-routing around each other in Discord instead of resolving in one place.
- Decision made in room:
  - design calls for Mercury activation / onboarding stay with Priya
  - canonical place for those decisions is Figma
  - release-readiness and dogfood gating stay with Marcus
  - canonical place for those concerns is the implementation checklist and release review, not Figma comment threads
  - if a checklist item requires a design change, link back to the exact Figma frame and reopen only that decision
  - stop adjudicating this in Discord side threads
- Not magically fixed:
  - Priya still feels implementation concerns keep arriving as late redesign
  - Marcus still feels risk gets labeled implementation detail too early
  - tone improved once the split was explicit, but still tense
- Cleanup from this meeting:
  - Priya keeps design decision notes in Figma
  - Marcus sends a cleaned implementation checklist with owners and blockers for the dogfood build
  - any Discord thread on this topic should point back to either the frame or the checklist instead of becoming a third system

Save this as the explicit decision path and post a short note to the Mercury team: design calls stay with Priya in Figma; release-readiness concerns stay with Marcus and the implementation checklist. Don’t make it sound like the interpersonal friction is magically solved.
