[2023-11-02T10:18:00-07:00] The October Mercury package draft is ready for a consolidated pass; Anna, Jake, Leo, and Devon have all added their sections.

October Mercury operating package - consolidated draft v0.7
Owner: Devon Hayes
Compiled: 2023-11-02 09:42 PT
Contributors: Anna Martinez, Jake, Leo Park, Devon Hayes
Status: working draft for owner pass

Audience note
- This draft is combining the board-operating view with a possible trimmed short-list diligence version.
- I left more in than we will likely send so we can decide what stays internal versus what can travel.
- Month cut is Oct 31, 2023. For any 7-day activation view, only cohorts with a full 7-day window by Nov 2 are treated as complete.

[Comment - Devon, 11/2 09:44] Please mark sections as: (a) okay for short-list diligence with caveats, (b) internal only, or (c) rewrite.

1) Draft selective-diligence narrative

Mercury is no longer telling a May story on activation. On completed windows, accounts reaching a real source connection or first live sync within 7 days are materially above the corrected May baseline, and the admin handoff into actual usage is less brittle than it was in the first external wave.

Evergreen's second admin group is the cleanest bounded enterprise-pattern example we have so far: the current preview path of org invite, magic-link access, preview/sample data, real-source connection, and first live sync is usable without exception handling. The open requests are now more clearly enterprise-readiness follow-up asks than "can the preview be used at all" asks.

Draft line for discussion: Mercury retention has turned the corner and expansion is starting to look repeatable.
[Comment - Anna, 11/2 08:54] I would split this. "Turned the corner" needs cohort-maturity language, and "repeatable" is too strong on expansion.
[Comment - Devon, 11/2 09:01] Fine with softer wording if the package still lands as stronger-than-May rather than "still early / nothing to see."

Cleaner version candidate:
- Activation is holding materially above May on the corrected definition.
- Mature cohorts show better early retention than the spring baseline, but we should keep the windowing explicit.
- Admin friction is improving inside the current bounded Mercury flow.
- Expansion exists but remains uneven across accounts and is not yet a smooth story.

Metric definition reminder
Activated account = account where real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed occurs within 7 days of workspace creation.
Excluded from activation = sample_import_completed by itself.

[Comment - Anna, 11/2 09:10] Yes on completed-window monthly rows only. No on mixing in late-Oct incomplete rows.

arguments.message:
Mercury October package — consolidated owner pass

Overall: keep the stronger-than-May story, but separate what is shareable from what is operating evidence. Suggested status labels below.

(a) Okay for short-list diligence, with caveats
• Table A: keep the corrected definition directly underneath: activated = real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed within 7 days; sample_import_completed alone and invite_sent alone do not count. Include completed windows only; exclude Oct 25–31 from the external trend.
• Table C: keep as mature-cohort evidence only. Say mature cohorts are tracking better than May, with the windowing and small/noisy base explicit. Do not characterize October retention as proven or solved.
• One aggregate live-sync line can travel: 21/37 completed-window workspaces reached first_live_sync_completed within 7 days in the Oct 1–24 cut. Do not use the 24/46 observed real_source_connected row as an external proof metric because it includes incomplete windows; keep the 18-minute median and support/stall counts out unless we define the denominator and purpose more clearly.
• Evergreen: use the second-admin pass only as a bounded enterprise-pattern example for the current flow (org invite → magic link → preview/sample data → real-source connection → first live sync). It demonstrates reduced admin friction in that path; it does not demonstrate enterprise completeness or generalize beyond the group.

(b) Internal only
• October weekly cuts (Table B): useful for operating decisions, not an external packet or appendix.
• Sample-preview-only stop diagnostic: retain for internal diagnosis, not as a shareable proof row.
• Small-n Evergreen directional box (2/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2): internal only; do not present as outside proof.
• MER-1279 and the ticket-by-ticket launch-readiness rows: internal operating evidence only, not external proof.
• Expansion Table D: keep internal for now or summarize only as uneven/incomplete signal; do not use it to imply a repeatable expansion motion while Sep/Oct windows are open.

(c) Rewrite
• Replace “retention has turned the corner,” “solved the activation and retention issues,” and “expansion is starting to look repeatable.” Also remove any wording that makes SSO, audit/change history, or admin-vs-billing-owner separation sound closed.
• Recommended center of gravity: “Mercury’s activation is materially stronger than the corrected May baseline, and mature cohorts are tracking better on early retention. The Evergreen second-admin pass is a bounded example that the current preview-to-live flow is becoming less brittle, while expansion remains uneven and enterprise-readiness follow-through is still being tightened.”
• Keep the enterprise-gaps page adjacent to the progress pages. Frame it as explicit scope and follow-up—not a defensive memo and not a near-term product promise.

Evergreen wording: retain the qualitative operating read (same-day invite acceptance, no resend, one remaining ownership question, and clearer live-sync status still needed). Label it illustrative and bounded; omit the small-n scorecard.

Final packet shape: narrative + Table A + Table C + bounded Evergreen example + separate enterprise-readiness gaps page. No weekly cuts, diagnostics, small-n scorecard, or non-external Linear rows.
Verification: the consolidated Mercury owner-pass notes were posted to #eng-team for Anna, Jake, Leo, and Devon (message id discord_1788579141281).

bookend_end.content:
Consolidated owner pass completed and sent to #eng-team for Anna, Jake, Leo, and Devon.

Key decisions:
- Preserve the corrected real-source/live-sync activation story as materially stronger than May.
- Keep Table A and mature-cohort Table C, with explicit completed-window and cohort-maturity caveats.
- Use Evergreen’s second-admin group only as bounded evidence of reduced friction in the current preview-to-live flow.
- Remove “solved,” “turned the corner,” and “repeatable expansion” language.
- Treat expansion as uneven and enterprise-readiness work as ongoing.
- Mark weekly cuts, sample-preview diagnostics, the small-n Evergreen scorecard, and Linear/launch-readiness rows as internal-only.
- Retain the enterprise-gaps page as explicit scope and follow-up, not as a defensive memo or product promise.

- Evidence test: show paid conversion, renewal, or expansion in more than one additional account, with similar time-to-value, implementation steps, and owner behavior and without bespoke roadmap work. Mercury / Atlas owner split
- Decision: keep the ownership boundary explicit rather than treating the work as one undifferentiated product motion.
- Mercury caveat: core funnel metrics reconcile across Looker and Mixpanel after the event-name fix, but week-two activity is the substantive watchout. For workspaces with unresolved admin setup, retained activity in week two was 18% in Looker versus 12% in Mixpanel; workspaces resolved by day seven were 44% versus 39%. Week-three repeat-admin activity remains unresolved pending workspace-filter validation.
- Atlas boundary: Rishi owns Scaffold's API, auth, and connectors side; keep Rishi off customer email threads unless Atlas comes up.
- Owner: Jake owns Mercury sequencing; Rishi owns the Atlas API/auth/connectors side.

Compass

- Owner: Compass owner group; owner split for April work still needs to be finalized.

- Renewal: show renewal or expansion evidence across more than one account; separate account-specific proof from repeatable motion.
- Reliable execution: show that the same implementation and owner-follow-up motion works without bespoke roadmap work, and make the Mercury/Atlas boundary observable in the operating evidence.
- Decision rule: do not promote exploratory evidence to a board conclusion until the definition, comparison boundary, owner, and behavior caveats are closed.
- Next checkpoint: Q3 operating review / next board evidence pass; date not set in the block.

Open risks / parking lot
- Launch-blocking versus deferrable work was not collapsed into one list in the block; keep that distinction visible in follow-up.

messages.content:
[2023-07-25T13:07:00-07:00] Sarah's design-partner questions are the right input for Thursday, but I don't want them dressed up as fundraising collateral.

From: Sarah Kim <sarah@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Cc: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>, Jake <jake@atlas-test.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Jul 2023 08:41:00 -0700
Subject: Mercury design-partner readiness questions

Sending the recurring launch-readiness questions I'm hearing in prospective design-partner conversations. I'm deliberately not naming anyone here because the conversations are still exploratory, but the themes are pretty consistent and seem useful before the Thursday checkpoint.

1) Source setup failure cases
- If the first source connection fails, what does the user actually see?
- Can they tell the difference between auth/permissions trouble, source unavailable/timeout, and an unknown failure without us translating it for them?
- Does recovery look self-serve, or does it feel like they would need vendor/API knowledge to continue?

2) Admin handoff
- If an admin starts setup and then invites an operator or teammate, does the invited person land in a sane next step?
- What happens if the invited member arrives before the first source is fully connected?
- Is the line between "waiting on admin/first source" and "something is broken" obvious?

3) Time to first sync
- How long from first connection to first live sync in the normal case?
- If the sync is queued or retried, what reassures the user that the system is working without inventing fake progress?

4) Which failure states are actually understandable
- Which states are legible on first read to an external user?
- Which ones still make sense only if someone from our side narrates what happened?

5) What evidence creates enough confidence to try Mercury
- a clean first-run path end to end
- one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails
- proof that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle
- clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state
- a credible sense of time-to-first-sync, even if it's a range rather than a promise

My read is that this is product-readiness input, not deck material. It's basically the bar people are using to decide whether they would be comfortable trying Mercury with a real but bounded workflow.

Create a one-page internal checklist for the Mercury headcount checkpoint: what external launch-readiness feedback we need before deciding any second Mercury engineering req. Keep it as product-readiness input only, not board, investor, or B-round material.

arguments.title: Mercury headcount checkpoint — external launch-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
MERCURY HEADCOUNT CHECKPOINT
External launch-readiness evidence required before deciding on a second Mercury engineering requisition
Internal product-readiness input only — not board, investor, or B-round material

Decision standard
Do not treat design-partner interest or recurring questions as evidence by itself. Before deciding on a second Mercury engineering req, review concrete evidence from bounded, real-user or realistic external design-partner workflows and identify the product gaps that still block a credible first run.

Checklist: evidence we need

[ ] 1. First source connection failure is understandable
    • Capture what an external user sees when the first source connection fails.
    • Distinguish auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown failure without internal narration.
    • Show a self-serve recovery path, or name the precise product gap if recovery still requires vendor/API knowledge.
    Evidence to bring: screenshots or recording of each state, observed user interpretation, recovery outcome.

[ ] 2. Admin-to-operator handoff is sane
    • Test an admin starting setup, then inviting an operator or teammate.
    • Verify the invitee lands on a clear next step, including arrival before the first source is fully connected.
    • Make “waiting on admin/first source” clearly different from “something is broken.”
    Evidence to bring: end-to-end invite path, timing, failure/edge-case notes, and unresolved handoff defects.

[ ] 3. Time to first sync is credible
    • Measure first connection → first live sync in the normal case across more than one bounded workflow where possible.
    • Exercise queued and retried syncs.
    • Confirm the UI reassures users that work is progressing without inventing fake progress or implying a guarantee.
    Evidence to bring: observed range, sample size/workflows, queue/retry behavior, and user comprehension.

[ ] 4. Failure states are legible on first read
    • Ask external participants to interpret setup, waiting, timeout, retry, and unknown-failure states without coaching.
    • Separate states they understand unaided from those that still require someone on our side to narrate.
    Evidence to bring: verbatim interpretations, misread states, severity, and proposed product changes.

[ ] 5. Confidence to try Mercury with a real but bounded workflow
    • Validate a clean first-run path end to end.
    • Show one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails.
    • Demonstrate that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle.
    • Clearly separate sample/preview data from real activated state.
    • Provide a credible time-to-first-sync range, not a promise.
    Evidence to bring: design-partner notes, observed workflow boundaries, activation/preview screenshots, and explicit blockers.

Headcount decision prompts

• Which gaps are launch blockers versus polish, and what user evidence supports that distinction?
• What additional engineering capacity would remove a specific blocker, rather than merely accelerate general roadmap work?
• If a second req is approved, what measurable product-readiness outcome must it own, by when, and how will we verify it with external users?
• If the evidence is insufficient, what smallest next design-partner test closes the uncertainty before we make the req decision?

Required checkpoint packet

[ ] One compact evidence table: workflow, participant/context, observed behavior, user interpretation, severity, owner, next gate.
[ ] Links to recordings/screenshots and the current build/version used.
[ ] Explicit list of states requiring internal narration.
[ ] Observed time-to-first-sync range with caveats and no roadmap or launch promise.
[ ] Clear recommendation: approve, defer pending evidence, or do not add the second req.

Out of scope

Fundraising narrative, board/investor collateral, B-round positioning, market-sizing, pricing, roadmap promises, and generalized hiring justification. Keep this checkpoint anchored to external product-readiness evidence only.

[2023-07-26T10:21:00-07:00] Devon's pre-checkpoint note is useful, but I want the meeting aimed at a rule rather than a vibe.

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Date: Wed, Jul 26, 2023 8:14 AM
Subject: Thursday Mercury headcount checkpoint

Morgan —

Ahead of Thursday's checkpoint, here's the frame I want us using so we don't spend the whole slot rehashing the month.

1) Candidate pipeline is stale.
Anything that looked interesting in June has either cooled off, drifted out of Mercury scope, or is not close enough to matter for an immediate decision. If we reopen now, we should be honest that we're effectively starting a fresh search, not pulling the trigger on a near-close candidate.

2) Jake still wants another senior engineer.
I get why. The argument is depth, less key-person risk, and another person who can independently carry ugly launch-critical issues if Leo turns up more real seams in auth/session/platform edges.

3) The new information is that Leo is finding actual seams, not writing a platform thesis.
That is a point in favor of letting the current shape settle. His readout was useful because it surfaced real Mercury risk, and the new ledger is already making that work more concrete.

4) Waiting also has a cost.
If we wait until late August and then decide we do need help, we will have burned time and the market does not get easier just because we were hesitant.

The thing I do not want Thursday to become is another "let's revisit in a few weeks" conversation with no trigger. We have done enough calendar-based decision making on this.

What I want out of the checkpoint is a rule:
- what evidence would mean "open the req now,"
- what evidence would mean "current team shape is enough through launch," and
- if we do reopen, what profile are we actually opening for.

Sarah Kim's design-partner questions are useful input here. The ones that feel most decision-relevant to me are:
- can an external admin get through setup without us narrating it,
- do invited-member/admin handoff states make sense,
- are failure states understandable and recoverable,
- does time-to-first-sync feel trustworthy enough to a real user.

If those are still muddy, I think that argues for using external readiness feedback before deciding profile. And if we do reopen, I don't think the answer should default to "another senior engineer because that was the old plan." The real options are at least:
- another senior engineer,
- a stronger mid-level implementer for launch cleanup / follow-through,
- or no immediate hire.

Not trying to decide it over email; just want the meeting pointed at the actual choice.

— Devon

Turn this into focused checkpoint questions for me. Do not decide the req in the prep. I want the questions to force the evidence triggers: what would justify opening now, what would show the current team is enough through launch, and if we do reopen, whether the profile is senior, mid-level implementer, or no immediate hire.

Mercury headcount checkpoint — focused question stack

1. Establish the evidence
- What has changed since the last checkpoint that is relevant to the hiring decision?
- Which findings from Leo’s risk readout are confirmed, and which are still hypotheses?
- What does the launch-readiness ledger show about work that is genuinely launch-critical versus work that can wait?
- Are we evaluating a staffing constraint, a product-readiness constraint, or both?

2. Test the “open the req now” trigger
- What specific evidence would justify opening a requisition now rather than waiting?
- Is there launch-critical work that the current team cannot cover without creating unacceptable schedule, reliability, or key-person risk?
- Which risks remain after assigning the current team’s available capacity?
- What evidence would show that an additional person would materially reduce those risks soon enough to matter?
- Would the role address an observed bottleneck, or are we reopening because the old hiring plan still exists?
- What would count as a sufficient threshold: a particular number of uncovered critical workstreams, a sustained capacity gap, or a specific launch-risk condition?

3. Test the “current team is enough through launch” trigger
- What evidence would allow us to say the current team is sufficient through launch?
- Can the current team cover the remaining launch-critical work with explicit owners and credible timing?
- Are Leo’s identified auth, session, or platform seams understood well enough to manage without another senior engineer?
- Which risks can be handled through sequencing, scope control, or temporary focus rather than hiring?
- What would make the current-team conclusion falsifiable?
- What leading signal would cause us to reopen the decision before launch rather than waiting for a calendar date?

4. Use external readiness as evidence
- Can an external admin complete setup without someone from Scaffold narrating the path?
- Do invited-member and admin handoff states make sense on first read?
- Are failure states understandable and recoverable to an external user?
- Can we point to one or two believable setup or sync recovery examples?
- Does the first-run path feel clean and bounded enough for a real design partner to try?
- Can we provide a credible time-to-first-sync range rather than an unconditional promise?
- Are sample or preview data clearly separated from the real activated state?
- Which of these answers would change the staffing conclusion, and which are product work regardless of headcount?

5. If we reopen, determine the profile from evidence
- What unmet need are we hiring for: architectural ownership, independent handling of launch-critical ambiguity, or execution capacity?
- What work specifically requires senior-level judgment and ownership?
- What work is well-defined enough for a strong mid-level implementer to take through launch?
- If the problem is follow-through and cleanup rather than system design, why would a senior hire be necessary?
- If the problem is risk discovery across auth/session/platform seams, what evidence shows that another senior engineer—not better sequencing or current-team focus—is the right response?
- What responsibilities would the new hire own in the first 30–60 days?
- What evidence would rule out the senior profile?
- What evidence would rule out the mid-level implementer profile?
- Under what conditions is “no immediate hire” the correct profile decision?

6. Close with an explicit rule
- What is the exact “open now” trigger?
- What is the exact “current team is enough through launch” trigger?
- What is the trigger for revisiting the decision, independent of a calendar date?
- If we reopen, which evidence determines senior versus mid-level implementer?
- Who owns collecting each missing piece of evidence, and by when?
- What decision will we record at the end of the checkpoint, and what evidence would change it?

Mercury engineering headcount checkpoint
Date: Thu, Jul 27, 2023
Attendees: Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes, Jake

Purpose
Decide whether to reopen the second Mercury engineering req now, and if not, what decision rule replaces the old month-end revisit habit.

Current context
- Leo's first release-risk readout was useful and has now been turned into a single Mercury launch-readiness ledger in Linear.
- Candidate pipeline is stale; there is no near-close candidate that would justify pretending this is an immediate hire / no-hire switch.
- External launch-readiness questions are getting sharper: source setup failure cases, admin handoff, time-to-first-sync, and whether failure states are legible without internal help.

Jake's case for reopening now
- Still wants more senior depth.
- Concern is not abstract headcount; it is too much launch-critical ambiguity resting on a small set of people.
- If Leo keeps finding cross-service seams, auth/invite edges, and release-discipline gaps, Jake does not want Marcus + Leo + himself absorbing everything while Priya is still holding activation UX decisions.
- Senior profile is still his default because he thinks the remaining risk is more about independent judgment through ugly edge cases than raw ticket throughput.

Devon's view
- Agrees the risk is real, but the pipeline does not support a reflex reopen.
- Reopening now means starting a fresh search from zero, not converting an active pipeline.
- Wants a decision rule tied to product-readiness evidence, not another calendar reminder.

Morgan's view
- July's actual signal is that Leo is finding the right seams.
- The new ledger gives the team one place to track launch readiness instead of burying risk in PRs, Figma comments, or Discord threads.
- The missing input is external launch-readiness feedback: can real users navigate setup, invited-member/admin handoff, failure recovery, and first-sync confidence without hand-holding.
- Do not force the old two-senior shape just because that used to be the plan.
- Keep this as launch-readiness operating logic, not an investor story.

Agreed owner split (unchanged)
- Marcus owns implementation gates and dogfood blockers.
- Priya owns design decisions / Figma source of truth.
- Leo owns cross-service platform-seam risk notes.
- Jake uses the ledger in the Mercury weekly.

Decision
- Do not reopen the second Mercury engineering req now.
- Do not set another arbitrary month-end revisit date.
- Revisit only after external launch-readiness feedback from design-partner conversations and trials is in hand.

Decision rule for the next req
1. Open a senior-engineer req if external feedback shows repeated platform / architecture-seam failures that need independent senior ownership to unblock launch confidence.
2. Open a more implementation-heavy mid-level req if the core user path is understandable but the limiting factor is cleanup throughput, follow-through, and launch hardening.
3. Open no immediate req if external users can get through setup, admin handoff, early sync, and failure recovery with manageable issues that the current owner split can close from the ledger.

Specific evidence required before reopening the question
- source setup failure cases seen by external users
- admin / invited-member handoff clarity
- time-to-first-sync comfort / trust
- which failure states are understandable vs confusing
- whether the remaining blockers look like depth problems or execution-throughput problems

Follow-up note
- Pipeline can stay cold until the external feedback points clearly to a profile.
- This replaces the old "revisit after July" placeholder with an evidence trigger.

arguments.title: September Mercury metrics package — board and H2 prep bounds
arguments.body:
September Mercury metrics package — board and H2 prep bounds

Prepared for: Morgan, Devon, and Anna
Source package: Anna Martinez’s first September Mercury package
Data cutoff: Sep 4, 2023 EOD PT
Status: Internal prep document

Purpose and boundary

Preserve the useful operating implications of the September Mercury package without turning it into outside proof. This document keeps two distinct reporting layers:

1. Board-operating alignment / selective H2 prep
2. Internal weekly diagnostics for operating decisions only

Board-operating layer: supported uses

The board-operating layer supports board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep context because:

- September design-partner activation is materially cleaner than the repaired May baseline under the current, sturdier 7-day activation definition.
- Activation here means an account hit either real_source_connected or first_live_sync_completed within 7 days of workspace creation; sample-preview-only accounts are excluded from the denominator.
- The repaired May comparable design-partner cut was 4 of 10 accounts activated within 7 days (40%).
- The current design-partner cohort, covering workspaces created Jul 31–Aug 27, was 8 of 11 (73%).
- Admin friction is down for the design-partner cohort: median time from workspace creation to first invited member accepted fell from 5.4 days to 2.3 days; accounts needing manual admin intervention fell from 6/10 to 2/11; and accounts reaching a first non-owner user within 7 days rose from 3/10 to 7/11.
- Evergreen Bank adds meaningful enterprise substance: 4 admin users touched setup/settings, 12 invited members were recorded, 3 real sources were connected, and successful live-sync activity occurred on 8 distinct days through Sep 4. This is repeated real-source/live-sync behavior after setup, not just a one-day preview spike.

The safe operating statement is: activation and admin handoff are materially cleaner than the repaired May operating read, and Evergreen contributes meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence. This supports board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep context.

Required caveats

- Expansion is still uneven account to account. The 30-day read shows 3 accounts meaningfully up, 3 mostly flat, and 2 choppy or down. Evergreen is the best positive signal, but the set does not support a solved expansion story.
- The weekly activation movement is internal-only. Do not use the weekly cuts in board notes, board charts, investor materials, or external/customer communications. They remain useful for operating decisions, debugging admin/setup friction, and reviewing sample-preview exclusions.
- This package does not prove retention.
- This package does not solve expansion.
- This package does not make the Mercury story external-ready.
- Evergreen is one account, not blanket enterprise validation.

Internal weekly diagnostics layer — internal only

Keep this layer separate from board/H2 framing. At the Sep 4 cutoff:

- Jul 31 week: 2 of 3 eligible accounts activated within 7 days (67%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 7 week: 2 of 3 (67%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 14 week: 2 of 3 (67%); no sample-preview-only exclusions.
- Aug 21 week: 2 of 2 (100%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 28 week: full 7-day window incomplete; pending.

These samples are small and sensitive to account mix. Use them for internal diagnosis and operating decisions only, never as external proof or as board-facing chart material.

Suggested one-sentence framing

The September package is materially better than the May operating read on cleaner real-source/live-sync activation and admin handoff, with Evergreen adding meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence; expansion remains uneven, the weekly activation movement is internal-only, and the package does not prove retention, solve expansion, or make the story external-ready.

Decision boundary

Use the board-operating layer for board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep. Keep the weekly diagnostics layer internal-only. Do not convert either layer into external claims without a later, separately reviewed evidence package.

[2023-07-25T13:07:00-07:00] Sarah's design-partner questions are the right input for Thursday, but I don't want them dressed up as fundraising collateral.

From: Sarah Kim <sarah@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Cc: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>, Jake <jake@atlas-test.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Jul 2023 08:41:00 -0700
Subject: Mercury design-partner readiness questions

Sending the recurring launch-readiness questions I'm hearing in prospective design-partner conversations. I'm deliberately not naming anyone here because the conversations are still exploratory, but the themes are pretty consistent and seem useful before the Thursday checkpoint.

1) Source setup failure cases
- If the first source connection fails, what does the user actually see?
- Can they tell the difference between auth/permissions trouble, source unavailable/timeout, and an unknown failure without us translating it for them?
- Does recovery look self-serve, or does it feel like they would need vendor/API knowledge to continue?

2) Admin handoff
- If an admin starts setup and then invites an operator or teammate, does the invited person land in a sane next step?
- What happens if the invited member arrives before the first source is fully connected?
- Is the line between "waiting on admin/first source" and "something is broken" obvious?

3) Time to first sync
- How long from first connection to first live sync in the normal case?
- If the sync is queued or retried, what reassures the user that the system is working without inventing fake progress?

4) Which failure states are actually understandable
- Which states are legible on first read to an external user?
- Which ones still make sense only if someone from our side narrates what happened?

5) What evidence creates enough confidence to try Mercury
- a clean first-run path end to end
- one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails
- proof that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle
- clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state
- a credible sense of time-to-first-sync, even if it's a range rather than a promise

My read is that this is product-readiness input, not deck material. It's basically the bar people are using to decide whether they would be comfortable trying Mercury with a real but bounded workflow.

Create a one-page internal checklist for the Mercury headcount checkpoint: what external launch-readiness feedback we need before deciding any second Mercury engineering req. Keep it as product-readiness input only, not board, investor, or B-round material.

arguments.title: Mercury headcount checkpoint — external launch-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
MERCURY HEADCOUNT CHECKPOINT
External launch-readiness evidence required before deciding on a second Mercury engineering requisition
Internal product-readiness input only — not board, investor, or B-round material

Decision standard
Do not treat design-partner interest or recurring questions as evidence by itself. Before deciding on a second Mercury engineering req, review concrete evidence from bounded, real-user or realistic external design-partner workflows and identify the product gaps that still block a credible first run.

Checklist: evidence we need

[ ] 1. First source connection failure is understandable
    • Capture what an external user sees when the first source connection fails.
    • Distinguish auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown failure without internal narration.
    • Show a self-serve recovery path, or name the precise product gap if recovery still requires vendor/API knowledge.
    Evidence to bring: screenshots or recording of each state, observed user interpretation, recovery outcome.

[ ] 2. Admin-to-operator handoff is sane
    • Test an admin starting setup, then inviting an operator or teammate.
    • Verify the invitee lands on a clear next step, including arrival before the first source is fully connected.
    • Make “waiting on admin/first source” clearly different from “something is broken.”
    Evidence to bring: end-to-end invite path, timing, failure/edge-case notes, and unresolved handoff defects.

[ ] 3. Time to first sync is credible
    • Measure first connection → first live sync in the normal case across more than one bounded workflow where possible.
    • Exercise queued and retried syncs.
    • Confirm the UI reassures users that work is progressing without inventing fake progress or implying a guarantee.
    Evidence to bring: observed range, sample size/workflows, queue/retry behavior, and user comprehension.

[ ] 4. Failure states are legible on first read
    • Ask external participants to interpret setup, waiting, timeout, retry, and unknown-failure states without coaching.
    • Separate states they understand unaided from those that still require someone on our side to narrate.
    Evidence to bring: verbatim interpretations, misread states, severity, and proposed product changes.

[ ] 5. Confidence to try Mercury with a real but bounded workflow
    • Validate a clean first-run path end to end.
    • Show one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails.
    • Demonstrate that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle.
    • Clearly separate sample/preview data from real activated state.
    • Provide a credible time-to-first-sync range, not a promise.
    Evidence to bring: design-partner notes, observed workflow boundaries, activation/preview screenshots, and explicit blockers.

Headcount decision prompts

• Which gaps are launch blockers versus polish, and what user evidence supports that distinction?
• What additional engineering capacity would remove a specific blocker, rather than merely accelerate general roadmap work?
• If a second req is approved, what measurable product-readiness outcome must it own, by when, and how will we verify it with external users?
• If the evidence is insufficient, what smallest next design-partner test closes the uncertainty before we make the req decision?

Required checkpoint packet

[ ] One compact evidence table: workflow, participant/context, observed behavior, user interpretation, severity, owner, next gate.
[ ] Links to recordings/screenshots and the current build/version used.
[ ] Explicit list of states requiring internal narration.
[ ] Observed time-to-first-sync range with caveats and no roadmap or launch promise.
[ ] Clear recommendation: approve, defer pending evidence, or do not add the second req.

Out of scope

Fundraising narrative, board/investor collateral, B-round positioning, market-sizing, pricing, roadmap promises, and generalized hiring justification. Keep this checkpoint anchored to external product-readiness evidence only.

[2023-07-26T10:21:00-07:00] Devon's pre-checkpoint note is useful, but I want the meeting aimed at a rule rather than a vibe.

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Date: Wed, Jul 26, 2023 8:14 AM
Subject: Thursday Mercury headcount checkpoint

Morgan —

Ahead of Thursday's checkpoint, here's the frame I want us using so we don't spend the whole slot rehashing the month.

1) Candidate pipeline is stale.
Anything that looked interesting in June has either cooled off, drifted out of Mercury scope, or is not close enough to matter for an immediate decision. If we reopen now, we should be honest that we're effectively starting a fresh search, not pulling the trigger on a near-close candidate.

2) Jake still wants another senior engineer.
I get why. The argument is depth, less key-person risk, and another person who can independently carry ugly launch-critical issues if Leo turns up more real seams in auth/session/platform edges.

3) The new information is that Leo is finding actual seams, not writing a platform thesis.
That is a point in favor of letting the current shape settle. His readout was useful because it surfaced real Mercury risk, and the new ledger is already making that work more concrete.

4) Waiting also has a cost.
If we wait until late August and then decide we do need help, we will have burned time and the market does not get easier just because we were hesitant.

The thing I do not want Thursday to become is another "let's revisit in a few weeks" conversation with no trigger. We have done enough calendar-based decision making on this.

What I want out of the checkpoint is a rule:
- what evidence would mean "open the req now,"
- what evidence would mean "current team shape is enough through launch," and
- if we do reopen, what profile are we actually opening for.

Sarah Kim's design-partner questions are useful input here. The ones that feel most decision-relevant to me are:
- can an external admin get through setup without us narrating it,
- do invited-member/admin handoff states make sense,
- are failure states understandable and recoverable,
- does time-to-first-sync feel trustworthy enough to a real user.

If those are still muddy, I think that argues for using external readiness feedback before deciding profile. And if we do reopen, I don't think the answer should default to "another senior engineer because that was the old plan." The real options are at least:
- another senior engineer,
- a stronger mid-level implementer for launch cleanup / follow-through,
- or no immediate hire.

Not trying to decide it over email; just want the meeting pointed at the actual choice.

— Devon

Turn this into focused checkpoint questions for me. Do not decide the req in the prep. I want the questions to force the evidence triggers: what would justify opening now, what would show the current team is enough through launch, and if we do reopen, whether the profile is senior, mid-level implementer, or no immediate hire.

Mercury headcount checkpoint — focused question stack

1. Establish the evidence
- What has changed since the last checkpoint that is relevant to the hiring decision?
- Which findings from Leo’s risk readout are confirmed, and which are still hypotheses?
- What does the launch-readiness ledger show about work that is genuinely launch-critical versus work that can wait?
- Are we evaluating a staffing constraint, a product-readiness constraint, or both?

2. Test the “open the req now” trigger
- What specific evidence would justify opening a requisition now rather than waiting?
- Is there launch-critical work that the current team cannot cover without creating unacceptable schedule, reliability, or key-person risk?
- Which risks remain after assigning the current team’s available capacity?
- What evidence would show that an additional person would materially reduce those risks soon enough to matter?
- Would the role address an observed bottleneck, or are we reopening because the old hiring plan still exists?
- What would count as a sufficient threshold: a particular number of uncovered critical workstreams, a sustained capacity gap, or a specific launch-risk condition?

3. Test the “current team is enough through launch” trigger
- What evidence would allow us to say the current team is sufficient through launch?
- Can the current team cover the remaining launch-critical work with explicit owners and credible timing?
- Are Leo’s identified auth, session, or platform seams understood well enough to manage without another senior engineer?
- Which risks can be handled through sequencing, scope control, or temporary focus rather than hiring?
- What would make the current-team conclusion falsifiable?
- What leading signal would cause us to reopen the decision before launch rather than waiting for a calendar date?

4. Use external readiness as evidence
- Can an external admin complete setup without someone from Scaffold narrating the path?
- Do invited-member and admin handoff states make sense on first read?
- Are failure states understandable and recoverable to an external user?
- Can we point to one or two believable setup or sync recovery examples?
- Does the first-run path feel clean and bounded enough for a real design partner to try?
- Can we provide a credible time-to-first-sync range rather than an unconditional promise?
- Are sample or preview data clearly separated from the real activated state?
- Which of these answers would change the staffing conclusion, and which are product work regardless of headcount?

5. If we reopen, determine the profile from evidence
- What unmet need are we hiring for: architectural ownership, independent handling of launch-critical ambiguity, or execution capacity?
- What work specifically requires senior-level judgment and ownership?
- What work is well-defined enough for a strong mid-level implementer to take through launch?
- If the problem is follow-through and cleanup rather than system design, why would a senior hire be necessary?
- If the problem is risk discovery across auth/session/platform seams, what evidence shows that another senior engineer—not better sequencing or current-team focus—is the right response?
- What responsibilities would the new hire own in the first 30–60 days?
- What evidence would rule out the senior profile?
- What evidence would rule out the mid-level implementer profile?
- Under what conditions is “no immediate hire” the correct profile decision?

6. Close with an explicit rule
- What is the exact “open now” trigger?
- What is the exact “current team is enough through launch” trigger?
- What is the trigger for revisiting the decision, independent of a calendar date?
- If we reopen, which evidence determines senior versus mid-level implementer?
- Who owns collecting each missing piece of evidence, and by when?
- What decision will we record at the end of the checkpoint, and what evidence would change it?

Mercury engineering headcount checkpoint

Purpose
Decide whether to reopen the second Mercury engineering req now, and if not, what decision rule replaces the old month-end revisit habit.

Current context
- Leo's first release-risk readout was useful and has now been turned into a single Mercury launch-readiness ledger in Linear.

- External launch-readiness questions are getting sharper: source setup failure cases, admin handoff, time-to-first-sync, and whether failure states are legible without internal help.

- Still wants more senior depth.
- Concern is not abstract headcount; it is too much launch-critical ambiguity resting on a small set of people.

Devon's view
- Agrees the risk is real, but the pipeline does not support a reflex reopen.
- Reopening now means starting a fresh search from zero, not converting an active pipeline.
- Wants a decision rule tied to product-readiness evidence, not another calendar reminder.

Morgan's view
- July's actual signal is that Leo is finding the right seams.
- The new ledger gives the team one place to track launch readiness instead of burying risk in PRs, Figma comments, or Discord threads.
- The missing input is external launch-readiness feedback: can real users navigate setup, invited-member/admin handoff, failure recovery, and first-sync confidence without hand-holding.
- Do not force the old two-senior shape just because that used to be the plan.
- Keep this as launch-readiness operating logic, not an investor story.

Agreed owner split (unchanged)
- Marcus owns implementation gates and dogfood blockers.
- Priya owns design decisions / Figma source of truth.
- Leo owns cross-service platform-seam risk notes.
- Jake uses the ledger in the Mercury weekly.

Decision
- Do not reopen the second Mercury engineering req now.
- Do not set another arbitrary month-end revisit date.
- Revisit only after external launch-readiness feedback from design-partner conversations and trials is in hand.

Decision rule for the next req
1. Open a senior-engineer req if external feedback shows repeated platform / architecture-seam failures that need independent senior ownership to unblock launch confidence.
2. Open a more implementation-heavy mid-level req if the core user path is understandable but the limiting factor is cleanup throughput, follow-through, and launch hardening.
3. Open no immediate req if external users can get through setup, admin handoff, early sync, and failure recovery with manageable issues that the current owner split can close from the ledger.

Specific evidence required before reopening the question
- source setup failure cases seen by external users
- admin / invited-member handoff clarity
- time-to-first-sync comfort / trust
- which failure states are understandable vs confusing
- whether the remaining blockers look like depth problems or execution-throughput problems

Follow-up note
- Pipeline can stay cold until the external feedback points clearly to a profile.
- This replaces the old "revisit after July" placeholder with an evidence trigger.

arguments.body:
Mercury / Evergreen procurement packet
Final — Sep 13, 2023

Prepared for Evergreen Bank
Commercial/procurement owner: Devon Hayes

1) Purpose

This packet summarizes the current Mercury design-partner deployment for procurement and security review: the commercial baseline, the present login and setup experience, the current bounded admin/security posture, and open enterprise-readiness gaps.

The statements below describe current Mercury facts and currently identified gaps. They do not constitute a commitment to future functionality, timing, or customer-specific packaging.

2) Commercial model

Mercury is priced on monthly active developer usage, not purchased seats or directory size.

Current pricing baseline:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Counting notes:
- Monthly active developer usage is the pricing driver.
- Scaffold internal and test users do not count toward usage.
- Preview/sample-only behavior is separate from activation reporting and is not usage proof by itself.

The commercial baseline is intended to support evaluation on a bounded usage model, with expansion available if usage later widens.

3) Current Mercury scope

Evergreen is in the first external design-partner wave, and the live bounded experience currently includes:
- Clerk-backed sessions
- Magic-link sign-in
- Organization invites
- A setup flow oriented around connecting a real source
- Preview/sample data available only as preview behavior and not activating by itself
- The first live sync path in the product

Current activation definition for operating review:
- real_source_connected within 7 days, or
- first_live_sync_completed within 7 days

The current launch scope does not include SSO, deeper admin controls, or audit history for admin changes.

4) Current login and setup experience

For the present Mercury flow, access is handled through magic links and organization invites, with Clerk-backed session handling. The intended path is:
1. An invited user enters through the magic-link or invite flow.
2. The user lands in the Mercury workspace context.
3. The user connects a real source.
4. The user reaches the first live sync.

Preview/sample behavior may be shown during evaluation. Preview/sample-only behavior does not activate the account and is not equivalent to a real source connection or live sync completion.

5) Current admin and security readiness

Current readiness is limited to the bounded design-partner experience; it is not a full enterprise admin/security package.

Current facts:
- Access uses the current magic-link and organization-invite flow.
- Organization-level invitation exists in the current Mercury experience.
- The launch experience is intentionally narrower than a full enterprise rollout.
- Current product facts should be evaluated against this present scope, rather than against a broader enterprise-control checklist.

This packet does not imply that Mercury currently includes full enterprise-ready login controls or that current admin behavior covers all enterprise audit and control requirements.

6) Open enterprise-readiness gaps

The following items remain open enterprise-readiness gaps identified through review:
- SSO
- Audit history for admin changes
- Clearer separation between admin permissions and billing-owner controls
- Stronger procurement and self-serve explanation materials that can stand on their own without live explanation

These items are not part of the current launch package. SSO, audit history, and deeper admin controls are roadmap-dependent add-ons and would be quoted only after the relevant capabilities ship. No timing, availability, or customer-specific packaging is stated here.

7) Product facts and activation measurement

Mercury is improving activation and setup clarity within the external design-partner wave. Activation is measured as real_source_connected or first_live_sync_completed within seven days, and sample-preview-only sessions are excluded from that activation definition.

The current product scope excludes SSO and deeper admin controls. Enterprise-readiness is not complete, and later-scope controls should not be read as available in the live launch package.

8) Review boundary

This packet is a current-state procurement and security summary. It is not a bespoke Evergreen roadmap, a promise of future delivery, or a commitment to custom commercial terms. Any future enterprise controls or expanded packaging will be assessed and quoted only after the applicable capabilities ship.

messages.content:
September 2024 cloud infrastructure variance note

Invoice period: September 2024  
September total: $8,642.18  
August total: $8,190.00  
Month-over-month variance: +$452.18 (+5.52%)

Summary

September cloud infrastructure spend increased by $452.18 versus August. The variance is concentrated in production Atlas API v2 traffic and a one-week staging increase for Mercury release validation. The supplied usage detail does not identify an unexplained production event, one-time restore, failover, or material change to the account-level support charge.

Variance by area

- Production: +$313.26
  - EC2 for atlas-api-v2: +$140.22, driven by higher production API v2 request volume.
  - Data Transfer for atlas-api-v2-egress: +$88.41, driven by higher response volume and webhook delivery traffic.
  - Application Load Balancer: +$47.16, consistent with increased traffic and request processing.
  - RDS PostgreSQL: +$23.58, described as normal production growth with no one-time restore or failover charge.
  - ElastiCache Redis: +$9.73, consistent with higher production request volume.
  - S3 connector payloads and archives: +$4.16, reflecting a slight increase in storage and requests.

- Staging: +$129.62
  - ECS Fargate: +$98.40.
  - CloudWatch: +$31.22.
  - Both increases are attributed to a one-week staging/test expansion for Mercury release validation.

- Shared services: +$7.12
  - NAT Gateway: +$5.30.
  - Route 53 and WAF: +$1.82.
  - These are minor increases consistent with higher external request volume; staging validation contributed a small portion of the NAT Gateway increase.

- Non-production baseline: +$2.18
  - Legacy us-west-2 compute and storage remained essentially flat.

- Support Plan: $0.00 variance
  - The account-level monthly support charge was unchanged.

Largest drivers

The three largest increases—production EC2, Data Transfer, and the production Application Load Balancer—account for $275.79 of the total variance. These are all consistent with increased Atlas API v2 production usage. The Mercury staging validation increase accounts for an additional $129.62.

Conclusion and approval context

The $8,642.18 invoice is above the AP manual-review threshold. Based on the supplied usage detail, the $452.18 increase is explainable and appears operationally consistent with:

1. Higher Atlas API v2 production request, response, and webhook traffic; and
2. A one-week Mercury release-validation effort in staging.

Recommended disposition: approve the invoice if the Mercury release-validation work was planned and authorized. If that staging work has not yet been confirmed, hold approval only for confirmation of the $129.62 staging variance; no other material anomaly is evident in the supplied data.

input.body: The Q3 2022 weekend incident should have made the risk of late deployments unmistakable before the later March outage: reduced staffing and slower escalation turn a manageable defect into prolonged customer impact. We should have treated late deploys as an exception requiring explicit coverage, a named decision-maker, clear rollback ownership, and live monitoring through the full risk window—not as a normal release with fewer people online. The durable fix is to make deploy timing, on-call coverage, rollback readiness, and escalation paths visible and auditable before approval.

results.snippet: ...Any such discussion is exploratory only and does not constitute a commitment or promise to provide any future feature, enhancement, permission >>>model<<<, role, operator control, sync capability, implementation, timing, >>>pricing<<<, or usage treatment. messages.content:
[2026-01-12T10:17:00-08:00] Excerpt — Evergreen Bank January renewal schedule draft

Section 2. Current Administrative Controls
Scaffold will document current administrative controls available in the Growth plan, including SAML login, admin audit lookup, invited teammate visibility, source owner visibility, and standard support escalation paths.

Section 3. Planned Advanced Administration Review
During the annual term, Scaffold and Evergreen Bank will review advanced administration needs, including a granular sync-operator role for department-specific source management. The parties understand this roadmap appendix is non-binding and does not alter fees unless mutually agreed.

Section 4. Usage and Overage
The renewal remains on Growth usage terms. If advanced administration scope moves forward during the term, the parties may revisit usage/overage treatment as part of that implementation discussion.

Sarah's question: is Section 3 safe if it says non-binding? Devon's instinct: keep Section 2, remove or sharply narrow Sections 3 and 4.

Sarah: No. “Non-binding” alone does not make Section 3 safe. The language still:

- Says the parties “will review,” which can create a continuing obligation.
- Identifies a specific future capability—a granular sync-operator role.
- Places that discussion within the annual term, creating a roadmap or delivery expectation.
- Could later be cited as acknowledgment that the requested functionality is part of the renewal conversation.

Recommendation: delete Section 3 from the customer-facing renewal schedule. If Evergreen insists on an acknowledgment, put it in a separate procurement note or use narrowly bounded language:

“During the term, the parties may discuss, separately from this renewal schedule, any additional administrative needs. Any such discussion is exploratory only and does not constitute a commitment or promise to provide any future feature, enhancement, permission model, role, operator control, sync capability, implementation, timing, pricing, or usage treatment. The renewal is not conditioned on any such functionality.”

Devon: I agree with keeping Section 2 and removing Sections 3 and 4. Section 2 should be expressly current-state and non-modifying:

“Scaffold will document the administrative controls currently available under the Growth plan as of the renewal date, including SAML login, admin audit lookup, invited teammate visibility, source owner visibility, and standard support escalation paths. This description is informational only and does not modify the Agreement, renewal terms, pricing, scope, service levels, support obligations, or product commitments.”

Section 4 should be deleted rather than merely softened. “May revisit usage/overage treatment” invites a later argument that advanced administration could trigger a pricing exception, department-specific package, or negotiated commercial change. The renewal should instead state, if needed:

“The renewal remains subject to the standard Growth plan usage and overage terms under the Agreement. No change to those terms is made or implied by this schedule.”

Bottom line: keep a current-state administrative description only; remove “roadmap,” the sync-operator request, the future review obligation, and any linkage between future functionality and usage or overage treatment.

# Mercury pricing decision — hybrid platform minimums

## Decision
We are no longer treating Mercury pricing as a pure-MAU-versus-pure-seat debate. For new Mercury design-partner and post-launch quotes, use the hybrid model below.

## Quote guidance
- Pilot platform minimum: $2,500/month, including up to 50 monthly active developers
- Growth platform minimum: $7,500/month, including up to 200 monthly active developers
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers
- Enterprise add-ons such as SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls are quoted separately only after those features actually ship

## Rationale
This keeps the usage-ramp logic honest while giving Devon a cleaner floor for forecasting and procurement conversations.

results.title: Diagnose Clerk replay JWT mapping failure
results.snippet:
...need the likely path and the evidence that would distinguish a Clerk payload issue from our JWT mapping bug.

>>>Auth rewrite<<< replay test — Clerk webhook replay failure
Date: 2024-04-02

Replay-test log excerpt
2024-04-02T10:42:17Z...

messages.content:
[2024-04-02T10:14:00-07:00] Can you reason through this replay failure? I need the likely path and the evidence that would distinguish a Clerk payload issue from our JWT mapping bug.

Auth rewrite replay test — Clerk webhook replay failure
Date: 2024-04-02

Replay-test log excerpt
2024-04-02T10:42:17Z clerk.replay event=user.updated replay_id=rep_041 source_user_id=user_7Q9 expected_workspace=wrk_evergreen_ops
2024-04-02T10:42:18Z auth-webhook normalized user_id=user_7Q9 external_id=clerk_user_7Q9 metadata_keys=[email,role,last_login] workspace_claim=<missing>
2024-04-02T10:42:18Z api_v2 jwt.build subject=user_7Q9 aud=graphql-api-v2 workspace=<nil> result=error code=JWT_METADATA_MISMATCH
2024-04-02T10:42:19Z replay assertion failed: expected user_id user_7Q9 present=true; expected workspace claim wrk_evergreen_ops present=false.

Test note
- Live create path passed yesterday with workspace claim present.
- Replay path is the only failing path so far.

The most likely path is:

1. Clerk replay delivers `user.updated` for `user_7Q9`.
2. `auth-webhook` parses and normalizes the event.
3. The normalized user contains `user_id=user_7Q9` and metadata:
   `email, role, last_login`
4. `api_v2` builds the JWT from that normalized object.
5. The JWT builder receives `workspace=<nil>`, so it fails with `JWT_METADATA_MISMATCH`.
6. The replay assertion fails because the workspace claim was never produced.

The important boundary is that `workspace_claim=<missing>` is already present in the normalized webhook log. That makes a signing problem or a downstream GraphQL problem unlikely. The failure is probably either:

- the replay payload does not contain the workspace value, or
- the replay-specific normalization/projection drops or misreads it.

The live-create success makes a replay-specific path difference more likely than a generally broken JWT mapper.

Evidence to collect at each boundary:

1. Raw Clerk replay payload

Capture the redacted raw `data` object, or at least the relevant metadata locations and their types:

- `data.public_metadata.workspace`
- `data.private_metadata.workspace`
- `data.unsafe_metadata.workspace`
- any top-level `workspace` or organization field
- event version/schema and replay source

Compare that with the raw payload from the successful live-create path.

Clerk payload issue indicators:

- The replay payload genuinely has no workspace value.
- The successful live payload has one.
- A fixture containing the replay payload, passed through the normalizer, also produces no workspace.
- Clerk’s replay response is an older user snapshot or a schema variant that does not include the metadata location used by the live path.

Mapping bug indicators:

- The raw replay payload contains `workspace=wrk_evergreen_ops`, but the normalized log still says `workspace_claim=<missing>`.
- The value is present under a different metadata container than the live path, and the replay normalizer only reads one container.
- The replay handler uses a reduced field projection such as `[email, role, last_login]` and omits `workspace`.
- The replay path uses a different normalizer, deserializer, or DTO than the live webhook path.

2. Normalized object immediately before JWT construction

Log a redacted, explicit field rather than only `metadata_keys`, for example:

`normalized.workspace_claim=<value>`
`normalized.metadata.workspace=<value>`
`jwt_input.workspace=<value>`

Do not rely on the metadata key list alone; it could be generated from one object while the JWT builder reads another.

Interpretation:

- `raw workspace present → normalized workspace absent`: replay normalizer/projection bug.
- `normalized workspace present → jwt_input workspace absent`: JWT input mapping bug.
- `jwt_input workspace present → signed JWT lacks workspace`: JWT claim serialization/mapping bug.
- `signed JWT contains workspace → assertion says absent`: assertion decoding or claim-name bug.

3. JWT builder output before signing

Inspect the unsigned claims or claim-construction structure:

- Is the intended claim called `workspace`, `workspace_id`, or something else?
- Is it conditionally omitted when the value is `nil`, empty, or the wrong type?
- Is the builder reading `metadata.workspace` while the normalizer emits `workspace_claim`?
- Does it reject a workspace value because it expects a different identifier format?

The current log says `workspace=<nil>` at `jwt.build`, which suggests the builder did not receive a value. That points upstream of signing, but this check confirms whether the log is reporting the builder input or merely its derived output.

A useful minimal matrix is:

| Input | Normalized workspace | JWT input workspace | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Successful live raw payload | present | present | passes |
| Failing replay raw payload | absent | absent | Clerk payload/replay snapshot issue |
| Failing replay raw payload | present | absent | replay normalization/projection bug |
| …

Dropped markup inline below. I cut the pure wishlist rows and left the stuff I think actually belongs in a 30-minute room.

Biggest thing from my side: don't let Mercury hardening and onboarding work blur together. They're related, but if we talk about them as one blob we won't call the tradeoff.

---
Q4 ship list — Devon markup
Legend: [keep] [cut] [decision] [owner follow-through] [wording]

1) Mercury hardening

- [keep] Q4 goal needs to read as safe expansion of the current Mercury wave, not a theatrical GA push.
  DH note: we still have real work in invited-member/admin handoff, queued-sync retry confidence, and failure-state legibility.

- [decision] Do we define the quarter around hardening the current path, or do we let ourselves get pulled into adjacent enterprise asks?
  My bias: harden the current path first.

- [keep / owner follow-through] Jake + Marcus own retry/recovery evidence and closeout on the ugly failure loops.
  Priya owns final pass on empty/error states once the latest evidence is in.

- [wording] Replace 'enterprise readiness story' with 'hardening against real design-partner failure cases.'
  The first phrase sounds like deck copy.

- [keep] Support is still eating manual Mercury setup + first-sync questions.
  If we don't pay that down, every additional account creates ops drag.

- [decision] Are SSO / audit / deeper admin controls actually in the Q4 ship list, or only bounded discovery?
  I would keep them out of core ship work unless a live partner forces the issue.

- [cut] Any line that implies Mercury is now 'proven.'
  Internally we can say the path is better and the rough edges are clearer. That's not the same thing.

2) Onboarding flow

- [decision] If we spend product/design cycles here, what are we buying?
  a) lower drop-off before first repo connect
  b) fewer 'what do I do now?' tickets after invite acceptance
  c) some combo, but we should say which one

- [keep] Empty-state copy and first-run guidance matter because users are landing before they're ready to connect a repo.
  UX goal should be a clear next step without turning the product into internal marketing copy.

- [tradeoff / keep] We cannot do a full onboarding rewrite and Mercury hardening at the same time.
  If onboarding stays in, it needs to be the narrowest set of changes that actually changes user behavior.

- [owner follow-through] Priya to lock copy/states.
  Jake + Rishi to say what instrumentation we can trust this quarter vs what is still too noisy to optimize against.

- [cut] 'Retention unlock' language.
  That belongs nowhere near a ship list unless we have actual shipping work under it.

3) Auth rewrite rollout

- [decision] Finish the Clerk session rollout behind an account allowlist first, or pick a date to flip everyone?
  My bias: bounded rollout first. The weirdness is in retry/refresh edges, not in the basic happy path anymore.

- [keep] API v2 auth surface is the real surface now.
  The remaining risk is rollout hygiene and token/session edge handling, not which auth direction we picked.

- [owner follow-through] Marcus + Rishi: refresh retry path, session invalidation, and cleanup for old verifier callers.

- [wording] Remove 'auth rewrite completed.'
  Not true. Core path exists; rollout and cleanup still don't.

- [keep] If we ship wider with…

Subject: Q4 ship list — 30-minute planning agenda

Devon —

Here’s the tight version for the product/engineering planning block.

Goal: make the Q4 scope decisions, explicitly separate Mercury hardening from onboarding work, and leave with owners only for work we are actually committing to. Park anything that is not a Q4 decision.

30-minute agenda

0:00–0:03 — Scope and decision criteria

- Q4 ship work should reflect concrete product and engineering commitments.
- Remove wishlist, broad platform-debt, narrative, and investor-facing language.
- Confirm that Mercury hardening and onboarding are separate workstreams with an explicit tradeoff.

0:03–0:10 — Mercury hardening: define the boundary

Decision in room:

- Do we focus Q4 on hardening the current Mercury path, or admit adjacent enterprise asks into the core ship list?
- Default recommendation: harden the current path first.
- Keep in scope: invited-member/admin handoff, queued-sync retry/recovery, failure-state legibility, and reducing manual setup and first-sync support load.
- Keep SSO, audit, and deeper admin controls to bounded discovery unless a live partner requires one for the committed path.
- Use “hardening against real design-partner failure cases,” not “enterprise readiness.”

Owner follow-through:

- Jake and Marcus: retry/recovery evidence and closeout of failure loops.
- Priya: final empty/error-state pass after the evidence is available.

0:10–0:15 — Onboarding: decide whether it earns Q4 capacity

Decision in room:

- If onboarding remains in Q4, what is the specific outcome:
  - lower drop-off before first repo connect,
  - fewer unclear-next-step tickets after invite acceptance,
  - or a defined combination?
- Confirm the tradeoff: we cannot do a full onboarding rewrite and Mercury hardening simultaneously.
- Default recommendation: include only the narrowest onboarding changes that are expected to change user behavior.

Owner follow-through:

- Priya: lock copy and states.
- Jake and Rishi: identify which instrumentation is reliable enough to use this quarter.
- Keep empty-state copy and first-run guidance focused on a clear next step.

0:15–0:21 — Auth rollout and API v2 docs

Decisions in room:

- Auth: finish the Clerk session rollout behind an account allowlist first, or choose a date for a full flip?
  - Default recommendation: bounded rollout first.
- Docs: publish a minimal “how auth works now” guide and migration examples first, or wait for a full docs sweep?
  - Default recommendation: publish the minimal version first.

Owner follow-through:

- Marcus and Rishi: refresh retry behavior, session invalidation, and cleanup for old verifier callers.
- Rishi: draft API v2 auth documentation.
- Morgan: edit for clarity.
- Support: validate examples against current JWT/header questions.

6:21–0:27 — Support backlog: commit product/engineering work versus response handling

Decision in room:

For each repeated row, decide whether it gets product/engineering work in Q4 or a templated support response:

- Invite accepted, but no clear next step.
- Repo-connect timing confusion.
- Stale or incomplete API v2 auth examples.
- Refresh timeout or forced re-login after long idle.
- Unclear ownership of initial admin/setup steps in shared workspaces.

Owner follow-through:

- Assign one explicit owner to every row receiving real work.
- Leave no item assigned to “shared.”
- Confirm which remaining rows are handled operationally rather than added to the ship list.

0:27–0:30 — Recap and parking lot

- Read back the actual Q4 decisions.
- Confirm owners and next checkpoints.
- Park future enterprise packaging, broad analytics cleanup, generalized platform debt, and any uncommitted discovery.
- Remove any remaining “proven,” “retention unlock,” “momentum,” or similar narrative language.

Morgan

HR REPLY PACKAGE
Post-all-hands follow-up and holiday coverage

Reply to HR

Thanks for sending this through. The pre-collected Q&A structure worked well: it kept the discussion focused, and tagging out-of-scope questions separately gives us a clean way to follow up without reopening the all-hands thread.

For the recap, please keep it broad and stay with the topics we covered in the all-hands. Please do not expand the recap into the unanswered buckets. Route those separately as follows:

- Fundraising/financing timing: hold for a January founder/finance follow-up.
- Enterprise roadmap questions, including SSO, auditability, and the admin model: hold for a January product/engineering follow-up.
- 2024 hiring: route to January HR planning.
- Pricing/packaging: hold for a January founder/product follow-up.
- The support-process question: route through Rishi Patel during coverage, with Priya as backup, and include it in the January follow-up if it needs broader discussion.

Holiday coverage announcement

Holiday coverage runs Saturday, December 23, 2023 through Monday, January 1, 2024. Our normal schedule resumes Tuesday, January 2, 2024.

During the coverage window:

- Customer support triage: Rishi Patel primary; Priya backup.
- Product/design clarification for active customer issues: Priya primary; Jake backup.
- Engineering on-call and production: Marcus primary; Leo Park backup.
- Deploy/rollback authority: Devon Hayes primary; Marcus backup.
- Billing and time-sensitive external follow-up already in flight: Sarah Kim primary; Devon Hayes backup.
- People and benefits: HR primary; Sarah Kim backup.

Please use Option B for standing meetings: cancel non-essential recurring meetings unless an owner confirms a real need. We should not ask for broad async updates during the reduced-schedule period.

For escalation, genuinely customer-impacting issues should go through the named owner/backup path first. Founders should be pulled in only when that path cannot resolve the issue.

Honeycomb line

For the same Saturday, December 23 through Monday, January 1 window: Honeycomb thresholds stay as they are. Page the named on-call owner first. Involve Morgan only for confirmed customer impact or if that path cannot reach anyone. Otherwise, roll a quiet week's alerts into Monday's digest.

Suggested closing

Thanks again to everyone who prepared questions and helped keep the all-hands focused. The coverage owners and escalation paths above should keep the holiday window clear and predictable, while the remaining questions can be handled deliberately in January.

messages.content:
- 0:00–1:00 — Frame and triage
  - Goal: identify only items needing action before the holiday week ends.
  - For each item, name one accountable owner, the next action, and the date.
  - Default rule: routine customer work stays with the account/support owner; no founder escalation without meeting a threshold.

- 1:00–4:00 — Account/customer owners
  - Prompt: “Which customer item has a concrete risk this week, and what is the next customer-facing action?”
  - Prompt: “Is there an active commitment, renewal risk, outage, or decision deadline—or only an open follow-up?”
  - Prompt: “What can you close directly without Devon or Morgan?”
  - Assign: owner, customer update date, and whether the item remains in the normal account thread.
  - Acme large-export follow-up: keep it as normal documentation/support work unless review identifies a new failure mode; no founder or Product rescue by default.

- 4:00–7:00 — Support/Product/Engineering owners
  - Prompt: “Is this an active reliability, product, security, or data issue, or a documentation/process gap?”
  - Prompt: “What evidence do we have, and what is the smallest action required before the holiday week?”
  - Prompt: “What is explicitly not being fixed or investigated this week?”
  - Do not escalate a single customer annoyance, routine documentation gap, stale follow-up, or known workaround with a named owner.

- 7:00–10:00 — Devon
  - Prompt: “Is there a commercial, procurement, contract, or selective cofounder-judgment question that specifically requires your input?”
  - Prompt: “What decision do you need to make, if any?”
  - Prompt: “Who remains the operating owner after your input?”
  - Devon is not the default cleanup path, customer follow-up owner, or substitute for an unassigned account owner.
  - Route routine customer work back to the account/support owner with a clear date; involve Devon only for the defined commercial or cofounder judgment issue.

- 10:00–13:00 — Morgan/founder escalation check
  - Escalate during the holiday week only if one of these is true:
    - Active production outage, material data loss, security/privacy issue, or legal/compliance exposure.
    - A customer or renewal commitment is at risk within the week and the accountable owner cannot resolve it with available authority.
    - The issue is recurring or reveals a new failure mode, rather than being a known support/documentation matter.
    - A founder-only decision is required on priority, customer commitment, commercial posture, or risk acceptance.
  - Do not escalate merely because:
    - The item is old, uncomfortable, or lacking a perfect update.
    - A customer has not yet replied.
    - The work needs routine cleanup, documentation, scheduling, or account follow-up.
    - Devon’s context would be convenient but is not necessary.
  - For every escalation: state the decision required, consequence of waiting until after the holiday, owner, and proposed recommendation.

- 13:00–15:00 — Lock decisions and defer list
  - Confirm no more than three pre-holiday actions, each with one owner and a due date.
  - Record deferred items explicitly as “after holiday week,” not as silent open work.
  - Defer:
    - Nonurgent documentation and process cleanup.
    - Exploratory product requests and roadmap debates.
    - Broad account reviews without an immediate deadline.
    - Routine customer follow-ups where the normal owner has a credible next step.
    - Any investor, deck, or strategic narrative work not tied to an active decision.
  - Close with: “If none of the escalation thresholds are met, this stays with the operating owner and we revisit after the holiday week.”
