[2024-06-18T10:43:00-07:00] Please turn Sofia’s email and my working notes into the plain operating-read section for the Q2 board update. Bullets are fine; keep it factual and don’t make it sound like we’re accelerating hiring, fully covered on Atlas, or declaring Mercury launch risk cleared.

From: Sofia Alvarez
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Tue, Jun 18, 2024, 7:42 AM
Subject: Q2 board update — plain operating read before the board note

Morgan — before you turn the Q2 board update into polished board language, can you send me the plain operating read on three things?

I’m not looking for the investor-story version yet. I want the factual version you are using internally, including the uncomfortable parts and what evidence changed your confidence.

1) Hiring pace after the Series B
- Did the Series B actually change the pace or shape of hiring, or did you mostly keep the same evidence-led posture?
- I’m especially interested in whether the customer-growth hire created a new org/hiring pull, and whether you are opening more GTM or Mercury engineering lanes in Q3.
- Please distinguish between “we hired the planned leader” and “we are accelerating headcount because we raised.”

2) Atlas risk after Rishi’s departure
- Now that Rishi has accepted Tessl, what is the real Atlas continuity risk?
- What is covered by Leo/Jake/support rotation, and what still depends too much on Rishi?
- If there has been any live test of the interim split, include that rather than only the transition plan.
- Please be explicit about dates — I know his last day has not happened yet.

3) Mercury release discipline and confidence
- Has the Mercury discipline actually improved release confidence, or are people just marking things green earlier?
- I’d like the raw operating evidence: release checks, observability evidence, incidents/anomalies, and what the team did when the evidence was missing.
- Please keep this separate from the larger retention/customer-growth story unless the evidence really connects.

If it is easier, send bullets under those headings. I’ll read it as operating evidence, not as proposed board copy.

Sofia

---

Morgan Chen working notes for Sofia request
Created: Jun 18, 2024, 9:06 AM
Last edited: Jun 18, 2024, 10:18 AM
Purpose: raw Q2 operating evidence for Sofia before drafting the board note. These are factual inputs only, not board language.

Cutoff: Jun 18, 2024. Rishi’s final Scaffold working day is scheduled for Jun 21, 2024. Atlas handoff is active and not complete.

1) Hiring pace after the Series B — raw evidence

Series B / operating posture
- Feb 22 Series B closed with Northstar as lead. Board milestones after the close have stayed centered on defensible retention evidence and repeatable enterprise expansion from Mercury/Evergreen learning, not on immediately launching a Series C narrative.
- Post-raise operating ownership was set without a broad hiring acceleration: Jake runs Mercury execution and launch evidence; Leo Park owns platform seams and release discipline; Priya owns activation/onboarding UX; Anna Martinez owns retention evidence; Devon Hayes owns enterprise-readiness commercial packaging with Sarah Kim; Morgan holds board narrative and hiring sequence.
- Post-raise hiring sequence decision: next new leadership search was customer-growth/GTM leader focused on repeatable enterprise expansion from Mercury and Evergreen learning. The second Mercury engineering req was not reopened; later hiring remained evidence-led.
- Existing Mercury engineering headcount plan still has the second Mercury engineering hire on hold. Revisit trigger is external launch-readiness feedback from design-partner conversations/trials, not an arbitrary calendar date. Decision rule still depends on whether blockers look like senior platform/architecture seams, implementation throughput, or manageable current-team follow-through.

Customer-growth leader
- Apr 15 Nadia Singh started as Head of Customer Growth. Reporting line: Morgan. First-90-day sc…

Q2 plain operating read
Cutoff: June 18, 2024

Hiring pace after the Series B

- The February 22 Series B did not lead to broad hiring acceleration. The operating posture remains evidence-led, with hiring tied to retention, enterprise expansion, and Mercury launch-readiness evidence rather than to the financing itself.
- One planned leadership hire was completed: Nadia Singh joined as Head of Customer Growth on April 15.
- Nadia’s initial mandate is to build a repeatable customer-growth motion around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and cross-functional handoffs. Her role is not a generic sales or bespoke enterprise-roadmap function.
- Nadia’s customer-growth cadence is producing useful pattern reads, including activation friction, admin handoff and role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls, and true product gaps. The process remains manual and depends on improving account-note quality.
- On June 14, Nadia asked for cleaner and more reliable account inputs before additional GTM headcount. Morgan and Devon decided not to open RevOps, CS, SDR, or field-sales hiring lanes in Q3.
- The second Mercury engineering requisition remains on hold. The decision to reopen it depends on external launch-readiness feedback and whether remaining blockers require senior platform or architecture capacity, implementation throughput, or can be handled by the current team.
- The customer-growth org shape will remain unchanged until Nadia has two more cadence cycles and the July Evergreen review provides better evidence. The current evidence supports the planned leader hire, not an accelerated headcount plan.

Atlas risk after Rishi’s departure

- Rishi accepted Tessl’s database-internals/platform offer on May 22. His final Scaffold working day is June 21, so the handoff is active but not complete.
- The interim coverage model assigns customer-facing ownership through the support rotation document, Leo to first-pass technical review of platform, auth, and API v2 seams, and Jake to product-priority and sequencing decisions.
- On May 24, an Atlas support item that initially routed directly to Rishi was redirected through the support rotation model. Leo handled the first technical read and Jake made the priority call.
- A second live test occurred on June 17 during Rishi’s final week. It was a low-severity issue, not a severe outage or high-pressure customer escalation. The support rotation named the customer-facing owner, Leo handled the technical pass, Jake made the sequencing decision, and Rishi remained available for correction.
- The transition work still includes the AT-03 verifier/auth note, AT-04 replay/backfill recovery steps, and AT-05 workspace/org-invite migration notes. Leo is shadowing the technical paths, while Jake remains responsible for product decisions.
- The principal remaining exposure is knowledge and written-procedure depth around replay/backfill recovery and idempotency, workspace/org-invite migration history, and Atlas-specific replay/verifier behavior during deployment or observability triage.
- The interim split has been exercised and is sufficient to route current issues, but it has not yet been tested under a severe outage or major customer escalation. Rishi’s availability through June 21 is still part of the current safety net, so Atlas continuity should not yet be treated as fully covered.

Mercury release discipline and confidence

- Mercury release confidence is being based more consistently on linked evidence, but the process is not proof that all launch risk has been cleared.
- On May 16, Marcus and Leo found two launch-readiness tickets marked green in Linear without linked Honeycomb evidence. They held the #eng-releases note until the evidence was attached and verified.
- This showed that green ticket status is not being accepted as sufficient on its own. It also exposed a workflow gap: tickets can still move to green before observabil…

messages.content: [2025-12-01T08:18:00-08:00] Sofia sent a Monday note about the Dec 12 Q4 operating review. She wants the pre-read to stay to one page if possible, separate facts from decisions, and not drift into Series C market-warming unless the evidence really supports that. I don't have all the inputs yet: Devon still owes the final November usage close, Anna is compiling the Compass behavior read, and Sarah/Jake/Leo may have customer/support examples. Give me a concise working agenda plus an owner-input checklist framed as questions to answer, not conclusions, so I can ask each person for the right material without implying the outcome is already decided.

Working agenda — Dec 12 Q4 operating review

- 10:00–10:10 — Frame the review
  - What facts are confirmed, what remains open, and which decisions—if any—are needed?
  - Can the pre-read remain one page without omitting material caveats?
- 10:10–10:30 — November operating close
  - What does the final November usage data show?
  - Which movements are real, and which require explanation or further validation?
- 10:30–10:50 — Compass behavior read
  - What behavior patterns are supported by the evidence?
  - What does the evidence not yet establish?
- 10:50–11:10 — Customer and support evidence
  - Do customer or support examples confirm, complicate, or contradict the operating read?
  - Are the examples representative, current, and attributable to a specific owner or action?
- 11:10–11:25 — Decisions and next actions
  - What action, if any, should change after reviewing the evidence?
  - What remains unresolved, and who owns closing each gap?
- 11:25–11:30 — Market-warming check
  - Does the evidence justify changing the current Series C market-warming posture?
  - If not, should that topic remain unchanged and out of the broader discussion?

Owner-input checklist

- Devon — November usage close
  - What is the final November usage number or range?
  - What methodology, exclusions, or late adjustments should be noted?
  - What changed from the prior view, and why?
  - Which conclusions are supported by the close, and which would be premature?
  - When can the final source or reconciliation be shared?

- Anna — Compass behavior read
  - What behaviors are directly observed in the current data?
  - How fresh, complete, and representative is the evidence?
  - What comparison period or baseline is being used?
  - Which findings are signals versus established patterns?
  - What caveats or missing data must appear in the one-page pre-read?
  - What owner actions or customer follow-up, if any, are supported by the evidence?

- Sarah — Customer/support examples
  - Which customer or support examples are most relevant to the operating questions?
  - What specifically happened, when, and what outcome followed?
  - Are the examples representative or isolated?
  - Do they confirm, complicate, or contradict the usage and Compass evidence?
  - What customer-sensitive details should be omitted or anonymized?

- Jake — Customer/business context
  - Which customer or commercial signals materially changed during the quarter?
  - What evidence supports the signal, and how current is it?
  - Are there relevant renewals, expansions, risks, or owner actions to include?
  - What should the team avoid inferring from the available examples?

- Leo — Product/operations context
  - Which product, support, or execution changes could explain the observed results?
  - What actions were completed, accepted, blocked, or still awaiting customer follow-up?
  - Which outcomes are attributable to those actions versus other factors?
  - What unresolved dependencies should be made explicit?

- Sofia — Review framing
  - Which facts must be on the one-page pre-read?
  - Which items belong under decisions rather than facts?
  - What evidence threshold would justify discussing a change in Series C market-warming?
  - If that threshold is not met, should the topic remain unchanged and be explicitly noted as unresolved or out of scope?

I don’t have the owner notes themselves—the internal search returned only placeholders—so I can’t safely invent owner-specific claims or questions. Here’s a bounded version you can use now; paste the notes and I’ll map each question to the relevant owner and evidence.

Opening script

“Thanks, everyone. This is an evidence read, not a decision meeting.

We’ll go owner by owner and keep three things separate: what we observed, what the evidence supports, and what it does not support. For each area, please give us the time window, source, scope, and any important limitations. We’ll distinguish facts from interpretation and interpretation from recommendation.

The goal today is to establish the durability read and its confidence level. We are not deciding on July market-warming activity or staffing posture in this meeting. Those questions remain deliberately undecided until we have heard and tested the evidence.

For each owner, we’ll close with four labels: supported, not supported, unknown, and follow-up evidence needed.”

Questions for each owner

1. What exactly did you observe?
   - What is the metric, event, or pattern?
   - What period and population does it cover?
   - What is the source of record?

2. What does that evidence support?
   - What claim can we make confidently?
   - How strong is the support?
   - Is this a trend, a point-in-time observation, or an anecdote?

3. What does it not support?
   - What stronger claim would be an overreach?
   - What conclusions should we explicitly avoid drawing?
   - Does it tell us anything about July market conditions or staffing needs? If not, say so plainly.

4. What could explain the result besides the proposed interpretation?
   - Are there confounders, selection effects, seasonality, or measurement changes?
   - What alternative explanation remains credible?

5. How does this compare with the prior read?
   - What changed?
   - What stayed stable?
   - Is the difference material or within expected noise?

6. What is your confidence level, and why?
   - What assumption is carrying the most weight?
   - What evidence would raise or lower your confidence?

7. What remains unknown?
   - What evidence is missing?
   - What follow-up would resolve the uncertainty?
   - Is that follow-up required for the durability read, or merely useful later?

8. What is the precise takeaway we should record?
   - Supported:
   - Not supported:
   - Unknown:
   - Follow-up:

Bounding prompts

- “Let’s stay with what the evidence shows before moving to implications.”
- “Which part of that is observed, and which part is inference?”
- “What does this specifically not allow us to conclude?”
- “What is the denominator and time window?”
- “Is that a durability conclusion, or a recommendation?”
- “Please separate the evidence from the staffing implication.”
- “Let’s park July market-warming for now; what does today’s evidence actually establish?”
- “What would we need to hear before treating that as supported?”
- “Can we label that as unknown rather than resolve it speculatively?”
- “I’m going to capture that as a follow-up, not a decision.”

Closing line

“We have recorded what the evidence supports, what it does not support, and what remains unresolved. We are leaving July market-warming and staffing posture open pending the completed read and any explicitly identified follow-up evidence.”

messages.content:
Replacement section: Verify Atlas webhook signatures

Atlas signs each webhook with the shared secret for the workspace and sends the signature in the request headers. Signature verification confirms that the request was signed for your workspace and that the signed bytes were not changed in transit. It does not guarantee delivery order, uniqueness, or successful processing.

Required request values

Read these values directly from the incoming request:

- X-Scaffold-Workspace: the Atlas workspace identifier
- X-Scaffold-Signature: the Atlas signature value
- The raw request body, as received, before parsing or decoding

Header names are case-insensitive in normal HTTP handling, but use the documented hyphenated names. Do not replace them with environment-variable-style names such as X_SCAFFOLD_SIGNATURE.

The signature is an HMAC-SHA256 digest computed with the workspace’s webhook secret. The signature base string is built from the exact signed timestamp and raw request payload according to Atlas’s signing format. Do not construct it from a parsed JSON object, a reserialized JSON string, or the event’s application timestamp. Whitespace, property order, escaping, and line endings must remain unchanged.

Recommended verification sequence

1. Read and retain the raw request bytes.
2. Read X-Scaffold-Workspace and X-Scaffold-Signature from the request headers.
3. Confirm that the workspace matches the endpoint or credential configuration you intend to use.
4. Parse the timestamp from the signature metadata using Atlas’s documented format. Use the signing timestamp, not the time at which your server received the request and not a timestamp inside the event payload.
5. Check the timestamp against the current UTC time and your configured Atlas tolerance. Reject requests outside that tolerance.
6. Compute the HMAC-SHA256 value over Atlas’s signature base string, using the workspace’s webhook secret.
7. Compare the computed digest with the supplied signature using a constant-time comparison.
8. Only after signature and timestamp checks succeed, parse and process the event. Apply normal idempotency checks before performing side effects.
9. Return a success response only after your receiver has accepted the verified event according to your normal processing policy.

Use Atlas’s current SDK verifier where one is available. Conceptually, the call should receive the raw payload, workspace identifier, signature, and the configured secret; it should not receive a parsed or reserialized JSON object.

Timestamp tolerance and clock skew

The tolerance is a replay-protection window, not a security bypass. It limits how long a captured signed request can remain acceptable. Keep the tolerance narrow and aligned with your processing and retry requirements; do not widen it simply to make a failing verification pass.

Keep the receiver’s clock synchronized to UTC. A timestamp failure can result from clock skew, delayed replay of an old request, or a request that was captured and retried outside the accepted window. If your clocks are synchronized and a fresh delivery still falls outside the configured tolerance, record the exact UTC times and contact Support rather than disabling the timestamp check.

Rotating webhook secrets

Treat a secret rotation as a coordinated receiver deployment:

- Store the new secret securely before switching verification.
- During the transition, allow verification with the new secret and, where necessary for in-flight retries, the previous secret.
- Try both secrets against the same raw body, workspace, signature, and timestamp. Do not modify the payload between attempts.
- Update every receiver instance, worker, queue consumer, and retry path that can process the webhook.
- Remove the previous secret only after the rotation window and relevant retries have cleared.
- Never include either secret in logs, support tickets, or webhook responses.

A receiver that is still using only the old secret can reject new deliveries a…

Purpose

- Produce internal account-owner evidence only.

Final boundary
- In scope: whether the internal owner workflow leads to a named owner, a dated next action, and usable follow-through on renewal-risk context, documented administrative friction, legitimate account follow-up, and post-first-live-sync expansion prompts.
- Administrative-workflow evidence is in scope.
- Post-first-live-sync prompts are gated: do not count them until the first sync is verified live.
- Teammate invites and role selection are valid owner actions when they are the explicit next step after a verified live sync.
- Keep rejected or thin rows visible with the source/date caveat; do not convert them into positive evidence.
- Out of scope: customer-facing behavior or communications, customer analytics or product-performance interpretation, staffing or org conclusions, fundraising or market conclusions, dashboard polish, relaunch language, or a broader product conclusion.

Evidence standard
- Every unresolved item has one named owner and one dated next action.
- Record the source, source date, account context, owner_action_status, next_action, and caveat.
- A prompt sighting without attached source/date support is not readout evidence.
- A source_freshness_warning is a caveat, not an automatic rejection.
- Reject only when the source or date is too thin to support the action; keep the rejected row visible.
- October output is bounded follow-through evidence, not a customer or market readout.

Workback

Sep 29–30 — lock the cycle
- Jake: confirm the October sequence and the owner-action definitions; keep the sequence limited to renewal risk, administrative friction, legitimate follow-up, teammate invites, and role selection.
- Anna: carry forward the September rows, preserve statuses/caveats, and assign one named owner plus one dated next action to each unresolved item.
- Sarah: attach internal account-thread context and source dates for items that need account-owner follow-up; do not turn the context into customer-facing or analytics evidence.
- Leo: confirm the administrative-workflow fields and the first-live-sync verification gate; no connector/API interpretation as Compass evidence.

Oct 1–3 — baseline and triage

Oct 6–10 — first owner-action cycle

- Anna checks that every unresolved row has a named owner and dated next action.
- Friday checkpoint: count statuses and list evidence gaps without interpretation beyond internal follow-through.

Oct 13–17 — verified-live-sync gate and expansion prompts

- After verification only, owners may log a teammate invite or role selection when it is the explicit next step.
- Sarah supplies dated internal account context for legitimate follow-up; Jake decides whether the action stays within the boundary.
- Anna keeps pre-verification prompts separate from evidence and retains caveats.

Oct 20–24 — second owner-action cycle

- Review post-first-live-sync actions for source/date support and clear separation from customer-facing or product claims.
- Remove no thin/rejected rows; mark their final status and caveat.

Oct 27–31 — closeout
- Anna freezes the evidence register and prepares the internal owner-action summary.
- Jake reviews the sequence, completion status, and remaining gaps against the final boundary.
- Sarah and Leo verify the supporting sources, dates, live-sync gate, and administrative-workflow evidence.
- Deliverable: October internal evidence pack showing completed, thin/rejected, awaiting-follow-up, and still-open rows.
- Conclusion allowed: bounded internal account-owner follow-through and remaining evidence gaps only.
- Conclusion not allowed: customer adoption/behavior, analytics, staffing, fundraising, market, relaunch, or broader product claims.

Operating rule
- If an item does not fit the boundary, park it rather than reinterpret it into Compass evidence.

arguments.title: Compass readout meeting frame — September 5, 2025
arguments.body:
PURPOSE
Keep the readout anchored to evidence and owner action. Review the current Compass prototype state without making the counts cleaner than the evidence supports.

BOUNDARY
Internal prototype/readout check only. Not a customer-facing result, GTM proof, staffing trigger, or fundraising claim.

OPEN WITH
“First we will establish the denominator and status counts. Then we will inspect caveats and owner actions. Unresolved or rejected evidence stays visible; we do not infer beyond the source.”

1. DENOMINATOR AND COUNTING RULES

Before discussing implications, confirm:
- Exact source snapshot and retrieval date.
- Total rows in scope.
- Whether Sarah’s seed_example=true rows are excluded from evidence readouts. They are instructional examples, not evidence.
- Whether rejected-thin rows remain visible and included in the counts. They do.
- Whether blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up remains a separate status. It does.

Status table — fill from the current source; do not estimate:
- not_started: [count]
- done: [count]
- rejected_thin_source_or_date: [count; visible and countable]
- blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up: [count; separate]
- Other/invalid status: [count; resolve before interpreting]
- Total in scope, excluding seed rows: [count]

Reconcile: status counts must sum to the stated denominator. If they do not, stop interpretation and resolve the discrepancy.

2. WHAT “DONE” MEANS

A done row is only counted as complete when it has:
- A named owner.
- Completion status.
- A dated next action.
- Supporting source and date sufficient to support the action.

If any of these are missing, do not silently promote the row to done. Name the exact gap and retain the appropriate status.

3. CAVEAT REVIEW

For each status count, inspect the evidence quality before discussing trends:
- source_freshness_warning is a caveat when the evidence source predates the owner action; it is not an automatic rejection.
- Reject only when the source/date evidence is too thin to support the action.
- Keep rejected-thin rows visible so the readout shows the evidence boundary rather than hiding it.
- Separate a thin source/date problem from a customer follow-up dependency; the latter remains blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up.

4. OWNER-ACTION REVIEW

For each owner, review only the rows that can be grounded in the current source:
- What action is assigned?
- Who owns it?
- What is complete versus still open?
- What is the dated next action?
- What evidence or customer follow-up is still required?

Do not convert an owner’s activity into a product, customer, GTM, staffing, or financing claim.

5. DECISION / CLOSE

Leave the room with:
- Confirmed denominator and reconciled status counts.
- Explicit list of rejected-thin rows that remain visible.
- Explicit list of blocked_waiting_customer_follow_up rows and required customer follow-up.
- Caveats attached to the relevant rows, including source_freshness_warning where applicable.
- Named owners and dated next actions for any follow-up.
- Any unresolved data-quality issue recorded as unresolved, not smoothed over.

PARKING LOT
- Product or GTM conclusions not directly supported by this prototype readout.
- Staffing or fundraising implications.
- Narrative cleanup that obscures rejected or blocked evidence.

CURRENT EVIDENCE NOTE
The available retrieval result did not expose the underlying Compass row-level counts. Populate the bracketed counts from the current mchen-notes-v3/source export before presenting them. Do not present placeholders as results.

[2023-07-25T13:07:00-07:00] Sarah's design-partner questions are the right input for Thursday, but I don't want them dressed up as fundraising collateral.

From: Sarah Kim <sarah@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Cc: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>, Jake <jake@atlas-test.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Jul 2023 08:41:00 -0700
Subject: Mercury design-partner readiness questions

Sending the recurring launch-readiness questions I'm hearing in prospective design-partner conversations. I'm deliberately not naming anyone here because the conversations are still exploratory, but the themes are pretty consistent and seem useful before the Thursday checkpoint.

1) Source setup failure cases
- If the first source connection fails, what does the user actually see?
- Can they tell the difference between auth/permissions trouble, source unavailable/timeout, and an unknown failure without us translating it for them?
- Does recovery look self-serve, or does it feel like they would need vendor/API knowledge to continue?

2) Admin handoff
- If an admin starts setup and then invites an operator or teammate, does the invited person land in a sane next step?
- What happens if the invited member arrives before the first source is fully connected?
- Is the line between "waiting on admin/first source" and "something is broken" obvious?

3) Time to first sync
- How long from first connection to first live sync in the normal case?
- If the sync is queued or retried, what reassures the user that the system is working without inventing fake progress?

4) Which failure states are actually understandable
- Which states are legible on first read to an external user?
- Which ones still make sense only if someone from our side narrates what happened?

5) What evidence creates enough confidence to try Mercury
- a clean first-run path end to end
- one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails
- proof that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle
- clear separation between sample/preview data and real activated state
- a credible sense of time-to-first-sync, even if it's a range rather than a promise

My read is that this is product-readiness input, not deck material. It's basically the bar people are using to decide whether they would be comfortable trying Mercury with a real but bounded workflow.

Create a one-page internal checklist for the Mercury headcount checkpoint: what external launch-readiness feedback we need before deciding any second Mercury engineering req. Keep it as product-readiness input only, not board, investor, or B-round material.

arguments.title: Mercury headcount checkpoint — external launch-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
MERCURY HEADCOUNT CHECKPOINT
External launch-readiness evidence required before deciding on a second Mercury engineering requisition
Internal product-readiness input only — not board, investor, or B-round material

Decision standard
Do not treat design-partner interest or recurring questions as evidence by itself. Before deciding on a second Mercury engineering req, review concrete evidence from bounded, real-user or realistic external design-partner workflows and identify the product gaps that still block a credible first run.

Checklist: evidence we need

[ ] 1. First source connection failure is understandable
    • Capture what an external user sees when the first source connection fails.
    • Distinguish auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown failure without internal narration.
    • Show a self-serve recovery path, or name the precise product gap if recovery still requires vendor/API knowledge.
    Evidence to bring: screenshots or recording of each state, observed user interpretation, recovery outcome.

[ ] 2. Admin-to-operator handoff is sane
    • Test an admin starting setup, then inviting an operator or teammate.
    • Verify the invitee lands on a clear next step, including arrival before the first source is fully connected.
    • Make “waiting on admin/first source” clearly different from “something is broken.”
    Evidence to bring: end-to-end invite path, timing, failure/edge-case notes, and unresolved handoff defects.

[ ] 3. Time to first sync is credible
    • Measure first connection → first live sync in the normal case across more than one bounded workflow where possible.
    • Exercise queued and retried syncs.
    • Confirm the UI reassures users that work is progressing without inventing fake progress or implying a guarantee.
    Evidence to bring: observed range, sample size/workflows, queue/retry behavior, and user comprehension.

[ ] 4. Failure states are legible on first read
    • Ask external participants to interpret setup, waiting, timeout, retry, and unknown-failure states without coaching.
    • Separate states they understand unaided from those that still require someone on our side to narrate.
    Evidence to bring: verbatim interpretations, misread states, severity, and proposed product changes.

[ ] 5. Confidence to try Mercury with a real but bounded workflow
    • Validate a clean first-run path end to end.
    • Show one or two believable recovery examples when setup or sync fails.
    • Demonstrate that invited-member/admin handoff is not brittle.
    • Clearly separate sample/preview data from real activated state.
    • Provide a credible time-to-first-sync range, not a promise.
    Evidence to bring: design-partner notes, observed workflow boundaries, activation/preview screenshots, and explicit blockers.

Headcount decision prompts

• Which gaps are launch blockers versus polish, and what user evidence supports that distinction?
• What additional engineering capacity would remove a specific blocker, rather than merely accelerate general roadmap work?
• If a second req is approved, what measurable product-readiness outcome must it own, by when, and how will we verify it with external users?
• If the evidence is insufficient, what smallest next design-partner test closes the uncertainty before we make the req decision?

Required checkpoint packet

[ ] One compact evidence table: workflow, participant/context, observed behavior, user interpretation, severity, owner, next gate.
[ ] Links to recordings/screenshots and the current build/version used.
[ ] Explicit list of states requiring internal narration.
[ ] Observed time-to-first-sync range with caveats and no roadmap or launch promise.
[ ] Clear recommendation: approve, defer pending evidence, or do not add the second req.

Out of scope

Fundraising narrative, board/investor collateral, B-round positioning, market-sizing, pricing, roadmap promises, and generalized hiring justification. Keep this checkpoint anchored to external product-readiness evidence only.

Give me a 15-min agenda with owner-by-owner prompts, explicit escalation thresholds, and what we should defer until after the holiday week — I don't want Devon becoming the default cleanup path or routine customer work turning into exec escalation.

messages.content:
- 0:00–1:00 — Frame and triage
  - Goal: identify only items needing action before the holiday week ends.
  - For each item, name one accountable owner, the next action, and the date.
  - Default rule: routine customer work stays with the account/support owner; no founder escalation without meeting a threshold.

- 1:00–4:00 — Account/customer owners
  - Prompt: “Which customer item has a concrete risk this week, and what is the next customer-facing action?”
  - Prompt: “Is there an active commitment, renewal risk, outage, or decision deadline—or only an open follow-up?”
  - Prompt: “What can you close directly without Devon or Morgan?”
  - Assign: owner, customer update date, and whether the item remains in the normal account thread.
  - Acme large-export follow-up: keep it as normal documentation/support work unless review identifies a new failure mode; no founder or Product rescue by default.

- 4:00–7:00 — Support/Product/Engineering owners
  - Prompt: “Is this an active reliability, product, security, or data issue, or a documentation/process gap?”
  - Prompt: “What evidence do we have, and what is the smallest action required before the holiday week?”
  - Prompt: “What is explicitly not being fixed or investigated this week?”
  - Do not escalate a single customer annoyance, routine documentation gap, stale follow-up, or known workaround with a named owner.

- 7:00–10:00 — Devon
  - Prompt: “Is there a commercial, procurement, contract, or selective cofounder-judgment question that specifically requires your input?”
  - Prompt: “What decision do you need to make, if any?”
  - Prompt: “Who remains the operating owner after your input?”
  - Devon is not the default cleanup path, customer follow-up owner, or substitute for an unassigned account owner.
  - Route routine customer work back to the account/support owner with a clear date; involve Devon only for the defined commercial or cofounder judgment issue.

- 10:00–13:00 — Morgan/founder escalation check
  - Escalate during the holiday week only if one of these is true:
    - Active production outage, material data loss, security/privacy issue, or legal/compliance exposure.
    - A customer or renewal commitment is at risk within the week and the accountable owner cannot resolve it with available authority.
    - The issue is recurring or reveals a new failure mode, rather than being a known support/documentation matter.
    - A founder-only decision is required on priority, customer commitment, commercial posture, or risk acceptance.
  - Do not escalate merely because:
    - The item is old, uncomfortable, or lacking a perfect update.
    - A customer has not yet replied.
    - The work needs routine cleanup, documentation, scheduling, or account follow-up.
    - Devon’s context would be convenient but is not necessary.
  - For every escalation: state the decision required, consequence of waiting until after the holiday, owner, and proposed recommendation.

- 13:00–15:00 — Lock decisions and defer list
  - Confirm no more than three pre-holiday actions, each with one owner and a due date.
  - Record deferred items explicitly as “after holiday week,” not as silent open work.
  - Defer:
    - Nonurgent documentation and process cleanup.
    - Exploratory product requests and roadmap debates.
    - Broad account reviews without an immediate deadline.
    - Routine customer follow-ups where the normal owner has a credible next step.
    - Any investor, deck, or strategic narrative work not tied to an active decision.
  - Close with: “If none of the escalation thresholds are met, this stays with the operating owner and we revisit after the holiday week.”

arguments.title: May 3 Quarterly All-Hands — Live Q&A Speaker Sheet
arguments.body:
May 3 Quarterly All-Hands — Live Q&A Speaker Sheet

Use short answers. Do not expand into feature timing, enterprise-readiness dates, personnel discussions, or individual-manager/process questions.

1. Nadia / Evergreen ownership

Q: Nadia was cc’d on Evergreen. Is customer ownership moving from Sarah, or does customer growth now own enterprise/customer threads?

A: No ownership change is implied by the cc. Sarah remains the customer owner. Nadia’s inclusion is for customer-growth context and coordination; customer growth does not automatically take over enterprise or customer threads.

Boundary: Do not speculate about future ownership changes or turn a cc into an org announcement.

2. Mercury support evidence

Q: How should teams handle Mercury support evidence without treating every ticket, screenshot, or one-off note as launch evidence?

A: Keep routine tickets, screenshots, and one-off customer notes as normal support signal. Bring evidence into the weekly Mercury truth check when it is material, repeated, and validated enough to change our understanding of usage or readiness. Do not label individual support artifacts as launch evidence by default.

Boundary: This does not create a launch claim or answer feature-timing or enterprise-readiness questions.

3. Kestrel Mercury newsletter

Q: Is the Kestrel Mercury newsletter an external launch marker, funding announcement, or broader go-to-market push?

A: No. The newsletter is not, by itself, a launch marker, funding announcement, or broader go-to-market announcement. Treat it as a communications item; it should not be read as a change in launch status.

Boundary: Do not use the newsletter to infer feature timing, enterprise-readiness dates, or a broader GTM commitment.

4. Atlas backup notes

Q: Are the Atlas backup notes related to Rishi’s outside technical conversations, or are they standard continuity work?

A: They are standard continuity and backup-coverage work. The point is to keep Atlas covered and reduce single-person dependency. There is no personnel or outside-conversation inference to make from the notes.

Boundary: Keep the answer at the coverage-discipline level; do not discuss Rishi’s outside conversations or personnel matters.

Not for live answer

- Mercury feature timing
- Broader enterprise-readiness dates
- Individual-manager or process questions; route these asynchronously through HR

Archive note: April 28, 2023 all-hands

What worked
- The effective format was a demo-day-style interactive show-and-tell.
- Each team received 5 minutes to present.
- The short, concrete team demos got people talking and re-engaged the room.

- The initial IMP-C Q&A attempt fell flat: the room was silent for roughly the first 30 minutes.

Comparison
- Open Q&A depended on people volunteering questions live and produced no useful interaction in the first half hour.
- Five-minute show-and-tells gave each team a defined turn and a concrete prompt, which created participation immediately.

Takeaway
- For future all-hands, prefer interactive, concrete show-and-tell segments over an open Q&A-only format.

Mercury auth v0.2 readout prep

Spent time in the sandbox on the two hosted paths we keep circling for Mercury auth. Not trying to re-open custom auth; this is just the practical readout on where Clerk is clean, where Auth0 is cleaner, and what still feels unresolved before we talk live.

- Sessions
  - Clerk: fastest path to a working session flow. I had middleware + server check working quickly, and the happy path feels boring in a good way.
  - Auth0: also works, but it took more setup to get to the same place. More knobs if we end up needing unusual policy or tenant-specific behavior.
  - Still unproven: session refresh after invite accept or org change.

- Magic links
  - Clerk: easiest end-to-end flow so far. New user + return user behavior was straightforward in the sandbox.
  - Auth0 passwordless: workable, but redirect/state handling was fussier and I hit more did-we-just-lose-the-return-path moments.
  - Need one more pass on link reuse and expiry behavior so support is not guessing on day one.

- Organization invites
  - Clerk's org model maps pretty well to the basic team-invite flow we want.
  - Main edge case: invited person already has a personal workspace, then accepts into a team workspace. That handoff is not fully burned down.
  - Auth0 can do it, but we would own more of the invite and membership stitching ourselves.

- SSO / admin gaps
  - This is still the squishiest area.
  - If Mercury launch only needs normal session auth + invites, Clerk remains the simpler path.
  - If we need deeper admin controls, domain or IdP management, or more enterprise-ish SSO behavior earlier than planned, Auth0 still looks stronger there.

- Pricing caveats
  - Clerk is better on speed right now.
  - I still do not have a satisfying pricing view if usage ramps fast and we end up with a large MAU footprint on top of org features.
  - Auth0 is less pleasant on implementation time, but the enterprise/contract shape may be less surprising later.

- Staging / deploy note
  - If anyone wants to validate either path on staging, please use the standard pipeline.
  - No one-off shortcut for staging auth testing. I do not want to learn the wrong lesson from a path we would not actually ship.

Happy to turn this into a short walkthrough once people have skimmed.

Create an internal pre-read doc for Thursday with the questions and non-decisions. I want scope risks and deploy-discipline checks called out, not a final provider recommendation.

arguments.title: Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read
arguments.body:
Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read

Purpose
This pre-read frames Thursday’s discussion around the practical gaps and risks in the two hosted auth paths tested in the sandbox. It is intentionally not a final provider recommendation and does not reopen custom auth.

What we know so far

- Sessions: Clerk reached a working middleware/server-check flow faster. Auth0 works but required more setup and exposes more policy/tenant configuration.
- Magic links: Clerk was the simpler end-to-end sandbox path. Auth0 passwordless worked but had more redirect/state-handling friction.
- Organization invites: Clerk’s organization model maps well to the basic team-invite flow. Auth0 would leave more invite and membership stitching to us.
- SSO/admin: Auth0 appears stronger for deeper admin controls, domain/IdP management, and earlier enterprise-style SSO needs.
- Pricing: The ramp/MAU economics of Clerk plus org features remain unresolved; Auth0’s implementation cost is higher, while its future enterprise/contract shape may be more predictable.
- Staging validation: Any validation must use the standard deployment pipeline. No one-off staging shortcut should be used for auth testing.

Questions for Thursday

1. Session lifecycle
   - What is the expected behavior when a user accepts an invite or changes organization membership while a session is active?
   - How will refresh, revocation, and re-authentication behave across those transitions?
   - What evidence do we need from each path before calling this flow proven?

2. Magic-link reliability
   - What are the exact link-reuse and expiry semantics for new and returning users?
   - What should support see and do when a link is expired, reused, or associated with the wrong browser/session?
   - What redirect/state guarantees are required so users do not lose the return path?

3. Organization and invite edge cases
   - How do we handle an invitee who already has a personal workspace and then joins a team workspace?
   - What happens when an invite is revoked, resent, accepted twice, or accepted after membership changes?
   - Which membership and workspace invariants must be enforced by the provider versus Mercury?

4. Enterprise/admin scope
   - Is normal session auth plus invites sufficient for the launch scope?
   - Which domain, IdP, admin, audit, or SSO capabilities are launch requirements versus later requirements?
   - What is the earliest credible date by which enterprise requirements could change the implementation choice?

5. Cost and operational shape
   - What usage assumptions should we use for MAU, organizations, and invite volume?
   - What pricing breakpoints or org-feature charges need validation before a provider decision?
   - What support, observability, and incident-response responsibilities remain with Mercury for each path?

6. Validation and rollout
   - What is the smallest staging matrix that exercises sessions, magic links, invite acceptance, org switching, revocation, and failure recovery?
   - Who owns the test evidence and sign-off for each unresolved flow?
   - What must be green in the standard pipeline before auth changes can be promoted?

Non-decisions for this meeting

- No final provider recommendation.
- No reopening of custom/in-house auth.
- No commitment to enterprise SSO, domain management, or advanced admin controls before scope is confirmed.
- No assumption that sandbox success proves refresh, invite/org handoff, link reuse/expiry, or production-scale behavior.
- No pricing or MAU commitment until usage assumptions and provider pricing details are validated.
- No staging validation through one-off deploys, direct kubectl, or other paths that differ from the path we would ship.
- No launch approval based solely on the happy path; failure, recovery, and support workflows remain part of the acceptance bar.

Scope risks to resolve or explicitly accept

- Session refresh and state continuity after invite acceptance or organization changes are unproven.
- Personal-workspace to team-workspace handoff may create duplicate, orphaned, or incorrectly scoped membership state.
- Magic-link reuse, expiry, and redirect/state behavior could create avoidable support load or account-access confusion.
- Auth0’s additional flexibility may expand implementation and ownership scope if requirements are not bounded.
- Clerk’s MAU/org-feature economics may become less predictable at higher usage.
- Enterprise SSO/admin requirements could arrive after implementation work has committed us to a less suitable shape.
- Provider-specific failure modes, logs, rate limits, recovery paths, and support tooling have not yet been compared systematically.
- A staging shortcut would give us misleading confidence and increase the risk of shipping an auth path that was not validated through the real deployment controls.

Deploy-discipline checks

- Use the standard/current deployment pipeline for every staging auth validation.
- Confirm the tested commit, environment, configuration, and provider tenant are recorded with the test evidence.
- Do not use direct kubectl or a one-off shortcut for staging auth testing.
- Verify secrets, redirect URLs, callback URLs, and environment separation through the normal configuration path; do not paste or manually mutate production values.
- Record pipeline result, deploy identifier, and rollback path before treating a test as comparable to a ship-ready flow.
- Keep any pre-green notes and findings in the engineering release channel/process until the deployment is green; do not broaden distribution prematurely.
- Define rollback and session invalidation behavior before testing a provider change against shared staging data.

Suggested Thursday outcome

Leave with a bounded validation matrix, named owners for each open question, explicit launch-versus-later scope, and a list of evidence required before the provider decision. The meeting should produce criteria and follow-up work—not a provider selection.

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury onboarding brief
arguments.body:
July 10 start — first-week focus

Purpose
Leo joins as Mercury’s senior technical anchor. His first week should put him directly into the work needed for launch readiness, not a generic codebase-ramp or meet-and-greet schedule.

First-week emphasis
- Mercury release discipline: understand the current release path, staging/validation expectations, ownership at each gate, and where release decisions or handoffs are still informal. Have Leo identify the smallest concrete improvements that make the next release safer and more repeatable.
- Platform seams: map the boundaries between product engineering and infrastructure, especially the points where auth/session, organization invites, activation, connectors, and related platform behavior meet Mercury. Pair on the seams that are most likely to create launch risk rather than assigning isolated feature work.
- Launch readiness: review the current launch-readiness signals, known blockers, operational gaps, and the evidence expected before launch. Leo should leave the week with a short, prioritized view of risks, owners, and next actions.

Handoff points
- Jake: give Leo the product/engineering context behind Mercury’s release-discipline needs, the current launch tradeoffs, and the open decisions or risks that need senior technical ownership. Jake should align with Leo on what “ready” means without presupposing the earlier two-senior hiring plan.
- Priya: coordinate the first-week schedule and onboarding flow, and hand over the working context from the Mercury activation/onboarding review. Priya should connect Leo with the people and recurring decision forums he needs, while keeping the schedule focused on launch-readiness work.
- Marcus: provide the implementation-level walkthrough of Mercury’s current platform seams and release path, including known handoff friction between product engineering and infrastructure. Leo and Marcus should identify where ownership, validation, or observability needs to be tightened before launch.

Hiring context
Do not force the second Mercury engineering hire before July launch-readiness feedback is available. Leo’s first-week observations and the July launch signals should inform whether a second hire is needed; the previous two-senior hiring plan is not an automatic commitment.

What this should feel like
A working week in the Mercury release and launch-readiness loop: focused pairing, concrete handoffs, and an initial risk/ownership map—not a generic “meet everyone” or “ramp on the codebase” program.

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

Date: July 10, 2023
Owner: Leo Park

Purpose

Keep Leo’s first month narrow, concrete, and useful: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a parallel process.

First-month center of gravity

- Work in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood.
- Identify where launch risk is actually hiding, where evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood or launch decisions.
- First useful output: an evidence-grounded release-risk readout—not abstract platform recommendations or a rewrite plan.
- Use the existing operating cadence. Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work is surfaced and forced to closure.
- Keep working material in internal docs, blockers, and owner tracking rather than investor-style packaging.

Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly / blockers

Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Its agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps; work that is not tied to launch readiness generally does not belong there.

Current blocker shape is primarily seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real product states behave as the design says they do. The current auth v0.2 baseline for internal builds is Clerk for sessions, magic links, and organization invites. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope.

There is no production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on:
- session path
- magic-link flow
- organization-invite flow

Org-invite / invited-member behavior remains a watch area because rendering depends on the correct server-role + source-state combination.

Retention and activation reporting have two audiences:
- directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions
- sturdier quarterly cohort views for board / investor use

Do not mix those audiences. In the weekly, point to risk and missing evidence; do not reopen settled product or design calls unless there is real launch impact.

Priya handoff — Figma / activation-onboarding source of truth

Priya’s Mercury activation surface v0.2 file and activation/onboarding frames are Leo’s starting point. Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file.

Key states to internalize first:
- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

Locked design logic:
- Sample data is preview-only and must remain visually separate from anything that looks activated.
- Invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state.
- Queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA.
- Failed sync uses normalized buckets and clear UI language, not raw vendor strings.

Locked CTA labels:
- No source: “Connect a data source”
- Invited member: “View setup guide”
- Queued: no primary CTA
- Failed: “Try again”

When something feels risky, point to the exact state/frame and the user consequence—not a general taste argument.

Marcus handoff — release-readiness checklist / thin evidence

Marcus’s focus is release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality—not reopening design ownership.

Be skeptical of “we saw it once in staging.” For each relevant path, distinguish among:
- behavior with repeated evidence
- behavior that only looks okay in demos or screenshots
- behavior technically implemented but still under-proven for launch

The release-risk readout should call out:
- seam risk
- severity
- evidence that exists now
- the one additional direct check still needed, where applicable

Separate true blockers from later cleanup or polish. Do not turn every rough edge into launch drama, but do not wave through regressions or states that mislead users.

Working expectations

- Stay centered on Mercury rather than broad platform abstraction work.
- Bring launch-critical risk, missing evidence, decisions, and owner gaps to Mercury weekly.
- Ground conclusions in direct checks and repeatable dogfood evidence.
- Preserve the existing ownership boundaries: use Figma reviews for design decisions and the release-readiness checklist for implementation/evidence gates.

Initial deliverable

A concise release-risk readout grounded in evidence, focused on activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams, with explicit user consequence, severity, evidence status, and next verification step.

Not abstract platform recommendations or a rewrite plan.

[2023-07-26T10:21:00-07:00] Devon's pre-checkpoint note is useful, but I want the meeting aimed at a rule rather than a vibe.

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Date: Wed, Jul 26, 2023 8:14 AM
Subject: Thursday Mercury headcount checkpoint

Morgan —

Ahead of Thursday's checkpoint, here's the frame I want us using so we don't spend the whole slot rehashing the month.

1) Candidate pipeline is stale.
Anything that looked interesting in June has either cooled off, drifted out of Mercury scope, or is not close enough to matter for an immediate decision. If we reopen now, we should be honest that we're effectively starting a fresh search, not pulling the trigger on a near-close candidate.

2) Jake still wants another senior engineer.
I get why. The argument is depth, less key-person risk, and another person who can independently carry ugly launch-critical issues if Leo turns up more real seams in auth/session/platform edges.

3) The new information is that Leo is finding actual seams, not writing a platform thesis.
That is a point in favor of letting the current shape settle. His readout was useful because it surfaced real Mercury risk, and the new ledger is already making that work more concrete.

4) Waiting also has a cost.
If we wait until late August and then decide we do need help, we will have burned time and the market does not get easier just because we were hesitant.

The thing I do not want Thursday to become is another "let's revisit in a few weeks" conversation with no trigger. We have done enough calendar-based decision making on this.

What I want out of the checkpoint is a rule:
- what evidence would mean "open the req now,"
- what evidence would mean "current team shape is enough through launch," and
- if we do reopen, what profile are we actually opening for.

Sarah Kim's design-partner questions are useful input here. The ones that feel most decision-relevant to me are:
- can an external admin get through setup without us narrating it,
- do invited-member/admin handoff states make sense,
- are failure states understandable and recoverable,
- does time-to-first-sync feel trustworthy enough to a real user.

If those are still muddy, I think that argues for using external readiness feedback before deciding profile. And if we do reopen, I don't think the answer should default to "another senior engineer because that was the old plan." The real options are at least:
- another senior engineer,
- a stronger mid-level implementer for launch cleanup / follow-through,
- or no immediate hire.

Not trying to decide it over email; just want the meeting pointed at the actual choice.

— Devon

Turn this into focused checkpoint questions for me. Do not decide the req in the prep. I want the questions to force the evidence triggers: what would justify opening now, what would show the current team is enough through launch, and if we do reopen, whether the profile is senior, mid-level implementer, or no immediate hire.

Mercury headcount checkpoint — focused question stack

1. Establish the evidence
- What has changed since the last checkpoint that is relevant to the hiring decision?
- Which findings from Leo’s risk readout are confirmed, and which are still hypotheses?
- What does the launch-readiness ledger show about work that is genuinely launch-critical versus work that can wait?
- Are we evaluating a staffing constraint, a product-readiness constraint, or both?

2. Test the “open the req now” trigger
- What specific evidence would justify opening a requisition now rather than waiting?
- Is there launch-critical work that the current team cannot cover without creating unacceptable schedule, reliability, or key-person risk?
- Which risks remain after assigning the current team’s available capacity?
- What evidence would show that an additional person would materially reduce those risks soon enough to matter?
- Would the role address an observed bottleneck, or are we reopening because the old hiring plan still exists?
- What would count as a sufficient threshold: a particular number of uncovered critical workstreams, a sustained capacity gap, or a specific launch-risk condition?

3. Test the “current team is enough through launch” trigger
- What evidence would allow us to say the current team is sufficient through launch?
- Can the current team cover the remaining launch-critical work with explicit owners and credible timing?
- Are Leo’s identified auth, session, or platform seams understood well enough to manage without another senior engineer?
- Which risks can be handled through sequencing, scope control, or temporary focus rather than hiring?
- What would make the current-team conclusion falsifiable?
- What leading signal would cause us to reopen the decision before launch rather than waiting for a calendar date?

4. Use external readiness as evidence
- Can an external admin complete setup without someone from Scaffold narrating the path?
- Do invited-member and admin handoff states make sense on first read?
- Are failure states understandable and recoverable to an external user?
- Can we point to one or two believable setup or sync recovery examples?
- Does the first-run path feel clean and bounded enough for a real design partner to try?
- Can we provide a credible time-to-first-sync range rather than an unconditional promise?
- Are sample or preview data clearly separated from the real activated state?
- Which of these answers would change the staffing conclusion, and which are product work regardless of headcount?

5. If we reopen, determine the profile from evidence
- What unmet need are we hiring for: architectural ownership, independent handling of launch-critical ambiguity, or execution capacity?
- What work specifically requires senior-level judgment and ownership?
- What work is well-defined enough for a strong mid-level implementer to take through launch?
- If the problem is follow-through and cleanup rather than system design, why would a senior hire be necessary?
- If the problem is risk discovery across auth/session/platform seams, what evidence shows that another senior engineer—not better sequencing or current-team focus—is the right response?
- What responsibilities would the new hire own in the first 30–60 days?
- What evidence would rule out the senior profile?
- What evidence would rule out the mid-level implementer profile?
- Under what conditions is “no immediate hire” the correct profile decision?

6. Close with an explicit rule
- What is the exact “open now” trigger?
- What is the exact “current team is enough through launch” trigger?
- What is the trigger for revisiting the decision, independent of a calendar date?
- If we reopen, which evidence determines senior versus mid-level implementer?
- Who owns collecting each missing piece of evidence, and by when?
- What decision will we record at the end of the checkpoint, and what evidence would change it?

- Still wants more senior depth.
- Concern is not abstract headcount; it is too much launch-critical ambiguity resting on a small set of people.

Devon's view
- Agrees the risk is real, but the pipeline does not support a reflex reopen.
- Reopening now means starting a fresh search from zero, not converting an active pipeline.
- Wants a decision rule tied to product-readiness evidence, not another calendar reminder.

Morgan's view
- July's actual signal is that Leo is finding the right seams.
- The new ledger gives the team one place to track launch readiness instead of burying risk in PRs, Figma comments, or Discord threads.
- The missing input is external launch-readiness feedback: can real users navigate setup, invited-member/admin handoff, failure recovery, and first-sync confidence without hand-holding.
- Do not force the old two-senior shape just because that used to be the plan.
- Keep this as launch-readiness operating logic, not an investor story.

Agreed owner split (unchanged)
- Marcus owns implementation gates and dogfood blockers.
- Priya owns design decisions / Figma source of truth.
- Leo owns cross-service platform-seam risk notes.
- Jake uses the ledger in the Mercury weekly.

Decision
- Do not reopen the second Mercury engineering req now.
- Do not set another arbitrary month-end revisit date.
- Revisit only after external launch-readiness feedback from design-partner conversations and trials is in hand.

Decision rule for the next req
1. Open a senior-engineer req if external feedback shows repeated platform / architecture-seam failures that need independent senior ownership to unblock launch confidence.
2. Open a more implementation-heavy mid-level req if the core user path is understandable but the limiting factor is cleanup throughput, follow-through, and launch hardening.
3. Open no immediate req if external users can get through setup, admin handoff, early sync, and failure recovery with manageable issues that the current owner split can close from the ledger.

Specific evidence required before reopening the question
- source setup failure cases seen by external users
- admin / invited-member handoff clarity
- time-to-first-sync comfort / trust
- which failure states are understandable vs confusing
- whether the remaining blockers look like depth problems or execution-throughput problems

Follow-up note
- Pipeline can stay cold until the external feedback points clearly to a profile.
- This replaces the old "revisit after July" placeholder with an evidence trigger.

Mercury October package — consolidated owner pass

Overall: keep the stronger-than-May story, but separate what is shareable from what is operating evidence. Suggested status labels below.

(a) Okay for short-list diligence, with caveats
• Table A: keep the corrected definition directly underneath: activated = real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed within 7 days; sample_import_completed alone and invite_sent alone do not count. Include completed windows only; exclude Oct 25–31 from the external trend.
• Table C: keep as mature-cohort evidence only. Say mature cohorts are tracking better than May, with the windowing and small/noisy base explicit. Do not characterize October retention as proven or solved.
• One aggregate live-sync line can travel: 21/37 completed-window workspaces reached first_live_sync_completed within 7 days in the Oct 1–24 cut. Do not use the 24/46 observed real_source_connected row as an external proof metric because it includes incomplete windows; keep the 18-minute median and support/stall counts out unless we define the denominator and purpose more clearly.
• Evergreen: use the second-admin pass only as a bounded enterprise-pattern example for the current flow (org invite → magic link → preview/sample data → real-source connection → first live sync). It demonstrates reduced admin friction in that path; it does not demonstrate enterprise completeness or generalize beyond the group.

(b) Internal only
• October weekly cuts (Table B): useful for operating decisions, not an external packet or appendix.
• Sample-preview-only stop diagnostic: retain for internal diagnosis, not as a shareable proof row.
• Small-n Evergreen directional box (2/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2): internal only; do not present as outside proof.
• MER-1279 and the ticket-by-ticket launch-readiness rows: internal operating evidence only, not external proof.
• Expansion Table D: keep internal for now or summarize only as uneven/incomplete signal; do not use it to imply a repeatable expansion motion while Sep/Oct windows are open.

(c) Rewrite
• Replace “retention has turned the corner,” “solved the activation and retention issues,” and “expansion is starting to look repeatable.” Also remove any wording that makes SSO, audit/change history, or admin-vs-billing-owner separation sound closed.
• Recommended center of gravity: “Mercury’s activation is materially stronger than the corrected May baseline, and mature cohorts are tracking better on early retention. The Evergreen second-admin pass is a bounded example that the current preview-to-live flow is becoming less brittle, while expansion remains uneven and enterprise-readiness follow-through is still being tightened.”
• Keep the enterprise-gaps page adjacent to the progress pages. Frame it as explicit scope and follow-up—not a defensive memo and not a near-term product promise.

Evergreen wording: retain the qualitative operating read (same-day invite acceptance, no resend, one remaining ownership question, and clearer live-sync status still needed). Label it illustrative and bounded; omit the small-n scorecard.

Final packet shape: narrative + Table A + Table C + bounded Evergreen example + separate enterprise-readiness gaps page. No weekly cuts, diagnostics, small-n scorecard, or non-external Linear rows.

arguments.title: Mercury product offsite — May 12 working agenda
arguments.body:
Mercury product offsite — May 12 working agenda

Purpose
This is an operating offsite, not a launch narrative or deck rehearsal.

Decisions to make
1. Launch scope: confirm what Mercury will ship by the end of Q2 and what is explicitly cut or deferred.
2. Activation/onboarding: decide which setup and first-value changes are in scope, and which UX cleanup is not.
3. Admin rollout: decide which admin issues are launch blockers versus follow-up work.
4. Retention instrumentation: agree which evidence is reliable enough to operate on, which caveats remain, and what must be true before broader claims are made.
5. Checkpoint: set the next review date and the evidence required at that checkpoint.

Cuts and scope
- Confirm the cut list and the rationale for each cut.
- Separate launch-critical setup/admin work from nice-to-have polish and one-off fixes.
- Do not add narrative slides, launch-story framing, or deck-rehearsal work to the offsite.

Blockers to resolve
- Activation/onboarding: valid setup order, first-success state after partial setup, and whether fallback paths are real product paths or edge-case patches.
- Invites: explicit outcomes for already-in-workspace, pending, failed, and otherwise restricted invites.
- Admin: invite reliability, permission confusion, account-level controls, and the engineering permission boundary behind role copy.
- Retention: mapping/instrumentation gaps that could change the readout or make a cut unsafe to operate on.

Owners
- Activation/onboarding: Priya — bring the unresolved product-intent and implementation-constraint questions; record the final scope decision.
- Admin/permissions: Engineering owner — confirm the actual permission boundary and owner for each admin blocker.
- Retention instrumentation: Anna — identify solid versus moving cuts and the caveats attached to each.
- Scope and cut list: Product lead — maintain the single decision log and flag anything that is not launch-critical.
- Follow-through: Each blocker owner — document the next action, due date, dependency, and evidence of resolution before the next checkpoint.

Working output
Leave with one operating page containing:
- launch-critical decisions
- explicit cuts and deferrals
- each blocker and its owner
- dependencies and next actions
- evidence required to determine whether the launch work is working

Timing
- Opening: review decisions and operating constraints.
- Working sessions: activation/onboarding, admin blockers, and retention instrumentation.
- Close: read back decisions, cuts, owners, blockers, and the next checkpoint.

The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities.
