Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist
Working session: January 21, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose and boundary
- Test whether a narrow set of signals produces a named action; do not build a prettier internal dashboard.
- Not building: a board dashboard, a new hiring lane, a general metrics layer, or a new product surface/platform while January Mercury activation is active.
- Jake owns keeping Compass narrow and subordinate to January Mercury activation.

Owner checklist

[ ] Renewal-risk / admin-friction — Anna + Nadia
    Signal: A specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion linked to a named account; do not collapse product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one risk bucket.
    Trigger/action: Nadia turns it into a named account-owner follow-up or account-team script addressing the specific friction; a category-only label remains internal FYI.
    Who sees it: First Nadia and the account owner; Anna sees the definition/caveat bundle. Do not circulate beyond the current team until the evidence and source-quality bars below are met.
    Evidence/caveat: Separate customer statement, support readout, observed account state, and internal interpretation; state what is known versus inferred. Define the minimum evidence package before Nadia permits an account-team script.
    Source-quality requirement: Sarah must rate the underlying account-thread note reliable, mixed, or too thin and provide provenance. Mixed notes carry an explicit caveat; too-thin notes stay internal.
    Not building: no generic renewal-risk score, dashboard tile, or risk category without a named follow-up.

[ ] Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt — Nadia + Jake + Leo
    Signal: First live sync is actually live, with teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough to ground a next step.
    Trigger/action: Nadia creates the smallest customer-growth/account-team prompt that changes the next action after first real traction; do not fire early or use generic upsell language.
    Who sees it: First Nadia and the account team for the relevant account; Jake gates scope. No broader audience until Leo completes the seam check.
    Evidence/caveat: Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage; record the live-sync state and the visible invite/admin-role evidence.
    Source-quality requirement: Leo checks that the data/platform seam and underlying event path are defendable before the signal leaves the current team; Sarah's source-quality bar applies where account notes are used.
    Not building: no new product surface, metrics view, or expansion dashboard.

[ ] Account-note source quality — Sarah + Anna + Nadia
    Signal: A provenance-labeled account note that can support follow-up: customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation.
    Trigger/action: Sarah marks each note reliable, mixed, or too thin; Anna attaches the caveat; Nadia uses it for outreach only when the bar is met. Weak notes remain internal or explicitly caveated.

    Evidence/caveat: Preserve traceability to the thread and separate the source types; record what is known, what is inferred, and any conflict or missing context.
    Source-quality requirement: Define the required note fields/source tags before this feeds real follow-up; a thin or mushy note cannot support external action.
    Not building: no cleanup project, automated source-quality score, or signal distribution based on untraceable notes.

Cross-signal gate
- [ ] Anna: definitions and caveats travel with every signal; prevent over-reading.
- [ ] Nadia: each signal names the follow-up/script and owner; reject signals that only create a metrics view.
- [ ] Jake: confirm v0.1 does not become a dashboard/platform build while January Mercury activation is active.
- [ ] Leo: complete the data/platform seam check before any signal is shown outside the current team.
- [ ] Sarah: make source hygiene a gating input, not cleanup after the fact.
- [ ] Morgan: keep the first pass narrow and test action, not signal volume.

- Minimum evidence package for renewal-risk/admin-friction to become an account-team script.
- Smallest useful post-first-live-sync prompt that changes behavior without becoming a product surface.
- Required account-note fields/source tags and the exact audience sequence for each signal.

output.link_hint: When referring the user to a session, write its `link` value verbatim inline mid-sentence (it renders as a titled link) — never as markdown, in backticks, on its own line, or next to the title/id/date. To read more around a compact result, scroll: session_search(session_id=..., around_message_id=match_message_id).

session_search.description: Recall past conversations: search or read old Hermes sessions (FTS5), or scroll inside one. Four shapes, picked by args: `query` = discovery (top-N matching sessions, top result fully hydrated); `session_id` + `around_message_id` = scroll (window of messages around an anchor); `session_id` alone = read a whole session — how you resolve an `@session:<profile>/<id>` link (split on '/' into profile + id); no args = browse recent sessions. Results are actual DB messages, no LLM. Searches conversation history ONLY — when the user gave a direct source (URL, file, contact, live system), inspect that first; never conclude 'not found' from history alone. Use for questions about past conversations: 'what did we do about X', 'where did we leave Y'. When referring the user to a session, write its `link` value verbatim inline (it renders as a titled link).

query.description: Search query (discovery shape). Keywords, phrases, or boolean expressions to find in past sessions. Omit to browse recent sessions. Ignored when session_id + around_message_id are set (scroll shape).

limit.description: Discovery shape only. Max sessions to return (default 3, max 10). Bump to 5–10 when the topic likely spans several sessions and you want to pick the right one to scroll into.

sort.description: Discovery shape only. Temporal bias on top of FTS5 ranking: omit for relevance-only (exploratory recall), 'newest' for "where did we leave X", 'oldest' for "how did X start".

detail.description: Discovery shape only. 'adaptive' (default) fully hydrates the top-ranked result and returns only the exact anchor message for lower-ranked results. 'full' returns bookends and the complete anchored window for every result.

session_id.description: Scroll shape. Session to read inside. Use the session_id returned from a prior discovery call. Must be paired with around_message_id.

around_message_id.description: Scroll shape. Message id to center the window on — use match_message_id from a discovery result, or any id from a prior window.

window.description: Scroll shape only. Messages to return on each side of the anchor (anchor itself always included). Clamped to [1, 20]. Default 5.

role_filter.description: Optional. Comma-separated roles to include. Discovery defaults to 'user,assistant' (tool output is usually noise). Pass 'user,assistant,tool' to include tool output (debugging tool behaviour) or 'tool' to search tool output only.

profile.description: Optional. Read sessions from another Hermes profile's database (read-only). Use when resolving an `@session:<profile>/<id>` link: pass the profile segment here with session_id as the id segment. Omit to use the current profile.

Please turn them into a tight internal owner-routing note so the team understands Compass without reading it as a new hiring lane or another board-dashboard project.

Project Compass kickoff notes
Date: January 17, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose of the meeting
- Name the next operating/product push before the January work turns into separate account threads, Mercury cleanup, and board shorthand.
- Use the signals Scaffold already has from internal operating work, but make them useful to customers and customer-growth follow-up instead of turning them into another internal reporting layer.

Working project name
- Project Compass

Why now
- We already have real signal categories showing up in Mercury/Evergreen work.
- The current-state Evergreen packet exists, so enterprise-readiness can be handled as actual evidence instead of vague sales language.
- The team does not want another board dashboard that looks clean internally but does not change what happens in an account.

Project intent
- Turn internal customer-health signals into customer-facing and customer-success/customer-growth follow-up that changes account behavior.
- The point is not to score accounts for internal consumption only.
- The point is to make the signal lead to a next action, better follow-up, or better customer-facing guidance.

Signals currently available from internal operating use
- Retention
- Activation
- Expansion
- Admin friction
- Enterprise readiness
- Account-note quality

Boundary / what Compass is not
- Do not build another board dashboard.
- Do not treat the first version as investor packaging.
- Do not turn this into a generic health-score project.
- Do not let it become a bespoke Evergreen side track.
- Do not use Compass as a reason to open a new hiring lane.
- Stay with the current lightweight staffing model.

Discussion notes

Morgan
- The framing should stay operational and customer-real, not presentation-ready.
- If Compass becomes a prettier internal dashboard, we missed the point.
- Board narrative matters later, but the first job is to make the signals produce better customer behavior and better follow-up.
- Keep the naming clean now so the work does not fragment into separate Mercury, Evergreen, and customer-growth side conversations.

Anna
- Signal definitions need caveats or they will get over-read immediately.
- “Renewal risk” can easily collapse together very different things: actual product weakness, admin handoff confusion, procurement packaging, or ordinary activation drag.
- Admin friction should not be treated as a churn prediction label by default.
- Every Compass signal needs source evidence attached, plus caveats about what the signal does and does not mean.
- Account-note quality is not separate housekeeping; it changes whether any of the other signals are trustworthy.

Nadia
- Useful only if the signal changes follow-up behavior.
- Customer-growth use cases need owner routing, not just visibility.
- A signal without a next action turns into an FYI bucket and then dies.
- The useful categories still look similar to what worked in the earlier Mercury/Evergreen read: activation friction, admin handoff/role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls after first live sync, and true product gaps. Compass should preserve that logic instead of flattening everything into one score.
- Need follow-up that distinguishes evidence from inference so customer-facing outreach does not sound made up.

Jake
- Keep v0.1 narrow enough that it can actually ship or be tested.
- If Compass starts asking for a big new product surface immediately, it will collide with Mercury work and stall.
- Initial product implementation should bias toward lightweight prompts, account workflow support, or a contained product assist rather than a broad new system.
- Anything that drifts into broad admin-policy product or general enterprise-controls work should be called out and kept separate.

Leo
- Data/platform seams need to stay light at first.
- Reuse existing signals and existing event paths where possible.
- Avoid building a separate scoring service or new platform layer just to make the project feel substantial.
- The seam question is: what is the minimum evidence bundle that can move from internal read to customer/action use without breaking trust?
- Need clear boundaries between usage evidence, account-note evidence, and inferred account state.

Sarah
- Current thread notes still mix customer quote, internal interpretation, support follow-up, and procurement context too easily.
- If account-note source quality stays messy, customer-growth follow-up will inherit the confusion.
- Need notes to say what came from the customer directly, what came from usage/readout, and what is internal interpretation.
- Hygiene work matters here because otherwise Compass will look more certain than the underlying record actually is.

Initial v0.1 scope
1. Renewal-risk/admin-friction evidence
- Build a first pass that can show when apparent renewal risk is actually admin friction, setup-control issues, or role confusion.
- Evidence should travel with the signal.
- Avoid binary risk labeling without context.

2. Expansion prompts after first live sync
- Focus on the post-first-live-sync moment.
- Identify what follow-up or prompt should happen after an account reaches first live sync and looks ready for broader usage.
- This is about timely action, not generic upsell language.

3. Cleaner account-note source quality for customer-growth follow-up
- Improve note quality enough that follow-up is based on traceable evidence.
- Source quality should distinguish customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal inference.
- Recency and provenance matter.

Owner split
- Anna Martinez owns signal definitions and caveats.
- Nadia Singh owns customer-growth and customer-success use cases.
- Jake owns product implementation and sequencing.
- Leo Park owns data/platform seams.
- Sarah Kim supplies account-thread hygiene.
- Morgan Chen owns board/customer narrative.

Staffing boundary
- Use the current lightweight staffing model.
- Do not open a new hiring lane for Compass.
- Keep the work inside the existing Nadia/Sarah operating model plus Jake/Leo implementation support.

Rough success test for v0.1
- A signal should trigger a clearer next action.
- The recipient should know why they are seeing it.
- The evidence and caveat should travel with it.
- The signal should improve follow-up quality rather than just improve internal visibility.

Open questions captured in the room
- What is the minimum evidence package that has to travel with each signal?
- Which signals should surface only internally first, and which can become customer-facing quickly?
- What is the smallest useful post-first-live-sync expansion prompt?
- How should admin friction be distinguished from true product gaps and from procurement/security packaging?
- What account-note fields or source tags are required before Nadia can trust a follow-up?
- How much Leo seam work is acceptable before Compass starts stealing too much attention from Mercury?

Immediate takeaways
- Compass is real and named.
- v0.1 stays narrow.
- No board-dashboard build.
- No investor-packaging framing.
- No new hiring lane.
- Owners are clear enough to proceed with a lightweight first pass.

COMPASS v0.1 — TUESDAY WORKING SESSION

Date: Tuesday, January 21, 2025
Participants: Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim
Length: 60 minutes

Outcome
Leave with one lightweight, testable definition for each v0.1 signal: a named action, audience/route, evidence and caveat bundle, minimum account-note/source-quality requirement, and explicit non-build boundary.

Working rule
Separate known evidence from inference. A signal is incomplete if it only creates visibility; it must change a follow-up action or customer-facing guidance.

Agenda

0:00–0:05  Frame and boundaries — Morgan
- Compass turns existing customer-health signals into better account behavior and follow-up.
- Keep v0.1 inside the current lightweight staffing model: Nadia/Sarah for operating and account work; Jake/Leo for implementation and seams.
- Explicitly out: no board dashboard, no investor-packaging surface, no generic health score, no bespoke Evergreen track, and no new hiring lane.

0:05–0:20  Signal 1: Renewal-risk / admin-friction evidence — Anna + Sarah
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Distinguish admin handoff, setup-control, role confusion, activation drag, procurement/security packaging, and true product gap before routing.
- Who sees it? Set internal owner and decide whether any version is safe for customer-facing use.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? No context-free or binary “renewal risk” label; state what is observed versus inferred.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Require provenance, recency, and source type (customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation).
- What are we explicitly not building? No churn-prediction score, broad admin-policy product, or general enterprise-controls system.

0:20–0:35  Signal 2: Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt — Nadia + Jake
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Define the smallest timely follow-up when an account appears ready for broader usage; avoid generic upsell language.
- Who sees it? Name the customer-success/customer-growth owner and any internal handoff; specify what stays internal first.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? Include first-live-sync evidence and the readiness basis; do not present customer pull as committed demand.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Record the sync milestone, account context, observed usage, and follow-up outcome with recency/provenance.
- What are we explicitly not building? No expansion-scoring platform, automated upsell campaign, or broad new product surface.

0:35–0:50  Signal 3: Account-note source quality — Sarah + Leo
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Define when to repair, suppress, or route a note before it informs customer-growth follow-up.
- Who sees it? Name the note owner, operating owner, and escalation path when the record is too weak for customer-facing use.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? Preserve the source, provenance, recency, and separation of fact from interpretation; flag missing or conflicting evidence.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Agree the minimum fields/tags and a clear “not enough evidence” state.
- What are we explicitly not building? No separate scoring service, data platform, or reporting/dashboard layer; reuse existing signals and event paths.

0:50–0:58  Cross-signal routing and seam check — all
- Confirm one owner, recipient, next action, evidence bundle, caveat, and minimum note quality for each signal.
- Confirm which signals are internal-only for the test and which can support customer-facing guidance.
- Keep Leo’s seam work limited to what is needed to test these flows without pulling focus from January Mercury activation.

0:58–1:00  Close — Morgan
- Record decisions, unresolved evidence gaps, and the smallest test for each signal.
- Reconfirm: no board dashboard and no new hiring lane.

Definition of done
For each signal, the group has a concrete next action and named route; the recipient knows why it surfaced; evidence and caveat travel with it; source quality is explicit; and the test improves follow-up rather than merely internal visibility.

COMPASS v0.1 — FIRST WORKING-SESSION AGENDA (RECONSTRUCTED)

Reconstructed from the January 17 kickoff and January 21, 2025 working-session notes.

Date: Tuesday, January 21, 2025
Participants: Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim
Length: 60 minutes

Purpose

Leave with one lightweight, testable definition for each Compass v0.1 signal:
- The action it should trigger
- The person or team that sees it first
- The evidence and caveat that travel with it
- The minimum account-note and source-quality requirement
- The explicit limit on what we are not building

Working rule

Compass is complete only when a signal changes a follow-up action or customer-facing guidance. Visibility alone is not a deliverable. Separate known evidence from inference; do not present an inference as a customer fact.

Limits on what we were building

- No investor-packaging surface or presentation-ready narrative as the first product.

messages.content:
[2023-08-01T09:06:00-07:00] Jake’s first-wave shape is finally concrete enough to review with Devon.

Discord group DM — Jake, Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
2023-08-01 08:47 PT

Jake:
Pulled together a first-pass view on the external Mercury design-partner wave.

My proposal is to use Evergreen Bank as the enterprise-shaped candidate in the first wave.

Why Evergreen:
- They are likely to stress the exact admin/security edges we still care about: admin handoff, role/state clarity, auditability questions, and how trustworthy the early sync/failure path feels.
- That gives us a real test of the standard Mercury path without immediately turning the rollout into bespoke build work.
- Put differently: hard enough to expose whether the product is enterprise-ready on the current path, but still within the boundaries of the product we are actually trying to ship.

I’m keeping the rest of the wave deliberately lighter; the enterprise question is whether Evergreen should be the anchor stress case.

On Acme, I would keep them in the not-now column.
- The NDA scope thread is still muddy enough that sending fresh Mercury material feels like asking for a document fight instead of product signal.
- I do still think their prior feedback is useful internally, especially on admin pain, failure-state legibility, and procurement/security questions.
- I would use that feedback to sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279, but not send Acme new packet/screens/notes unless the NDA thread gets narrowed first.

MER-1279 rows this would pressure-test most directly:
- invited-member/admin handoff confidence
- queued-sync trust / retry confidence
- failed-state legibility and recovery
- admin/security questions that show up before anyone asks for one-off treatment

Not calling any of those closed. This is just the cleanest first-wave shape I can see right now.

If you both agree with the direction, I can turn it into a tighter wave outline before the review.

Give me decision questions for that Devon review, not an announcement. I want them to pressure-test three things: why Evergreen Bank is a good enterprise stress case for admin/security without dragging us into bespoke work, what exactly keeps Acme out while the NDA scope thread is unresolved, and which parts of Acme’s prior feedback can still sharpen internal blocker rows in MER-1279 without sending Acme anything fresh.

Devon review — decision questions

1. Evergreen as the enterprise stress case
- What specific admin/security behaviors do we need the first wave to expose?
- Does Evergreen exercise those behaviors through the standard Mercury path, or are we already assuming custom workflow, permissions, integrations, or support?
- What would count as useful enterprise signal from Evergreen without turning their participation into a bespoke implementation?
- Which risks are we intentionally testing now, and which enterprise requirements are explicitly out of scope for this wave?
- What evidence would make us conclude that Evergreen is the wrong anchor—or that the standard path is not ready for this stress case?

2. Why Acme stays out for now
- What exactly remains unresolved in the NDA scope thread?
- Which categories of Mercury material are still unsafe or ambiguous to send under the current scope?
- Is the blocker the legal permission to share, the risk of starting a document-negotiation loop, or both?
- What narrow resolution would be sufficient to reconsider Acme, and who owns getting us there?

arguments.title: Nadia Singh — Final Interview Plan
arguments.body:
NADIA SINGH — FINAL INTERVIEW PLAN

Purpose

Run a tight, evidence-based final loop for the customer-growth role. Test whether Nadia can turn Mercury activation learning into a repeatable operating motion, interpret Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness pressure without creating bespoke commitments, diagnose expansion failure modes, and establish clean handoffs with Sarah and Devon.

This is not a generic VP Sales interview. Do not optimize for conventional enterprise-sales instincts, territory planning, comp design, pipeline theater, or closing a logo at any cost.

Decision to make

Can Nadia build the smallest useful customer-growth system at Scaffold’s current stage while preserving product truth, customer trust, and clear ownership?

Recommended format

Three tightly run conversations, using one shared scenario spine:

1. Morgan Chen + Devon Hayes — Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis (60 minutes)
2. Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim — Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals (45 minutes)
3. Sarah Kim + Morgan Chen — Handoffs, first 90 days, and stage fit (45 minutes)

Hold a same-day debrief immediately after the final conversation. Each interviewer should submit evidence against the scorecard before discussing general impressions.

Candidate opening brief

“Assume Scaffold has meaningful Mercury design-partner signal and a small set of enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven, context is distributed across founders and customer-facing people, and several enterprise-readiness requests are in view. We are looking for how you would build a repeatable customer-growth motion without making product promises that are not internally committed.”

Scenario guardrails for every interviewer

- Dates, quotes, feature promises, and account-specific exceptions are unavailable unless explicitly committed by the appropriate owner.
- Separate packaging/framing, onboarding/workaround, process/owner clarity, and genuine product gaps.
- Do not invite Nadia to negotiate hypothetical roadmap dates.
- Do not frame the exercise as “close the account no matter what.”
- Do not turn the discussion into territory coverage, quota, comp plans, or a conventional VP Sales org-design interview.
- Ask for sequencing, evidence, and ownership—not a complete future-state organization.

1. Mercury activation → repeatable motion

Interviewers: Morgan + Devon
Time: 60 minutes

Prompt

“Mercury has useful design-partner learning and some enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven and founder/customer context is spread across people. Walk us through your first 30, 60, and 90 days to turn that into a working customer-growth rhythm.”

Use the current activation definition: a real source connection or first live sync counts as activation. Invitation acceptance, preview viewing, or source selection alone does not.

Required follow-ups

- What is the minimum evidence set you would request in week one?
- How would you distinguish activation friction from admin/security blockers, procurement friction, expansion stall-outs, and true product deficiency?
- What would you instrument first if telemetry is incomplete?
- What would you personally do with customers versus route to product, founders, Sarah, or Devon?
- What would your weekly or biweekly synthesis and owner-routing cadence look like?
- What would you deliberately not build in the first quarter?

Expansion failure-mode probe

“An account reaches activation but does not broaden. Another is enthusiastic but stalls during setup. A third is active with one champion but loses internal air cover. How would you diagnose these cases, choose leading indicators, and decide whether the intervention is customer work, an internal process fix, better framing, or a product issue?”

Listen for

- Minimum viable evidence rather than a fantasy dashboard.
- A practical sequence from evidence → diagnosis → intervention → owner → review.
- Clear distinction between activation and durable value realization.
- Specific failure modes: champion weakness, admin friction, setup trust, unclear value, procurement drag, poor handoff, and product gaps.
- Comfort with incomplete instrumentation and founder-led context.
- No assumption that customer-growth owns everything customer-related.

2. Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals without bespoke promises

Interviewers: Devon + Sarah
Time: 45 minutes

Prompt

“An Evergreen-like account asks about SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet. Some needs may be addressed through packaging or clearer materials; others may require product work. How would you help the company learn from these signals and communicate credibly without turning each conversation into custom roadmap negotiation?”

Required follow-ups

- Classify each request: framing/materials, onboarding/workaround, owner/process clarity, customer-specific out-of-scope request, or product gap.
- What would you say to the customer today when there is no committed date?
- When do you pull in Devon for commercial/procurement framing?
- When do you preserve Sarah’s ownership of the live customer thread?
- What evidence would change your classification or prioritization?
- How would you capture the pattern so the next account does not restart from zero?

Listen for

- “Current constraint + credible workaround/path + evidence needed to revisit,” not implied certainty.
- Respect for the distinction between a procurement packet and a product commitment.
- Clear escalation triggers and owner boundaries.
- Customer empathy paired with firm product truth.
- A mechanism for aggregating repeated signals without promising that repetition guarantees roadmap priority.
- No “we can probably make that work,” informal dates, or bespoke concessions.

3. Handoffs with Sarah and Devon; first build and stage fit

Interviewers: Sarah + Morgan
Time: 45 minutes

Prompt

“Sketch how you would work with Sarah on live customer threads and with Devon on commercial/procurement framing. Consider a request that is partly packaging, partly a product gap, and partly account education. Who owns what, how is the customer kept informed, and how does the learning become reusable?”

Required follow-ups

- What would you take over, and what would you explicitly leave with the existing owner?
- How would you reduce founder dependence without bypassing the people who currently hold customer context?
- What information must be in the handoff record?
- What is the escalation path when ownership is unclear?
- How would you prevent customer-growth from becoming founder cleanup or reactive deal support?

First-90-day probe

“What support do you need to be effective here, what would you build yourself, and what signals would tell you the motion is becoming repeatable? What would you refuse to build in quarter one?”

Listen for

- Explicit owner boundaries and lightweight operating cadence.
- Respect for live-thread continuity and existing commercial/procurement ownership.
- A bias toward systematizing rather than bypassing or absorbing every decision.
- Realistic support requirements: reliable notes, activation milestones, decision owners, and access to product truth—not a large team or full RevOps stack.
- Sequence over completeness.
- A clear definition of repeatability based on evidence and handoffs, not organizational prestige.

Scoring rubric

Score each dimension 1–4, with written evidence:

4 — Strong evidence: specific, sequenced, stage-appropriate answer; preserves product truth and names owners.
3 — Positive evidence: sound approach with limited gaps that appear coachable.
2 — Mixed evidence: useful instincts but relies on assumptions, vague process, or unclear boundaries.
1 — Concern: defaults to promises, bespoke concessions, generic sales machinery, or ownership blur.

Dimensions

1. Mercury activation reasoning: understands the activation boundary and can convert evidence into a lightweight rhythm.
2. Prioritization under mixed evidence: separates signal types and chooses what to address first.
3. Expansion diagnosis: identifies failure modes and selects practical leading indicators and interventions.
4. Product-promise judgment: communicates constraints without inventing dates, exceptions, or certainty.
5. Enterprise-readiness judgment: distinguishes packaging, process, workaround, and genuine product gaps.
6. Handoff and ownership discipline: works cleanly with Sarah, Devon, product, and founders.
7. Stage fit and first-90-day sequencing: builds what is needed now and deliberately defers what is not.

Debrief format

Complete independently before discussion:

- Strongest evidence for hire:
- Most important unresolved concern:
- Example of product-promise judgment:
- Example of prioritization under mixed evidence:
- Example of clean ownership/handoff thinking:
- Would we trust Nadia with an important customer thread before the company has a mature system? Yes / No / Unclear
- Overall recommendation: Strong yes / Yes / Mixed / No

Debrief rule

Discuss evidence against the seven dimensions first. Do not substitute executive presence, charisma, or generic “VP-level” impression for the scenario-based assessment. If the group is split, identify the exact missing evidence and whether it can be tested in one targeted follow-up rather than expanding the loop.

Topics to avoid

- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- “Close this enterprise logo no matter what.”
- Territory, pipeline, quota, comp-plan, or large-sales-org scaling questions.
- Any prompt that rewards bespoke roadmap promises for Evergreen-like accounts.
- Product-scope debates outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.

Northstar underwrote the round on the bounded story we can actually support: Mercury activation and admin-path improvement are real, the current Evergreen read is useful enterprise signal, hybrid MAU pricing is credible, and we did not need to invent a vanity-growth version of the business to get there.

Why the narrow process was the right call
We kept the path through Sofia and the current Mercury evidence set instead of reopening a broader fundraising process. That let us hold the story to something defensible rather than smoothing over uneven expansion or spending another month creating theatrical price tension. At this point, that trade looks right.

The remaining steps are largely closing mechanics: board consent, signature packet circulation, and final document cleanup. The only substantive governance items left are the Sofia board-seat / board-size mechanics, the written-consent structure, and the matching director-designation language.

Operating implication
This round gives us enough room to operate against the current Mercury / enterprise-expansion path without continuing to manage every decision like a survival bridge. Northstar completed final diligence on the existing Mercury package and is closing an $18M Series B with Scaffold on February 22. The package held because it stayed on current evidence rather than a broadened process story.

The main lesson from this process is that a narrower, defendable path beat extra weeks of fundraising theater. We should treat that as a useful operating constraint even once the money is in.

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 — Tuesday working-session agenda
arguments.body:
COMPASS v0.1 — TUESDAY WORKING SESSION

Date: Tuesday, January 21, 2025
Participants: Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim
Length: 60 minutes

Outcome
Leave with one lightweight, testable definition for each v0.1 signal: a named action, audience/route, evidence and caveat bundle, minimum account-note/source-quality requirement, and explicit non-build boundary.

Working rule
Separate known evidence from inference. A signal is incomplete if it only creates visibility; it must change a follow-up action or customer-facing guidance.

Agenda

0:00–0:05  Frame and boundaries — Morgan
- Compass turns existing customer-health signals into better account behavior and follow-up.
- Keep v0.1 inside the current lightweight staffing model: Nadia/Sarah for operating and account work; Jake/Leo for implementation and seams.
- Explicitly out: no board dashboard, no investor-packaging surface, no generic health score, no bespoke Evergreen track, and no new hiring lane.

0:05–0:20  Signal 1: Renewal-risk / admin-friction evidence — Anna + Sarah
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Distinguish admin handoff, setup-control, role confusion, activation drag, procurement/security packaging, and true product gap before routing.
- Who sees it? Set internal owner and decide whether any version is safe for customer-facing use.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? No context-free or binary “renewal risk” label; state what is observed versus inferred.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Require provenance, recency, and source type (customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation).
- What are we explicitly not building? No churn-prediction score, broad admin-policy product, or general enterprise-controls system.

0:20–0:35  Signal 2: Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt — Nadia + Jake
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Define the smallest timely follow-up when an account appears ready for broader usage; avoid generic upsell language.
- Who sees it? Name the customer-success/customer-growth owner and any internal handoff; specify what stays internal first.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? Include first-live-sync evidence and the readiness basis; do not present customer pull as committed demand.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Record the sync milestone, account context, observed usage, and follow-up outcome with recency/provenance.
- What are we explicitly not building? No expansion-scoring platform, automated upsell campaign, or broad new product surface.

0:35–0:50  Signal 3: Account-note source quality — Sarah + Leo
Decide:
- What action should this trigger? Define when to repair, suppress, or route a note before it informs customer-growth follow-up.
- Who sees it? Name the note owner, operating owner, and escalation path when the record is too weak for customer-facing use.
- What evidence and caveat travel with it? Preserve the source, provenance, recency, and separation of fact from interpretation; flag missing or conflicting evidence.
- What account note/source quality must be true? Agree the minimum fields/tags and a clear “not enough evidence” state.
- What are we explicitly not building? No separate scoring service, data platform, or reporting/dashboard layer; reuse existing signals and event paths.

0:50–0:58  Cross-signal routing and seam check — all
- Confirm one owner, recipient, next action, evidence bundle, caveat, and minimum note quality for each signal.
- Confirm which signals are internal-only for the test and which can support customer-facing guidance.
- Keep Leo’s seam work limited to what is needed to test these flows without pulling focus from January Mercury activation.

0:58–1:00  Close — Morgan
- Record decisions, unresolved evidence gaps, and the smallest test for each signal.
- Reconfirm: no board dashboard and no new hiring lane.

Definition of done
For each signal, the group has a concrete next action and named route; the recipient knows why it surfaced; evidence and caveat travel with it; source quality is explicit; and the test improves follow-up rather than merely internal visibility.

Devon Hayes and Sarah Kim own current-state commercial and procurement packaging, using shipped or current product facts only. Jake and Leo provide current product facts and seam-risk input; they must not backdoor roadmap promises into customer material.

No Evergreen-specific commitments, feature dates, or enterprise add-on quoting before the relevant work ships. Evergreen Bank remains a useful stress case for the current path, not a reason to turn wave-one learning into bespoke-build behavior.

The enterprise-readiness review remains a separate lane from current Mercury release work. Sarah keeps the customer-coordination lane; owners now take back their operating lanes.

Board and investor follow-through
The first post-close board framing will focus on defensible retention evidence and repeatable enterprise expansion learned through Mercury and Evergreen—not a rush to spin a Series C story. MER-1279 and Leo Park’s risk readout are internal operating evidence, not board or investor proof claims.

Anna Martinez and Morgan Chen will keep the board pack tight: retention truth, expansion truth, and bounded enterprise-readiness next steps.

Hiring decision
The second Mercury engineering requisition is not reopened.

The first new search to scope is a customer-growth / GTM leader—not an immediate Mercury engineering search. The role is intended to build a repeatable customer-growth motion from Mercury- and Evergreen-like pull without turning accounts into bespoke commitments or product-roadmap negotiating sessions.

Devon Hayes and HR will draft the initial role description. Morgan reviews it before it goes beyond the small reset group.

If Mercury engineering hiring is reconsidered later, the existing evidence rule applies:
• Senior hire for repeated platform or architecture seam failures requiring independent ownership
• Implementation-heavy mid-level hire for hardening or throughput constraints
• No requisition if the current split can close the remaining work

Near-term cadence
• Keep the short weekly Mercury truth check focused on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and material product change.
• Keep enterprise-readiness review as a separate lane from Mercury release work.
• Close-thread handoff is complete: Sarah retains customer coordination, while operating owners resume their respective lanes.

Core decisions to carry forward
Mercury ownership is explicit. Enterprise-readiness scope is bounded. No one should use the close as permission to describe Mercury as enterprise-ready now or to reopen every deferred initiative.

arguments.title: Nadia Singh — Final Interview Plan
arguments.body:
NADIA SINGH — FINAL INTERVIEW PLAN

Purpose

Run a tight, evidence-based final loop for the customer-growth role. Test whether Nadia can turn Mercury activation learning into a repeatable operating motion, interpret Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness pressure without creating bespoke commitments, diagnose expansion failure modes, and establish clean handoffs with Sarah and Devon.

This is not a generic VP Sales interview. Do not optimize for conventional enterprise-sales instincts, territory planning, comp design, pipeline theater, or closing a logo at any cost.

Decision to make

Can Nadia build the smallest useful customer-growth system at Scaffold’s current stage while preserving product truth, customer trust, and clear ownership?

Recommended format

Three tightly run conversations, using one shared scenario spine:

1. Morgan Chen + Devon Hayes — Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis (60 minutes)
2. Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim — Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals (45 minutes)
3. Sarah Kim + Morgan Chen — Handoffs, first 90 days, and stage fit (45 minutes)

Hold a same-day debrief immediately after the final conversation. Each interviewer should submit evidence against the scorecard before discussing general impressions.

Candidate opening brief

“Assume Scaffold has meaningful Mercury design-partner signal and a small set of enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven, context is distributed across founders and customer-facing people, and several enterprise-readiness requests are in view. We are looking for how you would build a repeatable customer-growth motion without making product promises that are not internally committed.”

Scenario guardrails for every interviewer

- Dates, quotes, feature promises, and account-specific exceptions are unavailable unless explicitly committed by the appropriate owner.
- Separate packaging/framing, onboarding/workaround, process/owner clarity, and genuine product gaps.
- Do not invite Nadia to negotiate hypothetical roadmap dates.
- Do not frame the exercise as “close the account no matter what.”
- Do not turn the discussion into territory coverage, quota, comp plans, or a conventional VP Sales org-design interview.
- Ask for sequencing, evidence, and ownership—not a complete future-state organization.

1. Mercury activation → repeatable motion

Interviewers: Morgan + Devon
Time: 60 minutes

Prompt

“Mercury has useful design-partner learning and some enterprise-leaning accounts, but activation evidence is uneven and founder/customer context is spread across people. Walk us through your first 30, 60, and 90 days to turn that into a working customer-growth rhythm.”

Use the current activation definition: a real source connection or first live sync counts as activation. Invitation acceptance, preview viewing, or source selection alone does not.

Required follow-ups

- What is the minimum evidence set you would request in week one?
- How would you distinguish activation friction from admin/security blockers, procurement friction, expansion stall-outs, and true product deficiency?
- What would you instrument first if telemetry is incomplete?
- What would you personally do with customers versus route to product, founders, Sarah, or Devon?
- What would your weekly or biweekly synthesis and owner-routing cadence look like?
- What would you deliberately not build in the first quarter?

Expansion failure-mode probe

“An account reaches activation but does not broaden. Another is enthusiastic but stalls during setup. A third is active with one champion but loses internal air cover. How would you diagnose these cases, choose leading indicators, and decide whether the intervention is customer work, an internal process fix, better framing, or a product issue?”

Listen for

- Minimum viable evidence rather than a fantasy dashboard.
- A practical sequence from evidence → diagnosis → intervention → owner → review.
- Clear distinction between activation and durable value realization.
- Specific failure modes: champion weakness, admin friction, setup trust, unclear value, procurement drag, poor handoff, and product gaps.
- Comfort with incomplete instrumentation and founder-led context.
- No assumption that customer-growth owns everything customer-related.

2. Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals without bespoke promises

Interviewers: Devon + Sarah
Time: 45 minutes

Prompt

“An Evergreen-like account asks about SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet. Some needs may be addressed through packaging or clearer materials; others may require product work. How would you help the company learn from these signals and communicate credibly without turning each conversation into custom roadmap negotiation?”

Required follow-ups

- Classify each request: framing/materials, onboarding/workaround, owner/process clarity, customer-specific out-of-scope request, or product gap.
- What would you say to the customer today when there is no committed date?
- When do you pull in Devon for commercial/procurement framing?
- When do you preserve Sarah’s ownership of the live customer thread?
- What evidence would change your classification or prioritization?
- How would you capture the pattern so the next account does not restart from zero?

Listen for

- “Current constraint + credible workaround/path + evidence needed to revisit,” not implied certainty.
- Respect for the distinction between a procurement packet and a product commitment.
- Clear escalation triggers and owner boundaries.
- Customer empathy paired with firm product truth.
- A mechanism for aggregating repeated signals without promising that repetition guarantees roadmap priority.
- No “we can probably make that work,” informal dates, or bespoke concessions.

3. Handoffs with Sarah and Devon; first build and stage fit

Interviewers: Sarah + Morgan
Time: 45 minutes

Prompt

“Sketch how you would work with Sarah on live customer threads and with Devon on commercial/procurement framing. Consider a request that is partly packaging, partly a product gap, and partly account education. Who owns what, how is the customer kept informed, and how does the learning become reusable?”

Required follow-ups

- What would you take over, and what would you explicitly leave with the existing owner?
- How would you reduce founder dependence without bypassing the people who currently hold customer context?
- What information must be in the handoff record?
- What is the escalation path when ownership is unclear?
- How would you prevent customer-growth from becoming founder cleanup or reactive deal support?

First-90-day probe

“What support do you need to be effective here, what would you build yourself, and what signals would tell you the motion is becoming repeatable? What would you refuse to build in quarter one?”

Listen for

- Explicit owner boundaries and lightweight operating cadence.
- Respect for live-thread continuity and existing commercial/procurement ownership.
- A bias toward systematizing rather than bypassing or absorbing every decision.
- Realistic support requirements: reliable notes, activation milestones, decision owners, and access to product truth—not a large team or full RevOps stack.
- Sequence over completeness.
- A clear definition of repeatability based on evidence and handoffs, not organizational prestige.

Scoring rubric

Score each dimension 1–4, with written evidence:

4 — Strong evidence: specific, sequenced, stage-appropriate answer; preserves product truth and names owners.
3 — Positive evidence: sound approach with limited gaps that appear coachable.
2 — Mixed evidence: useful instincts but relies on assumptions, vague process, or unclear boundaries.
1 — Concern: defaults to promises, bespoke concessions, generic sales machinery, or ownership blur.

Dimensions

1. Mercury activation reasoning: understands the activation boundary and can convert evidence into a lightweight rhythm.
2. Prioritization under mixed evidence: separates signal types and chooses what to address first.
3. Expansion diagnosis: identifies failure modes and selects practical leading indicators and interventions.
4. Product-promise judgment: communicates constraints without inventing dates, exceptions, or certainty.
5. Enterprise-readiness judgment: distinguishes packaging, process, workaround, and genuine product gaps.
6. Handoff and ownership discipline: works cleanly with Sarah, Devon, product, and founders.
7. Stage fit and first-90-day sequencing: builds what is needed now and deliberately defers what is not.

Debrief format

Complete independently before discussion:

- Strongest evidence for hire:
- Most important unresolved concern:
- Example of product-promise judgment:
- Example of prioritization under mixed evidence:
- Example of clean ownership/handoff thinking:
- Would we trust Nadia with an important customer thread before the company has a mature system? Yes / No / Unclear
- Overall recommendation: Strong yes / Yes / Mixed / No

Debrief rule

Discuss evidence against the seven dimensions first. Do not substitute executive presence, charisma, or generic “VP-level” impression for the scenario-based assessment. If the group is split, identify the exact missing evidence and whether it can be tested in one targeted follow-up rather than expanding the loop.

Topics to avoid

- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- “Close this enterprise logo no matter what.”
- Territory, pipeline, quota, comp-plan, or large-sales-org scaling questions.
- Any prompt that rewards bespoke roadmap promises for Evergreen-like accounts.
- Product-scope debates outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.

arguments.title: Mercury operating and offsite decisions — activation, invites, and first value
arguments.body:
Mercury — decision agenda for operating/offsite review
Source: Customer Success blocker digest, May 8–9, 2023 (received May 10)

Purpose
Turn the setup blocker pattern into decisions and owners, not a narrative summary. The common issue is uncertainty during setup: users do not know which path is valid, whether an action succeeded, or who should act next.

Decision 1 — Activation path after workspace creation
Evidence:
- 7 accounts hit activation dead ends.
- Users stall at the first connect/import/continue choice.
- Failed or skipped connector attempts can leave an empty state that looks unfinished and offers no clear next action.
- “Connect data” reads as mandatory even for sample-data or manual-setup paths.
- 3 accounts required manual CSM intervention; 2 questioned whether rollout was still in beta.

Decision required:
Do we redesign the post-workspace state to offer explicit, equivalent paths (connect data, use sample data, or manual setup), with a recoverable fallback after connector failure, instead of implying one required order?

Questions to resolve:
- What is the default first-value path for a new workspace?
- After a failed connection, should the primary action be retry, switch method, or continue without a connector?
- What state and confirmation make it clear what was saved and what remains?

Proposed owner: Product + Engineering, with Customer Success validation.
Acceptance signal: a new admin always sees one unambiguous next action and can reach first value without CSM intervention, including after a failed or skipped connector.

Decision 2 — Invite send and invite-state contract
Evidence:
- 5 accounts reported admin invite failures or confusing states.
- Invites sometimes appeared to send without recipient delivery; “pending” could persist for existing or already-joined teammates.
- 2 accounts paused rollout; 1 repeated the flow three times and created support noise.

Decision required:
What explicit invite-state contract will we expose: preflight permission/domain/role checks, clear send confirmation, duplicate handling, and a trustworthy pending/accepted state?

Questions to resolve:
- Which restrictions must be surfaced before email entry or send?
- What exact confirmation proves the invite was accepted by the system?
- How should existing users, duplicate invites, bounced mail, and already-joined teammates appear?
- What plain-language role labels replace overloaded “admin” terminology at invite time?

Proposed owner: Product + Engineering, with Customer Success support instrumentation.
Acceptance signal: an admin can tell whether an invite was sent, blocked, duplicate, delivered, or accepted without contacting support or retrying blindly.

Decision 3 — Onboarding order and first-value definition
Evidence:
- 6 accounts showed confusion before first value.
- Users did not know whether to invite teammates before or after creating the first source/project/setup object.
- 4 accounts contacted support because they were not confident enough to proceed; 2 reached value only after a live walkthrough.
- The checklist explains too much, steers too little, and implies a single order.

Decision required:
What is the minimum guided sequence and explicit “done” state for first value, and when should team invitations become available or recommended?

Questions to resolve:
- What event counts as first value for a new workspace?
- Should the checklist adapt to the chosen activation path rather than enforce one order?
- Which role terms need rewriting, and which explanation should move out of the critical path?
- Do we recommend inviting teammates before or after the first source/project is ready?

Proposed owner: Product Design + Product, with Customer Success usability checks.
Acceptance signal: a new admin can state what “done” means, complete the first-value path, and understand the next step without a walkthrough.

Cross-cutting operating decision
Prioritize ambiguity reduction in setup over adding net-new capability for this cycle. Track the three decisions separately, but measure them together through: first-session completion, time to first value, connector recovery, invite-state support contacts, and CSM-assisted setup.

Immediate follow-ups to assign in the meeting
1. Product/Engineering: bring one proposed activation state diagram, including failed/skipped connector paths.
2. Product/Engineering: bring the invite-state model and preflight validation list.
3. Design/Product: bring a revised adaptive checklist and proposed first-value event.
4. Customer Success: provide funnel-step breakout and a small set of representative flows for validation.

Not a decision
The May 8–9 digest is evidence, not a proposed solution. Counts overlap and are not additive.

messages.content: [2023-05-12T12:46:00-07:00] The first demo block helped, but open Q&A is starting to go dead-air. Give me quick facilitation prompts to turn the afternoon into three working blocks: activation, expansion, admin pain. I want decisions and owner calls, not wandering opinions.

Use the same structure for each block:

“Name the decision, name the owner, and name the next proof point. Opinions without a proposed action go to the parking lot.”

Block 1: Activation

Open:
“We are not diagnosing activation in the abstract. Where exactly does a new workspace fail to reach its first key action?”

Prompts:
- “Which step is the highest-leverage break: workspace creation, invites, first admin action, or first key action?”
- “What evidence makes that the priority?”
- “What will we change in the product or onboarding this week?”
- “What are we explicitly not fixing yet?”
- “Who owns shipping the change, and who owns measuring it?”
- “What result would tell us within seven days that this worked?”

Close:
“Decision: [priority step]. Owner: [name]. Experiment: [specific change]. Metric and date: [具体].”

Block 2: Expansion

Open:
“Assume activation improves. What is the next behavior that makes Mercury expand inside an account?”

Prompts:
- “Who is the next user or team after the initial admin?”
- “What action creates a natural reason to invite or adopt more broadly?”
- “Which expansion path are we choosing first?”
- “What customer signal would disprove that path?”
- “What can we test with existing customers without building a large feature?”
- “Who owns the customer test, and who owns the product follow-up?”

Force the call:
“We have three plausible expansion ideas. Which one gets the next two weeks, and which two are parked?”

Close:
“Decision: [expansion motion]. Owner: [name]. Customer test: [specific accounts/action]. Success signal: [metric/date].”

Block 3: Admin Pain

Open:
“Let’s focus on the administrative friction that blocks value—not every rough edge.”

Prompts:
- “Which admin failure causes the most delay or abandonment?”
- “Is this a product defect, an unclear state, a missing permission, or an onboarding problem?”
- “What is the smallest change that removes the pain?”
- “What should the admin understand or be able to do in one screen?”
- “What workaround are we willing to support temporarily?”
- “Who owns the fix, and who will validate it with an admin?”

Force prioritization:
“Rank the top three admin pains by customer impact and frequency. We are choosing one to address now.”

Close:
“Decision: [admin pain/fix]. Owner: [name]. Validation customer: [name/account]. Ship-or-revisit date: [date].”

If discussion starts drifting:

- “What decision are we trying to make?”
- “What would you recommend we do?”
- “Who owns the next step?”
- “What evidence would change your mind?”
- “Is this blocking today’s decision? If not, parking lot.”
- “We have two minutes left—what is the call?”
- “Disagreement is fine; unresolved ownership is not.”

End with a visible decision log:

1. Decision
2. Owner
3. First action
4. Success metric
5. Date to review
6. Explicitly parked items

arguments.title: Mercury offsite closeout — owners, cuts, launch blockers
arguments.body:
Mercury offsite closeout
Owners, cuts, launch blockers
Photo transcription / closeout notes — 2023-05-12

Purpose
This is working material, not a deck. Ship work, owners, cuts, and blockers. The weekly spine is Jake. If discussion turns into narrative polish, cut it.

Launch bar
- Activation works without founder handholding.
- The expansion path is visible in the product, not in slides.
- The top admin pain is reduced enough that calls stop repeating the same three complaints.
- Every blocker has one owner.

ACTIVATION

Owners
- Priya: path, copy, and screens.
- Jake: implementation, feature flag, and rollout sequence.
- Anna: event definitions and success cut.

Needed by next review
- Single primary CTA: connect first source.
- Invite teammates becomes optional after first value, not before.
- Use sample data only if there is no real event in the first session.
- Define the activation event chain in plain English and as actual events.

Blockers
- Billing gate timing is unresolved:
  - Before the first real run is probably too much friction.
  - After first value is better, but requires an abuse cap / usage limit.
- Event names are still fuzzy. Anna needs an exact handoff; Jake will not wire to vibes.
- Role-setup copy is too abstract. Admins do not know what changes later versus now.
- Feature-flag rollout criteria are not written anywhere.

Scope cuts
- No template gallery for v1.
- No SSO in the first-run path.
- No advanced permissions setup during activation.
- No logo upload or custom branding in first-run.

Decisions / guardrails
- “First value” means connected source plus first successful action, not an invited teammate.
- Stop debating the empty-state illustration.
- Do not reopen the entire settings IA here.

EXPANSION

Owners
- Jake: overall.
- Priya: upgrade moments and UI.
- Anna: usage-threshold sanity check and measurement.

What stays in
- Expose the upgrade trigger where usage actually hits the limit.
- Provide one clean in-app path from cap hit to plan / owner action.
- Show the admin why the workspace is constrained.
- Keep copy light; no packaging essay.

Blockers
- Mercury feature-flag rollout remains ambiguous:
  - Who flips it?
  - What are the merge criteria?
  - Where is the rollback note?
  - What is the target date?
- The usage-threshold cut is noisy; choose one number the team will actually use.
- Upgrade copy is split between product / admin language and billing language.

Scope cuts
- No annual-plan flow work for launch.
- No seat-management overhaul.
- No contract-specific enterprise branching in product.
- No pricing-story work in this room.

Decisions / guardrails
- The expansion path must exist even if monetization details evolve later.
- If it requires sales explanation every time, it is not launch-ready.

ADMIN PAIN

Owners
- Jake: backend, account actions, and audit surfaces.
- Priya: admin home and settings grouping.
- Anna: tag incoming issues by severity and frequency.

Repeated pain to fix
1. Permissions / roles are unclear.
2. Bulk user actions are too manual.
3. There is no clean audit trail for “who changed what.”
4. The wrong person gets admin / billing noise.
5. Settings are scattered across too many places.

Blockers
- Audit-log scope is unclear: which events are mandatory for launch?
- CSV / import failures do a poor job explaining what broke.
- The permission-model explanation is too hand-wavey for security-conscious customers.
- Notification-routing rules are not explicit enough.

Scope cuts
- No full settings redesign.
- No granular notification matrix.
- No admin analytics dashboard.
- No custom role builder.

Decision / guardrail
- Fix repeated pain, not every admin complaint anyone has ever had.
- If a problem matters only after launch scale, write it down and move on.

CROSS-CUTTING
- Jake runs the weekly from this; Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon can pressure-test logic, but should not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner comes to weekly with: what moved, what slipped, and what we cut.
- Customer examples beat opinions.
- Keep the launch-blocker list short and named.

OPEN BLOCKERS TO CARRY FORWARD
1. Billing gate timing.
2. Activation instrumentation definitions.
3. Mercury feature-flag rollout owner plus merge / rollback criteria.
4. Admin audit-log minimum scope.

DECISIONS DUE
- Decide billing-gate placement and abuse-cap / usage-limit approach.
- Lock the activation event chain and exact event-name handoff.
- Name the Mercury feature-flag rollout owner; document merge criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- Set the single usage threshold for the expansion path.
- Define the minimum launch audit-log event scope.

MONDAY GUARDRAIL
Do not let Monday become “can we make this story cleaner.”

arguments.title: Mercury activation empty states — working decision note (v7 review)
arguments.body:
Mercury activation empty states — working decision note

Working-team material; not for external circulation.
Source: Figma export for Mercury / Activation empty states, page “Activation empty + transitional states,” section “v7 review.” Exported 2023-06-19 17:18 PT.

Purpose
Separate product decisions from release-readiness and implementation constraints so the next review can close the remaining gaps without using Figma comments as the sole source of truth.

PRODUCT DECISIONS

1. No source connected — admin
- The state has one job: get an admin to connect a real source.
- Primary CTA: “Connect a data source.”
- Secondary option may link to the setup guide.
- Sample import must not appear on this card in a way that reads as activation.
- If sample import remains in v0.2, label it “preview only.” It must not produce a success state, “you’re ready” language, or a green-check treatment for sample data.

2. Invited member before first source
- Do not show a generic blank page.
- Explain that the workspace exists but an admin still needs to connect the first source.
- A non-admin must not be teased with a CTA they cannot complete.
- The user should land in a coherent explanatory state rather than dead air.

3. First sync queued
- Treat this as a transitional state, not an empty state.
- Reassure the user that the source was found and the first live sync is running.
- Do not use a fake percentage, countdown, stepper, or language implying precise/resumable progress.
- Neutral copy such as “This usually takes a couple of minutes” is acceptable if it remains accurate.
- Add a docs link only when the state has run long enough to justify it; do not add it by default if it creates noise.

4. Sync failed
- Make the state actionable, not merely apologetic.
- Provide retry plus help docs.
- Keep copy at the product level; do not expose connector internals or raw vendor errors.
- Day-one failure presentation does not need five distinct user-facing variants.
- Support contact is not part of the state unless support routing is wired.

5. Sample data
- Sample data must not create an activated-looking success card.
- If retained in v0.2, it belongs to a sandbox/preview branch with its own copy and no shared “activated” treatment.
- Sample import may help exploration but cannot masquerade as a live source connection.

6. Measurement language and success framing
- Do not expose internal activation-measurement language in the UI.
- User-facing copy should talk about connecting a real source and seeing the first live data arrive.
- Invite acceptance is not equivalent to activation.
- Sample data is not equivalent to activation.
- No celebratory success card until real data is present; invite acceptance and sample data must not feel equivalent to that outcome.

7. CTA labels locked for now (C-221 resolved)
- No source: “Connect a data source”
- Invited member: “View setup guide”
- Queued: no primary CTA
- Failed: “Try again”

8. Mobile copy
- Shorten invited-member and failure-state copy so the CTA remains usable on small widths, including iPhone SE.
- Prefer cutting words over shrinking type.

RELEASE-READINESS / IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS

1. State derivation
- Distinguish “member lacks permission” from “organization has no source yet.”
- Use server-provided role/source state, including org_has_connected_source where applicable.
- Do not infer the client-side role from the session token; token-based guessing can flicker on refresh and create false CTAs.
- Wait for server role/source state before rendering the invited-member branch. A short loading state is preferable to showing the wrong action.

2. Queued-state behavior
- Define and implement a threshold for when queued becomes “taking longer than usual.” QA cannot test that branch until the timeout is agreed.
- Do not promise an ETA or percentage that the system cannot substantiate.

3. Failure handling
- Normalize connector failures before release into these implementation buckets:
  - auth / permissions
  - source unavailable / timeout
  - unknown / retry
- Map those buckets to simplified product copy.
- Retry must be idempotent; double-clicking must not create duplicate jobs.

4. Event and activation mapping
- Engineering, QA, and Anna need one agreed event mapping behind the scenes.
- invite_sent is supporting activity only, not activation.
- sample_import_completed stays out of the activation definition.
- Product copy should remain free of the internal formula/measurement language.

5. QA freeze
- Final invited-member and failure strings are needed before QA screenshots are frozen.
- Small-width rendering must be checked for both states, including CTA position on iPhone SE.

6. Success trigger implementation
- Engineering needs a concrete trigger definition for the success treatment. Candidate checkpoints discussed were real_source_connected, first_live_sync_completed, or both in practice.
- Do not fill the product-definition gap with a fake happy path; carry it to the next review if it cannot be resolved now.

UNRESOLVED ITEMS FOR NEXT REVIEW

1. Success trigger: Should the success treatment fire on real_source_connected, first_live_sync_completed, or only after both are true?
2. Queued timeout: What exact threshold changes the state to “taking longer than usual,” and what copy/docs behavior follows that transition?
3. Long-running queued state: When exactly should the docs link appear?
4. Support routing: Is support contact wired for v0.2? If not, confirm docs-only behavior for the failed state.
5. Activation/event contract: Finalize the canonical event mapping and ownership for engineering, QA, and Anna, including how real-source connection and first live sync relate to activation.
6. Failure copy mapping: Approve the simplified user-facing copy for each normalized failure bucket while keeping vendor details out of the UI.
7. Final strings: Lock the shortened invited-member and failure-state strings before QA screenshot freeze.
8. Sample-data scope: Confirm whether sample import remains in v0.2; if yes, approve the sandbox/preview branch, labels, separate event names, and explicit exclusion from activation treatment.
9. Loading branch: Confirm the exact loading behavior and copy while server role/source state is pending.
10. Ownership/checklist: Assign one canonical home and owner for the release-readiness checklist and the event/QA contract so these constraints do not remain split across Figma comments and review threads.

Proposed next-review output
- Approved success trigger and event mapping.
- Agreed queued timeout and long-running-state behavior.
- Confirmed support/docs decision.
- Final mobile-safe strings.
- Explicit v0.2 decision on sample data.
- Named owner and canonical location for the release-readiness checklist.

[2023-08-01T09:06:00-07:00] Jake’s first-wave shape is finally concrete enough to review with Devon.

Discord group DM — Jake, Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
2023-08-01 08:47 PT

Jake:
Pulled together a first-pass view on the external Mercury design-partner wave.

My proposal is to use Evergreen Bank as the enterprise-shaped candidate in the first wave.

Why Evergreen:
- They are likely to stress the exact admin/security edges we still care about: admin handoff, role/state clarity, auditability questions, and how trustworthy the early sync/failure path feels.
- That gives us a real test of the standard Mercury path without immediately turning the rollout into bespoke build work.
- Put differently: hard enough to expose whether the product is enterprise-ready on the current path, but still within the boundaries of the product we are actually trying to ship.

I’m keeping the rest of the wave deliberately lighter; the enterprise question is whether Evergreen should be the anchor stress case.

On Acme, I would keep them in the not-now column.
- The NDA scope thread is still muddy enough that sending fresh Mercury material feels like asking for a document fight instead of product signal.
- I do still think their prior feedback is useful internally, especially on admin pain, failure-state legibility, and procurement/security questions.
- I would use that feedback to sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279, but not send Acme new packet/screens/notes unless the NDA thread gets narrowed first.

MER-1279 rows this would pressure-test most directly:
- invited-member/admin handoff confidence
- queued-sync trust / retry confidence
- failed-state legibility and recovery
- admin/security questions that show up before anyone asks for one-off treatment

Not calling any of those closed. This is just the cleanest first-wave shape I can see right now.

If you both agree with the direction, I can turn it into a tighter wave outline before the review.

Give me decision questions for that Devon review, not an announcement. I want them to pressure-test three things: why Evergreen Bank is a good enterprise stress case for admin/security without dragging us into bespoke work, what exactly keeps Acme out while the NDA scope thread is unresolved, and which parts of Acme’s prior feedback can still sharpen internal blocker rows in MER-1279 without sending Acme anything fresh.

Devon review — decision questions

1. Evergreen as the enterprise stress case
- What specific admin/security behaviors do we need the first wave to expose?
- Does Evergreen exercise those behaviors through the standard Mercury path, or are we already assuming custom workflow, permissions, integrations, or support?
- What would count as useful enterprise signal from Evergreen without turning their participation into a bespoke implementation?
- Which risks are we intentionally testing now, and which enterprise requirements are explicitly out of scope for this wave?
- What evidence would make us conclude that Evergreen is the wrong anchor—or that the standard path is not ready for this stress case?

2. Why Acme stays out for now
- What exactly remains unresolved in the NDA scope thread?
- Which categories of Mercury material are still unsafe or ambiguous to send under the current scope?
- Is the blocker the legal permission to share, the risk of starting a document-negotiation loop, or both?
- What narrow resolution would be sufficient to reconsider Acme, and who owns getting us there?
- Until that resolution exists, are we aligned that Acme receives no fresh packets, screens, notes, or other Mercury materials?

3. Using Acme’s prior feedback internally
- Which parts of Acme’s existing feedback are clearly usable without sharing anything new: admin pain, failure-state legibility, procurement/security questions, or specific examples?
- How should those points sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279 without being treated as fresh customer validation?
- Which rows should be updated first: invited-member/admin handoff, queued-sync and retry trust, failed-state recovery, or admin/security clarity?
- What evidence would distinguish a real launch-readiness blocker from a useful design concern or future enterprise requirement?
- Who will convert the usable feedback into explicit blocker criteria, and what would we need to see before calling any row materially improved?

4. Decision at the end of the review
- Do we agree to make Evergreen the first-wave enterprise-shaped stress case on the standard Mercury path?
- Do we agree to keep Acme out until the NDA scope is narrowed?
- Do we agree on the specific Acme feedback that can inform MER-1279 internally, with no new external sharing?

From: HR
To: Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
Cc: Sarah Kim
Date: Mon, Mar 25, 2024 8:52 AM PT
Subject: Nadia Singh final loop debrief + next-step recommendation

Morgan / Devon / Sarah —

Final loop is complete for Nadia plus the alternate finalist. Consolidating notes from Friday's scenarios and this morning's close debrief below.

Bottom line: Nadia is the clear recommendation for the Head of Customer Growth brief as we actually defined it. The alternate finalist is not weak, but reads as a first VP Sales / revenue-leader archetype for a later stage and kept pushing us toward a motion we explicitly said we do not want to build yet.

Shared final-interview notes

1) Morgan + Devon scenario — Mercury activation to repeatable motion
Date: Fri Mar 22
Format: 55 min

Nadia Singh
- Started by asking for the minimum evidence set she would trust in week one: current activation stages, account-level failure points, owner handoffs, and where founder memory still substitutes for a system.
- Proposed a lightweight first pass: one shared weekly review of activation friction, expansion stalls, enterprise-readiness asks, and owner routing rather than separate customer, product, and commercial stories.
- Kept distinguishing signal from theater. She said she would rather have six durable account patterns than a polished dashboard full of blended anecdotes.
- Good instinct on sequencing: instrument where activation and adoption break first, then decide what deserves packaging work, workflow fixes, or true product investment.
- Did not ask for early headcount or a large customer-success org to make the role viable.

Alternate finalist
- Went quickly to pipeline shape, account segmentation by ARR band, and when he would be expected to carry a number.
