results.title: Facilitate working blocks with decisions
results.snippet: [2023-05-12T12:46:00-07:00] The first >>>demo<<< block helped, but open Q&A is starting to go dead-air. Give me quick facilitation prompts to turn the afternoon into three working blocks: activation, expansion, admin pain. I...

messages.content: [2023-05-12T12:46:00-07:00] The first demo block helped, but open Q&A is starting to go dead-air. Give me quick facilitation prompts to turn the afternoon into three working blocks: activation, expansion, admin pain. I want decisions and owner calls, not wandering opinions.

Use the same structure for each block:

“Name the decision, name the owner, and name the next proof point. Opinions without a proposed action go to the parking lot.”

Block 1: Activation

Open:
“We are not diagnosing activation in the abstract. Where exactly does a new workspace fail to reach its first key action?”

Prompts:
- “Which step is the highest-leverage break: workspace creation, invites, first admin action, or first key action?”
- “What evidence makes that the priority?”
- “What will we change in the product or onboarding this week?”
- “What are we explicitly not fixing yet?”
- “Who owns shipping the change, and who owns measuring it?”
- “What result would tell us within seven days that this worked?”

Close:
“Decision: [priority step]. Owner: [name]. Experiment: [specific change]. Metric and date: [具体].”

Block 2: Expansion

Open:
“Assume activation improves. What is the next behavior that makes Mercury expand inside an account?”

Prompts:
- “Who is the next user or team after the initial admin?”
- “What action creates a natural reason to invite or adopt more broadly?”
- “Which expansion path are we choosing first?”
- “What customer signal would disprove that path?”
- “What can we test with existing customers without building a large feature?”
- “Who owns the customer test, and who owns the product follow-up?”

Force the call:
“We have three plausible expansion ideas. Which one gets the next two weeks, and which two are parked?”

Close:
“Decision: [expansion motion]. Owner: [name]. Customer test: [specific accounts/action]. Success signal: [metric/date].”

Block 3: Admin Pain

Open:
“Let’s focus on the administrative friction that blocks value—not every rough edge.”

Prompts:
- “Which admin failure causes the most delay or abandonment?”
- “Is this a product defect, an unclear state, a missing permission, or an onboarding problem?”
- “What is the smallest change that removes the pain?”
- “What should the admin understand or be able to do in one screen?”
- “What workaround are we willing to support temporarily?”
- “Who owns the fix, and who will validate it with an admin?”

Force prioritization:
“Rank the top three admin pains by customer impact and frequency. We are choosing one to address now.”

Close:
“Decision: [admin pain/fix]. Owner: [name]. Validation customer: [name/account]. Ship-or-revisit date: [date].”

If discussion starts drifting:

- “What decision are we trying to make?”
- “What would you recommend we do?”
- “Who owns the next step?”
- “What evidence would change your mind?”
- “Is this blocking today’s decision? If not, parking lot.”
- “We have two minutes left—what is the call?”
- “Disagreement is fine; unresolved ownership is not.”

End with a visible decision log:

1. Decision
2. Owner
3. First action
4. Success metric
5. Date to review
6. Explicitly parked items

Read:

Safe for internal operating decisions this week

- Use the mature monthly cohorts from November through February for directional decisions. They show a reasonably consistent shape:
  - Wk1 activation: 68–73%
  - Wk4 active: 58–63%
  - M2 retention: 55–59%
  - M3 retention: 53–56%
- The January cohort is the clearest positive signal: best activation, Wk4 activity, and retention, consistent with the onboarding fixes helping.
- February looks broadly stable, not like a regression. Its expansion count is lower than January, but Anna notes that some expansion is still arriving later, so do not treat four accounts as a final result.
- Operationally, investigate the invitation step first. April 24 shows a clear invite_sent drop-off: 6 of 11 signups reached that stage, versus 9 of 14 the prior week.
- Treat the May 1 funnel as an early warning, not a verdict: 3 of 8 reached the 7-day key action, and late events may still move it. It is worth checking now for an onboarding or instrumentation issue.
- Keep using weekly activation as a diagnostic funnel, not as a performance trend. The small weekly samples are appropriate for finding where onboarding breaks, especially when the same-stage drop appears across adjacent weeks.

Too noisy for board or external charts

- Do not chart the weekly activation series as a trend. The 9–14 signup weekly samples can swing materially from one account, and the reported 38–58% range will invite overinterpretation.
- Do not use the May 1 week externally; it is both small and still subject to late event arrival.
- Do not make retention claims from the March cohort: M2 is only 50%, but the cohort is still maturing and has no M3 result.
- Exclude April from retention charts entirely. It is explicitly too early for a retention read.
- Avoid showing raw expansion-account counts as evidence of a trend. The counts are small, have different cohort maturity, and February’s result is not final.
- Be cautious even with November–February externally: they are the most usable data, but the cohorts are only 28–37 accounts each. They are suitable for a clearly labeled mature-cohort directional chart, not a strong claim about company-wide retention or a precise forecast.

Bottom line: use the mature monthly cohorts to preserve the onboarding direction and use the weekly funnel to investigate the invite/action break. For external or board material, show only the mature monthly cohorts, label cohort sizes and maturity, and leave out weekly activation, March/April retention, and expansion-count conclusions.

[2023-02-13T14:00:00-08:00] meeting was good i think. room felt fine. but the Feb 13 lead-investor partner meeting is still stuck in my head bc the partner had two pointed questions on retention and i kind of hand-waved one, half-answered the other. not catastrophic, just bad in the specific way where you know they found the soft spot.

i keep messing with that slide like the label order is the issue. it's not. the problem is we show top-line logo retention cleanly enough, but the usage cohort gets muddy after month 4 once teams collapse into annual and seat expansion hides the drop. i need a real answer on what we believe is product improvement vs segmentation artifact vs instrumenting this badly in Stripe + app events. leaning pull raw cohort cuts tonight and stop trying to pretty it up -- if i can't say it plainly in the room, deck polish is useless.

That sounds like a real soft spot, but also a much better diagnosis than “the slide is confusing.”

The issue seems to be that three different things are being blended:

1. Product behavior: are teams actually using less after month 4?
2. Segmentation: are annual conversions or expansion-heavy accounts distorting the cohort?
3. Instrumentation: are Stripe billing events and app events failing to line up cleanly?

I’d stop touching the label order tonight. Pull the raw account-month cuts and separate:

- logo retention
- usage retention
- annual-vs-monthly status
- seat expansion/contraction
- billing activity versus app-event activity
- event completeness by cohort

Then you can say plainly in the room:

“We have clean top-line logo retention, but the usage cohort is less settled after month 4. Annual conversion and seat expansion may be masking lower engagement, and we’re validating whether part of the shape is an instrumentation issue. We’re not going to present a polished interpretation until those effects are separated.”

That is a credible answer. It acknowledges the weakness without turning it into a catastrophe—and it gives the partner a concrete path to resolution.

arguments.body:
Mercury product offsite — May 12 working agenda

Purpose
This is an operating offsite, not a launch narrative or deck rehearsal.

Decisions to make
1. Launch scope: confirm what Mercury will ship by the end of Q2 and what is explicitly cut or deferred.
2. Activation/onboarding: decide which setup and first-value changes are in scope, and which UX cleanup is not.
3. Admin rollout: decide which admin issues are launch blockers versus follow-up work.
4. Retention instrumentation: agree which evidence is reliable enough to operate on, which caveats remain, and what must be true before broader claims are made.
5. Checkpoint: set the next review date and the evidence required at that checkpoint.

Cuts and scope
- Confirm the cut list and the rationale for each cut.
- Separate launch-critical setup/admin work from nice-to-have polish and one-off fixes.
- Do not add narrative slides, launch-story framing, or deck-rehearsal work to the offsite.

Blockers to resolve
- Activation/onboarding: valid setup order, first-success state after partial setup, and whether fallback paths are real product paths or edge-case patches.
- Invites: explicit outcomes for already-in-workspace, pending, failed, and otherwise restricted invites.
- Admin: invite reliability, permission confusion, account-level controls, and the engineering permission boundary behind role copy.
- Retention: mapping/instrumentation gaps that could change the readout or make a cut unsafe to operate on.

Owners
- Activation/onboarding: Priya — bring the unresolved product-intent and implementation-constraint questions; record the final scope decision.
- Admin/permissions: Engineering owner — confirm the actual permission boundary and owner for each admin blocker.
- Retention instrumentation: Anna — identify solid versus moving cuts and the caveats attached to each.
- Scope and cut list: Product lead — maintain the single decision log and flag anything that is not launch-critical.
- Follow-through: Each blocker owner — document the next action, due date, dependency, and evidence of resolution before the next checkpoint.

Working output
Leave with one operating page containing:
- launch-critical decisions
- explicit cuts and deferrals
- each blocker and its owner
- dependencies and next actions
- evidence required to determine whether the launch work is working

Timing
- Opening: review decisions and operating constraints.
- Working sessions: activation/onboarding, admin blockers, and retention instrumentation.
- Close: read back decisions, cuts, owners, blockers, and the next checkpoint.

[2023-09-27T19:31:00-07:00] Devon’s rough pass for tomorrow is here.

From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Wed, 27 Sep 2023 19:12:00 -0700
Subject: Thursday prep — rough October investor path

Morgan —

Rough pass before tomorrow so we can decide whether to put real walls around this instead of letting random September inbound set the agenda.

What I think is supportable now

- We finally have a real Mercury story grounded in external use, not just planned-launch narrative.
- The September package is usable if we keep the framing disciplined: activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave; Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context; the corrected weekly cuts are helpful operating read, not proof.
- Evergreen is useful evidence in two ways: (1) there is real enterprise pull serious enough to get procurement/commercial attention, and (2) the enterprise-readiness gaps are now concrete rather than abstract.
- Hybrid pricing gives us a cleaner commercial frame. Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands is much easier to explain than the earlier seat-ish ambiguity.

What I do not think we can blur

- We cannot tell a “retention is solved” story. It still is not.
- We cannot present expansion as clean. Some rows are moving; some are still uneven.
- We cannot use Evergreen’s procurement motion as proof that enterprise readiness is already there. Their feedback is basically the current gap list: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, clearer admin vs billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without one of us live-explaining it.
- We cannot let the pricing decision imply enterprise add-ons are in-market beyond what is actually shipped.

How I would frame the investor path

I think there is a version of reopening that is disciplined and a version that turns into cosplay. The disciplined version is: selective, October, and explicitly based on whether the investor can underwrite the real Mercury story. Not “market is hot again, let’s spray meetings.”

Elena feels like the right first conversation in that frame. She already engaged seriously once and her pass was thoughtful, not generic. If we go back to her, the point is calibration and context: does the more honest Mercury picture change the read at all? That is very different from treating Elena as the start of a broad process.

Short-list criteria

Only keep firms that can handle all of the following without pushing us into story inflation:
1. uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention
2. enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped
3. a usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young
4. a deliberately narrow process instead of a manufactured auction

Rough list

1) Elena Volkov — warm-context bucket
- Best use: first calibration conversation
- Why: prior feedback was substantive; she'd pressure-test the actual story
- Caveat: only useful if we stay honest about what still is not proven

2) Firm A — possible fit if we keep the narrative operational
- Tends to understand infra/devtools motion
- Biggest risk is they will immediately push on expansion consistency

3) Firm B — possible fit if the commercial story is crisp
- Could appreciate the cleaner pricing frame
- Risk is enterprise checklist bias if the packet still requires too much live explanation

4) Firm C — maybe
- Thoughtful and patient
- Might be more useful as signal than as an actual lead if we are keeping the list tight

September inbound / coffee noise

I have three stray September asks that I think should probably stay out:
- two mutual-intro coffee requests that feel more social than decision-relevant
- one “in town next week” inbound that looks like calendar tax
Given where we are, I think saying yes to these just makes the whole thing feel broader than it is.

Questions for tomorrow
- Are we comfortable calling this a selective October reopen internally, or do we want even tighter language?
- Is Elena definitely first, or do we want one more p…

Decision-prep read

Bottom line

There is enough for a disciplined, selective October calibration process—but not enough for a broad fundraising reopen or a “traction is now proven” narrative.

The honest frame is:

“Mercury has moved from planned-launch narrative to externally observed usage and a clearer commercial model. Activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave, and enterprise demand is real. Retention and expansion are not yet fully proven, and enterprise readiness still has specific gaps we are actively closing.”

I would use “selective October calibration” internally rather than “reopen” unless the team wants to signal a more active process. The operating behavior should remain the same: one conversation first, a very small list only if that conversation and the package support it.

What can support the story

1. External use, not just roadmap
   - Mercury now has a credible external-use basis.
   - The design-partner wave provides evidence that activation and admin friction improved.
   - This is a meaningful change from a planned-launch story, but it should not be inflated into proof of durable product-market fit.

2. September data as operating evidence
   - Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context.
   - The corrected weekly cuts are useful for understanding operating movement.
   - Neither should be presented as definitive proof of retention or expansion.

3. Evergreen as both demand and diagnostic evidence
   - Evergreen demonstrates that enterprise interest is serious enough to reach procurement and commercial review.
   - More importantly, its feedback turns enterprise-readiness concerns into a concrete, bounded gap list.
   - That supports a story of real pull plus known execution work—not a claim that enterprise readiness is complete.

4. Cleaner commercial framing
   - Hybrid pricing, with Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands, is easier to explain than the earlier seat-like ambiguity.
   - The model is clearer, but still young.
   - The pricing decision must not imply that enterprise add-ons are already shipped or broadly in-market.

Gaps we cannot blur

- Retention is not solved. Do not use “retention is improving” as shorthand for “retention is durable” or “retention is solved.”
- Expansion is uneven. Some rows are moving, but the overall picture is not clean enough to present as a consistent expansion engine.
- Evergreen procurement interest is not enterprise readiness. The current gap list remains:
  - SSO timing
  - audit history for admin changes
  - clearer separation between admin and billing-owner roles
  - a procurement packet that does not require live explanation from the team
- The commercial model is clearer, not mature. Do not present usage-based pricing as a validated enterprise monetization system.
- Enterprise add-ons should be described only according to what is actually shipped.
- The selective process itself matters. A broad set of meetings would create pressure to turn partial evidence into a larger story.

Short-list criteria

Keep a firm only if it can engage constructively with all four of these:

1. Uneven expansion and not-yet-solved retention
   - They should be able to underwrite progress without demanding that the data be cleaner than it is.

2. Scoped enterprise-readiness gaps
   - They should distinguish “important work remains” from “there is no enterprise opportunity.”
   - They should not require premature promises on SSO, audit controls, admin permissions, or procurement timing.

3. A usage-based commercial model that is clearer but still early
   - They should understand MAU-based platform bands without forcing the company into a more mature pricing narrative than the evidence supports.

4. A narrow, deliberate process
   - They should be comfortable with calibration before process-building.
   - Avoid firms or partners whose default response is to manufacture urgency, auction dynamics, or story inflation.

arguments.body:
PROJECT COMPASS — v0.1 OWNER-ROUTING NOTE

Purpose
Compass turns customer-health signals we already see in Mercury/Evergreen operating work into a customer-facing or customer-growth next action. It is an operating/product push, not a new reporting layer: every signal should improve account behavior, follow-up, or customer guidance.

What Compass is not
- Not another board dashboard or investor-packaging exercise.
- Not a generic health-score project.
- Not a bespoke Evergreen side track.
- Not a reason to open a new hiring lane.
- Not broad admin-policy or general enterprise-controls product work.

Staffing boundary
Keep Compass inside the current lightweight model: Nadia/Sarah for operating and account work, with Jake/Leo for implementation and seams. No new headcount lane.

Routing rules
1. Route the signal, evidence bundle, caveat, and proposed next action together.
2. Separate what is known from what is inferred. Do not present an inference as a customer fact.
3. Do not use binary “renewal risk” language without context. Admin friction, role confusion, setup-control issues, procurement/security packaging, activation drag, and true product gaps require different follow-up.
4. A signal without a next action is an FYI and is not complete.
5. Account-note quality is part of signal quality: record provenance and recency before customer-growth follow-up.

Owner routing
Anna Martinez — signal definitions and caveats
- Define the available categories: retention, activation, expansion, admin friction, enterprise readiness, and account-note quality.
- Specify what each signal does and does not mean, including how admin friction differs from product weakness, procurement/security packaging, and ordinary activation drag.
- Define the minimum evidence package and confidence/caveat language.

Nadia Singh — customer-success and customer-growth use cases
- Turn a validated signal into a concrete follow-up motion and owner.
- Own the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt: timely, evidence-based follow-up for accounts showing readiness for broader usage, not generic upsell copy.
- Decide which signals remain internal first and which can support customer-facing guidance.

Jake — product implementation and sequencing
- Keep v0.1 narrow and shippable.
- Bias toward lightweight prompts, account-workflow support, or a contained product assist; do not start with a broad new product surface.
- Call out and keep separate any drift into broad admin-policy or general enterprise-controls work.

Leo Park — data/platform seams
- Reuse existing signals and event paths; do not build a separate scoring service or platform layer for v0.1.
- Define the minimum evidence bundle that can move from internal read to customer/action use without breaking trust.
- Keep usage evidence, account-note evidence, and inferred account state clearly separated.

Sarah Kim — account-thread and note hygiene
- Clean up source quality so follow-up can be traced to customer statements, observed usage, support-derived facts, or internal interpretation.
- Preserve provenance and recency; keep customer quotes, internal interpretation, support follow-up, and procurement context from blending together.
- Flag when the record is too weak for customer-facing or growth follow-up.

Morgan Chen — board/customer narrative
- Keep the framing operational and customer-real while v0.1 is being tested.
- Protect the boundary against dashboard drift, investor-packaging framing, and fragmented Mercury/Evergreen/customer-growth threads.
- Board narrative comes later, after Compass changes account behavior.

v0.1 focus
1. Renewal-risk/admin-friction evidence
Show when apparent renewal risk may actually be admin friction, setup-control issues, or role confusion. Evidence travels with the signal; no context-free risk label.

2. Expansion prompt after first live sync
Identify the smallest useful prompt or follow-up after first live sync when an account appears ready for broader usage. Optimize for timely action, not generic expansion language.

3. Account-note source quality
Make notes reliable enough for customer-growth follow-up by tagging source type, provenance, and recency, and separating observed facts from inference.

Definition of done for a v0.1 signal
- It triggers a clearer next action and named route.
- The recipient knows why it surfaced.
- Evidence and caveat travel with it.
- Follow-up quality improves; internal visibility alone does not count.
- The implementation remains within the lightweight staffing and existing-signal boundary.

Open questions to resolve in the first pass
- What is the minimum evidence package for each signal?
- Which signals are internal-only initially, and which can become customer-facing quickly?
- What is the smallest useful post-first-live-sync expansion prompt?
- How do we distinguish admin friction, true product gaps, and procurement/security packaging?
- Which account-note fields/source tags must exist before Nadia can trust follow-up?
- How much Leo seam work is acceptable before Compass starts taking attention from Mercury?

Immediate next step
Owners should return a lightweight first-pass proposal against their sections—definition/evidence, use case/action, implementation, seam, or note hygiene—without opening a new staffing lane or dashboard build.

results.title: Validate retention drop across cohorts
results.snippet: ...but the Feb 13 lead->>>investor<<< partner meeting is still stuck in my head bc the partner had two pointed questions on retention and i kind of hand-waved one, half-answered the other. not catastrophic, just bad in the...

messages.content:
[2023-02-13T14:00:00-08:00] meeting was good i think. room felt fine. but the Feb 13 lead-investor partner meeting is still stuck in my head bc the partner had two pointed questions on retention and i kind of hand-waved one, half-answered the other. not catastrophic, just bad in the specific way where you know they found the soft spot.

i keep messing with that slide like the label order is the issue. it's not. the problem is we show top-line logo retention cleanly enough, but the usage cohort gets muddy after month 4 once teams collapse into annual and seat expansion hides the drop. i need a real answer on what we believe is product improvement vs segmentation artifact vs instrumenting this badly in Stripe + app events. leaning pull raw cohort cuts tonight and stop trying to pretty it up -- if i can't say it plainly in the room, deck polish is useless.

That sounds like a real soft spot, but also a much better diagnosis than “the slide is confusing.”

The issue seems to be that three different things are being blended:

1. Product behavior: are teams actually using less after month 4?
2. Segmentation: are annual conversions or expansion-heavy accounts distorting the cohort?
3. Instrumentation: are Stripe billing events and app events failing to line up cleanly?

I’d stop touching the label order tonight. Pull the raw account-month cuts and separate:

- logo retention
- usage retention
- annual-vs-monthly status
- seat expansion/contraction
- billing activity versus app-event activity
- event completeness by cohort

Then you can say plainly in the room:

“We have clean top-line logo retention, but the usage cohort is less settled after month 4. Annual conversion and seat expansion may be masking lower engagement, and we’re validating whether part of the shape is an instrumentation issue. We’re not going to present a polished interpretation until those effects are separated.”

That is a credible answer. It acknowledges the weakness without turning it into a catastrophe—and it gives the partner a concrete path to resolution.

[2023-05-10T08:48:00-07:00] Customer Success sent the blocker digest. From: Customer Success
Date: Wed, May 10, 2023 8:21 AM PT
To: Morgan Chen, Jake, Priya, Anna Martinez, Devon Hayes
Subject: Mercury blocker digest — May 8-9 (account names removed)

Account names removed as requested. This is just the blocker pattern digest from the last two days, not a proposed plan.

Top themes across the May 8-9 calls/tickets
- Activation dead ends: 7 accounts
- Admin invite failures / confusing invite states: 5 accounts
- Onboarding confusion before first value: 6 accounts
- Several accounts showed up in more than one bucket, so counts are not additive.

1) Activation dead ends
What we heard
- New admins are getting through workspace creation and then stalling on the first "connect / import / continue" decision.
- When the connector step fails or is skipped, people are landing in an empty state that reads like setup is still in progress but does not give a clear next action.
- In a few cases the champion assumed the product was not fully enabled yet and stopped instead of trying another path.

Observed patterns
- The setup checklist implies a single correct order, but users are hitting paths where that order breaks.
- "Connect data" is reading as mandatory even for teams that expected to start with sample data or manual setup.
- Error text after a failed connection attempt is too generic; users are not sure whether to retry, switch methods, or ask an admin.

Representative notes
- "I connected, got bounced back, and now I can't tell if it saved anything."
- "We wanted to invite the team first and come back to the source later, but the flow kept pushing us back into setup."
- "The page looked unfinished, so we waited for your team instead of clicking around."

Impact
- 3 accounts did not complete first-session setup without manual CSM intervention.
- 2 accounts asked whether the rollout was still in beta because the post-create state looked incomplete.

2) Admin invite failures / confusing invite states
What we heard
- Admins are sending teammate invites and not trusting the result.
- Some invites appear to send but recipients never receive them.
- Some admins see a "pending" state that stays around even when the teammate already exists or has already tried to join.

Observed patterns
- Duplicate-invite handling is not obvious from the UI.
- Domain / role restrictions are surfacing late, after the admin thinks the invite already went out.
- The distinction between workspace admin vs other roles is unclear at the exact moment people are inviting their first teammates.

Representative notes
- "It said pending, but the person was already in there on their side."
- "I invited two people and got no confirmation other than the spinner stopping."
- "If this is blocked because of permissions, say that before I type the emails."

Impact
- 2 accounts paused rollout until their internal admin could verify whether invites had actually been sent.
- 1 account attempted the same invite flow three times and created support noise because nobody trusted the state.

3) Onboarding confusion before first value
What we heard
- Teams are not getting to a crisp first success moment fast enough.
- Users are reading the setup screens as product documentation rather than guided onboarding.
- The copy around roles, first project/setup object, and team invite timing is still muddy.

Observed patterns
- People do not understand whether they should invite teammates before or after the first source/project is set up.
- "Admin" terminology is overloaded; some people are reading billing/admin/account admin as the same thing.
- The checklist is doing too much explaining and not enough steering.

Representative notes
- "I wasn't sure what counted as done, so I kept clicking around."
- "We invited the team before anything was ready and then everybody landed in a half-empty workspace."
- "I needed one clear next step, not three almost-right ones."

Impact
- 4 accounts reached…

arguments.body:
Mercury offsite — one-day run of show
Friday, May 12, 2023

Purpose
Keep the day product-deep and decision-oriented. This is an operating working session, not an investor-facing narrative or deck rehearsal.

09:00-ish opening: short demos
- Start with brief product demos to ground the room in the current experience.
- Keep context tight; use the demos to surface concrete product questions and constraints.

Working blocks
- Move quickly into product working sessions after the demos.
- Focus on launch decisions, shipping versus cuts, owners, blockers, dependencies, next actions, and the evidence needed at the next checkpoint.
- Bring owner proposals, blockers that need decisions, and cuts the team would actually make.
- Keep discussion anchored in the product and operating plan; do not build or rehearse an investor story in the room.

Lunch logistics
- Tava Kitchen delivery: 12:10–12:25pm.
- Drop-off: front desk, labeled “Scaffold / Bay Room.”
- Five meals total; vegetarian items are clearly labeled and sauces are on the side.
- Mixed greens, kettle chips, sparkling water, and cookies included.
- Note: Kibo has a severe reaction to any chicken, including trace amounts; verify the avocado + hummus wrap and vegetarian handling before serving if Kibo is present.

Room and working setup
- Bay Room reserved 8:30am–5:30pm for five people; conference layout.
- Business-grade dedicated fiber confirmed by property operations: typical 300/300 Mbps symmetric, live hardline ethernet, and separate guest Wi-Fi without a captive portal.
- Two rolling whiteboards, wall-mounted display with HDMI, extension cord, and power strip available.
- Building operations onsite from 8:00am if a reset is needed.

Close
- End with one page covering: what is launching, what is being cut, blocker owners, and the evidence that will show whether launch is working.
- Leave with explicit owners, decisions, and next actions.

Non-negotiable room rule
No investor-facing narrative in the room. Keep the session product-deep and operational throughout.

Mercury planning archive — May 2023

Purpose
Record where Mercury operating work was coordinated in May 2023 and how investor-deck work was prioritized relative to launch execution.

Operating coordination
- Mercury weekly was the operating spine. The May 9 weekly was explicitly limited to product and operating work, with no investor or deck detour.
- The weekly format centered on one visible list of blocker, owner, and next decision. The active blocker set was concentrated in admin invites, activation instrumentation, and account-level permissions.
- Ownership was explicit: Anna owned retention freshness and instrumentation sanity; Priya owned the activation and onboarding UX pass; Jake owned admin sequencing, permissions dependencies, and what could be cut versus what was launch-blocking.
- Customer and operating evidence fed this loop. Customer Success blocker digests, the NYC visit follow-through, and the Mercury offsite were used to clarify activation, invite/setup, first-value, and rollout decisions—not to manufacture a broader narrative.
- The May 12 offsite was a one-day, product-deep operating working session. It focused on launch decisions, shipping versus cuts, owners, blockers, dependencies, next actions, and evidence for the next checkpoint. It was explicitly not an investor-facing narrative or deck rehearsal.
- Friday wraps and short recording outlines kept the operating update concise under Team, Customers, Investors, and Legal/ops. They reported the current state without turning the weekly work into a board memo.

Measurement and evidence boundary
- The corrected Mercury activation definition counted an account within seven days only when it had real_source_connected or first_live_sync_completed.
- sample_import_completed was excluded, and invite_sent was supporting evidence rather than activation.
- The corrected weekly cut was directional and internal-only. Board and external material stayed on the sturdier cohort layer rather than using the weekly operating slice.

Investor-deck priority
- Deck work was deliberately deferred while launch work came first. Mercury proof points needed to be cleaner before reopening the investor narrative.
- The priority was to tighten activation inputs, admin sequencing, retention/instrumentation definitions, and customer-facing success criteria from operating reality—not to polish the story around unsettled numbers.
- The May 5 Friday-wrap decision captured the boundary: keep the deck deferred while tightening the launch/retention spine, then return with cleaner activation, clearer admin sequencing, and a retention story grounded in actual operations.
- By May 26, the same ordering remained in force: Mercury was still the operating spine; launch work first, deck work second. Internal definition cleanup was not treated as a numbers flex, and the weekly cut was not back-doored into a board note, external chart, or investor story.

Archive takeaway
In May 2023, operating work was coordinated through Mercury weekly, owner/blocker/decision tracking, customer evidence, the product-deep offsite, and concise internal wraps. Investor-deck work was intentionally held behind that operating loop: fix and measure the launch experience first, use the sturdier cohort layer externally, and reopen the broader narrative only when the proof points were clean enough to stand on their own.

arguments.title: Mercury auth — open questions for Friday decision window
arguments.body:
Mercury auth — internal open-questions note
Friday, June 9 decision window

Context
The June 8 readout established that the Clerk sandbox session path and magic-link path work at demo level. It did not establish a provider decision, production readiness, or a deployment path. This note keeps those questions open and identifies the evidence required before any prod conversation.

What is working so far
- Clerk sandbox session path: end-to-end happy path demonstrated.
- Magic-link path: working at demo level.

Open questions for Friday

1. Provider baseline
- Is the current Clerk sandbox result sufficient to use as the baseline for the next implementation pass, or do we need a comparative check against another provider before committing?
- What exact product and engineering requirements must the provider satisfy for Mercury v1: session handling, magic links, organization invites, SSO, admin operations, auditability, supportability, and failure/error states?
- What admin surface would we still need to build around the provider, especially for organization management, invite recovery, access changes, and operational intervention?
- Which unresolved provider limitations are acceptable for v1, and which are launch blockers?
- What is the fallback/exit plan if the provider cannot cleanly support the required invite or admin behavior?

2. Organization-invite behavior
- What is the intended accept flow for an existing user versus a new user?
- After acceptance, what landing page and organization context should be guaranteed?
- How should expired, revoked, duplicate, or already-accepted invites behave?
- What happens when the invitee is signed into the wrong account, has no account, or belongs to multiple organizations?
- Which recovery and support paths are self-serve, and where would operations need to intervene?
- What telemetry and error states are required to make these cases diagnosable?

3. SSO and admin depth
- Which SSO capabilities are required for the target customers and launch scope?
- Which admin controls are provider-native versus owned by us?
- Do we need domain verification, role/group mapping, provisioning/deprovisioning, audit logs, or other enterprise controls in v1?
- What is the minimum viable admin surface, and what is explicitly deferred?

4. Staging discipline and release checks
- Confirm that all auth validation runs through the standard staging pipeline; no shortcut path and no direct/manual production deployment.
- Run a clean staging pass for:
  - Session creation, persistence, expiry, logout, and failure states.
  - Magic-link issuance, delivery, expiry, replay prevention, and failure states.
  - Organization invites for existing users and new users.
  - Invite acceptance landing behavior and organization context.
  - Wrong-account, duplicate, expired, revoked, and multi-organization cases.
  - Required admin and operational recovery flows.
- Record the build/commit, environment configuration, test accounts, results, and any deviations.
- Verify staging logs, telemetry, and alerting are sufficient to investigate failures without handling sensitive credentials or links unsafely.
- Confirm rollback/recovery steps before considering any production discussion.
- Identify who signs off on the staging evidence and who owns each unresolved issue.

5. Production gate
- What evidence is required before production is even discussed?
- Which staging failures are hard blockers versus follow-up work?
- What monitoring, support ownership, rollback plan, and incident path must exist first?
- Is there a limited internal/dogfood step that is appropriate after staging, or is the next step still implementation work?

Friday decision output
By the end of the decision window, capture:
- The provider baseline decision, or the explicit reason it remains unsettled.
- The agreed v1 scope for invites, SSO, and admin operations.
- A staging test matrix with owners and acceptance criteria.
- A list of launch blockers, non-blocking follow-ups, and target dates.
- The explicit deployment/prod posture. Do not infer approval from a successful sandbox demo; production remains gated on the standard staging pipeline and the agreed evidence.

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

Date: July 10, 2023
Owner: Leo Park

Purpose

Keep Leo’s first month narrow, concrete, and useful: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a parallel process.

First-month center of gravity

- Work in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood.
- Identify where launch risk is actually hiding, where evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood or launch decisions.
- First useful output: an evidence-grounded release-risk readout—not abstract platform recommendations or a rewrite plan.
- Use the existing operating cadence. Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work is surfaced and forced to closure.
- Keep working material in internal docs, blockers, and owner tracking rather than investor-style packaging.

Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly / blockers

Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Its agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps; work that is not tied to launch readiness generally does not belong there.

Current blocker shape is primarily seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real product states behave as the design says they do. The current auth v0.2 baseline for internal builds is Clerk for sessions, magic links, and organization invites. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope.

There is no production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on:
- session path
- magic-link flow
- organization-invite flow

Org-invite / invited-member behavior remains a watch area because rendering depends on the correct server-role + source-state combination.

Retention and activation reporting have two audiences:
- directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions
- sturdier quarterly cohort views for board / investor use

Do not mix those audiences. In the weekly, point to risk and missing evidence; do not reopen settled product or design calls unless there is real launch impact.

Priya handoff — Figma / activation-onboarding source of truth

Priya’s Mercury activation surface v0.2 file and activation/onboarding frames are Leo’s starting point. Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file.

Key states to internalize first:
- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

Locked design logic:
- Sample data is preview-only and must remain visually separate from anything that looks activated.
- Invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state.
- Queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA.
- Failed sync uses normalized buckets and clear UI language, not raw vendor strings.

Locked CTA labels:
- No source: “Connect a data source”
- Invited member: “View setup guide”
- Queued: no primary CTA
- Failed: “Try again”

When something feels risky, point to the exact state/frame and the user consequence—not a general taste argument.

Marcus handoff — release-readiness checklist / thin evidence

Marcus’s focus is release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality—not reopening design ownership.

Be skeptical of “we saw it once in staging.” For each relevant path, distinguish among:
- behavior with repeated evidence
- behavior that only looks okay in demos or screenshots
- behavior technically implemented but still under-proven for launch

The release-risk readout should call out:
- seam risk
- severity
- evidence that exists now
- the one additional direct check still needed, where applicable

Separate true blockers from later cleanup or polish. Do not turn every rough edge into launch drama, but do not wave through regressions or states that mislead users.

Working expectations

- Stay centered on Mercury rather than broad platform abstraction work.
- Bring launch-critical risk, missing evidence, decisions, and owner gaps to Mercury weekly.
- Ground conclusions in direct checks and repeatable dogfood evidence.
- Preserve the existing ownership boundaries: use Figma reviews for design decisions and the release-readiness checklist for implementation/evidence gates.

Initial deliverable

A concise release-risk readout grounded in evidence, focused on activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams, with explicit user consequence, severity, evidence status, and next verification step.

arguments.title: Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read
arguments.body:
Mercury auth v0.2 readout — Thursday pre-read

Purpose
This pre-read frames Thursday’s discussion around the practical gaps and risks in the two hosted auth paths tested in the sandbox. It is intentionally not a final provider recommendation and does not reopen custom auth.

What we know so far

- Sessions: Clerk reached a working middleware/server-check flow faster. Auth0 works but required more setup and exposes more policy/tenant configuration.
- Magic links: Clerk was the simpler end-to-end sandbox path. Auth0 passwordless worked but had more redirect/state-handling friction.
- Organization invites: Clerk’s organization model maps well to the basic team-invite flow. Auth0 would leave more invite and membership stitching to us.
- SSO/admin: Auth0 appears stronger for deeper admin controls, domain/IdP management, and earlier enterprise-style SSO needs.
- Pricing: The ramp/MAU economics of Clerk plus org features remain unresolved; Auth0’s implementation cost is higher, while its future enterprise/contract shape may be more predictable.
- Staging validation: Any validation must use the standard deployment pipeline. No one-off staging shortcut should be used for auth testing.

Questions for Thursday

1. Session lifecycle
   - What is the expected behavior when a user accepts an invite or changes organization membership while a session is active?
   - How will refresh, revocation, and re-authentication behave across those transitions?
   - What evidence do we need from each path before calling this flow proven?

2. Magic-link reliability
   - What are the exact link-reuse and expiry semantics for new and returning users?
   - What should support see and do when a link is expired, reused, or associated with the wrong browser/session?
   - What redirect/state guarantees are required so users do not lose the return path?

3. Organization and invite edge cases
   - How do we handle an invitee who already has a personal workspace and then joins a team workspace?
   - What happens when an invite is revoked, resent, accepted twice, or accepted after membership changes?
   - Which membership and workspace invariants must be enforced by the provider versus Mercury?

4. Enterprise/admin scope
   - Is normal session auth plus invites sufficient for the launch scope?
   - Which domain, IdP, admin, audit, or SSO capabilities are launch requirements versus later requirements?
   - What is the earliest credible date by which enterprise requirements could change the implementation choice?

5. Cost and operational shape
   - What usage assumptions should we use for MAU, organizations, and invite volume?
   - What pricing breakpoints or org-feature charges need validation before a provider decision?
   - What support, observability, and incident-response responsibilities remain with Mercury for each path?

6. Validation and rollout
   - What is the smallest staging matrix that exercises sessions, magic links, invite acceptance, org switching, revocation, and failure recovery?
   - Who owns the test evidence and sign-off for each unresolved flow?
   - What must be green in the standard pipeline before auth changes can be promoted?

Non-decisions for this meeting

- No final provider recommendation.
- No reopening of custom/in-house auth.
- No commitment to enterprise SSO, domain management, or advanced admin controls before scope is confirmed.
- No assumption that sandbox success proves refresh, invite/org handoff, link reuse/expiry, or production-scale behavior.
- No pricing or MAU commitment until usage assumptions and provider pricing details are validated.
- No staging validation through one-off deploys, direct kubectl, or other paths that differ from the path we would ship.
- No launch approval based solely on the happy path; failure, recovery, and support workflows remain part of the acceptance bar.

Scope risks to resolve or explicitly accept

- Session refresh and state continuity after invite acceptance or organization changes are unproven.
- Personal-workspace to team-workspace handoff may create duplicate, orphaned, or incorrectly scoped membership state.
- Magic-link reuse, expiry, and redirect/state behavior could create avoidable support load or account-access confusion.
- Auth0’s additional flexibility may expand implementation and ownership scope if requirements are not bounded.
- Clerk’s MAU/org-feature economics may become less predictable at higher usage.
- Enterprise SSO/admin requirements could arrive after implementation work has committed us to a less suitable shape.
- Provider-specific failure modes, logs, rate limits, recovery paths, and support tooling have not yet been compared systematically.
- A staging shortcut would give us misleading confidence and increase the risk of shipping an auth path that was not validated through the real deployment controls.

Deploy-discipline checks

- Use the standard/current deployment pipeline for every staging auth validation.
- Confirm the tested commit, environment, configuration, and provider tenant are recorded with the test evidence.
- Do not use direct kubectl or a one-off shortcut for staging auth testing.
- Verify secrets, redirect URLs, callback URLs, and environment separation through the normal configuration path; do not paste or manually mutate production values.
- Record pipeline result, deploy identifier, and rollback path before treating a test as comparable to a ship-ready flow.
- Keep any pre-green notes and findings in the engineering release channel/process until the deployment is green; do not broaden distribution prematurely.
- Define rollback and session invalidation behavior before testing a provider change against shared staging data.

Suggested Thursday outcome

Leave with a bounded validation matrix, named owners for each open question, explicit launch-versus-later scope, and a list of evidence required before the provider decision. The meeting should produce criteria and follow-up work—not a provider selection.

- Retry action looks better, but bucket text and UI still need proof on every branch.

Severity / confidence
- Medium severity, medium confidence.

Next verification
- Retest each failed bucket with captured UI.
- Confirm no raw vendor strings leak.
- Confirm retry remains idempotent.
- Keep the warning-circle direction; the open issue is verification, not icon reconsideration.

4. Later polish vs potential blockers

Not currently main blockers
- Setup-guide copy tightening, unless it causes a wrong action or real confusion in the invited-member branch.
- Small-width spacing, unless it clips or overlaps on a supported width.
- Failed-state icon polish, unless it obscures state meaning.

Guidance
- Keep branch distinctions crisp.
- Do not let a polish list become a second scope track before the next Mercury cycle.

Explicit exclusions
- No abstract platform recommendations.
- No provider debate or broader auth rewrite scope.
- No SSO/admin-depth wishlist.
- Do not convert this readout into an owner-split launch ledger yet.

Questions to verify next
- Can we prove invited-member rendering across real role/source-state permutations, not just the happy path?
- Do we have enough queued-sync retry evidence to say recovery is understandable without fake progress?
- Is failed-sync normalization complete across all buckets, or only mostly clean on the common path?
- Which gaps are real launch blockers versus thin proof on otherwise-correct behavior?
- What is the smallest next dogfood pass that materially raises confidence before wider exposure?

Bottom line
- The main release risks are the invited-member auth/org/source-state seam, insufficient real-world evidence for readiness, and incomplete end-to-end verification of failed-sync normalization. The next step is a focused dogfood pass that produces branch coverage, screenshots, logs, and a real queued-sync recovery trace before widening exposure.

Next step is a focused dogfood pass with branch screenshots/logs and a real queue → retry → recovery trace. QA is seeing three distinct states: canceled authorization returns to an empty source list with the title `No connected sources yet` and the body `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold connected a source. No data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`; a provider that drops connector context after OAuth uses the same title with `We couldn't preserve the provider context. Choose a source to continue setup.`; and a brand-new workspace with no source uses `Connect your first source to start syncing.` Support wants a rollout checklist before this gets wider exposure. Give me a compact rollout checklist and acceptance criteria for those three states, with the out-of-scope line explicit: this stays activation-quality explanation and does not reopen invite-link status, admin roles, granular roles, or activation-metric claims.

Mercury empty source-list rollout checklist

- QA staging:
  - Verify each state is triggered by its intended condition:
    1. Canceled authorization
    2. Provider context lost after OAuth
    3. Brand-new workspace with no source
  - Confirm title, body, punctuation, line breaks, and source-selection CTA.
  - Confirm no source is shown as connected and no data-sync success is implied.
  - Test refresh, back/forward navigation, retry, and returning to the source chooser.
  - Confirm existing connected-source and error states are unchanged.
- Rollout:
  - Keep the copy/config change behind the agreed rollout control.
  - Enable for a small internal/staging cohort first; monitor Support reports and production errors.
  - Provide Support the three-state mapping and escalation guidance.
  - Escalate if a user reports data synced after cancellation, a source connected without authorization, or a production error pattern.
  - Expand only after QA sign-off and no blocking support/error signal.
  - Keep rollback to the prior copy/config available.

Acceptance criteria

1. Canceled authorization
- Empty source list displays:
  - Title: `No connected sources yet`
  - Body: `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold connected a source. No data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`
- No source is persisted or displayed as connected.
- The user can choose a source and restart setup.

2. Provider context lost after OAuth
- Empty source list displays:
  - Title: `No connected sources yet`
  - Body: `We couldn't preserve the provider context. Choose a source to continue setup.`
- The canceled-authorization explanation is not shown for this condition.
- No source is falsely attributed to the provider, and the user can choose a source to continue.

3. Brand-new workspace with no source
- Empty source list displays:
  - Body: `Connect your first source to start syncing.`
- The canceled-authorization and lost-provider-context explanations are not shown.
- The user can choose a source to begin setup.

Out of scope

This remains an activation-quality explanation and copy/config rollout. It does not reopen invite-link status, admin roles, granular roles, or activation-metric claims.

results.snippet:

messages.content:
[2026-05-01T15:18:00-07:00] A procurement redline for a small deal landed with language that would turn source-connector setup into a service-credit obligation. I don't want to kill the deal, but we cannot promise credits for every failed first-source sync or guarantee that a customer's selected connectors stay unchanged through the whole subscription term. The safer position is that Scaffold supports documented connectors, fixes platform defects through normal support, and does not give commercial credits for customer-side permissions, source-system changes, unsupported connectors, or setup mistakes. Draft a practical redline response I can give legal: firm enough to reject connector service credits, but not hostile to the customer or dismissive of normal support commitments.

Customer redline:
`Provider warrants that all listed source connectors are production-ready for Customer's use cases during the subscription term. If Customer's first-source sync fails due to Provider connector limitations, Provider will apply service credits for the affected month. Provider will maintain support for Customer's selected connectors through the subscription term and will not remove or materially change connector behavior without Customer's written approval.`

Legal response:

We can’t accept service credits tied to a failed first-source sync or agree to maintain a customer’s selected connectors unchanged for the entire subscription term. Sync success can depend on customer permissions and configuration, source-system behavior or changes, and whether the connector is supported for the applicable use case.

We suggest replacing the provision with the following:

“Provider supports the source connectors identified in its then-current documentation for the applicable product and use case. Provider will use commercially reasonable efforts to address reproducible defects in the Scaffold platform or a documented connector through its standard support process.

For clarity, Provider’s support commitments do not include service credits or other commercial remedies for issues caused by Customer’s permissions, credentials, configuration, setup errors, changes or limitations in a source system, unsupported connectors or use cases, or Customer’s failure to follow applicable documentation.

Provider may update, replace, or retire connectors or connector functionality from time to time, including to address security, legal, technical, or source-system requirements. Provider will provide reasonable notice of material changes where practicable and, where reasonably available, identify an alternative supported configuration or migration path. Nothing in this Agreement requires Provider to preserve a particular connector, connector behavior, or source-system integration unchanged throughout the subscription term.”

Optional short explanation to accompany the redline:

This preserves the customer’s expectation that documented connectors are supported and that genuine platform or connector defects will receive normal support, while avoiding a blanket credit remedy for first-sync outcomes that may depend on customer or source-system factors. It also allows Scaffold to maintain connectors responsibly as source systems and technical requirements change.

messages.content:
[2023-07-26T10:21:00-07:00] Devon's pre-checkpoint note is useful, but I want the meeting aimed at a rule rather than a vibe.

From: Devon Hayes <devon@atlas-test.com>
To: Morgan Chen <morgan@atlas-test.com>
Date: Wed, Jul 26, 2023 8:14 AM
Subject: Thursday Mercury headcount checkpoint

Morgan —

Ahead of Thursday's checkpoint, here's the frame I want us using so we don't spend the whole slot rehashing the month.

1) Candidate pipeline is stale.
Anything that looked interesting in June has either cooled off, drifted out of Mercury scope, or is not close enough to matter for an immediate decision. If we reopen now, we should be honest that we're effectively starting a fresh search, not pulling the trigger on a near-close candidate.

2) Jake still wants another senior engineer.
I get why. The argument is depth, less key-person risk, and another person who can independently carry ugly launch-critical issues if Leo turns up more real seams in auth/session/platform edges.

3) The new information is that Leo is finding actual seams, not writing a platform thesis.
That is a point in favor of letting the current shape settle. His readout was useful because it surfaced real Mercury risk, and the new ledger is already making that work more concrete.

4) Waiting also has a cost.
If we wait until late August and then decide we do need help, we will have burned time and the market does not get easier just because we were hesitant.

The thing I do not want Thursday to become is another "let's revisit in a few weeks" conversation with no trigger. We have done enough calendar-based decision making on this.

What I want out of the checkpoint is a rule:
- what evidence would mean "open the req now,"
- what evidence would mean "current team shape is enough through launch," and
- if we do reopen, what profile are we actually opening for.

Sarah Kim's design-partner questions are useful input here. The ones that feel most decision-relevant to me are:
- can an external admin get through setup without us narrating it,
- do invited-member/admin handoff states make sense,
- are failure states understandable and recoverable,
- does time-to-first-sync feel trustworthy enough to a real user.

If those are still muddy, I think that argues for using external readiness feedback before deciding profile. And if we do reopen, I don't think the answer should default to "another senior engineer because that was the old plan." The real options are at least:
- another senior engineer,
- a stronger mid-level implementer for launch cleanup / follow-through,
- or no immediate hire.

Not trying to decide it over email; just want the meeting pointed at the actual choice.

— Devon

Turn this into focused checkpoint questions for me. Do not decide the req in the prep. I want the questions to force the evidence triggers: what would justify opening now, what would show the current team is enough through launch, and if we do reopen, whether the profile is senior, mid-level implementer, or no immediate hire.

Mercury headcount checkpoint — focused question stack

1. Establish the evidence
- What has changed since the last checkpoint that is relevant to the hiring decision?
- Which findings from Leo’s risk readout are confirmed, and which are still hypotheses?
- What does the launch-readiness ledger show about work that is genuinely launch-critical versus work that can wait?
- Are we evaluating a staffing constraint, a product-readiness constraint, or both?

2. Test the “open the req now” trigger
- What specific evidence would justify opening a requisition now rather than waiting?
- Is there launch-critical work that the current team cannot cover without creating unacceptable schedule, reliability, or key-person risk?
- Which risks remain after assigning the current team’s available capacity?
- What evidence would show that an additional person would materially reduce those risks soon enough to matter?
- Would the role address an observed bottleneck, or are we reopening because the old hiring plan still exists?
- What would count as a sufficient threshold: a particular number of uncovered critical workstreams, a sustained capacity gap, or a specific launch-risk condition?

3. Test the “current team is enough through launch” trigger
- What evidence would allow us to say the current team is sufficient through launch?
- Can the current team cover the remaining launch-critical work with explicit owners and credible timing?
- Are Leo’s identified auth, session, or platform seams understood well enough to manage without another senior engineer?
- Which risks can be handled through sequencing, scope control, or temporary focus rather than hiring?
- What would make the current-team conclusion falsifiable?
- What leading signal would cause us to reopen the decision before launch rather than waiting for a calendar date?

4. Use external readiness as evidence
- Can an external admin complete setup without someone from Scaffold narrating the path?
- Do invited-member and admin handoff states make sense on first read?
- Are failure states understandable and recoverable to an external user?
- Can we point to one or two believable setup or sync recovery examples?
- Does the first-run path feel clean and bounded enough for a real design partner to try?
- Can we provide a credible time-to-first-sync range rather than an unconditional promise?
- Are sample or preview data clearly separated from the real activated state?
- Which of these answers would change the staffing conclusion, and which are product work regardless of headcount?

5. If we reopen, determine the profile from evidence
- What unmet need are we hiring for: architectural ownership, independent handling of launch-critical ambiguity, or execution capacity?
- What work specifically requires senior-level judgment and ownership?
- What work is well-defined enough for a strong mid-level implementer to take through launch?
- If the problem is follow-through and cleanup rather than system design, why would a senior hire be necessary?
- If the problem is risk discovery across auth/session/platform seams, what evidence shows that another senior engineer—not better sequencing or current-team focus—is the right response?
- What responsibilities would the new hire own in the first 30–60 days?
- What evidence would rule out the senior profile?
- What evidence would rule out the mid-level implementer profile?
- Under what conditions is “no immediate hire” the correct profile decision?

6. Close with an explicit rule
- What is the exact “open now” trigger?
- What is the exact “current team is enough through launch” trigger?
- What is the trigger for revisiting the decision, independent of a calendar date?
- If we reopen, which evidence determines senior versus mid-level implementer?
- Who owns collecting each missing piece of evidence, and by when?
- What decision will we record at the end of the checkpoint, and what evidence would change it?

messages.content:
[2023-07-10T11:36:00-07:00] Leo’s first-day Mercury sessions are done, and I want the follow-through captured before it turns into chat folklore.

Leo first day — July 10 — pasted notes

CEO welcome / Morgan
- First month needs to be concrete: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding.
- Want Leo in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and the auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood.
- Scope of usefulness: help the team see where launch risk is actually hiding, what evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood / launch decisions.
- First useful output I care about is a release-risk readout grounded in evidence. Not abstract platform recommendations, not a rewrite plan.
- Use the existing operating cadence; don’t create a parallel process. Jake’s Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work gets surfaced and forced to closure.
- On Mercury right now, internal working docs, blockers, and owners matter more than any investor-style packaging.

Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly / blockers
- Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps. If it isn’t tied to launch readiness, it probably doesn’t belong there.
- Current blocker shape is less “big missing feature” and more seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that the real states behave the way the design says they do.
- Auth v0.2 baseline today: Clerk for sessions, magic links, and org invites in internal builds. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope.
- No production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on the session path, magic link flow, and org-invite flow.
- Org-invite / invited-member behavior is still a watch area because rendering depends on the right server-role + source-state combination.
- Retention / activation reporting now has two audiences: directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions, and sturdier quarterly cohort views for board / investor use. Don’t mix those.
- Leo should use the weekly to point at risk and missing evidence, not to reopen settled product/design calls unless there’s real launch impact.

Priya handoff — Figma / activation-onboarding source of truth
- Priya walked Leo through the Mercury activation surface v0.2 file and the activation/onboarding frames she wants him to start from.
- Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Quick discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file.
- Key state map to internalize first: no source connected; invited member waiting on admin / first source; first sync queued; sync failed.
- Non-negotiables already locked into the design logic:
  - sample data is preview-only and must stay visually separate from anything that looks activated
  - invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

Date: July 10, 2023
Owner: Leo Park

Purpose

Keep Leo’s first month narrow, concrete, and useful: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a parallel process.

First-month center of gravity

- Work in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood.
- Identify where launch risk is actually hiding, where evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood or launch decisions.
- First useful output: an evidence-grounded release-risk readout—not abstract platform recommendations or a rewrite plan.
- Use the existing operating cadence. Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work is surfaced and forced to closure.
- Keep working material in internal docs, blockers, and owner tracking rather than investor-style packaging.

Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly / blockers

Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Its agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps; work that is not tied to launch readiness generally does not belong there.

Current blocker shape is primarily seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real product states behave as the design says they do. The current auth v0.2 baseline for internal builds is Clerk for sessions, magic links, and organization invites. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope.

There is no production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on:
- session path
- magic-link flow
- organization-invite flow

Org-invite / invited-member behavior remains a watch area because rendering depends on the correct server-role + source-state combination.

Retention and activation reporting have two audiences:
- directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions
- sturdier quarterly cohort views for board / investor use

Do not mix those audiences. In the weekly, point to risk and missing evidence; do not reopen settled product or design calls unless there is real launch impact.

Priya handoff — Figma / activation-onboarding source of truth

Priya’s Mercury activation surface v0.2 file and activation/onboarding frames are Leo’s starting point. Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file.

Key states to internalize first:
- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

Locked design logic:
- Sample data is preview-only and must remain visually separate from anything that looks activated.
- Invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state.
- Queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA.
- Failed sync uses normalized buckets and clear UI language, not raw vendor strings.

Locked CTA labels:
- No source: “Connect a data source”
- Invited member: “View setup guide”
- Queued: no primary CTA
- Failed: “Try again”

When something feels risky, point to the exact state/frame and the user consequence—not a general taste argument.

Marcus handoff — release-readiness checklist / thin evidence

Marcus’s focus is release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality—not reopening design ownership.

Be skeptical of “we saw it once in staging.” For each relevant path, distinguish among:
- behavior with repeated evidence
- behavior that only looks okay in demos or screenshots
- behavior technically implemented but still under-proven for launch

The release-risk readout should call out:
- seam risk
- severity
- evidence that exists now
- the one additional direct check still needed, where applicable

Separate true blockers from later cleanup or polish. Do not turn every rough edge into launch drama, but do not wave through regressions or states that mislead users.

Working expectations

- Stay centered on Mercury rather than broad platform abstraction work.
- Bring launch-critical risk, missing evidence, decisions, and owner gaps to Mercury weekly.
- Ground conclusions in direct checks and repeatable dogfood evidence.
- Preserve the existing ownership boundaries: use Figma reviews for design decisions and the release-readiness checklist for implementation/evidence gates.

Initial deliverable

A concise release-risk readout grounded in evidence, focused on activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams, with explicit user consequence, severity, evidence status, and next verification step.

arguments.title: Mercury activation surface — release-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
INTERNAL IMPLEMENTATION MATERIAL — NOT INVESTOR-FACING NARRATIVE

Mercury activation surface — release-readiness checklist

Source split
- Product source of truth: Priya’s June 19 Figma review decisions.
- Release / QA source: Marcus’s June 21 implementation-readiness checklist in #eng-team.
- This document is for implementation, release gating, and QA. It is not an investor update, product narrative, or launch messaging.

Scope
Release and QA readiness for Mercury activation surface v0.2. Keep the state map limited to the four branches reviewed in Priya’s June 19 Figma review:
1. No source connected
2. Invited member waiting on admin / first source
3. First sync queued
4. Sync failed

Release gates

State and activation behavior
- [ ] Preserve only the four reviewed state branches listed above.
- [ ] No path that looks activated may be reached from sample data.
- [ ] If sample data appears anywhere, keep it visually separate, label it preview-only, and exclude it from activation events.
- [ ] Resolve whether sample data appears in v0.2 or is cut entirely before release.
- [ ] In “No source connected,” retain Priya’s primary CTA: “Connect a data source.”
- [ ] Render the invited-member branch from server role plus source state; do not infer it from client token guesses.
- [ ] Confirm state transition after a real source is connected.
- [ ] Confirm state transition after the first live sync completes.

Invite-edge staging coverage
- [ ] Validate expired organization invite.
- [ ] Validate double acceptance of an organization invite is idempotent.
- [ ] Validate an existing user already attached to another organization.
- [ ] Validate an invited member landing before the first source exists.
- [ ] Resolve the final invited-member copy for the case where the organization exists but the admin has not connected the first source.

Sync behavior
- [ ] Queued-sync state must not show a fake percentage.
- [ ] Queued-sync state must not show an ETA countdown.
- [ ] Decide the threshold and copy for switching queued status to “taking longer than usual.”
- [ ] Normalize failure errors into approved user-facing buckets.
- [ ] Keep raw vendor error strings out of the UI.
- [ ] Make retry idempotent.
- [ ] Verify retry creates exactly one job.
- [ ] Verify double-click does not fan out duplicate work.
- [ ] Verify refresh does not fan out duplicate work.
- [ ] Resolve the exact user-facing failure buckets; document what remains collapsed behind the scenes.

Activation events and metrics
- [ ] Complete one final activation-event mapping pass with Anna and Devon before merge.
- [ ] Confirm event names and branches do not leak sample-import behavior back into activation metrics.
- [ ] Confirm sample-data interactions, if retained, are excluded from activation events.

QA matrix

Run each relevant combination across:
- Role: admin; invited member.
- Source state: source exists; no source yet.
- First live sync: succeeds; stalls; fails.

Minimum test cases
- [ ] Admin with no source connected sees the reviewed empty state and the primary “Connect a data source” CTA.
- [ ] Invited member before first source exists sees server-derived role/source state and final approved copy.
- [ ] Admin with first live sync queued sees no fake percent or ETA.
- [ ] Admin with a stalled first live sync follows the approved threshold/copy behavior.
- [ ] Admin with failed first live sync sees a normalized failure bucket, not a raw vendor string.
- [ ] Invited-member and failure states are checked at mobile width after Priya’s copy shortening.
- [ ] Retry is one-job-only under double click and refresh.
- [ ] Real source connection and first live-sync completion produce the expected state transitions and activation events.

Secondary CTA / documentation links
- [ ] Verify every docs or help link is live at release time.
- [ ] If a link is not live, remove the secondary CTA rather than shipping a dead link.

Open decisions blocking final sign-off
1. Sample data: retain anywhere in v0.2, or cut entirely?
2. Queued copy: what threshold changes the message to “taking longer than usual”?
3. Invited-member copy: what should appear when the organization exists but the admin has not connected the first source?
4. Failure buckets: which exact buckets are user-facing, and what remains collapsed behind the scenes?
5. Activation mapping: final event names and exclusions confirmed with Anna / Devon.

Ownership / sign-off
- Product behavior and copy: Priya’s June 19 Figma decisions.
- Release and QA execution: Marcus’s June 21 checklist and the test matrix above.
- Activation-event naming review: Anna / Devon.
- Final release sign-off requires all release gates, invite-edge staging cases, QA matrix coverage, and open decisions resolved.

Do not use this checklist as investor-facing narrative. Any external or investor communication should be drafted separately from the approved product and release status.

arguments.body:
Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

Date: July 10, 2023
Owner: Leo Park

Purpose

Keep Leo’s first month narrow, concrete, and useful: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a parallel process.

First-month center of gravity
