Atlas runbook draft v1
Status: working draft
Purpose: close the two biggest Atlas runbook holes without changing support routing. Customer-facing ownership still starts with the named weekly owner in the support rotation doc.

AT-04 - Replay / backfill

When this section applies
- Replay job can rerun when the source event ID is stable and downstream derived state is missing or inconsistent.
- Do not start from the first failed customer-visible row if a last confirmed checkpoint exists.

Checkpoint rule
- Backfill starts from the last confirmed checkpoint.
- If checkpoint is absent, stop and get Atlas owner review before manual replay.

PR-1187 verifier seam
- Duplicate internal attempts may appear during replay/backfill while verifier emits one customer-visible state.
- Support should not describe internal duplicate attempts as duplicate customer action.

Support language
- Avoid promising manual replay.
- Say recovery is automatic after transient failures only when the replay path is already active and the evidence matches.

Evidence to collect before escalation
- source event ID
- last confirmed checkpoint
- current customer-visible state
- verifier output
- current API v2 support path or docs pointer used in the thread; if docs/search confusion is involved, use the current GraphQL API v2 quickstart: https://docs.atlas-test.com/api/v2/graphql-quickstart

Escalation / lane
- Customer-facing thread stays with the named weekly owner in the support rotation doc.
- Pull Rishi only for manual replay recovery, idempotency-key mismatches, or last-run-marker correction.
- Leo Park can do a first-pass verifier/auth seam read and PR-1187 behavior check, but should not be named as the default Atlas owner.

AT-05 - Workspace / org-invite migration history

What to assume first
- Old org-invite records can point at workspace IDs that were renamed during migration.
- Invite email header is not authoritative.

First support step
- Ask the weekly support owner to verify the membership record before escalating to Atlas.
- Keep customer-facing ownership with support; do not create a direct route to me for normal invite failures.

Customer / support boundary
- Do not expose raw prior org label to support or customers.
- If the issue is standard invite failure, keep it in the Atlas app lane first.

Escalation / backup notes
- Pull Jake only for time-sensitive product-priority or sequencing cuts, not implementation debugging.
- Leo can first-pass verifier/auth seams and PR-1187 behavior, but should not be named as default Atlas owner.
- Legacy org-alias collisions, wrong-workspace landings, and invite-accepted-but-membership-not-materialized cases are still the edge paths most likely to need Atlas owner review.

Open questions
- Need clearer stop condition for manual replay request.
- Unsure whether support language still says too much.
- Check Jake/Leo backup descriptions.

Review: v1 is directionally right, but I would not publish it yet. The two largest remaining gaps are an executable manual-replay procedure and explicit support/internal boundaries.

1. Missing operational steps

AT-04 — Replay/backfill

Add these steps:

- Confirm the named weekly owner has approved the replay request.
- Verify the source event ID, tenant/workspace, affected object, and last confirmed checkpoint.
- Confirm no replay is already active for the same event or scope.
- Check the idempotency key and last-run marker before starting.
- Record the operator, approval, timestamp, scope, and pre-replay customer-visible state.
- Define the replay scope and maximum retry/attempt limit.
- State what happens if the checkpoint is missing, inconsistent, or moves during execution.
- Define an abort condition: unexpected state transition, repeated verifier mismatch, duplicate customer-visible state, or any impact outside the approved scope.
- After replay, verify the customer-visible state and verifier output.
- Close the escalation only after the weekly owner confirms the result.
- If replay fails, preserve evidence and escalate to Rishi rather than retrying indefinitely.

The open question should become an explicit stop condition:

“Stop and obtain Atlas owner approval if the checkpoint is absent, the source event is not stable, an active replay exists, the idempotency key does not match, the replay would cross tenant/object scope, or the first attempt does not produce the expected customer-visible state. Do not manually retry after an abort without a new approval.”

AT-05 — Workspace/org-invite migration

Add:

- Verify the workspace ID, current membership record, invite status, recipient identity, and current account/workspace association.
- Confirm the invite is for the intended workspace before resending or changing anything.
- Check whether an accepted invite created or failed to create the membership record.
- Define the safe remediation for each supported case: resend, repair membership, or escalate.
- State whether support may perform the remediation or only collect evidence.
- Record the migration mapping and remediation in the internal ticket/audit trail.
- Add a stop condition for ambiguous identity, multiple matching workspaces, conflicting membership records, or any request to expose historical organization names.
- Define the escalation severity and expected handoff when the weekly owner is unavailable.

2. Support-language leakage

The draft still contains several phrases that should remain internal-only, or should be clearly marked as internal escalation terminology:

- “replay/backfill”
- “source event ID”
- “last confirmed checkpoint”
- “verifier seam”
- “PR-1187”
- “internal duplicate attempts”
- “idempotency-key mismatch”
- “last-run-marker correction”
- “legacy org-alias collisions”
- “wrong-workspace landings”
- “membership-not-materialized”
- raw prior organization labels

The evidence list is appropriate for an internal escalation packet, but label it explicitly:

“Internal-only evidence; do not paste these fields into customer-facing threads.”

The current support wording is also too operational:

“Say recovery is automatic after transient failures only when the replay path is already active and the evidence matches.”

That still exposes recovery mechanics and risks an unsupported promise. Replace it with something like:

“We’re reviewing the current account state and will follow up once we confirm the result. No action is needed unless we ask you to retry.”

If the customer must retry:

“Please wait for our confirmation before retrying the invite.”

Do not tell customers or ordinary support contacts that duplicate attempts were generated, that a verifier collapsed them, or that a manual replay is running.

3. Leo’s role is still too broad

This wording appears twice:

“Leo Park can do a first-pass verifier/auth seam read and PR-1187 behavior check…”

It is narrower than making Leo the owner, but still…

[2023-10-11T08:58:00-07:00] Marcus’s auth-rewrite rollout checklist is here:

Auth rewrite rollout checklist
Owner: Marcus
Date: 2023-10-11
Scope: API v2 auth path only. Existing API behavior remains GraphQL + JWT on the client-facing side; this rollout changes how session revalidation happens behind that path.

Status snapshot
- Staging pass completed on the happy path.
- JWT refresh behavior looks correct in the tested web flows.
- Rollback path is defined, but I have not finished the last prod-like dry run on the rollback toggle.
- Release note wording is still open, mainly on whether we name Clerk directly or keep the note provider-neutral.

Preflight items
[x] Staging login -> dashboard load on API v2 with fresh JWT
[x] Expired JWT on API v2 GraphQL request triggers background revalidation and returns a fresh token without user-visible signout
[x] Retry-once refresh path matches the already-live auth refresh retry behavior
[x] Accepted-org-invite flow still lands the user in the correct org after session revalidation
[x] Existing browser session survives page refresh after token expiry
[ ] Canary owner + 30-minute watch window confirmed
[ ] Rollback toggle exercised end-to-end in prod-like config
[ ] Final release note wording approved for #eng-releases

Clerk session revalidation steps
1. Start with an existing signed-in web session on API v2.
2. Let the short-lived JWT age past TTL or force-expire it in the browser.
3. Hit a normal GraphQL read and then a write.
4. Expected result: request chain gets a fresh JWT through the session revalidation path; user stays signed in; org context does not change.
5. Confirm session revalidation does not bounce the user to auth, lose the selected workspace, or break invite-derived org membership.
6. Watch for a one-request 401 blip versus a sticky 401 loop; only the sticky case is a rollout stopper.

JWT refresh checks
- Fresh-token path: no regression in normal API v2 reads/writes.
- Expired-token path: refresh occurs once, request succeeds, no manual retry needed.
- Concurrent-tab check: second tab should accept the new token without drifting into repeated 401s.
- Metrics to watch during canary: 401 rate, refresh retry count, session revalidation latency, and any spike in auth-related support pings.

Rollback flag
- Rollback is a single toggle that disables Clerk-backed session revalidation and returns API v2 to the legacy validator path.
- Intended use: only if canary shows sustained auth failures, sticky 401 loops, or org-context mismatches.
- Expected rollback behavior: JWT format exposed to API v2 callers stays the same; the internal session source changes back.
- Still open: I want one more dry run to confirm the toggle clears cleanly without leaving mixed auth state on already-warm pods.

Draft release-note wording
Option A — provider named
API v2 auth now uses Clerk-backed session revalidation behind the scenes for expired sessions. No customer action is expected.

Option B — provider-neutral
API v2 auth now revalidates expired sessions more consistently in the background. No customer action is expected.

Open wording note
I’m not sure whether naming Clerk in the release note is useful precision for the team or unnecessary provider callout. Everything else in the note can stay narrow to API v2 auth behavior.

Please review it and DM Marcus the remaining go/no-go questions in our internal team chat. Also prepare a narrow #eng-releases note that describes the API v2 auth behavior change without making Clerk customer-facing positioning or implying any customer action is needed.

arguments.message:
Diagnosis: your read is supported. Clerk revalidation succeeds and advances the session to v27/rt_4b22, but the inline retry starts before the cookie write and reuses cached v26/rt_4b21. The refresh exchange then rejects the retry (expected v27/rt_4b22, got v26/rt_4b21), so the original request returns 401; hard reload passes because it picks up the new context. Before calling the patch green, please answer:
1) Does the retry consume the revalidation result directly (or otherwise wait for the new cookie/session context) instead of rereading the stale cache?
2) Is the update/refresh exchange atomic under concurrent expired-token requests, including single-flight behavior and old-refresh-token invalidation?
3) Do tests cover this exact expired-mid-flight ordering, plus concurrent retries and a failed refresh, and verify the original request succeeds without requiring a hard reload?
4) Do logs/metrics distinguish successful Clerk revalidation followed by stale-context retry failure, so we can confirm the race is gone in staging?

Evergreen current-flow examples pack

Purpose

A compact pack of demonstrable current-state examples for internal circulation. Each example should use the same structure:

- What the admin is trying to do
- Current-flow steps
- What the admin sees or receives
- Where the flow stops or requires follow-up
- Direct current-state statement
- Any limitation that must not be mistaken for an enterprise variant

The pack should not include dates, roadmap sequencing, or language suggesting that an alternate enterprise flow exists behind the current one.

1. First admin: entering the current Mercury flow

Example scenario

A first administrator is given access to a new workspace and needs to enter the current bounded Mercury flow.

Current-flow walkthrough

1. The admin receives the initial access or invitation email.
2. The admin follows the link and uses the current magic-link authentication flow.
3. The admin enters the assigned workspace.
4. The admin completes the currently supported workspace setup steps.
5. The admin proceeds to the available source-connection step, if applicable.
6. The admin reaches the current Mercury workspace state.

Required written statement

“This is the current Mercury admin path. It uses the current magic-link flow. There is no SSO or SAML step in this flow.”

Also state explicitly:

- This is the same current path for Evergreen as for other customers.
- There is no separate enterprise branch being omitted from the example.
- The example covers the presently bounded admin experience, not a future enterprise configuration.

2. Second admin: adding another administrator

Example scenario

The first admin adds a second admin to the same workspace.

Current-flow walkthrough

1. The first admin opens the current organization or workspace invitation control.
2. The first admin enters the second admin’s email address.
3. Mercury sends the organization invite.
4. The second admin follows the invite link.
5. The second admin completes the current magic-link flow.
6. The second admin enters the same workspace.
7. Both admins can be shown in the resulting current workspace state.

Required written statement

“This is the same current organization-invite and magic-link flow used to add another administrator to an existing workspace. It is not an Evergreen-only variant.”

Clarify the scope:

- The example demonstrates adding an admin through the current invitation model.
- It should not imply a separate SSO, directory-sync, or enterprise-provisioning path.
- Any permissions shown should be described only as the permissions currently available in the flow.

- What action, if any, the admin can retry.
- When the admin must involve Mercury.
- What information should accompany follow-up, such as workspace, source, connection time, and observed sync state.

arguments.body:
Sarah, Devon —

Below is a short FAQ you can forward to Evergreen. It is intentionally limited to the current test and avoids roadmap dates or bespoke commitments.

Evergreen Mercury test — FAQ

1) Invite and testing scope

Can our current admin invite additional testers now?
Yes. The current admin can invite additional testers under the existing Mercury test.

Is this a broader rollout?
No. This remains bounded testing / preview use, not a broader rollout.

What guardrails should we keep in mind?
Please keep the additional access within the intended invited tester group and treat the activity as part of the bounded test. Adding the second admin group does not change the test into a general rollout.

2) Login flow

What is the current login path?
The current login path is magic link.

Are organization invites part of the setup flow?
Yes. Organization invites are part of the current setup flow.

What happens if a magic link expires?
The user should request a fresh magic link. There is no separate support step required for the normal expired-link case.

3) Pricing interpretation

How should we interpret Pilot and Growth for budgeting?
Pilot and Growth are the current budgetary guidance bands. They are based on active usage, not seat count or directory size.

Is this a custom quote?
No. This is budgetary guidance only, not a custom quote.

4) Current scope and enterprise-readiness gaps

Is SSO in the current launch/test scope?
No. SSO remains an enterprise-readiness gap.

Is audit history for admin changes in the current scope?
No. Audit history for admin changes remains an enterprise-readiness gap.

Does Mercury currently separate admin permissions from billing-owner controls?
That separation is not currently available; it remains an enterprise-readiness gap.

Do these gaps block adding invited testers under the current bounded test?
No. They do not block adding invited testers under the current bounded test, provided the access remains within that bounded testing scope.

5) Procurement and commercial follow-up

Who owns procurement follow-up on our side?
Devon Hayes is the commercial/procurement owner for follow-up. Product questions can remain in the coordination thread, while Devon handles procurement and paperwork.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold

arguments.title: Mercury auth — open questions for Friday decision window
arguments.body:
Mercury auth — internal open-questions note
Friday, June 9 decision window

Context
The June 8 readout established that the Clerk sandbox session path and magic-link path work at demo level. It did not establish a provider decision, production readiness, or a deployment path. This note keeps those questions open and identifies the evidence required before any prod conversation.

What is working so far
- Clerk sandbox session path: end-to-end happy path demonstrated.
- Magic-link path: working at demo level.

Open questions for Friday

1. Provider baseline
- Is the current Clerk sandbox result sufficient to use as the baseline for the next implementation pass, or do we need a comparative check against another provider before committing?
- What exact product and engineering requirements must the provider satisfy for Mercury v1: session handling, magic links, organization invites, SSO, admin operations, auditability, supportability, and failure/error states?
- What admin surface would we still need to build around the provider, especially for organization management, invite recovery, access changes, and operational intervention?
- Which unresolved provider limitations are acceptable for v1, and which are launch blockers?
- What is the fallback/exit plan if the provider cannot cleanly support the required invite or admin behavior?

2. Organization-invite behavior
- What is the intended accept flow for an existing user versus a new user?
- After acceptance, what landing page and organization context should be guaranteed?
- How should expired, revoked, duplicate, or already-accepted invites behave?
- What happens when the invitee is signed into the wrong account, has no account, or belongs to multiple organizations?
- Which recovery and support paths are self-serve, and where would operations need to intervene?
- What telemetry and error states are required to make these cases diagnosable?

3. SSO and admin depth
- Which SSO capabilities are required for the target customers and launch scope?
- Which admin controls are provider-native versus owned by us?
- Do we need domain verification, role/group mapping, provisioning/deprovisioning, audit logs, or other enterprise controls in v1?
- What is the minimum viable admin surface, and what is explicitly deferred?

4. Staging discipline and release checks
- Confirm that all auth validation runs through the standard staging pipeline; no shortcut path and no direct/manual production deployment.
- Run a clean staging pass for:
  - Session creation, persistence, expiry, logout, and failure states.
  - Magic-link issuance, delivery, expiry, replay prevention, and failure states.
  - Organization invites for existing users and new users.
  - Invite acceptance landing behavior and organization context.
  - Wrong-account, duplicate, expired, revoked, and multi-organization cases.
  - Required admin and operational recovery flows.
- Record the build/commit, environment configuration, test accounts, results, and any deviations.
- Verify staging logs, telemetry, and alerting are sufficient to investigate failures without handling sensitive credentials or links unsafely.
- Confirm rollback/recovery steps before considering any production discussion.
- Identify who signs off on the staging evidence and who owns each unresolved issue.

5. Production gate
- What evidence is required before production is even discussed?
- Which staging failures are hard blockers versus follow-up work?
- What monitoring, support ownership, rollback plan, and incident path must exist first?
- Is there a limited internal/dogfood step that is appropriate after staging, or is the next step still implementation work?

Friday decision output
By the end of the decision window, capture:
- The provider baseline decision, or the explicit reason it remains unsettled.
- The agreed v1 scope for invites, SSO, and admin operations.
- A staging test matrix with owners and acceptance criteria.
- A list of launch blockers, non-blocking follow-ups, and target dates.
- The explicit deployment/prod posture. Do not infer approval from a successful sandbox demo; production remains gated on the standard staging pipeline and the agreed evidence.

input.body:
March 2023 board framing: separating the financing miss from company execution

The financing miss and the operating result were related, but they were not the same event. We treated the missed financing as a capital-markets outcome: the planned raise did not close on the expected timing or terms. We did not automatically translate that outcome into a verdict on the company’s execution.

To separate the two, we reviewed the business against the operating plan independently of the fundraising process: customer and revenue progress, product delivery, operating discipline, and the milestones management directly controlled. We then isolated the financing-specific factors—funding availability, investor appetite, timing, and the resulting cash constraint—from execution gaps that required management action.

That framing produced a more useful board discussion. The financing miss required a liquidity response and a revised capital plan. Execution was judged on the evidence in the operating KPIs and milestone record, with any genuine gaps named separately and assigned owners. In short: the financing outcome changed our runway and choices; it did not, by itself, prove that the company had failed to execute.

  - implying the corrected weekly activation work gives us external-ready proof

September 2024 cloud infrastructure variance note

Invoice period: September 2024  
September total: $8,642.18  
August total: $8,190.00  
Month-over-month variance: +$452.18 (+5.52%)

Summary

September cloud infrastructure spend increased by $452.18 versus August. The variance is concentrated in production Atlas API v2 traffic and a one-week staging increase for Mercury release validation. The supplied usage detail does not identify an unexplained production event, one-time restore, failover, or material change to the account-level support charge.

Variance by area

- Production: +$313.26
  - EC2 for atlas-api-v2: +$140.22, driven by higher production API v2 request volume.
  - Data Transfer for atlas-api-v2-egress: +$88.41, driven by higher response volume and webhook delivery traffic.
  - Application Load Balancer: +$47.16, consistent with increased traffic and request processing.
  - RDS PostgreSQL: +$23.58, described as normal production growth with no one-time restore or failover charge.
  - ElastiCache Redis: +$9.73, consistent with higher production request volume.
  - S3 connector payloads and archives: +$4.16, reflecting a slight increase in storage and requests.

- Staging: +$129.62
  - ECS Fargate: +$98.40.
  - CloudWatch: +$31.22.
  - Both increases are attributed to a one-week staging/test expansion for Mercury release validation.

- Shared services: +$7.12
  - NAT Gateway: +$5.30.
  - Route 53 and WAF: +$1.82.
  - These are minor increases consistent with higher external request volume; staging validation contributed a small portion of the NAT Gateway increase.

- Non-production baseline: +$2.18
  - Legacy us-west-2 compute and storage remained essentially flat.

- Support Plan: $0.00 variance
  - The account-level monthly support charge was unchanged.

Largest drivers

The three largest increases—production EC2, Data Transfer, and the production Application Load Balancer—account for $275.79 of the total variance. These are all consistent with increased Atlas API v2 production usage. The Mercury staging validation increase accounts for an additional $129.62.

Conclusion and approval context

The $8,642.18 invoice is above the AP manual-review threshold. Based on the supplied usage detail, the $452.18 increase is explainable and appears operationally consistent with:

1. Higher Atlas API v2 production request, response, and webhook traffic; and
2. A one-week Mercury release-validation effort in staging.

Recommended disposition: approve the invoice if the Mercury release-validation work was planned and authorized. If that staging work has not yet been confirmed, hold approval only for confirmation of the $129.62 staging variance; no other material anomaly is evident in the supplied data.

arguments.body:
September Mercury metrics package — board and H2 prep bounds

Prepared for: Morgan, Devon, and Anna
Source package: Anna Martinez’s first September Mercury package
Data cutoff: Sep 4, 2023 EOD PT
Status: Internal prep document

Purpose and boundary

Preserve the useful operating implications of the September Mercury package without turning it into outside proof. This document keeps two distinct reporting layers:

1. Board-operating alignment / selective H2 prep
2. Internal weekly diagnostics for operating decisions only

Board-operating layer: supported uses

The board-operating layer supports board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep context because:

- September design-partner activation is materially cleaner than the repaired May baseline under the current, sturdier 7-day activation definition.
- Activation here means an account hit either real_source_connected or first_live_sync_completed within 7 days of workspace creation; sample-preview-only accounts are excluded from the denominator.
- The repaired May comparable design-partner cut was 4 of 10 accounts activated within 7 days (40%).
- The current design-partner cohort, covering workspaces created Jul 31–Aug 27, was 8 of 11 (73%).
- Admin friction is down for the design-partner cohort: median time from workspace creation to first invited member accepted fell from 5.4 days to 2.3 days; accounts needing manual admin intervention fell from 6/10 to 2/11; and accounts reaching a first non-owner user within 7 days rose from 3/10 to 7/11.
- Evergreen Bank adds meaningful enterprise substance: 4 admin users touched setup/settings, 12 invited members were recorded, 3 real sources were connected, and successful live-sync activity occurred on 8 distinct days through Sep 4. This is repeated real-source/live-sync behavior after setup, not just a one-day preview spike.

The safe operating statement is: activation and admin handoff are materially cleaner than the repaired May operating read, and Evergreen contributes meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence. This supports board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep context.

Required caveats

- Expansion is still uneven account to account. The 30-day read shows 3 accounts meaningfully up, 3 mostly flat, and 2 choppy or down. Evergreen is the best positive signal, but the set does not support a solved expansion story.
- The weekly activation movement is internal-only. Do not use the weekly cuts in board notes, board charts, investor materials, or external/customer communications. They remain useful for operating decisions, debugging admin/setup friction, and reviewing sample-preview exclusions.
- This package does not prove retention.
- This package does not solve expansion.
- This package does not make the Mercury story external-ready.
- Evergreen is one account, not blanket enterprise validation.

Internal weekly diagnostics layer — internal only

Keep this layer separate from board/H2 framing. At the Sep 4 cutoff:

- Jul 31 week: 2 of 3 eligible accounts activated within 7 days (67%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 7 week: 2 of 3 (67%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 14 week: 2 of 3 (67%); no sample-preview-only exclusions.
- Aug 21 week: 2 of 2 (100%); 1 sample-preview-only exclusion.
- Aug 28 week: full 7-day window incomplete; pending.

These samples are small and sensitive to account mix. Use them for internal diagnosis and operating decisions only, never as external proof or as board-facing chart material.

Suggested one-sentence framing

The September package is materially better than the May operating read on cleaner real-source/live-sync activation and admin handoff, with Evergreen adding meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence; expansion remains uneven, the weekly activation movement is internal-only, and the package does not prove retention, solve expansion, or make the story external-ready.

Decision boundary

Use the board-operating layer for board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep. Keep the weekly diagnostics layer internal-only. Do not convert either layer into external claims without a later, separately reviewed evidence package.

Discord DM — Devon Hayes → Morgan Chen
2024-01-16 08:31 PT

Rough cut before the Sofia call. I’m writing this as the compare/contrast if the partnership discussion turned into a real proposal, not assuming we already have paper.

| Dimension | Possible Northstar lead option | Delay and widen process |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | If Sofia comes back with something like an $18M Northstar-led Series B, plus board seat and normal confirmatory work | Reopen the process, spend the next few weeks trying to get more firms engaged, and see if we can create actual competition |
| Runway / oxygen | Likely enough real breathing room to stop optimizing every decision for fundraising survival | Maybe a better headline if the process works, but only if multiple firms move fast instead of browsing |
| Story defensibility | Built around the version we can actually defend now: Mercury activation/admin progress, bounded Evergreen signal, hybrid MAU pricing, expansion caveats intact | The longer we widen, the more temptation there is to smooth over uneven expansion or tell a cleaner story than we really have |
| Diligence / legal timing | Immediate refs + legal cleanup + January cash/runway + governance work | Same work anyway, plus more repetition across firms and more founder cycles |
| Time cost | Contained if Sofia is serious | High; we burn operating time exactly while Mercury follow-through and enterprise gaps still need attention |
| Price-shopping tradeoff | Probably not the loudest outcome, but could be a credible enough one | Upside exists only if we believe there is real price tension to create, not just theoretical upside |
| Main downside | We could accept something workable but less euphoric than the dream case | We could spend 3–4 more weeks widening, get nothing materially better, and come back with less leverage |
| Hidden risk | We talk ourselves into "good enough" too quickly | We turn it into theater and lose the ability to say we picked the narrow, defensible path on purpose |

My rough take:
- If the number is actually around $18M and the frame is still the defendable one, that is probably enough oxygen to matter.
- The real question is whether their milestone language is just how they describe the bet, or whether they try to wire in something we can’t honestly control yet.
- Best argument for delay: if we think one more pass can produce real competition, not just a prettier maybe.
- Best argument against delay: the market story does not get more defensible just because we spend extra weeks telling it to more people.

Not polished. Just wanted the tradeoff in one place before we talk.

Turn this into a decision memo Devon and I can actually use: workable Northstar-led runway and a story we can defend versus the time cost and maybe-upside of widening the process. Make the tradeoff explicit, including price-shopping risk and founder-cycle cost, and don’t write it like we already have accepted paper.

Decision memo: Northstar-led financing versus widening the process

Date: January 16, 2024
For: Morgan Chen and Devon Hayes
Status: Decision framework; no paper accepted

Decision to make

If Sofia’s proposal is in the range of an $18M Northstar-led Series B, with a board seat and ordinary confirmatory diligence, do we prioritize advancing that path or spend the next three to four weeks widening the fundraising process in search of stronger price tension or a better headline?

Working conclusion

Prioritize the Northstar-led path if the economics are genuinely around $18M and the structure is workable, while keeping the process disciplined until the key terms are understood. Do not widen the process merely to create the appearance of competition.

The Northstar path is attractive because it could provide meaningful runway and operating room without requiring us to improve the story beyond what we can currently defend. Widening is justified only if we have a credible reason to believe additional firms can engage quickly and create real competitive tension—not simply more meetings, hypothetical interest, or pressure to smooth over the company’s uneven evidence.

This is not a recommendation to accept paper before reviewing the terms.

The core tradeoff

Northstar-led path

Potential benefits

1. Meaningful runway and operating oxygen

An approximately $18M financing could give the company enough breathing room to make operating decisions based on product and customer priorities rather than near-term fundraising survival. That has value beyond the headline valuation: it could reduce distraction, preserve optionality, and give Mercury follow-through and enterprise readiness time to develop.

2. A story we can defend now

The strongest version of the case is already available:

- Mercury activation and administrative progress are real.
- Evergreen provides a bounded signal, not proof of fully repeatable expansion.
- MAU pricing can be explained, with caveats around slower-expanding accounts.
- Enterprise readiness remains an open area rather than a solved problem.

A Northstar-led process may allow us to raise against that narrower, credible story instead of spending additional weeks trying to make the evidence look more uniform than it is.

3. Lower founder-cycle cost

The core diligence, references, legal cleanup, January cash and runway work, pricing follow-up, and governance work will be required regardless. A focused process contains that work. Widening would add repeated management presentations, partner meetings, follow-up questions, data-room maintenance, negotiation cycles, and internal preparation while the same operating gaps still need attention.

4. Faster conversion of uncertainty into usable runway

If Sofia is serious, the Northstar path could turn an uncertain fundraising process into a concrete diligence and governance process sooner. That would let the team spend more time improving Mercury and closing enterprise gaps rather than continuing to explain them to new firms.

Risks and costs

1. We may accept “good enough” too quickly

The principal risk is not that Northstar is obviously bad. It is that the relief of having a workable option causes us to stop testing whether the terms, governance, and price are actually fair.

2. Milestone or control language may make the financing less workable

The proposal may be described as an investment in future milestones. That framing is acceptable only if it reflects an underwriting view rather than conditions tied to outcomes we cannot honestly control yet.

We need to distinguish between:

- Normal confirmatory diligence and standard financing conditions; and
- Milestones, covenants, governance rights, or other mechanisms that effectively require Mercury expansion, Evergreen repeatability, or enterprise readiness to be solved on a particular schedule.

We should not accept a structure that converts known operating uncertainty into founder-controlled financing risk.

Midweek board block notes — June 25, 2025

Purpose

The motion needs to work in at least two or three additional accounts before it is called repeatable.

Mercury / October calibration draft for Elena Volkov

Why this note
We are considering a selective October reopen, starting with a short list and using this as a calibration conversation rather than a broad process update. The goal is to test whether the Mercury story is now honest and credible enough to reopen narrowly.

What has changed since February
- Product signal is less theoretical. The design-partner wave produced real evidence on setup, activation, and admin friction.
- The activation/admin story is better than it was earlier in the year because the team corrected the biggest early setup and handoff failures.
- Pricing is now structured instead of bespoke.

September Mercury package — usable summary

Board-facing context
- The quarterly cohort view is directionally better in the recent design-partner wave than in the earliest Mercury cohorts.
- That improvement is useful context, but it is not proof that retention or expansion is solved.

Operating read
- Activation improved after the onboarding/admin fixes in the design-partner wave.
- Admin friction came down in the latest wave.
- Expansion remains uneven: some accounts deepen after setup, others stall after initial usage.
- The package is best used as evidence that the team improved the early path and clarified the failure points, not as proof of a finished growth engine.

How to talk about Evergreen
What Evergreen gives us
- a real buyer process in a regulated environment
- concrete evidence on where Mercury still needs deeper enterprise-readiness work
- a better read on packaging gaps around security/admin expectations and procurement handling

What Evergreen does not give us
- proof that enterprise readiness is solved
- proof that the motion is repeatable across multiple accounts
- proof that procurement converts cleanly into expansion

Pricing frame

Pilot
- $2,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 50 monthly active developers

Growth
- $7,500/month platform minimum
- includes up to 200 monthly active developers

Overage
- $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Enterprise add-ons
- SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls are separate add-ons only after those features ship
- we should be explicit that those are not being pre-sold as current capability

Caveats to keep explicit
- Expansion is still uneven.
- Evergreen is a strong signal, but still a single signal.
- Enterprise-readiness gaps are clearer than before; they are not closed.
- This would be a narrow October reopen, not a broad fundraising process.
- I do not think we should put random investor coffees on the calendar off this package.

1. Is this package materially more credible than the February version?
2. What would make the Evergreen signal feel repeatable rather than anecdotal?

4. How much more explanation do we need on uneven expansion before widening beyond a short list?

Title: Northstar diligence — retention methodology note (September / October Mercury cohorts)

Purpose
This note stays on the existing September / October 2023 external Mercury cohort package. It does not introduce a broader pipeline view, weekly operating cuts, or sample-preview diagnostics.

1) Cohort construction / scope
For the September and October 2023 external cohorts, 'entered the bounded Mercury flow' means an account entered the current bounded Mercury setup path used in the external package: invited into the product, able to access by the current invite / magic-link path, able to interact with preview-only sample data if present, and then progress toward connecting a real source and completing a first live sync. The construction is intentionally limited to that bounded Mercury flow and does not widen into a broader top-of-funnel or sales-pipeline view.

2) Activation definition
For the outside-reader view, activated within 7 days means that within the first seven days after entering the bounded Mercury flow, the account either:
- connected a real source, or
- completed a first live sync.

The following do not count as activation:
- sample import / preview-only behavior
- invite sent
- invite accepted
- preview viewed
- source selected in-product
- similar first-week motion that does not reach real-source connection or first live sync

3) October 19/27 versus 16/27
In the October 2023 cohort, 19 of 27 accounts were activated within 7 days and 16 of 27 completed first live sync within 7 days. The full gap between those two numbers is 3 accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but did not complete first live sync in that same seven-day window.

There is no additional preview-only, invite-only, or source-selected-only state inside the activation numerator.

4) Expansion / longer-window caveat
The external package stays week-one focused because that is the defensible read from the current September / October cohort set. The improved signal is that more accounts are getting through the first-admin path to real-source connection and, from there, into first live sync inside the first seven days.

That does not mean downstream expansion is clean. Expansion after the initial admin/setup path remains uneven, and late-October accounts still do not support a clean longer-window expansion read. The appropriate outside-reader takeaway is improved activation/admin path rather than expansion solved.

[2023-09-27T19:31:00-07:00] Devon’s rough pass for tomorrow is here.

From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Wed, 27 Sep 2023 19:12:00 -0700
Subject: Thursday prep — rough October investor path

Morgan —

Rough pass before tomorrow so we can decide whether to put real walls around this instead of letting random September inbound set the agenda.

What I think is supportable now

- We finally have a real Mercury story grounded in external use, not just planned-launch narrative.
- The September package is usable if we keep the framing disciplined: activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave; Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context; the corrected weekly cuts are helpful operating read, not proof.
- Evergreen is useful evidence in two ways: (1) there is real enterprise pull serious enough to get procurement/commercial attention, and (2) the enterprise-readiness gaps are now concrete rather than abstract.
- Hybrid pricing gives us a cleaner commercial frame. Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands is much easier to explain than the earlier seat-ish ambiguity.

What I do not think we can blur

- We cannot tell a “retention is solved” story. It still is not.
- We cannot present expansion as clean. Some rows are moving; some are still uneven.
- We cannot use Evergreen’s procurement motion as proof that enterprise readiness is already there. Their feedback is basically the current gap list: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, clearer admin vs billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without one of us live-explaining it.
- We cannot let the pricing decision imply enterprise add-ons are in-market beyond what is actually shipped.

How I would frame the investor path

I think there is a version of reopening that is disciplined and a version that turns into cosplay. The disciplined version is: selective, October, and explicitly based on whether the investor can underwrite the real Mercury story. Not “market is hot again, let’s spray meetings.”

Elena feels like the right first conversation in that frame. She already engaged seriously once and her pass was thoughtful, not generic. If we go back to her, the point is calibration and context: does the more honest Mercury picture change the read at all? That is very different from treating Elena as the start of a broad process.

Short-list criteria

Only keep firms that can handle all of the following without pushing us into story inflation:
1. uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention
2. enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped
3. a usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young
4. a deliberately narrow process instead of a manufactured auction

Rough list

1) Elena Volkov — warm-context bucket
- Best use: first calibration conversation
- Why: prior feedback was substantive; she'd pressure-test the actual story
- Caveat: only useful if we stay honest about what still is not proven

2) Firm A — possible fit if we keep the narrative operational
- Tends to understand infra/devtools motion
- Biggest risk is they will immediately push on expansion consistency

3) Firm B — possible fit if the commercial story is crisp
- Could appreciate the cleaner pricing frame
- Risk is enterprise checklist bias if the packet still requires too much live explanation

4) Firm C — maybe
- Thoughtful and patient
- Might be more useful as signal than as an actual lead if we are keeping the list tight

September inbound / coffee noise

I have three stray September asks that I think should probably stay out:
- two mutual-intro coffee requests that feel more social than decision-relevant
- one “in town next week” inbound that looks like calendar tax
Given where we are, I think saying yes to these just makes the whole thing feel broader than it is.

Questions for tomorrow
- Are we comfortable calling this a selective October reopen internally, or do we want even tighter language?
- Is Elena definitely first, or do we want one more p…

Decision-prep read

Bottom line

There is enough for a disciplined, selective October calibration process—but not enough for a broad fundraising reopen or a “traction is now proven” narrative.

The honest frame is:

“Mercury has moved from planned-launch narrative to externally observed usage and a clearer commercial model. Activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave, and enterprise demand is real. Retention and expansion are not yet fully proven, and enterprise readiness still has specific gaps we are actively closing.”

I would use “selective October calibration” internally rather than “reopen” unless the team wants to signal a more active process. The operating behavior should remain the same: one conversation first, a very small list only if that conversation and the package support it.

What can support the story

1. External use, not just roadmap
   - Mercury now has a credible external-use basis.
   - The design-partner wave provides evidence that activation and admin friction improved.
   - This is a meaningful change from a planned-launch story, but it should not be inflated into proof of durable product-market fit.

2. September data as operating evidence
   - Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context.
   - The corrected weekly cuts are useful for understanding operating movement.
   - Neither should be presented as definitive proof of retention or expansion.

3. Evergreen as both demand and diagnostic evidence
   - Evergreen demonstrates that enterprise interest is serious enough to reach procurement and commercial review.
   - More importantly, its feedback turns enterprise-readiness concerns into a concrete, bounded gap list.
   - That supports a story of real pull plus known execution work—not a claim that enterprise readiness is complete.

4. Cleaner commercial framing
   - Hybrid pricing, with Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands, is easier to explain than the earlier seat-like ambiguity.
   - The model is clearer, but still young.
   - The pricing decision must not imply that enterprise add-ons are already shipped or broadly in-market.

Gaps we cannot blur

- Retention is not solved. Do not use “retention is improving” as shorthand for “retention is durable” or “retention is solved.”
- Expansion is uneven. Some rows are moving, but the overall picture is not clean enough to present as a consistent expansion engine.
- Evergreen procurement interest is not enterprise readiness. The current gap list remains:
  - SSO timing
  - audit history for admin changes
  - clearer separation between admin and billing-owner roles
  - a procurement packet that does not require live explanation from the team
- The commercial model is clearer, not mature. Do not present usage-based pricing as a validated enterprise monetization system.
- Enterprise add-ons should be described only according to what is actually shipped.
- The selective process itself matters. A broad set of meetings would create pressure to turn partial evidence into a larger story.

Short-list criteria

Keep a firm only if it can engage constructively with all four of these:

1. Uneven expansion and not-yet-solved retention
   - They should be able to underwrite progress without demanding that the data be cleaner than it is.

2. Scoped enterprise-readiness gaps
   - They should distinguish “important work remains” from “there is no enterprise opportunity.”
   - They should not require premature promises on SSO, audit controls, admin permissions, or procurement timing.

3. A usage-based commercial model that is clearer but still early
   - They should understand MAU-based platform bands without forcing the company into a more mature pricing narrative than the evidence supports.

4. A narrow, deliberate process
   - They should be comfortable with calibration before process-building.
   - Avoid firms or partners whose default response is to manufacture urgency, auction dynamics, or story inflation.

Head of Customer Growth — recruiter screen plan v2

Purpose

Test whether the candidate can turn early enterprise customer learning into repeatable adoption and expansion—not merely close large deals or manage an established sales organization.

The screen should emphasize:

- Converting Mercury/Evergreen-style account learning into a repeatable enterprise motion
- Driving activation, adoption, and expansion after the initial sale
- Exercising judgment about product gaps and avoiding unsupported commitments
- Operating hands-on without mature SDR, AE, CSM, RevOps, or marketing infrastructure
- Working effectively with founders, product, and engineering in major accounts

30-minute flow

- 3 min — company and role overview
- 5 min — candidate background and relevant operating context
- 14 min — evidence-based questions and scenario prompts

- 3 min — compensation, logistics, travel, and next steps

“The first senior commercial and customer-growth builder around our Mercury and Evergreen enterprise motion. The job is not simply to sell more logos. Replacement prompts

1. From customer learning to a repeatable motion

“Tell me about a time when your team learned something important from one or two early customers and converted it into a repeatable sales, onboarding, or adoption motion. What was the original observation, what changed in the process, and what measurable result followed?”

Required probes:

- What was the specific customer behavior or signal?
- How did you distinguish a repeatable pattern from a one-off account?
- What did you document or standardize?
- Who adopted the new process?
- How did you know it was working?

Strong signals:

- Uses behavioral evidence rather than anecdotes
- Separates discovery, activation, adoption, and expansion
- Can explain how an individual account insight became a playbook, qualification rule, onboarding step, or product priority
- Measures more than bookings—for example time to first value, stakeholder adoption, usage depth, renewal, or expansion

Watch-outs:

- Describes only a large deal win
- Treats customer requests as automatically representative
- Cannot explain what became repeatable

2. Enterprise adoption after the initial sale

“Describe an enterprise customer that signed but did not immediately achieve meaningful adoption. How did you diagnose the problem, decide what intervention was needed, and get the account to sustained usage?”

Required probes:

- What did the customer commit to do, and what did they actually do?
- Which user, admin, executive, or workflow was blocking adoption?
- What was the first measurable activation milestone?
- What did you personally own versus what product, implementation, or support owned?
- Did the account eventually expand, renew, or churn?

Optional scenario prompt:

“Imagine an account has signed, invited several users, but has not connected a live source or completed the first meaningful workflow within the expected activation window. What would you investigate in the first week?”

Strong signals:

- Establishes an explicit activation definition
- Finds the operational or organizational blocker instead of simply scheduling more check-ins
- Identifies the next smallest customer action
- Builds a structured learning loop across sales, onboarding, product, and engineering
- Does not confuse enthusiasm, invitations, or a signed contract with adoption

3. Knowing when not to promise product

The issue seems to be that three different things are being blended:

3. Instrumentation: are Stripe billing events and app events failing to line up cleanly?

- logo retention

- event completeness by cohort

That is a credible answer. It acknowledges the weakness without turning it into a catastrophe—and it gives the partner a concrete path to resolution.

arguments.title: Leadership Recap — February 26 Reset
arguments.body:
INTERNAL LEADERSHIP RECAP
February 26 leadership reset

Operating line
More room, same discipline. We will build a defensible story, not a bigger story.

Mercury operating ownership
• Jake owns Mercury execution and the weekly launch-evidence path. MER-1279 remains the internal operating ledger for launch-relevant evidence, with links back to source evidence rather than summary theater.
• Leo Park owns platform seams, release discipline, and cases where sync trust or system behavior crosses from cleanup into architecture or system-risk work.
• Priya owns activation and onboarding UX, admin/setup clarity, and failure-state legibility. Settled design decisions remain settled unless new evidence changes the conclusion.
• Anna Martinez owns retention evidence, cohort-definition discipline, and the board-consistent outside-reader package.
• Morgan Chen owns board follow-through, sequencing, dates and promises, not-yet lines, and the hiring sequence.

Enterprise-readiness lane
The next-phase scope remains bounded to:
• SSO timing
• Admin-change audit history
• Clearer separation between the admin and billing owner
• A standalone procurement packet

Devon Hayes and Sarah Kim own current-state commercial and procurement packaging, using shipped or current product facts only. Jake and Leo provide current product facts and seam-risk input; they must not backdoor roadmap promises into customer material.

No Evergreen-specific commitments, feature dates, or enterprise add-on quoting before the relevant work ships. Evergreen Bank remains a useful stress case for the current path, not a reason to turn wave-one learning into bespoke-build behavior.

The enterprise-readiness review remains a separate lane from current Mercury release work. Sarah keeps the customer-coordination lane; owners now take back their operating lanes.

Board and investor follow-through
The first post-close board framing will focus on defensible retention evidence and repeatable enterprise expansion learned through Mercury and Evergreen—not a rush to spin a Series C story. MER-1279 and Leo Park’s risk readout are internal operating evidence, not board or investor proof claims.

Anna Martinez and Morgan Chen will keep the board pack tight: retention truth, expansion truth, and bounded enterprise-readiness next steps.

Hiring decision
The second Mercury engineering requisition is not reopened.

The first new search to scope is a customer-growth / GTM leader—not an immediate Mercury engineering search. The role is intended to build a repeatable customer-growth motion from Mercury- and Evergreen-like pull without turning accounts into bespoke commitments or product-roadmap negotiating sessions.

Devon Hayes and HR will draft the initial role description. Morgan reviews it before it goes beyond the small reset group.

If Mercury engineering hiring is reconsidered later, the existing evidence rule applies:
• Senior hire for repeated platform or architecture seam failures requiring independent ownership
• Implementation-heavy mid-level hire for hardening or throughput constraints
• No requisition if the current split can close the remaining work

Near-term cadence
• Keep the short weekly Mercury truth check focused on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and material product change.
• Keep enterprise-readiness review as a separate lane from Mercury release work.
• Close-thread handoff is complete: Sarah retains customer coordination, while operating owners resume their respective lanes.

Core decisions to carry forward
Mercury ownership is explicit. Enterprise-readiness scope is bounded. No one should use the close as permission to describe Mercury as enterprise-ready now or to reopen every deferred initiative.

Head of Customer Growth — recruiter screen plan v2

Purpose

Test whether the candidate can turn early enterprise customer learning into repeatable adoption and expansion—not merely close large deals or manage an established sales organization.

The screen should emphasize:

- Converting Mercury/Evergreen-style account learning into a repeatable enterprise motion
- Driving activation, adoption, and expansion after the initial sale
- Exercising judgment about product gaps and avoiding unsupported commitments
- Operating hands-on without mature SDR, AE, CSM, RevOps, or marketing infrastructure
- Working effectively with founders, product, and engineering in major accounts

30-minute flow

- 3 min — company and role overview
- 5 min — candidate background and relevant operating context
- 14 min — evidence-based questions and scenario prompts
- 5 min — leadership, operating model, and founder partnership
- 3 min — compensation, logistics, travel, and next steps

Positioning

Describe the role as:

“The first senior commercial and customer-growth builder around our Mercury and Evergreen enterprise motion. The job is not simply to sell more logos. It is to learn why enterprise customers activate, adopt, and expand; turn those learnings into a repeatable motion; and help shape the product and team without overpromising to customers.”

Replacement prompts

1. From customer learning to a repeatable motion

“Tell me about a time when your team learned something important from one or two early customers and converted it into a repeatable sales, onboarding, or adoption motion. What was the original observation, what changed in the process, and what measurable result followed?”

Required probes:

- What was the specific customer behavior or signal?
- How did you distinguish a repeatable pattern from a one-off account?
- What did you document or standardize?
- Who adopted the new process?
- How did you know it was working?

Strong signals:

- Uses behavioral evidence rather than anecdotes
- Separates discovery, activation, adoption, and expansion
- Can explain how an individual account insight became a playbook, qualification rule, onboarding step, or product priority
- Measures more than bookings—for example time to first value, stakeholder adoption, usage depth, renewal, or expansion

Watch-outs:

- Describes only a large deal win
- Treats customer requests as automatically representative
- Cannot explain what became repeatable

2. Enterprise adoption after the initial sale

“Describe an enterprise customer that signed but did not immediately achieve meaningful adoption. How did you diagnose the problem, decide what intervention was needed, and get the account to sustained usage?”

Required probes:

- What did the customer commit to do, and what did they actually do?
- Which user, admin, executive, or workflow was blocking adoption?
- What was the first measurable activation milestone?
- What did you personally own versus what product, implementation, or support owned?
- Did the account eventually expand, renew, or churn?

Optional scenario prompt:

“Imagine an account has signed, invited several users, but has not connected a live source or completed the first meaningful workflow within the expected activation window. What would you investigate in the first week?”

Strong signals:

- Establishes an explicit activation definition
- Finds the operational or organizational blocker instead of simply scheduling more check-ins
- Identifies the next smallest customer action
- Builds a structured learning loop across sales, onboarding, product, and engineering
- Does not confuse enthusiasm, invitations, or a signed contract with adoption

3. Knowing when not to promise product

“Tell me about a deal where a product gap threatened the opportunity. What did the customer want, what did you promise—or deliberately refuse to promise—and how did you reach a decision?”

- What evidence did you have that the request was important and r…

messages.content: [2024-03-04T10:18:00-08:00] HR’s early customer-growth calibration is in. Please draft wording for my response to HR and Devon that keeps the search centered on turning design-partner learning into a repeatable customer-growth motion — not a generic enterprise-sales VP brief and not a permission slip for bespoke product promises.

Subject: Re: Early customer-growth calibration

Thanks for the early read. I’d like to keep the search tightly centered on the motion we’re actually trying to build from our design-partner learning.

This is not a generic enterprise-sales VP search. We need someone who can turn what we’re learning with design partners into a repeatable customer-growth system: identify the patterns that are genuinely reusable, sharpen the path from initial value to broader adoption, and build the operating discipline around qualification, activation, expansion, and customer feedback.

The role should be able to work credibly across customers, product, and engineering, but the test is not whether someone can sell large bespoke deals. It’s whether they can distinguish a repeatable customer problem from a one-off request, and then help us scale the former without turning the latter into product commitments.

I’d suggest we make the following explicit in the brief:

- Design-partner insight must be converted into repeatable segmentation, messaging, onboarding, and expansion motions.
- Customer feedback should improve the product and go-to-market system, not create a queue of bespoke promises.
- The candidate should be comfortable saying no—or not yet—when a request is outside the product direction or cannot be supported repeatably.
- Success should be measured by evidence of a durable customer-growth motion: repeatable activation, expansion patterns, clear qualification, and disciplined feedback loops—not just enterprise-logo acquisition or near-term bookings.
- The person needs enough product judgment to partner closely with us without operating as a second product leader or making roadmap commitments independently.

I’m supportive of continuing the search, provided we preserve that center of gravity. If the profile starts reading like a conventional enterprise-sales VP brief, I’d rather recalibrate it now than optimize for the wrong candidate pool.

[2024-03-18T09:42:00-07:00] Devon’s customer-growth debrief is here.

Discord DM — Devon Hayes → Morgan Chen
Mon Mar 18, 2024

9:14 AM Devon:
Got off with the strongest customer-growth candidate so far. Keeping the name out of chat for now, so labeling her CG-A below.

Pasted notes — CG-A

Background
- Last two roles were at technical B2B / developer-tooling companies where the job started as founder-heavy design-partner cleanup and became repeatable rollout plus expansion.
- Built the first real adoption motion around a product that had early enterprise pull but uneven packaging: onboarding map, success criteria by account stage, security / procurement prep, and a weekly readout that kept current product facts separate from later asks.
- Not a classic big-team VP Sales profile. Feels much more like a customer-growth / GTM builder who can translate messy early learning into a motion.

Debrief against the search
- Repeatable enterprise adoption: 4/4. Best answer was on turning five noisy lighthouse accounts into one common rollout sequence instead of running five bespoke plans forever. She talked concretely about where she standardized discovery, rollout milestones, and expansion triggers.
- Judgment about not promising product: 4/4. Very clear that design-partner pressure is useful only if someone keeps a hard line between current capability, packaging work, and later roadmap. Said once you trade custom promises for urgency, you teach the org the wrong lesson.
- Ability to work without a mature sales org: 4/4. Has worked with no SDR layer, no real RevOps, and founders still in the biggest accounts. Did not sound romantic about chaos, but also did not act like she needs a full team before she can do the job.
- Technical-buyer comfort: 4/4. Comfortable with security, IT, and technical evaluators directly. Could explain procurement-packet gaps, rollout sequencing, admin handoff problems, and where credibility gets lost if the external story outruns the product.
- Stage fit: 3/4. Strong on builder fit and founder-adjacent work. Only reason I am not calling this a clean 4 is that most of her success stories had at least one junior operator by the time the motion stabilized. Need to test how she prioritizes when it is still this manual.

What stood out
- She naturally spoke about adoption and expansion as one system rather than separate sales vs. CS buckets.
- Good answer on saying no: gave an example of refusing to promise a security-feature date to unblock a deal, then reframing around what was already true plus a clear recheck point.
- Understood that early enterprise pull can mislead a company into building a packet factory or a roadmap-by-escalation habit.
- Asked sensible questions about how Sarah stays on active customer threads versus where product / engineering boundaries get held.
- Did not oversell closing heroics. More credible than flashy.

Watch-outs / open questions
- I want references to test whether she can still create top-of-funnel leverage or whether she is strongest only once there is already real founder-driven demand.
- Need one more pass on how she would work with Sarah on active threads and with product / engineering when enterprise asks are real but not yet shippable.
- She is thoughtful, not loud. I liked that, but worth checking board / external presence in a higher-pressure setting.

My read
- Best match to the reset so far.
- If we keep the role centered on repeatable adoption and expansion from Mercury / Evergreen-type learning, she fits the actual brief.
- If we secretly want a first VP Sales, she is not that.

Happy to compare against the rest once HR finishes the next round.

Can you turn this into a calibration summary against the current search? I want fit, watch-outs, and what to test next, anchored on the reset role rather than generic VP Sales language.

Calibration summary: CG-A against the reset role

Overall read

CG-A is the strongest match so far for the role as reset: building a repeatable customer-adoption and expansion motion from Mercury/Evergreen-type learning, without prematurely turning the search into a first VP Sales hire.

Her profile is customer-growth/GTM builder rather than traditional sales leader. That is a strength if the role is genuinely about converting founder-led enterprise pull into a disciplined rollout, adoption, and expansion system. It would be a mismatch only if we are quietly looking for a large-team sales executive or a top-of-funnel owner first.

Fit

1. Repeatable enterprise adoption — Strong

She gave the clearest answer so far on turning five noisy lighthouse accounts into a common rollout sequence rather than maintaining five bespoke plans. She appears able to standardize:

- Discovery and account-stage definitions
- Rollout milestones
- Success criteria
- Security and procurement preparation
- Expansion triggers
- Weekly operating readouts

This maps directly to the reset role: extracting a durable motion from early enterprise learning instead of treating every account as a special project.

2. Customer growth and expansion as one system — Strong

She naturally connected adoption and expansion rather than separating Sales and Customer Success into different motions. That is important for the current stage, where expansion should follow demonstrated value and product usage—not simply a downstream quota process.

3. Product-truth discipline — Strong

Her judgment around current capability, packaging work, and roadmap asks was unusually clear. The example of declining to promise a security-feature date, then reframing around what was already true and setting a recheck point, is highly relevant.

She seems unlikely to create a roadmap-by-escalation habit or a packet factory around individual enterprise pressure.

4. Operating without mature infrastructure — Strong, with one remaining test

She has worked without an SDR layer, mature RevOps, or a fully built sales organization. She is comfortable operating alongside founders in major accounts without romanticizing the chaos.

The open question is whether she can prioritize effectively when the work remains highly manual and there is no junior operator available to absorb execution. Her strongest examples became more scalable once she had at least one junior person.

5. Technical-buyer and cross-functional credibility — Strong

She is comfortable with security, IT, technical evaluators, procurement preparation, rollout sequencing, and administrative handoff issues. She also understands how credibility is lost when the external story gets ahead of the product.

Her questions about Sarah’s role on active customer threads and about product/engineering boundaries suggest she is thinking about the actual operating model, not just the title.

6. Stage fit — Good, not yet fully proven

The 3/4 rating is appropriate. She has strong builder and founder-adjacent experience, but we still need evidence that she can create leverage when the motion is still manual, demand is uneven, and there is little operating support.

Watch-outs

- Top-of-funnel leverage: Her experience may be strongest after founder-driven demand already exists. We need to determine whether she can help create enough repeatable demand or partner effectively with founders when the pipeline is not yet self-sustaining.
- Zero-support prioritization: Test how she decides what to do when five customers have legitimate asks, none can receive a fully bespoke plan, and there is no junior operator to delegate to.
- Working model with Sarah: Clarify how she would divide ownership of active customer threads, especially when customer urgency crosses into product, engineering, or roadmap territory.
- Product/engineering escalation: Confirm that her boundary-setting remains practical under pressure and does not become either overpromising or excessi…

Cutoff: June 18, 2024

- Nadia’s customer-growth cadence is producing useful pattern reads, including activation friction, admin handoff and role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls, and true product gaps. The process remains manual and depends on improving account-note quality.

- The customer-growth org shape will remain unchanged until Nadia has two more cadence cycles and the July Evergreen review provides better evidence. The current evidence supports the planned leader hire, not an accelerated headcount plan.

- The interim coverage model assigns customer-facing ownership through the support rotation document, Leo to first-pass technical review of platform, auth, and API v2 seams, and Jake to product-priority and sequencing decisions.

The support rotation named the customer-facing owner, Leo handled the technical pass, Jake made the sequencing decision, and Rishi remained available for correction.
- The transition work still includes the AT-03 verifier/auth note, AT-04 replay/backfill recovery steps, and AT-05 workspace/org-invite migration notes. Leo is shadowing the technical paths, while Jake remains responsible for product decisions.
- The principal remaining exposure is knowledge and written-procedure depth around replay/backfill recovery and idempotency, workspace/org-invite migration history, and Atlas-specific replay/verifier behavior during deployment or observability triage.
- The interim split has been exercised and is sufficient to route current issues, but it has not yet been tested under a severe outage or major customer escalation. Rishi’s availability through June 21 is still part of the current safety net, so Atlas continuity should not yet be treated as fully covered.

messages.content:
[2023-10-19T15:39:00-07:00] HR’s parked all-hands questions are here:

Discord DM — HR → Morgan Chen
Thu, 19 Oct 2023 15:21 PT

- Unanswered / parked questions from today's all-hands:
- Q4 hardening: Does hardening mean planned feature work slips again, or just that the ship bar is higher?
- Q4 hardening: Which issues are explicitly in the first hardening pass versus the longer tail?
- Mercury boundary: Are SSO, admin-change audit history, and role separation in the current Mercury promise, or are those follow-up items?
- Mercury boundary: Why are design partners allowed into bounded testing before every enterprise control exists?
- Mercury boundary: Does bounded testing include real-source connections now, or only preview/sample data?
- Fundraising-adjacent: Was the Mercury section in the CEO update mostly for the board / upcoming raise?
- Fundraising-adjacent: Are current Q4 hardening choices being driven by fundraising timing or by product readiness?
- Process: a couple people also asked whether we should keep doing collected questions instead of reopening live Q&A.
- Need guidance on what to post as the written follow-up versus what should stay parked.

Please draft a concise follow-up HR can send. Answer the product-hardening and Mercury-boundary questions, keep fundraising out of it, and direct future questions back into the collected-question format instead of reopening live Q&A.

HR follow-up:

Thanks for the questions from today’s all-hands. Here’s the written follow-up on the product questions:

Q4 hardening does not mean all planned feature work slips again. It means we are raising the ship bar and prioritizing the issues that could affect reliability, correctness, data handling, permissions, or safe onboarding. Those release-blocking issues are in the first pass; lower-severity edge cases, polish, and non-blocking feature work will follow in the longer tail.

For Mercury, the current promise is bounded design-partner testing—not full enterprise readiness. SSO, admin-change audit history, and role separation are follow-up enterprise controls, not requirements of the current bounded-testing promise. Design partners can participate because the testing is scoped, opt-in, monitored, and limited to preview/sample data; real-source connections are not included at this stage.

We’ll continue using the collected-question format for future all-hands questions. We will post written answers where appropriate rather than reopening live Q&A. Fundraising-related questions will remain parked and are not part of this follow-up.
